one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 6 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 1), CJP's July 20, 2008 Inquirer column, asks whether GMA could legally extend her reign beyond June 30, 2010, and answers: yes, but only by revising the Constitution to a parliamentary system, and only if Congress, the Supreme Court, the Comelec and the people all agree. He recaps, as a first-hand participant, the failed 2006 Charter-change bid during his term as Chief Justice: the de Venecia-allied 'people's initiative' (the Sigaw ng Bayan and Ulap, with 6.3 million alleged signatures) was struck down 8-7 in Lambino as 'a deception' and 'a gigantic fraud' -- the signatures gathered 'without first showing to the people the full texts' -- and because shifting to a parliamentary system is a 'revision, not a mere amendment' beyond the reach of an initiative (Carpio for the majority, which included CJP; Puno in dissent). With the initiative foreclosed and a constitutional convention too 'tedious,' he predicts the Palace's vehicle will be a constituent assembly (Con-ass), where the decisive legal question is whether the two houses vote jointly or separately on a three-fourths proposal: a joint count would let GMA's 200-plus House majority prevail 'even if all the senators' opposed. He forecasts that a Supreme Court thinned by retirements -- and with GMA 'lately... winning controversial cases' -- might validate a joint vote and 'wash its hands' to a Yes/No plebiscite that is 'easy to manipulate,' recalling that the Marcos Constitution was 'approved by a mere raising of hands during citizens' assemblies,' validated by 'a compliant Supreme Court.' Laying out a timeline (congressional approval by December 2008, a Court decision by mid-2009, a plebiscite in September 2009, and a 2010 election for a new Parliament in which GMA takes a Pampanga seat and becomes prime minister), he closes with the question that frames the next column: can GMA, 'unlike Ferdinand Marcos,' extend her reign 'without martial law'?

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 8 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 1), CJP's August 23, 2009 Inquirer column, corrects the loose talk of 'emergency rule' -- prompted by former Ambassador del Rosario and others -- and uses David v. Arroyo (2006) to map the constitutional limits of presidential power. To be precise, he writes, GMA did not impose 'emergency rule' on February 24, 2006; she issued Presidential Proclamation 1017 'declaring a State of National Emergency,' directing the Armed Forces to suppress lawless violence, to enforce all laws and decrees 'promulgated by me,' and to take over public utilities. David v. Arroyo (per Sandoval-Gutierrez) then parsed three powers: the 'call out' power is valid to contain lawless violence but cannot justify the warrantless arrest of Randy David, the banning of Kilusang Mayo Uno assemblies, or the censorship of the Daily Tribune; the 'take care' power reaches only laws relevant to lawless violence (not customs, family relations or contracts) and cannot authorize Marcos-style decrees -- the Court noting that the offending proviso was 'lifted from PP 1081'; and the 'take over' power, purportedly used to threaten Meralco, PLDT, PAL, the Inquirer and ABS-CBN, belongs to Congress, not the President, who lacks any delegating law. So while the President may declare a national emergency and call out the military, without an enabling law she cannot issue decrees, enforce unrelated laws, or seize utilities -- and the 'brazen attempt to smuggle extraneous powers tainted an otherwise valid exercise of executive power.' CJP closes by reprising his own concurrence as Chief Justice: those drafting such proclamations 'are playing with fire, and unless prudently restrained, they may one day wittingly or unwittingly burn down the country,' adding that the nation might have been spared 'the wrenching pain of dictatorship' had the Court of Marcos's era had 'the moral courage' to remind him of 'the historical damnation of despots and tyrants' -- and pleading that no one, 'friend or foe,' pipe GMA 'into the same precipice.'

It was patently unconstitutional, he writes, because the 1987 Charter permits martial law only for 'invasion or rebellion' -- actual, not 'looming' or 'brewing' -- when 'public safety requires' it, and the Ampatuan-clan massacre of 57 people, however unpardonable, was not 'rebellion' under RA 6968, which requires 'rising publicly and taking arms against the Government... to deprive' it of its powers. The 'rebellion' theory collapses on common sense, he says: the Ampatuans controlled the entire province (the governorship, most mayoralties, both congressmen) and were GMA's 'close political ally and generous patron,' so they had nothing to rise against -- the killings were 'plain murder' solvable by 'normal police powers.' In CJP's reading, the belated edict was an attempt to 'test her hold on Congress, and more important, on the Supreme Court,' and lifting it before the Court could act was a bid to dodge a 'judicial dressing down' by having the petitions dismissed as 'moot and academic.' But, he argues, the petitions should not be dismissed: three years earlier, in David v. Arroyo, the Court refused to let the lifting of PP 1017 evade review because the violation was grave and 'capable of repetition yet evading review,' striking it down 'to prevent future constitutional aberrations.' Warning that an emboldened President could mask 'feigned or real' attacks or 'automated election glitches' as excuses for 'iron rule again and again,' he reprises his David v. Arroyo opinion ('playing with fire... burn down the country'; the condemnation of 'legal hocus pocus' like the moot-and-academic theory) and urges that the Court 'should not tire of firmly striking down the trifling of civil liberties.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 1 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 2), CJP's December 28, 2008 Inquirer column, explains why the Philippine Supreme Court is 'extraordinary' -- wielding, he argues, more powers and duties than any comparable tribunal, even the United States'. He opens with the diplomats' amazement at the Court's recent feats: halting the 1997 and 2006 people's-initiative Charter revisions, defrocking Estrada and validating Arroyo's ascent in 2001, annulling PP 1017, and voiding acts of Congress and government contracts. The 1987 Constitution armed the judiciary this way, he says, because of the martial-law experience, imposing two judicial DUTIES: to settle actual controversies and to determine 'grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction' by any branch. He stresses that these are duties, not mere powers -- 'a power can be relinquished but a duty cannot... be evaded' -- so the Court 'cannot shirk, waver or equivocate,' and is in this sense mandated to be 'activist' and 'interventionist'; its 'democratic constituency is the Constitution,' so its loyalty runs to the Charter, not the President or Congress. The first duty (reviewing lower courts) is the 'ordinary' one most supreme courts share; the second (striking down grave abuse) is extraordinary and, he notes, unknown to foreign courts that split such work among constitutional (Thailand) and administrative (Russia) tribunals. Beyond judging, the Court holds 'quasi-legislative' power (promulgating court rules, running the bar, regulating lawyers, the IBP and triennial MCLE, and issuing the writs of amparo and habeas data) and 'quasi-executive' power ('administrative supervision over all courts,' overseeing 2,000-plus judges and 26,000 personnel through a court administrator). Endowed with more than any comparable tribunal, he concludes, the Court is expected to use these powers solely for the people, as 'the last bulwark of democracy and the impregnable citadel of liberty' -- 'to whom much is given, much is expected.'

The Court, he concludes, 'faces a historic moment' and must not 'cower or cop-out or hide behind legalisms' or invent excuses from 'a false sense of gratitude': 'Rare is the opportunity for greatness. JBC (March 17, 2010), in which the Court voted 9-3 that the constitutional ban on 'midnight appointments' does not apply to the chief magistracy, directing the JBC to submit its short list by May 17 so GMA could appoint Chief Justice Puno's successor. CJP marshals fifty years of settled understanding to the contrary: the ban was judicially originated in Aytona v. Castillo (1962), which voided President Garcia's last-day appointments on 'plain common sense and old-fashioned delicadeza'; it was written into the present Charter on Commissioner Davide's suggestion expressly to stop a President 'prolonging his rule indirectly by appointing people to these sensitive positions'; and it was unanimously applied to the judiciary, including the Supreme Court, in In Re Valenzuela (1998) -- penned by CJ Narvasa and concurred in by all, including three future chiefs (Davide, Puno and CJP), with Davide, the ban's own sponsor, joining. That understanding, honored even by Marcos, is now 'twisted,' he says, so GMA could seat not just the 14 incumbent justices she had already named but also an 'Arroyo Chief Justice.' He rebuts the pro-appointment argument: the 90-day deadline to fill a Court vacancy is 'legally suspended' during the ban (and even unsuspended ends Aug. 15, leaving the next president 45 days), while the Judiciary Act of 1948 and a century of practice provide for the most senior justice to serve as acting CJ. With reversal unlikely after a lopsided 9-3 vote, he proposes the 'easier way' out: since the Court directed only that the JBC submit a list and did not command an appointment, GMA could heed her own candidate Gibo Teodoro and refrain from naming a midnight Chief Justice -- muffling the public outcry against 'the Arroyo Court' and even boosting Teodoro's poll numbers. 'In the end, it is really GMA's call.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 8 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 2), CJP's August 22, 2010 Inquirer column, answers readers who -- reacting to his earlier piece on the Malaya Lolas Organization's plagiarism complaint -- asked whether it is 'awkward, if not legally baseless, for the justices to discipline their own. If not they, who will?' He begins with removal: the Constitution permits a justice to be 'removed from office' only by impeachment, initiated 'exclusively' by the House for six grounds (culpable violation of the Constitution, treason, bribery, graft and corruption, other high crimes, or betrayal of public trust) and tried by the Senate's 'sole' power. No justice has ever been successfully impeached; the closest was the Oct. 23, 2003 attempt by Reps. Teodoro and Fuentebella against CJ Davide, which Francisco v. House of Representatives halted under the rule barring more than one impeachment 'within a period of one year.' Since those six offenses exclude plagiarism, and the only penalty Congress may impose is removal, no body is expressly empowered to mete lighter penalties -- so the Court itself assumed the task, censuring a member for the first time in 100 years in Bar Matter 979 (2000) and, in In Re Biraogo (2009), finding a justice liable for grave misconduct for leaking a confidential document, fining him a record P500,000 from his retirement benefits and later suspending him from law practice -- a power now institutionalized in the Internal Rules' Ethics Committee. Finally, answering readers who bristled at his 'How the Supreme Court can help P-Noy' column, he distinguishes checking from sabotage: an independent Court must check the President's 'excesses and abuses,' not 'blur his vision and ambush his programs,' upholding executive acts under the presumption of good faith and reversing only upon 'grave abuse of discretion' -- an act 'contrary to the Constitution, the law or jurisprudence' or done 'whimsically, capriciously or arbitrarily,' so 'patent and so gross as to amount to an evasion of a positive duty.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 2 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 3), CJP's July 29, 2007 Inquirer column, argues that the rule of law alone cannot rescue the poorest, who also need 'legal empowerment' and 'social justice.' He opens with 'Jose Cruz' (a pseudonym), a boy 'barely in his teens' who wakes at 4 a.m. to sell newspapers at a Makati intersection, lives in 'an all-purpose shanty along the riles' on the South Super Highway, and helps his 'partly paralyzed mother' mind a makeshift store, with no time for school or skill. Having migrated from Sorsogon, Jose and his two sisters are 'informal settlers' with no birth certificates, no legal residence, no title to their shack-stall and no medical care -- legally invisible, their hut once demolished so they could be 'banished from the view' of visiting foreign VIPs. For such a family, CJP writes, the Bill of Rights is 'empty rhetoric,' because poverty denies 'access to effective legal protection, to the social security system, and to integration into the economy,' leaving Jose 'a hairline away from a life of crime and violence.' Drawing on a July 25-26 conference convened by ESCR-Asia with the UNDP and the UN-affiliated Commission on Legal Empowerment for the Poor on 'the legal exclusion of the poor,' he explains why 'orthodox' rule of law fails them: its courts, lawyers, fees and complex laws are 'alien to the day-to-day existence of the very poor,' who are not consulted when laws are made and cannot afford to invoke them. Jose's disadvantages are concrete -- no legal status (he is a minor), an unregistered store, and no lawyer willing to help. Because society has 'a big stake' in keeping such families from sliding 'from the legally excluded poor to socially condemned criminals,' they need 'legal empowerment, not just the rule of law' and 'social justice, not just empty legalisms.' The conference, he says, produced an 'awakening': a jurist who long thought the rule of law sufficient for his 'twin vision of safeguarding liberty and nurturing prosperity' now believes 'liberty and prosperity for all requires not just the rule of law but also the legal empowerment of the poor' -- thanking organizers Glenda Litong, Resurreccion Lao and Dr. Naresh Singh, and noting the Commission's co-chairs, Madeleine Albright and Hernando de Soto.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 1 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 4), CJP's April 8, 2007 Inquirer column, explains why courts use 'strict scrutiny' when liberty is endangered but 'deferential interpretation' when prosperity is promoted -- a question readers pressed after the Supreme Court ordered Rep. Satur Ocampo's release. On liberty: the Bill of Rights (Article III) exists 'to restrict the State's power to interfere' and shields the people 'from the misuse and abuse of the awesome powers of the State'; its provisions, like the due-process and equal-protection clause, are 'self-executory' (courts 'need no other law' to enforce them), so any government action encroaching on rights is 'presumed invalid' and strictly scrutinized -- the reverse of the usual presumption that laws and orders are valid. On prosperity: the Constitution's development mandates are 'general policies or instructions' to Congress and the President (to 'promote a just and dynamic social order' freeing the people 'from poverty' and to pursue 'a more equitable distribution of opportunities, income and wealth'), not self-executory rights, so they generally need 'enabling' legislation. Because the judiciary 'has no power to pass upon the wisdom, merit, and propriety' of the political branches' discretionary acts, it is 'loathe to interfere' -- holding, for instance, that whether to adopt deregulation or globalization is for the political branches, reversible by the people at the polls, not by judges substituting their judgment. That deference, however, yields to the judiciary's 'unique duty, not just power' to nullify acts tainted with 'grave abuse of discretion' -- those that clearly violate the Constitution, laws or jurisprudence, or are issued with 'patent arbitrariness, whim, bias or personal hostility.' He illustrates with the Court's striking down of the first Oil Deregulation Law for offending the ban on monopolies (after which a corrected statute admitted Total, PTT and Seaoil) and its invalidation of the Manila airport terminal, Manila Bay reclamation, and automated election-counting contracts.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 3 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 4), CJP's February 17, 2008 Inquirer column, hails 'the Puno court for championing press freedom' after it stopped the National Telecommunications Commission (NTC) from canceling the licenses of radio and television stations that aired the 'Hello Garci tapes' -- once more proving the Court 'the bastion of liberty.' Written by Chief Justice Puno, the decision branded the NTC threat 'an unconstitutional prior restraint... a naked means to prevent the free exercise of speech... a patent invasion of a constitutionally protected right,' capped by the line that 'a blow too soon struck for freedom is preferred than a blow too late.' Reaffirming a century of jurisprudence, the Court held that 'content-based' restrictions on speech cannot stand except under the 'clear and present danger rule,' which the NTC 'miserably failed to prove' -- airing the conversation 'allegedly between the President... and a high-ranking [Comelec] official' endangered no national security, even if it caused 'adverse effect on a person's private comfort.' CJP adds that 'the duty of the judiciary is not to soothe private discomfort but to uphold the Bill of Rights,' warning that had the NTC prevailed, 'no self-respecting and independent broadcast station would be spared' and the people would be left to 'government propaganda.' He commends the ruling as 'compulsory reading' for its 'scholarly dissertation on media freedom,' praising Justice Sandoval-Gutierrez's invocation of the Universal Declaration and of Canadian Chief Justice Beverley McLachlin (whom he had invited to the country), and Justice Carpio's view that the NTC has no 'content-based censorship power.' He notes the dissenters' observation that only a private citizen, Francisco Chavez, complained, and that the broadcasters' association (KBP) had itself stated that the 'NTC respects and will not hinder freedom of the press.' His moral lesson: media 'must be more careful' about agreeing to 'constitutionally infirm "guidelines... or joint statements"' that can become 'legal traps,' for 'the parameters are already set by the Constitution. There is no need for any other "guidelines."'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 4 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 4), CJP's April 27, 2008 Inquirer column, weighs the pending bills to decriminalize libel -- either abolishing it as a crime or replacing imprisonment with fines. He presents retired Justice Vicente Mendoza's Senate testimony against outright decriminalization: free speech 'can and has been used as a calumny... to destroy the reputation' of others, and 'the right to one's honor is oftentimes more valuable than the right to property,' since a defamed reputation is 'more difficult to restore than stolen goods.' Yet CJP balances this against abuse from the other side -- 'the powerful and the rich' who file libel suits in 'inconvenient venues' with 'odious lawyers' to harass penniless journalists, some of whom suffer 'disappearances and extralegal killings.' Mendoza's middle way, which CJP favors, is to distinguish 'political' from 'private' libel: criticism of public officials for their official conduct would be 'privileged' and presumed in good faith, so a writer could be convicted only on proof of 'actual malice' (the imputation false and known to be false), while ordinary protection would remain for private individuals. The Senate was split -- Sen. Gordon backed the distinction; Sens. Enrile and Joker Arroyo had 'reservations' since 'the law is already lenient on media.' The proposal, CJP notes, tracks Vasquez v. Court of Appeals (1999), which made truth a complete defense and required proof of 'actual malice' for statements on official conduct, reversing older jurisprudence. And even before Congress acts, the Court had already moved: Administrative Circular 08-2008 declared a 'rule of preference for... fine only rather than imprisonment,' applied in Fermin v. People (2008), where Justice Nachura's ruling fined 'Gossip Tabloid' publisher Cristy Fermin just P6,000 'in lieu of imprisonment' for libel against Annabelle Rama and Eddie Gutierrez -- part of the judiciary's care, CJP writes, to 'encourage fair criticism especially of public officials, and to protect journalists from harassment.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 8 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 4), CJP's July 11, 2010 Inquirer column, argues that the Supreme Court 'partially defanged' the Anti-Money Laundering Act (Amla) by requiring courts to notify depositors before issuing bank inquiry orders -- a rule he likens to 'telling a thief to hide his loot lest the police discover and seize it.' Enacted as RA 9160 (2001) and amended by RA 9194 (2003), Amla defines money laundering as transacting unlawful proceeds to make them 'appear to have originated from legitimate sources' (a crime, he notes, for which a Paris court had just convicted ex-dictator Manuel Noriega), and provides two tools: 'freeze orders' and 'bank inquiry orders.' After Agan v. Piatco voided the NAIA Terminal 3 concession, the Anti-Money Laundering Council used bank inquiries -- winning lower-court ex parte access to four people's accounts, including a former Cabinet member's -- until one holder and a wife (over a joint conjugal account) challenged the orders as violating privacy and due process. In Republic v. Eugenio (2008, per Justice Tinga), the Court allowed ex parte inquiries for kidnapping, drugs, hijacking, arson and murder, but not for graft -- since Section 11, unlike Section 10's explicit 20-day freeze orders, 'omits any reference to ex parte applications' -- and required prior notice and a hearing, reasoning the bank records would remain intact. CJP rejects that reasoning: 'the depositor, once alerted, will... surely empty the account too.' Worse, the Court leaned on the Bank Secrecy Act (RA 1405) to hold that 'the absolute confidentiality of bank deposits remains a basic state policy' and to exempt the joint conjugal account -- so, he notes wryly, 'to frustrate bank inquiry orders, one needs only to utilize a joint account. Hmmm.' To make its anti-corruption campaign succeed, he concludes, the Aquino administration must 'restore the fangs of Amla' -- petitioning the Court to allow ex parte inquiries or at least reverse the joint-account exemption, and asking Congress to amend Amla to authorize ex parte inquiries and to modify the bank-secrecy policy as to ill-gotten wealth.

Carlos Garcia are 'in my humble view, invalid' -- the undated Plea Bargaining Agreement (PBA) with the Ombudsman, the May 4, 2010 Sandiganbayan (SBN) resolution, and the December 16, 2010 resolution granting bail. His second ground: a plea to a lesser crime must come 'at arraignment' or 'before trial,' yet Garcia's came after the prosecution had rested; the narrow exception applies 'only when the prosecution does not have sufficient evidence' and requires a finding on 'the weight of the evidence' (People v. Villarama, 1992) -- a finding the May 4 resolution never made, and one contradicted by the SBN's own January 7, 2010 denial of bail because the evidence was 'strong.' The December 16 bail-and-release order, resting on the invalid May 4 resolution, is therefore 'likewise irregular,' and CJP flags that only Garcia signed even as the deal's benefits reached his wife and sons 'in the United States, outside the jurisdiction of our courts.' Still, 'all is not lost': the Sandiganbayan 'can still correct these lapses... by recalling its two Resolutions and ordering the re-confinement of the accused.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 1 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 5), CJP's April 1, 2007 Inquirer column, is a civic-education primer exposing 'the ways used by politicians to subvert the popular will' at every stage of an election. He opens with the PPCRV's 'three Gs' -- guns, goons, and gold -- and the quipped fourth, 'Garci.' Before and during election day, cheats pad the voters' list, register 'flying' voters, print fake or excess ballots and returns, and field 'nuisance' like-named candidates to spoil votes for genuine aspirants; the 'lansadera' scheme smuggles a pre-filled ballot into the box (often with BEI connivance) while the blank one is carried back out to be filled again; hostile voters are paid off and their fingernails inked so the law bars them; and bought ballots are covertly identified by quirks like middle names. After the ballots are cast, precinct 'misreading' adds or subtracts votes, while 'wholesale' fraud -- 'dagdag-bawas' -- alters the election returns and statements of votes (SOVs), where changing 'one number, say, from 10 to 100,' or an SOV 'from 1,000 to 10,000,' can decide a race, since the SOVs feed the Boards of Canvassers' Certificates of Canvass and the proclamation. The 'critical struggles,' he stresses, come after precinct counting but before proclamation, in 'pre-proclamation controversies' over the returns' validity -- a vigilance many candidates neglect after spending everything on the campaign. After proclamation, results may be contested by 'timely election protests' (RTCs for municipal offices, the Comelec for provincial/city, the House and Senate Electoral Tribunals for Congress), even as ballots are substituted in the treasurers' custody. He closes with a 'dubious' adjudication: a governor's race (margin 2,700) where the Comelec voided 3,500 of the winner's ballots as 'marked' even though the ballot boxes' seals were intact -- 'How then were the ballots examined?' -- concluding that until a 'credible Comelec' checks the cheating, 'eternal vigilance at all stages of the polls is the price of democracy.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 3 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 5), CJP's July 15, 2007 Inquirer column, explains the 'law and mathematics' of party-list seat allocation. With commentators calling the system a 'conundrum' (Pangalangan) and an 'experiment' (Bernas), and the Comelec having named 13 winners with one 'qualifying' seat each, the 'Gordian question' is which winners get more than one. The answer, he writes, lies in Veterans Federation Party v. Comelec (2000) -- a 53-page decision he ranks among 'the most debated' of his 11 years -- which drew from the Constitution and RA 7941 'four inviolable parameters': the 20-percent allocation, the 2-percent threshold, the three-seat limit, and proportional representation. Litigants argued the threshold and limit were arbitrary and that the 20-percent allocation must always be filled, but the Court 'unanimously' upheld them, since the system is 'provided by law' and Congress has 'wide latitude.' What divided the Court was how to turn the parameters into a formula. A simple '2 percent = one seat, 4 percent = two' proposal was discarded because lopsided votes (a 20-percent party getting 10 seats) broke the three-seat limit and ignored proportionality; Justice Mendoza's German 'Niemeyer Formula' was inapplicable because German law has no seat limits, whereas RA 7941 imposes one 'to encourage small parties.' So CJP devised the 'Panganiban Formula' to honor all four parameters: the 'first party' (topnotcher) gets one more seat at 4-to-under-6 percent and two at 6 percent or more, while the other qualified parties' additional seats are computed proportionally (their votes divided by the topnotcher's, times the topnotcher's seats). The majority accepted his math, so he wrote the decision (Mendoza, with two others, dissented; Puno concurred), and though criticized, the formula drew no viable alternative and was 'unanimously reiterated' in Partido ng Manggagawa (2006) and CIBAC (2007).

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 4 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 5), CJP's July 22, 2007 follow-up column, answers the critics of his party-list 'Panganiban Formula.' He first rejects Rep. Satur Ocampo's charge that the formula was meant to 'marginalize... progressive party-list groups' as 'unfair, uncalled for, and totally baseless,' insisting 'no partisan or ideological bias' shaped the Court's deliberations. He then takes up the mathematical objections: Oscar Franklin Tan faulted the formula for not justifying the 'two percent per seat ratio' and not graphing as a 'rough straight line,' and would discard the 2-percent threshold (which he called 'mathematically absurd') to seat even 1-percent parties; Felix Muga II called Tan's scheme 'unacceptable' and noted true proportionality also needs the three-seat limit junked; and Luis Baltazar proposed 'rounding off' (above 1.5 to 2 percent) to reach 53 seats. CJP rebuts: any failure to graph a straight line arises 'only because the formula reflects the distortions in the law' it converts; 'rounding off may make sense in abstract math' but not in 'flesh-and-blood law' that demands 'at least two percent' (so 199,000 votes cannot satisfy a 200,000-vote requirement); and the topnotcher's seat-per-2-percent rule flows from the statute itself. Crucially, the critics' 'obsession to fill up the 20-percent allocation' (to 53 or 55 seats) would push the House past the constitutional ceiling of 'not more than two hundred fifty members,' meaning 265-267 lawmakers and 'more salaries, more allowances, and more pork barrel' -- all requiring a law. The remedy, he concludes, is for Congress to amend the statute (on the allocation, thresholds, limits, rounding and House size), since these are 'policy matters addressed to the discretion of Congress'; despite seven years of party-list practice Congress has not acted, so the Court cannot be faulted for reiterating a formula whose provisions, however 'unwise or mathematically imprecise,' are 'not unconstitutional' -- for 'the Supreme Court does not make the law, it merely applies it.'

Comelec, which raised party-list seats 'from 22 to 55' and enlarged the House toward 271. The Court upheld the 'first clause' of Section 1(b) of RA 7941 (an initial seat for a party-list with 'at least two percent of the total votes cast') but struck down the 'second clause' (proportional additional seats) as unconstitutional for making it 'mathematically impossible to achieve the maximum number of available party-list seats when the number... exceeds 50.' Preposterous, but certainly possible!' If filling 55 seats 'was its passion,' CJP argues, the Court should have struck down both the three-seat limit and the 2-percent threshold entirely (as Justice Nachura urged) to compute with 'legal, mathematical, and proportional precision.' He flags a 'doctrinal contradiction': the Court called the 20-percent allocation 'merely a ceiling' yet made reaching it mandatory, and it 'quietly overlooked' its own recent decisions unanimously reaffirming the Veterans formula -- even those ponentes concurring in Banat 'with nary a mention' ('So much for doctrinal stability and depth of conviction!'). He suggests the true defect may be 'the reckless creation of the excessive districts' (220 of them), not the 'second clause,' and warns that inflating party-list seats past the constitutional cap of 'not more than two hundred and fifty members' may have 'usurp[ed] the law-making function of Congress,' leaving unanswered what becomes of the new solons' salaries, pork and three-fourths Charter-change votes. The fix, he concludes, belongs to the legislature: 'only Congress has the constitutional mandate to formulate policy solutions... It is not too late.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 2 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 7), CJP's June 20, 2010 Inquirer column, warns that it 'would not be easy to serve in the Cabinet of President Noynoy Aquino.' Because P-Noy 'promised to hold Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo and her officials accountable,' he will demand of his own subalterns 'a very high standard of accountability and transparency.' Under 'leadership by example,' Cabinet members 'should exemplify trustworthiness, integrity, and probity (TIP)' and the 'courage, humility, and heroism' of Ninoy and Cory, serving as 'alter egos' who 'must instinctively know his mind' -- like Mar Roxas, who shares 'the same mindset, the same vision' -- and subordinating personal ambition to teamwork. They must 'forego their privacy' before the 'tri-media, the freest in the world' (to be 'headlined... tweeted, YouTubed, and Facebooked'), survive Commission on Appointments scrutiny of their 'public and private lives,' 'leave their professions and divest from their businesses,' disclose assets and relatives, and -- since 'the Constitution requires them to live simply' -- explain how they acquired their houses; it is 'not enough to serve well,' for 'even the purest of officials must undergo public scrutiny,' 'the price of public service.' CJP holds up Jovito Salonga -- on his 90th birthday -- who 'dissolved his famous law office' (his 'only source of income') on joining Cory's Cabinet, though 'not required by law,' 'to set a new standard in ethical conduct': a 1944 bar topnotcher, Harvard and Yale graduate, three-time Senate-race topnotcher and 'the best president the country never had' (losing to Ramos in 1992), and CJP's 'lifetime guru' since 1956. His 'supreme teaching': beyond 'the things that money can buy,' we must aspire for what it 'cannot buy' -- 'integrity, moral courage, character, honor, humility, dignity, and an abiding faith in the love and mercy of God.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 13 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 7), CJP's March 18, 2007 Inquirer column, explains why the CBCP does not endorse candidates. 'Prior to 1965,' he notes, 'the Catholic Church's involvement in politics was largely unheard of,' a change he traces to the Second Vatican Council (1962-1965), which 'underscored the need for the Christians' total or integral development' -- believers acting out their faith 'in all facets,' Christianity not 'merely sav[ing] souls for the next life' but liberating people to develop 'spiritually, economically, socially, culturally, and politically,' making the Church 'pro-life, pro-poor... pro-human rights.' A Vatican II-era document, 'Christifideles Laici,' asked the laity 'never to relinquish participation in public life,' and 'Lumen Gentium' proclaimed 'the empowerment of the faithful' as 'co-workers' equal 'in dignity and in mission.' Echoing this, the Second Plenary Council of the Philippines (1991) set out in Resolution 28 that the laity 'must... promote the election... of leaders of true integrity,' while 'bishops, priests and religious... must refrain from partisan politics,' avoiding 'the pulpit for partisan purposes.' The Holy See, CJP adds, 'does not encourage direct clergy intervention,' lest the Church's work in 'China and Vietnam' be hindered. So CBCP president Archbishop Lagdameo 'rejected the proposal of Bro. Mike Velarde to choose candidates for the May 14 senatorial elections,' since to 'dictate... whom to vote for is as bad as buying their votes,' and 'no national Catholic authority' can command a vote, each bishop being 'autonomous' and 'responsible directly to Rome.' Bishops thus issue only 'guidelines' and back the nonpartisan PPCRV's call -- akin to CJP's own for 'visionary leaders by example' -- for 'principles, programs and performance' over 'payoff, personality... and patronage'; this 'indirect and extremely cautious' path, he argues, is wiser than a 'confrontational method' that would harm 'both the Church and the State.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 14 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 7), CJP's March 4, 2007 Inquirer column, honors Jose Wright 'Ka Pepe' Diokno on his 85th birthday and 20th death anniversary, presenting him as the living answer to a homily by Archbishop Oscar Cruz. Cruz preached that loving one's neighbor (Matthew 25) means feeding the hungry and visiting prisoners -- then pressed beyond the Gospel: 'Shall we just feed the hungry but not punish the greedy who deprived them of food?... visit the prisoners without bringing to justice the tyrants who jailed them?' Reflecting at home, CJP thought of Diokno, whose anniversaries De La Salle marked with the 'Ka Pepe Diokno Human Rights Award' and the launch of 'Diokno on Trial.' As keynote speaker, CJP 'remembered him as the answer.' Diokno 'easily exemplified... ethics and competence': he 'topped both the CPA and the bar examinations' and, 'with special permission,' took the bar 'without having formally graduated' -- a feat 'unsurpassed.' In an age of plunderers, CJP distinguishes the merely 'honest public servants' who 'did nothing to stamp out the evil around them' from those of true 'integrity, not mere honesty' -- for 'honesty is a virtue taught in grade school,' but the country needs the 'moral courage to punish the greedy, chase the robbers, and prosecute the tyrants.' Diokno had it: though he 'twice supported the presidential candidacy of... Marcos,' he 'did not hesitate to part from him' and 'denounce his excesses,' risking 'his own safety, health... and career' and enduring 'solitary confinement without being charged or tried' -- 'a visionary leader of exemplary integrity.' Pointing to the Bantayog ng mga Bayani heroes (Ninoy, Climaco, Concepcion, Tañada, Teehankee and more, 'all... in the Great Beyond') and Salonga's words that 'a nation is measured by the quality of the men and women it honors,' CJP leaves readers -- especially the Ayala Young Leaders -- to name the living leaders worth honoring.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 15 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 7), CJP's February 11, 2007 Inquirer column -- his very first, and the volume's closing piece -- opens with 'one of the ringing joys' of his life: the journey 'from hawking newspapers in the backstreets of Sampaloc... to becoming the president of the most widely read newspaper,' and now, after 'more than 11 years on the Supreme Court,' his return to the Inquirer 'as a column writer.' Keynoting the Ayala Young Leaders Congress (75 student leaders, on 'Leading in Challenging Times'), he argued that 'every leader and every organization... must have a clear idea of what they ultimately want to accomplish': as a journey needs 'a pre-selected destination, and a specific mode of how to get there' (like a pilot's announced route), 'so must every leader have a vision-mission' -- one 'specific and quantifiable, not a mere collection of motherhood principles,' value-laden and 'achievable within a declared period.' Quoting George Patton that wars 'are won by soldiers' -- by 'the spirit of the men who follow and of the man who leads' -- he points to the Inquirer (the largest daily, on a clear vision to be 'the dominant, most respected and influential' media organization) and GMA Network (whose values place 'God above all'), pursued 'doggedly... into fruition' by Marixi Prieto and Felipe Gozon. But beyond vision, he insists, 'leading by example is the best, if not the only, way': a new CEO of 'a huge Philippine company,' finding 'more than five dozen' cars assigned to his office, kept one and sold the rest; banked a briefcase of commission cash; and quietly began arriving at '8 a.m.' That CEO was Manuel V. Pangilinan, whose three days of modeling 'prudent use of corporate assets, integrity in money matters, and on-time office arrival' multiplied PLDT's worth 'tenfold' and 'its corporate ethics, a hundredfold' -- proof that 'using visionary leadership by example, the Inquirer, GMA7, and PLDT climbed to the top,' as 'can any organization,' and perhaps 'the Philippines.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 2 of 'A Centenary of Justice' reproduces the Centenary Lecture Series lecture CJP delivered on February 13, 2001 in the SC Session Hall, surveying how the Court used 'old but reliable doctrines' to meet new e-age paradigms across four domains. His premise, anchored in Judge Learned Hand, is that judges need both liberal education and legal expertise -- 'it is no longer enough for judges to be walking encyclopedias of the Constitution.' On the new economy (globalization, liberalization, deregulation, privatization): Tanada v. Angara upheld WTO membership on grave-abuse deference, holding the 'Filipino First' provisions non-self-executing and the Constitution interpretable for 'future and unknown circumstances'; Manila Prince Hotel was distinguished as a self-executing exception; Tatad v. Secretary of Energy voided the Oil Deregulation Law (RA 8180) 9-2 for entrenching the Petron-Shell-Caltex oligopoly ('the Constitution mandates this Court to be the guardian not only of the people's political rights but their economic rights as well'), while Garcia v. Corona upheld the corrected RA 8479; and Pimentel v. Aguirre affirmed LGU fiscal autonomy. On constitutional and political law he canvasses free expression (ABS-CBN v. Comelec protecting exit polls; Vasquez's actual-malice libel standard), the death penalty (his Dissent in People v. Echegaray that the 1987 Constitution abolished rather than suspended capital punishment and that executions are 'nightmarishly irreversible'), due process for workers (his Serrano Dissent that due process binds private power, not just government) and extraditees (Lantion), privacy (Ople v. Torres), citizenship (Frivaldo; Mercado on dual citizenship; the 'reluctant hinges'), automated elections (Loong; Bush v. Gore), initiative/referendum/recall (Santiago and PIRMA finding RA 6735 inadequate to amend the Constitution), the party-list four parameters (Veterans Federation Party v. Comelec -- 'the Philippine style party list system is a unique paradigm,' rejecting the German Niemeyer formula because 'one cannot grow Washington apples in the Philippines'), and the environment (Oposa; Tano). He treats the Court's role in swearing in President Arroyo on January 20, 2001 only guardedly under the sub judice rule, and closes on medical-malpractice res ipsa loquitur (Batiquin; Ramos). His epilogue concedes the Court has yet to catch up on the death penalty and private-power due process, but credits the 1987 Constitution as 'a beacon of light and a rock of stability,' ending on his Tanada paean that a Constitution 'can withstand the assaults of bigots and infidels but at the same time bend with the refreshing winds of change.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 3 of 'A Centenary of Justice' reproduces the Prologue CJP wrote for the Court's centenary anthology, the three-volume 'Centenary Reader' -- Supreme Court Decisions as Literature, as Philosophy, and as History -- which he calls the Court's 'obra maestra.' He frames the Court's twofold responsibility under Article VIII: the traditional duty to review 'reversible errors' and settle controversies, and the 'more sensitive, if sometimes controversial' duty to strike down any branch's act done with grave abuse of discretion. Posing the question of who corrects a branch that abuses its powers -- 'The military? The police? An armed revolution? People Power?' -- he answers that the US Supreme Court 'long answered this question by placing that responsibility upon itself,' a doctrine that in the Philippines 'solidified into a granite doctrine': the Court strikes transgressions by the Presidency or Congress 'not because it has any superior-inferior relationship with the violator, but because the Constitution must be upheld as truly paramount.' He traces the political-question theory (Tanada v. Cuenco -- matters of 'wisdom, not legality') and how the 1987 Constitution narrowed it by expressly vesting grave-abuse review, rooted in Avelino v. Cuenco, where Justice Gregorio Perfecto branded the 'judicial hands-off policy... a showing of official inferiority complex'; and his own Santiago v. Guingona, taking jurisdiction over the Senate's minority-leader selection because 'jurisdiction... is determined by the allegations of the complaint or petition.' Turning to craft, he sets out the '4 Cs' of effective legal writing -- correct, complete, clear and concise -- from his PhilJA seminars, cites Nicos Industrial against 'kilometric decisions' (the ideal decision arrives 'with welcome economy of words... and, having done so, ends') and Francisco v. Permskul on 'pride of authorship' ('a judicial decision does not have to be a bore'). His governing thesis is that Supreme Court decisions are 'veritable sources of history, philosophy and literature' -- the Estrada v. Desierto succession Decision exemplifying all three -- capped by Morales v. Enrile: 'when the judgment of history is written... we shall be asked to account... for what visions we have today of our tomorrow.' He closes by acknowledging the five editors, the Philippine Judiciary Foundation and 'Legal Write,' who produced and donated 1,000 copies of the trilogy.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 10 of 'A Centenary of Justice' reproduces CJP's plenary remarks of July 1, 2001 at the Einstein Institute (Einshac) 'Working Conversation' on biosciences and biotechnology in Kona, Hawaii -- a conference of about 100 leaders of law and science he attended on a judicial scholarship with Justice Leonardo A. Quisumbing and PhilJA Chancellor Ameurfina A. Melencio Herrera, framing it as ushering 'the bio-age into the Philippine judiciary' during its centenary. Building on Canadian Justice Claire L'Heureux-Dube's account of judicial and constitutional globalization (with her 'Harvard mouse and Monsanto's canola' examples), he surveys the new paradigms confronting the world's courts: economic deregulation, liberalization and privatization dissolving sovereign borders under the WTO; the information highway shifting wealth 'from the exploitation of natural resources to the exploration and use of knowledge'; and -- 'most daunting' -- genomics, genetic engineering and biotechnology reshaping health, ethics and 'the very essence of life itself.' Answering for the Philippines, he restates that the SC is reckoned from 1901 (after the 1898 Treaty of Paris) because only then did an independent tribunal arise, with decisions appealable to the US Supreme Court until 1946, and defines judicial independence as non-reviewable decisions, constitutionally guaranteed funding, and security of tenure (to age 70) and compensation. He then enumerates the Court's five powers -- ordinary review; certiorari review of any agency, including the Presidency and Congress, for grave abuse of discretion; administrative supervision and discipline of judges; control of the bar; and rule-making -- and maps each to bioscience readiness: reviewing the DOH, DA, Bureau of Patents and FDA, voiding laws on cloning, genetic testing and privacy, promulgating rules on DNA and electronic evidence, shaping curricula through bar exams and PhilJA, ensuring uniform ethical application, and entering international judicial agreements unaided. He closes on truth: Time magazine's report that 80 US convicts were later exonerated by DNA leads him to 'shudder' that Philippine trial courts had imposed death on more than 1,500 persons in five years -- 'a penalty which, incidentally, I personally oppose on constitutional and philosophical grounds' -- concluding that scientific breakthroughs can ensure 'mistakes in the discovery of truth can be minimized, if not totally avoided.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 11 of 'A Centenary of Justice' reproduces CJP's August 24, 2001 address to the Calamba City Lawyers League, inducting Atty. Emilio C. Capulong Jr. -- a Bantay Katarungan and Kilosbayan figure who 'equates being a lawyer with being a servant of the Lord.' Against this, he offers his three personal cornerstones, the '3 E-values.' Excellence is more than competence; it is responsibility, sincerity and 'making a difference,' pursued not for 'power, wealth or acclaim' but in service of the underprivileged, as the Code of Professional Responsibility requires. Ethics is fidelity to a threefold hierarchy of responsibilities -- the interest of justice first (lawyers are officers of the court), the client's cause a 'far second,' and the lawyer's personal interest a 'farther third' -- a hierarchy some have inverted but which, he stresses, the Supreme Court has issued no circular to reverse; ethics flows from integrity, which is moral courage, and 'only one who is clear of mind and pure of heart can act with integrity.' Eternity, the third E, is the belief that life on earth is not all there is: just as there are human and physical laws, there are spiritual laws, and placing God at the center transforms one's entire value system and reveals 'what is true and just.' He closes that lawyers can stand 'on a level with any other pontificate' through excellence, ethics and eternity -- and that 'if there is truth to the aphorism that saints are sinners who keep trying,' then 'let us begin our journey to sainthood,' becoming 'holy in a not-so-holy profession.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 13 of 'A Centenary of Justice' is CJP's detailed analysis of Estrada v. Desierto and Estrada v. Arroyo (decided March 2, 2001, per Puno, J., by a 13-0 vote), the landmark ruling upholding Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo's succession, from which both CJ Davide and CJP voluntarily inhibited. The Court held Arroyo the de jure President: applying the 'totality test,' it found Estrada had resigned before her noon January 20, 2001 oath -- the Angara Diary serving as the 'authoritative window' on his intent and his final press release a 'valedictory' in which 'his presidency is now in the past tense' -- and that she took office as President (not merely acting), with Congress's recognition (House Resolutions 175/176/178), Guingona confirmed as Vice-President, and the Impeachment Court declared functus officio. It denied Estrada immunity (citing Nixon and Clinton v. Jones) and drew its pivotal distinction: EDSA I was an 'extra constitutional' revolution beyond judicial review (Lawyers League v. Aquino), whereas EDSA II was 'intra constitutional' -- an exercise of free speech and assembly affecting only the presidency -- so 'EDSA I presented a political question; EDSA II involves legal questions.' CJP canvasses the concurrences (Bellosillo on permanent 'functional' disability; Vitug on abandonment as resignation and EDSA II as non-revolutionary; Mendoza on Estrada's total disability and the existence of only one government) and the separate opinions concurring 'in the result' (Kapunan and Gutierrez doubting voluntary resignation yet accepting Arroyo's legitimacy as 'an irreversible fact'; Santiago's disquietude over 'people power' -- even 2 million at EDSA being only 2.67% of 75 million Filipinos -- and her insistence that 'the situation should conform to the Constitution'). The 13-0 reconsideration (April 3, 2001) listed twenty-three prior events building the pressure to resign, debunked the 'duress' claim ('no tanks... no shooting'), and upheld the Angara Diary as an adoptive admission. Finally, CJP recounts his own inhibition, distinguishing compulsory disqualification (Rule 137) from voluntary inhibition and recusal, and explaining that he stepped aside 'pro hac vice... to hold myself above petitioner's reproach,' even as the Court rightly refused the tactical mass disqualification of the twelve 'mere spectator' justices.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 14 of 'A Centenary of Justice' surveys the death-penalty jurisprudence of CJP's sixth year (October 2000-October 2001), its title 'More of the Same' signaling both doctrinal continuity and the persistence of his opposition (developed in 'Battles in the Supreme Court,' 'Leadership by Example' and 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity'). He reports the de facto no-execution policy: President Estrada's Jubilee-Year moratorium (March 25, 2000), continued by the Arroyo government through automatic commutation ('no executions... during [Arroyo's] three-year term'), so no one had entered the lethal-injection chamber since March 2000, even as repeal bills were filed and the Court kept reviewing sentences. The governing safeguard is that special qualifying circumstances under Section 11 of RA 7659 must be BOTH alleged in the information AND proven -- a rule many trial courts violated, so the Court reduced numerous death sentences to reclusion perpetua (for failures to allege a deadly weapon, to independently prove minority, or to establish a qualifying relationship). He catalogues developments including People v. Catubig (exemplary damages on the civil side even when an aggravating circumstance is unalleged) and People v. Gonzales (treachery not lightly inferred from the Loyola Park killing of Feliber Andres -- over a Pardo dissent, joined by CJP, finding treachery and aberratio ictus). A major thread is the improvident-plea line -- People v. Aranzado (per Davide), CJP's own People v. Sta. Teresa, and People v. Chua (per Puno) -- enforcing the mandatory 'searching inquiry' under Rule 116, Section 3 and condemning 'lackadaisical' counsel, since the right to counsel must be 'efficient and truly decisive, not perfunctory' and courts must not sacrifice due process to 'sheer speed' when the penalty 'is irrevocable.' Finally, he approvingly cites Justice Vitug's article that a mandatory single death penalty unconstitutionally infringes judicial prerogative -- marshalling US precedents (Furman, Woodson, Roberts, McGautha, Trop v. Dulles, grounded in 'the dignity of man') -- and closes on the worldwide abolition trend, with about 110 countries now supporting a ban and the UN Secretary-General backing a moratorium.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 17 of 'A Centenary of Justice' analyzes Perez v. Estrada (AM No. 01-4-03-SC, June 29, 2001), in which the Court, by 8-6, denied a petition to allow LIVE radio and TV coverage of former President Estrada's plunder trial before the Sandiganbayan and reaffirmed its absolute 1991 prohibition (rooted in Estes v. Texas and US Federal Rule 53). The request came from the Kapisanan ng mga Brodkaster ng Pilipinas and was formalized by a petition of Justice Secretary Hernando Perez invoking the public's right to know and to dispel 'railroad' suspicions. Writing for the majority, Justice Vitug held that in balancing press freedom and the public's right to information against the accused's right to a fair and impartial trial, 'the right of the accused must be preferred': a 'public trial is not synonymous with publicized trial,' television 'can work profound changes' in witnesses and judges, and requiring proof of actual prejudice would ignore 'the subtle threats to justice.' Justice Kapunan concurred ('the balance is never weighed against the accused'; televising could reignite the EDSA II/EDSA III divide), as did Justice Gutierrez (media sensationalism as an 'offensive force'). Justice Puno dissented -- Estes had been modified by later cases and most US states now allow cameras -- favoring the trial judge's discretion under detailed standards and warning of 'new Rip Van Winkles.' CJP also dissented, arguing that 2001 technology could satisfy the people's right to information without prejudicing the accused via a single fixed, court-controlled camera at the rear of the courtroom, fed to outside broadcast stations, so home viewers would be no more disruptive than courtroom spectators; he lamented that the Court 'refused to march in cadence with the music created by the chimes of changing technology' and urged that 'the light of truth be beamed to all the people through the advances of science and technology.' In a Postscript, the Court on reconsideration kept the live-coverage ban (9-6) but, by 8-7 (per Mendoza), ordered an audio-visual RECORDING of the entire trial for documentary purposes only -- released after judgment and deposited in the National Museum -- over Vitug's view that even recording would prejudice the accused.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 19 of 'A Centenary of Justice' analyzes Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal (GR 142840, May 7, 2001, per Kapunan, J.), which held that repatriation under RA 2630 restores a person's ORIGINAL citizenship. Teodoro C. Cruz, natural-born in 1960, lost his Philippine citizenship by enlisting in the US Marine Corps (1985) and being naturalized American (1990), repatriated in 1994, and in 1998 was elected to the House from Pangasinan's Second District; the HRET dismissed Antonio Bengson III's quo warranto and upheld Cruz, who then charged the tribunal with grave abuse. The Court reasoned that citizenship is acquired by birth or naturalization, yielding only two classes -- natural-born and naturalized -- and since Cruz reacquired his status by repatriation rather than naturalization or a direct act of Congress, he 'perforce' is natural-born, the Constitution providing no separate category for reacquirers. CJP -- whose dissent became a Concurring Opinion after he deferred to the senior Justice Kapunan -- gave five reasons: (1) repatriation is the recovery of original citizenship (citing Salonga's 'Private International Law' and Webster), 'not a grant of a new citizenship'; (2) not being naturalized, Cruz is natural-born; (3) the HRET, as 'sole judge' of its members' qualifications, committed no grave abuse, since a good-faith interpretation of an unsettled question is not capricious or whimsical ('there is a line between perceived error and grave abuse'); (4) in case of doubt the popular will prevails -- Cruz won 80,119 votes, more than all opponents combined -- and 'it would be better to err in favor of the people's choice than to be right in complex but little understood legalisms' (Frivaldo v. Comelec); and (5) the global trend favors welcoming back former Filipinos who are 'Filipinos by blood, by origin and by culture.' Justice Gutierrez dissented, arguing that natural-born status is a privilege that cannot be reacquired once a person must perform acts (oath, renunciation, registration) to regain citizenship, and that the constitutional trend has made natural-born status 'more narrow and qualified over the years.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 2 of 'Justice and Faith' is a curated anthology of direct quotations from CJP's first-two-years ponencias and opinions (October 1995 to October 1997), arranged in ten lettered topical subsections (A through K, with E omitted): A. On Promoting Substantial Justice, B. On Upholding the People's Sovereignty, C. On Protecting the People's Rights, D. On Interpreting the Constitution and the Laws, F. On Protecting Human Life, G. On Comforting the Innocent, H. On Compassion for the Repentant, I. On Promoting Cultural Values and Religious Faith, J. On Enhancing Trade and Industry, and K. On the Conduct of Judicial Officers. Signature passages anchor each section -- from Frivaldo v. Comelec's titular 'the real essence of justice does not emanate from quibblings over patchwork legal technicality. It proceeds from the spirit's gut consciousness of the dynamic role of law as a brick in the ultimate development of the social edifice'; through Philippines Today v. NLRC's 'each case has its own flesh and blood and cannot be decided simply on the basis of isolated clinical classroom principles'; Leonor v. CA's 'the Supreme Court is not just a toothless promoter of procedural niceties... [but] the fountain of speedy, adequate and substantial justice'; Obosa v. CA's 'law must be understood not by the letter that killeth but by the spirit that giveth life'; the Tabuena Dissent's Nuremberg-analogy holding that 'a moral choice was not only possible. It was in fact available' and that 'before [mercy] can be invoked, there must first be justice'; Santiago v. Comelec's Separate Opinion treating initiative, referendum and recall as 'institutionalized legacies of the world-admired EDSA people power' that must be 'carefully nurtured and zealously protected' while abuse is 'resolutely struck down'; the Manila Prince Hotel Dissent's bidding-as-ridiculous-sham critique with its closing 'do not do unto others what you do not want others to do unto you'; and Valat v. Judge Ramos's standard that 'ignorance of the law on the part of a judge is not only most ignominious, it is also prejudicial to litigants and the administration of justice as a whole.' Together the subsections present CJP's signature doctrinal voice across his first two years on the bench.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 6 of 'Love God, Serve Man' reproduces the legal opinion Atty. Artemio V. Panganiban rendered at the request of former Ambassador to Germany and Manila Bulletin columnist Melchor P. Aquino, printed in full in the Bulletin on January 14, 1987. The facts he sets out are that Minister Aquilino Pimentel, head of the Philippine panel negotiating with the MNLF, had announced that the government preferred all talks to be held in the Philippines and not the Middle East, yet left unceremoniously for Jeddah on December 30, 1986 with panel members Agapito 'Butz' Aquino and Norberto Gonzales and Deputy Minister Saidamen Pangarungan, pursuant to a ceasefire signed in a Jolo convent; on January 3, 1987 an agreement was signed under the auspices of the 46-member Organization of the Islamic Conference, the MNLF dropping its demand for full independence and agreeing to negotiate autonomy that chairman Nur Misuari said would mean a 'state within a state' for Mindanao, Sulu, Basilan, Tawi-Tawi and Palawan. Asked what the international-law effects of meeting in a third country under such auspices were, Panganiban restated his earlier opinion that neither the MNLF nor the NDF had a status of belligerency, subject to the caveat that there is no purely legal right to be recognized, so recognition is discretionary, political, and hardly reviewable in an international tribunal. He observed that the practice was not new -- the Tripoli Agreement of 1977 was concluded in Libya by the Marcos government -- so that refusal would have prevented nothing and the present government is estopped from denouncing the prior regime, though he doubted Britain would meet the IRA, or India Sikh separatists, on comparable terms. Tracing the doctrine from Grotius, when only states had international personality, through the ICJ's Reparations advisory opinion recognizing action by entities that are not states, he stressed that international law derives from the collective acts of states and has evolved -- more than 100 new states in fifty years, and exceptions now allowing humanitarian intervention, as with India in East Bengal in 1971. He concluded that belligerency had not been accorded, but frowned upon acquiescing to meet outside Philippine territory under OIC auspices, warning that 46 states could by agreement spawn new principles vesting 'quasi' personality in the MNLF and warranting intervention in a domestic affair. Still, he refused to blame the government, holding that peace must be pursued regardless of legal and political niceties.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 7 of 'Love God, Serve Man' reprints the letter Atty. Artemio V. Panganiban addressed on February 1, 1994 to Hon. Eufemio C. Domingo, Chairman of the Presidential Commission Against Graft and Corruption, placing in writing the constitutional and legal questions he had raised about his appointment, made by President Fidel V. Ramos on January 21, 1994, as the Commissioner representing the private sector. He quotes Section 2 of Executive Order No. 151-A, which provides that one of the two Commissioners shall represent the private sector and may serve on a part-time basis, and sets against it Article VII, Section 13 of the 1987 Constitution, which forbids the President, Vice-President, Members of the Cabinet and their deputies or assistants to hold other office, to practice any other profession, to participate in any business or to be financially interested in government contracts, as well as Section 7(b)(2) of Republic Act 6713, the Ethical Standards Law, which repeats the bar on private practice with penal sanctions and reaches all public officials and employees. Reading the executive order purposively, he argues that its objective is people empowerment through a Commissioner who remains in the private sector, since the office would be meaningless if the appointee could not continue his private work, and notes that many others have been appointed part-time on that understanding. He then poses the threshold questions of coverage and distinguishes Civil Liberties Union versus The Executive Secretary, 194 SCRA 317, whose August 1, 1991 resolution confined the prohibition to department heads, undersecretaries and assistant secretaries but concerned the holding of another office rather than private practice and did not pass on part-time office under the Ethical Standards Law. His two formal questions ask whether he may continue as senior partner of Panganiban Benitez Parlade Africa and Barinaga and as an officer and director of Baron Travel Corporation and the Philippine Daily Inquirer, Inc., and whether he is subject to the Statements and Disclosure provisions. He asks that the matter be settled by a definitive ruling, such as an Opinion of the Secretary of Justice, before he takes his oath, since the PCAGC of all bodies should set the example of following the anti-graft laws and its acts and his own should not be open to attack or doubt.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 3 of 'Battles in the Supreme Court' recounted the two Charter change cases that CJP considered the most controversial of his first three years: Santiago v. Comelec and PIRMA v. Comelec. In the first, Senator Miriam Defensor Santiago and others sought to stop the Comelec and Jesus Delfin from conducting a people's initiative to let an incumbent President seek reelection. The March 1997 Decision by Justice Davide, concurred in by eight justices, held RA 6735 inadequate to cover initiatives on constitutional amendments. CJP dissented with Justices Puno, Francisco, Melo and Mendoza. The dissenters accepted that the Comelec could not act without the constitutionally required signatures, twelve percent nationwide and three percent per district, but rejected the thesis of statutory insufficiency; CJP called the majority's position all too sweeping and all too extremist, equivalent to burning the whole house to exterminate the rats, and reported that his research staff could find no authority for the novel concept of an insufficient law. His epilogue placed initiative, referendum and recall among the institutionalized legacies of EDSA people power. Motions for reconsideration deadlocked six to six and were denied with finality. PIRMA, led by the Pedrosa spouses, then filed nearly six million signatures; the Comelec dismissed the petition under the Court's order, and in September 1997 the Court unanimously found no grave abuse of discretion while seven justices refused to re-examine the insufficiency ruling. CJP argued that upholding the law's adequacy would not have validated PIRMA's petition, which still had to answer whether the change was an amendment rather than a revision, which registry would verify signatures, whether the clamor came from the people or from the beneficiaries of term extension, and whether the signatures were genuine. He rebutted claims of partisan alignment by noting that Ramos appointees voted against PIRMA, and closed with his credo that initiative is an alternative to bloody revolution.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 4 of 'Battles in the Supreme Court' recounted the Court's battles over capital punishment, written under the constraint that death-penalty decisions are per curiam, so CJP named neither ponentes nor dissenters. He set out Section 19, Article III, which permits death only for compelling reasons involving heinous crimes, and RA 7659, under which trial courts had imposed at least 748 death sentences by October 1998. In Echegaray the Court upheld the law 12 to 3, reasoning that death is not cruel or unusual, that the covered offenses are heinous, that the statute contains safeguards, and that no statistical proof of rising crime is required. He reproduced the two dissents at length, especially a 32-page opinion arguing that Congress merely made penalties more severe for crimes already punishable by death, that the framers had in mind organized murder or the brutal murder of a rape victim, that heinousness requires new offenses or new aggravating elements, that no empirical proof links death to deterrence, that the Charter shows an explosion of concern for man more than property, and that the penalty falls hardest on the poor and unlettered, closing with Scripture and Evangelium Vitae. He then traced Esparas and Prades on whether an escaped appellant's sentence must still be reviewed and judgment rendered, recording his own middle position of review without judgment until rearrest. He described the quarrel over repetitive dissents in Escala, settled by a standard clause reproduced in all later affirmations, and printed that dissent in full, with its warning of one execution every working day. He summarized the 10-4 ruling sustaining the Lethal Injection Law while voiding two implementing rules, and the dissents on dual delegation and the international abolition trend. He closed by predicting the dissenters would eventually win and warning that an innocent man could die through plain human error.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 5 of 'Battles in the Supreme Court' gathered three cases CJP treated as battles over the people's sovereignty. In Osmena v. Comelec the Court, speaking through Justice Mendoza, dismissed by 10 to 4 a challenge to the political ad ban of Section 11 (b) of RA 6646, holding the restriction regulatory, incidental and limited in time and scope, and finding no empirical data that it disadvantaged poor candidates. CJP dissented with figures, showing by actual computation that thirty quarter-page newspaper ads cost less than mailing an equivalent number of posters, and argued that since candidates need to advertise precisely during the election period the ban is total rather than limited; far from leveling the playing field, he wrote, the Court had abolished it, favoring the rich and popular who can afford costlier propaganda. He rejected stare decisis as a reason to preserve error, citing Roscoe Pound, and urged that clean elections require not only the absence of guns, goons and gold but the presence of principles, platforms and programs. In the companion case, Telebap v. Comelec, the Court upheld by 11 to 3 the compulsory grant of free broadcast time as a condition of a franchise; he dissented that the State does not own the airwaves, that stations already pay fees and have invested billions, and that the distinction from Philippine Press Institute, which shielded print media from the same compulsion, was too flimsy to justify the taking. Justice Romero dissented separately on eminent domain and police power. Finally, in his own ponencia in Frivaldo v. Comelec he held that citizenship must be possessed when an elective official begins to govern, so the thrice-elected Sorsogon governor, repatriated on the very day his term began, was qualified. Justice Davide dissented on fragmentized sovereignty; Justice Puno concurred.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 7 of 'Battles in the Supreme Court' gathers three further constitutional controversies in which Justice Panganiban wrote separately. In Manila Prince Hotel v. GSIS, written by Justice Bellosillo, the Court unanimously held that the 'Filipino First' clause of Article XII, Section 10 is a mandatory, positive command needing no implementing law, that national patrimony embraces cultural heritage, and that the Manila Hotel -- 'a living testimonial of Philippine heritage' -- was covered, making the sale of the government's 51 percent a state action. The division came over the degree of preference: the majority and Justice Padilla would let a losing qualified Filipino match the highest foreign bid and win, while Justice Puno dissented that the clause is 'pro-Filipino and not anti-alien' and gives preference only on a tie. CJP joined Puno and added his own dissent, arguing that with no statute empowering a losing bidder to raise his bid, the majority's reading was 'unadulterated judicial legislation' that 'makes bidding a ridiculous sham,' invited reverse comity and retaliation abroad, and should be confined to equal bids -- 'a victory for the qualified Filipino only when the scores are tied.' In Iglesia ni Cristo v. Court of Appeals, the majority through Justice Puno upheld the MTRCB's power to screen religious programs while still allowing the banned series to air; Justices Melo, Padilla, Kapunan and Mendoza attacked administrative censorship as prior restraint, invoking Chief Justice Teehankee's standard in American Bible Society. CJP concurred in granting the petition but insisted the Board act 'according to a standard and/or a limit,' urging that the martial-law-vintage 'dangerous tendency' test be struck down in favor of 'clear and present danger,' and that the statute's own 'contemporary Philippine cultural values' govern questions of immorality and indecency -- illustrating the point with Filipino core values and with the 'Children of God' free-sex example. Finally, in Ople v. Torres, the Court voided President Ramos' AO 308 creating a national identification system; CJP voted to grant the petition only because the subject was 'beyond the powers of the President to regulate without a legislative enactment,' leaving the privacy and freedom-of-thought questions to ripen if and when Congress legislates.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 9 of 'Battles in the Supreme Court' collects three fights in which Justice Panganiban took the side of strict legality against expedience. He begins with warrantless arrests. In Malacat v. Court of Appeals the Court, through Justice Davide, unanimously acquitted a man convicted of possessing a hand grenade, holding that a lawful arrest must precede a search and that shifty eyes and flight, without personal knowledge or an overt act, supported neither an in flagrante delicto nor a hot pursuit arrest; CJP wrote a full concurrence comparing the case with four decisions he had authored, concluding that to convict on queer behavior alone would be 'wrong, unjust and inhuman.' Six weeks later, in People v. Montilla, the majority through Justice Regalado upheld a dawn seizure of 28 kilos of marijuana made on an informer's tip and urged a realistic appreciation of police problems. Joined by Justices Melo and Puno, CJP dissented: the officers had no personal knowledge, the case paralleled Aminnudin where 'the furtive finger' of an informer triggered the arrest, and the police had held the tip since 2:00 p.m. the previous day and could have obtained a warrant even on a Sunday. He warned that accepting 'reliable tips' as probable cause would leave everyone at the mercy of informants 'reminiscent of the makapilis during the Japanese occupation,' noting with relief that the majority's pronouncement was only obiter because the issue had been waived. He next dissented in Tabuena and Peralta v. Sandiganbayan, where an 8-6 majority acquitted officials who remitted P55 million on Marcos' memorandum, calling the defense of superior orders an 'internationally discredited Nazi defense' that Nuremberg and the United Nations had already answered with the test of whether moral choice was possible, and insisting on 'justice first before mercy.' The chapter closes with his 27-page dissent from the en banc acquittal of Imelda R. Marcos in the LRTA-PGHFI lease-and-sublease cases: the statute punishes 'entering,' not signing; the two contracts prove a loss of P189 million and are 'more than enough monument to graft,' since 'Opinion cannot prevail over hard fact'; the Sandiganbayan's irregularities were errors in the exercise of jurisdiction, not defects voiding its judgment; and far from being denied due process she had received 'over-due' process. Writing against an October 10, 1998 book deadline, he ends by submitting the Court's conduct to the judgment of history.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 10 of 'Battles in the Supreme Court' takes up two civil-rights battles fought inside private law. The first is De Santos v. Angeles, on the successional rights of natural children by legal fiction. After a primer on the Civil Code's categories of filiation and the three rights that vary with them -- surname, support and succession -- Justice Panganiban recounts the facts: Dr. Antonio de Santos married Sofia Bona in 1941, secured an unrecognized Nevada divorce in 1949, married Conchita Talag in Tokyo and had eleven children by her, and married her validly in Tagaytay in 1967 after Sofia's death. The trial court treated those children as legitimated and coequal heirs with the lone legitimate daughter, but an 8-7 majority through Justice Romero reversed, holding that 'a natural child by legal fiction cannot rise beyond that to which an acknowledged natural child is entitled' and that legitimation is a privilege, not a demandable right. Dissenting with Justices Vitug and Kapunan, CJP read Article 89 as placing such children on the plane of acknowledged natural children, so that they satisfy the first two requisites of legitimation from inception and need only the parents' subsequent valid marriage -- available here because the bigamous impediment, unlike incest, ended with the first spouse's death. He answered the objection that legitimation would cut the legitimate daughter's share by showing that Article 272 intends exactly that effect, the legislature having cast 'a mantle of protection upon the children of void marriages,' and he defended the children in moral terms: they had no fault in nor control over their parents' impediments, and 'there are really no illegitimate children; there are only illegitimate parents.' The second battle is Equatorial Realty v. Mayfair Theater, where a lease clause giving the lessee a thirty-day exclusive option to purchase was breached by a sale of the Recto property to Equatorial. The Court through Justice Hermosisima treated the clause as a right of first refusal needing no separate consideration, rescinded the sale and let Mayfair buy at P11,300,000. Over Justice Vitug's dissent that such a breach sounds only in damages, CJP concurred separately: the covenant had the force of law, the offer was wrongfully directed to Equatorial at a fixed price, and Mayfair's prompt suit for specific performance was an unqualified acceptance, so consensuality was satisfied.
