one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 6 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' recounted the January 1999 confrontation over capital punishment. Justice Panganiban reported that the Court, voting 8-5 on January 4, issued a temporary restraining order hours before Leo Echegaray's scheduled execution, holding that the merest chance Congress might reconsider the Death Penalty Law entitled him to a stay, and that nearly the entire officialdom reacted furiously, with rallies demanding the eight justices' resignation and threats reaching magistrates, employees and families -- his own daughters requiring extra security because he had publicly opposed the penalty in his earlier book. After the President vowed to veto any repeal and the House passed Resolution No. 629 rejecting review, the Court lifted the order on January 19 in a Resolution by Justice Puno, which insisted the Court had changed not a comma of its decision, had exercised only its power to control the execution of its own judgments, and had refused to constitutionalize haste because all rights stop at the graveyard. CJP reproduced his own short opinion refusing to vote for lifting, since that would enforce a law he considers unconstitutional, while deferring to the rule of law. He then set out four years of statistics -- 164 death cases reviewed, 53 affirmed, 74 reduced to reclusion perpetua, 12 reduced further, 9 remanded, 23 acquittals -- and catalogued the grounds for reduction, chiefly the failure to allege in the Information both the victim's minority and her relationship to the offender, illustrated through Perez, Dimapilis, Manggasin, Ponado, Larena, Puertollano and the reopened Gallo case. Applying that doctrine, he argued Echegaray himself should have received reclusion perpetua, an error no jurisprudence could now undo. He discussed Parazo, the refusal to reopen Esparas, his objection to reviewing appeals of escaped convicts, and the vote-splitting that could leave death short of a majority. The chapter closed with his Separate Opinion in Echegaray reproduced in full, arguing that the 1987 Constitution abolished the penalty, that RA 7659 defined neither heinousness nor compelling reasons, that crime statistics contradicted its premises, and that the law fell on the poor and had no place in the legal firmament.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 7 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' revisited the rules on warrantless arrests and seizures, beginning with Justice Panganiban's observation that apparently guilty persons are often acquitted because police violated the accused's constitutional rights, and his admission that the governing law is not easy to understand even for judges and lawyers. He recalled his Dissent in People v. Montilla, where the majority suggested that the doctrines on illegal arrests be relaxed so the Court could be of understanding assistance to law enforcement, and reported that a year later People v. Doria, written by Justice Puno, unanimously restored the original principles, holding the arrest of Gaddao and the consequent search illegal. He then reproduced his Concurring Opinion in Doria, written to guide law enforcers. Quoting Section 5 of Rule 113, he stressed that in both in flagrante delicto and hot pursuit arrests the officer must have personal knowledge of the commission of an offense: an overt act done in the officer's presence, as Malacat and Mengote showed, is not supplied by fast-moving eyes, darting looks or a hand over the abdomen, nor, as Aminnudin, Encinada and Burgos showed, by an informant's tip or raw intelligence information; Umil v. Ramos was distinguished as involving the continuing offenses of subversion and rebellion. Items seized after an unlawful arrest, he wrote, are inadmissible even when contraband. He then enumerated the six allowable warrantless searches -- incident to a lawful arrest, plain view, moving vehicles, customs searches, consent, and stop and frisk -- setting out the requisites of each, quoting the American rationale for vehicle searches and Terry v. Ohio for stop and frisk, and noting Lacerna, Posadas and Manalili. He added the eleven guidelines laid down in People v. Mahinay on custodial investigation, called Doria and Mahinay the most significant cases of his fourth year, and closed with a passage from his own decision warning that courts cannot expect people to be law-abiding if they do not insist on the full protection of rights, since the end never justifies the means.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 8 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' took up a question left open by Justice Panganiban's ponencia in Ho v. People: after a court issues a void warrant of arrest, does it retain jurisdiction over the accused? He first reproduced the three-part holding of Ho, written for a unanimous Court en banc to reconcile doctrines that were then still fluid. First, the prosecutor and the judge determine probable cause for different purposes -- the prosecutor whether the accused should be held for trial, the judge whether immediate custody is necessary -- so their objectives remain distinct even on the same evidence. Second, because the objectives differ, the judge cannot rely solely on the prosecutor's report but must decide independently on supporting evidence, a responsibility lodged in him by the most basic law of the land; prosecutors, he added, could ease that burden by forwarding the records and evidence on hand. Third, the complete record of the preliminary investigation need not be examined, only sufficient supporting documents such as affidavits, counter-affidavits, sworn statements or transcripts, since a judge fails in his bounden duty if he relies merely on the investigating officer's certification. A warrant issued on the bare charge is therefore void. In Cojuangco v. Sandiganbayan, the majority through Justice Quisumbing held that the graft court nevertheless retained jurisdiction, because the accused posted bail and participated in proceedings seeking other affirmative reliefs, thereby waiving his objections, and because he could have sought certiorari and prohibition instead, as had worked in Allado v. Diokno. CJP's Concurring and Dissenting Opinion argued the contrary: the accused had opposed the warrant immediately, posted bail expressly without prejudice to that Opposition, amplified it, moved for reconsideration and moved to dismiss once the Ombudsman found no probable cause, and had been arraigned only conditionally to accommodate a request to travel. These were special appearances to obtain urgent relief and avoid incarceration, not voluntary appearance. To hold otherwise, he wrote, was most unfair and unjust, since a court could indefinitely detain an accused by sitting on his objection -- as this one had for three years. He voted to remand the case so that evidence sufficient for determining probable cause could be submitted, a procedure he conceded was cumbersome but which the Constitution commands.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 11 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' recorded CJP's dissent from one of Philippine election law's settled equations -- that 'residence' in the Constitution means 'domicile.' He recalled that the first extended Opinion he wrote as a member of the Supreme Court was his Dissent from the Resolution denying reconsideration in Marcos v. Comelec, promulgated fifteen days after he assumed office, and that the majority there held that when the Constitution speaks of residence in election law it actually means only domicile. In Domino v. Comelec, Chief Justice Davide Jr.'s ponencia reiterated that rule, applied the three-fold traditional test of domicile, and held that Juan Domino, whose domicile of origin was Candon, Ilocos Sur and whose 1991 domicile of choice was in Quezon City, had not established a new domicile of choice in Sarangani. CJP agreed that Domino failed the one-year requirement but rejected the reasoning. Reiterating his Marcos dissent, he argued that residence should be interpreted as ordinary lay persons understand it, since the common people who ratified the Constitution would consult a dictionary rather than the journals of the Constitutional Commission, so that Webster's definition should control and residence should mean actual, physical and personal presence substantial enough to show by overt acts an intention to fulfill the duties of the office. He admitted this contradicted the textbook rule taught by his political law professors, but said that even as a student he had frowned upon such a contortive way of interpreting the charter. He added that domicile arose in American conflict-of-laws cases about the estates of men who left home before the steamboat and the oceanic cable, and was later used in taxation and divorce cases, never to govern political rights; that the domicile test defeats the purpose of the residence period, which is to make officials acquainted with their constituents and let the electorate judge their fitness, since legal domicile survives absence so long as the animus revertendi remains; and that the Constitution, being the people's document and not a lawyer's, must be read in the sense of common use. He closed by repeating that Domino had still failed to prove actual presence in Sarangani for a year before the 1998 elections.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 12 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' reproduced and explained CJP's lengthy Dissenting Opinion in Loong v. Comelec, the first case to test the Philippine automated election system. He began by describing how repeated fraud and delay in manual balloting led Congress to enact RA 8436 on December 22, 1997, and how the law's automated system -- pre-printed ballots with shaded ovals, optical scanning machines, audit trails, minimum human intervention and twenty-three statutory features -- was first used in the ARMM on May 11, 1998. He then reconstructed the Sulu controversy in detail: at dawn on May 12, watchers complained about PATA returns, Atty. Jose Tolentino Jr. pulled three already-counted ballots showing votes credited as zero, traced the fault to misaligned ovals in the printing of the local ballots, and suspended the automated count across the entire province when it was already 65 percent complete; the Comelec en banc then issued a chain of Minute Resolutions airlifting ballots, machines and canvassers by C130 to the PICC and ordering a parallel manual count, but in the end conducted only a manual count by public school teachers in Pasay City, on which Abdusakur Tan was proclaimed governor. Justice Reynato S. Puno's majority upheld the Comelec on nine grounds, including the avoidance of a bloodbath and the reliability of the hand count. CJP dissented on five grounds: the stoppage rested on three ballots and on an official who admitted he had no legal authority; the threat of violence was contradicted by the PNP's own report and would at most justify a change of venue, not of method; the Comelec disobeyed its own Resolution requiring an automated count; the BEIs appreciated automated ballots by Omnibus Election Code rules, producing systematic divergences from the machine count; and the Resolutions issued without notice or hearing denied due process. He concluded that a void order yields a void count, that the only equitable remedy was a special election for governor alone, that only Congress could fill the law's gap without judicial or administrative legislation, and that time would tell whether the Court had applied a Jurassic-age solution to a third-millennium problem.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 13 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' set CJP's dissent in Miranda v. Comelec against the Court's own recent declaration in Loong v. Comelec that upholding the sovereignty of the people is what democracy is all about. He recounted that Jose 'Pempe' Miranda, incumbent mayor of Santiago City, Isabela, filed his certificate of candidacy on March 24, 1998; that on Antonio M. Abaya's petition the Comelec First Division on May 5, 1998 resolved to disqualify him, a ruling that became final for want of appeal; that his son Joel G. Miranda filed the next day as substitute and then won the May 11 election with 22,002 votes to Abaya's 20,336; and that Abaya nevertheless persuaded the Comelec en banc to nullify the victory. Speaking through Justice Jose A.R. Melo, the Court agreed, holding that Section 77 of the Election Code permits substitution only for death, withdrawal or disqualification, that a merely cancelled certificate leaves no candidate to substitute for under expressio unius est exclusio alterius, and that since the second placer could not be proclaimed under Nolasco, Section 44 of the Local Government Code required the vice mayor to succeed. CJP said he could not in conscience accept that reasoning. He conceded that the Comelec Resolution was less than perfect, even confusing or contradictory, but insisted that such confusion should not be used to thwart the will of the electorate, that sound public policy requires offices to be filled by the choice of the voters, and that election laws must be liberally construed to give fullest effect to the people's mandate. He quoted Loong's own warning against kicking away the people's will by a literal reading of the law, and the en banc decision in Frivaldo v. Comelec framing the question as a choice between the letter and the spirit and concluding that it is far better to err in favor of popular sovereignty than to be right in little understood legalisms. Imposing on Santiago City a vice mayor nobody had voted for as mayor was, he wrote, an unwarranted imposition on the people. He closed by quoting the longer dissent of Justice Flerida Ruth P. Romero, who argued that Section 77 replaces the disqualified candidate rather than his certificate and that formal defects in the certificate of nomination were harmless irregularities that could not nullify a sovereign choice.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 14 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' used CJP's own ponencia in Santiago v. Guingona to explain when the Supreme Court may look into the internal acts of Congress. He began with the Court's role as guardian of the Constitution and conscience of society, and with the limit on that role: it will strike down acts of the political departments only for unconstitutionality or grave abuse of discretion, never for want of wisdom or propriety. The case arose when the Senate elected Marcelo B. Fernan its President on July 27, 1998 by a vote of 20 to 2, Senator Francisco S. Tatad, the losing nominee supported only by Senator Miriam Defensor Santiago, claimed the minority leadership, and Fernan instead recognized Teofisto T. Guingona Jr. on the strength of a letter from seven Lakas-NUCD-UMDP senators. Santiago and Tatad sued in quo warranto, arguing that Article VI, Section 16 (1) required the Court to define 'majority' and 'minority' and that Guingona, having voted for Fernan, could not lead the minority. The Court unanimously denied the petition, holding that absent any showing of a constitutional violation or grave abuse, constitutional respect for a coequal branch forbade prying into the Senate's internal workings, and that Fernan and Guingona had acted within their competence. Three Justices led by Vicente V. Mendoza would have dismissed for lack of jurisdiction, calling the composition of the Senate minority a political question and invoking Marbury v. Madison for the proposition that such a court has no jurisdiction except to declare itself without jurisdiction. CJP answered that jurisdiction is determined by the allegations of the petition, is not lost when the petition proves meritless, and extends to Congress because the Constitution's grave abuse clause covers 'any branch or instrumentality of the government.' He conceded that where a petition shows only a breach of internal rules the Court may indeed dismiss for want of jurisdiction, and he reproduced the Separate Opinions of Justice Jose C. Vitug, who urged judicial statesmanship rather than judicial tyranny and said only a clear disregard of a specific constitutional precept can unbolt the door to intervention, and of Justice Flerida Ruth P. Romero, who reaffirmed her position in Arroyo v. De Venecia. Neither, he noted, addressed jurisdiction -- and had the majority followed Mendoza, the Court would have announced that it will never review internal legislative acts, however grave the allegations.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 12 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' recounted Republic v. Molina, the unanimous ponencia Artemio V. Panganiban wrote after Article 36 of the Family Code had swamped the courts with petitions and had been, in his words, used, abused and misused as a convenient divorce law -- the Office of the Solicitor General itself calling it the most liberal divorce procedure in the world and asking the Court for guidelines. Roridel Molina had won a declaration of nullity in the RTC of La Trinidad and in the Court of Appeals on the strength of her husband Reynaldo's immaturity, irresponsibility, squandering of money and eventual abandonment; the Republic sought review. The Court reversed, holding that psychological incapacity is confined to the most serious personality disorders indicating utter insensitivity or inability to give meaning and significance to the marriage, marked by gravity, juridical antecedence and incurability and existing when the marriage was celebrated. What Reynaldo showed was difficulty, negligence or refusal, and mere irreconcilable differences and conflicting personalities do not qualify. The real significance of the decision, CJP wrote, lay not in refusing to void the marriage but in the eight guidelines it issued, since the function of the Supreme Court is to teach and to open new vistas: the plaintiff bears the burden, with doubt resolved for the marriage the Constitution calls inviolable; the root cause must be medically identified, pleaded, proven by qualified psychiatrists or psychologists and explained in the decision; the incapacity must exist at the time of the celebration, be permanent or incurable, and be grave enough that mere characteriological peculiarities or emotional outbursts will not do; the obligations are those in Articles 68 to 71 and 220, 221 and 225; interpretations of the Church's National Appellate Matrimonial Tribunal, given Article 36's origin in Canon 1095, deserve great respect; and the Solicitor General must certify his position as the equivalent of a defensor vinculi. Answering critics of the ruling's strictness, he replied that Molina is strict only insofar as Article 36 is construed as a divorce law, and he recorded the concurring Separate Opinions of Justices Padilla, Romero and Vitug.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 13 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' set out Obosa v. Court of Appeals, the unanimous ponencia Artemio V. Panganiban wrote on who may approve bail in an appealed case. Jose T. Obosa, an escapee from the National Penitentiary who had been let out on a subpoena illegally issued by an MTC judge of Sariaya, was charged with the double murder of Secretary of Local Governments Jaime N. Ferrer and his driver Jesus D. Calderon. The Makati RTC convicted him instead of homicide on two counts, granted his manifestation to appeal and post bail, approved the bond the following day and ordered his release, which the prison authorities carried out. On the Solicitor General's motion a special five-person Division of the Court of Appeals cancelled the bond, nullified the order and ordered his arrest. The Supreme Court agreed: the trial court had power to grant bail when it did but not to approve the bond and release him after the appeal was perfected, and Obosa had no right to bail because the Information charged murder, because an appeal in a criminal case opens the whole case for review as Quemel held, and because the earlier showing that the evidence of guilt was strong survived his conviction for a lesser offense. Although the grant of bail is initially the trial court's discretion, CJP wrote, that discretion must be exercised with caution and only for strong reasons, and is best lodged in the appellate court. He answered the academe's objection that jurisdiction persists while the records remain below by weighing the special circumstances of an escapee who could offend again and would probably jump bail, calling his release bad judicial policy, while declining to fault trial judge Nemesio Felix. The Court's July to September 2000 deliberations wrote his stand into Section 5 of Rule 114, and the later conviction of Obosa for double murder, affirmed in toto on May 31, 2000, confirmed that bail would have let him make a mockery of judicial processes.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 14 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' took up Cabaero v. Cantos and the question it posed: since the civil action is impliedly instituted with the criminal one, may the accused file an answer with counterclaim for damages in the same criminal proceeding? Amado Cabaero and Carmen Perez, charged with estafa, had done exactly that, claiming damages for malicious prosecution and invoking Javier v. Intermediate Appellate Court, which had called such a compulsory counterclaim procedurally sound and otherwise barred forever; Judge Alfredo C. Cantos expunged the pleading. Writing for the Court, Artemio V. Panganiban acknowledged Javier's cogency but set out ten difficulties his colleagues had raised in deliberation, all flowing from the obvious lacuna in the Rules of Court: the criminal rules are silent where the civil rules are explicit; a criminal judgment need not award a counterclaim; counterclaims would delay a prosecution whose issue is guilt; civil-only doctrines like admission of actionable documents and waiver of affirmative defenses would intrude; an information filed for the People states no ultimate facts of civil liability, so the accused is not apprised of the claim; bills of particulars and discovery would follow; no reckoning date exists for an answer since summons is alien to a criminal action; the answer could come only after the initial hearing; interlocutory challenges would stall cases and deprive a detained accused of speedy trial; and a malicious prosecution claim may be premature. Without expressly reversing Javier, the Court ordered the trial to proceed and set the counterclaim aside without prejudice, citing the absence of clear-cut rules. As postscript he recounted the July to September 2000 revision: the Puno committee's three proposals, Justice Mendoza's adopted amendment confining the implied institution to civil liability ex delicto, the deletion of the reservation requirement for the independent civil actions under Articles 32, 33, 34 and 2176, and the new sixth paragraph of Section 1, Rule 111 flatly barring counterclaims, crossclaims and third-party complaints by the accused -- on which he pointedly declined to comment further.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 15 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' recounted Ho v. People, the unanimous en banc Decision Artemio V. Panganiban wrote to settle what had been confusing jurisprudence on the basis for an arrest warrant. The Anti-Graft League had complained to the Ombudsman against Doris Teresa Ho, Rolando S. Narciso and others under Section 3(g) of RA 3019; Ombudsman Conrado M. Vasquez authorized the charges and the Sandiganbayan issued warrants on the strength of the prosecutor's resolution alone. That, the Court held, violated Section 2 of Article III, which requires probable cause to be determined personally by the judge. Surveying Soliven, Inting, Lim, Allado, Webb and Roberts, CJP summarized three points: the prosecutor decides whether to hold the accused for trial while the judge decides whether immediate custody is necessary; because their objectives differ the judge must decide independently on evidence beyond the prosecutor's bare report; and yet the complete records need not be examined, only sufficient supporting documents such as affidavits, counter-affidavits and transcripts, on which the judge can make or at least verify a finding. He corrected a misreading of Webb, where sworn statements and counter-affidavits had also been before the trial court, and found grave abuse of discretion in a Sandiganbayan that had nothing before it but a resolution, a memorandum and its own conjecture. He noted his pleasure at the unanimous vote, won by reconciling the divided opinions in Roberts. A wrinkle followed in Cojuangco Jr. v. Sandiganbayan, where the majority held that posting bail and participating waived objections to a void warrant; dissenting, he traced the petitioner's continuing objections -- an Opposition, bail posted expressly without prejudice, a Memorandum in Amplification, a motion to dismiss -- and argued that a conditional arraignment sought only to permit travel was no voluntary appearance, that three years of inaction by the graft court made the majority's rule unjust, and that remand was constitutionally commanded however cumbersome. The Revised 2000 Rules abandoned Cojuangco and adopted his Dissent as Section 26 of Rule 114.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 16 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' surveyed the death penalty cases decided between October 11, 1999 and October 10, 2000, framed by the eleven-month moratorium on executions that the news dailies reported on March 25, 2000 President Joseph Ejercito Estrada had declared the previous day, made out of respect for the Jubilee Year opened by Pope John Paul II, on the Presidential Conscience Commission's recommendation after an appeal by the CBCP, and sparing 18 convicts then scheduled for lethal injection. Artemio V. Panganiban contrasted the muted criticism of that omnibus reprieve with the conflagration that had followed the Court's January 4, 1999 postponement of Leo Echegaray's execution, when officialdom demanded the resignation or impeachment of the eight justices who voted for the TRO. The Court kept reviewing capital sentences, and the trend held: only about a third were affirmed, over half commuted to reclusion perpetua, most of them rape cases. The commonest ground was the prosecution's failure to allege in the Information or prove the qualifying circumstances of relationship and minority -- Delos Santos, where a final judgment was reopened because the Information never said the accused was the stepfather; Mendez and its line, where stepdaughter was alleged but only a common-law relationship proven; Ferolino, where alleging a niece was too vague because even a cousin's daughter is called a pamangkin; and the age cases from Javier through Tabanggay, with a Separate Opinion insisting that between 13 and 18 the mother's word will not do because the proof of age spells the difference between life and death. Other sentences fell for unalleged aggravating circumstances, unproven penetration in Campuhan, the offender's own minority, incomplete fulfillment of duty, crimes predating RA 7659, and the RA 8294 firearms rulings; still others were remanded for improvident pleas taken without a searching inquiry, or for a denied mental examination. He also recorded his Genosa Resolution reopening a case to receive expert evidence on the battered woman syndrome, and his continuing Dissent, reiterated in Contreras, against deciding a death appeal while the appellant remains at large. Throughout he pressed his conviction that errors in imposing death are nightmarishly irreversible, since human reversals do not affect the graveyard.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 18 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' recounts Secretary of Justice v. Lantion and Jimenez, the extradition case in which the Supreme Court first held, by a vote of 9-6 in a forty-page Decision penned by Justice Jose A.R. Melo, that Mark Jimenez was entitled to copies of the extradition documents and an opportunity to comment even during the executive department's preliminary evaluation of the United States' request. CJP set out the chronology -- the November 13, 1994 RP-US Extradition Treaty, the US request of June 18, 1999 by Note Verbale No. 0522, the evaluation panel created that same day, Jimenez's denied request through counsel Estelito P. Mendoza, and the status quo order of Manila RTC Judge Ralph C. Lantion -- and then distinguished the two phases of an extradition proceeding: an evaluation stage that is essentially executive, and an extradition hearing that is judicial. He summarized the Melo majority's six reasons, including that the evaluation could lead to provisional or temporary arrest, that it was akin to a preliminary investigation, that notice and hearing pervade administrative proceedings, and that the constitutional right to information applied. He then reproduced his own Dissent: in the peculiar factual milieu of the case there was no danger that Jimenez would lose life, liberty or property, because Article 9 of the Treaty required urgency, a corresponding request, and priority to the extradition request, none of which was present, and the justice secretary had disclaimed any intent to seek provisional arrest; the evaluation stage was ministerial, confined to checking the Treaty's documentary requirements, so there was nothing the extraditee could genuinely comment on; and his remedy for reputational injury lay in fighting the charges in the US courts. He also summarized Justice Puno's scholarly dissent, which traced extradition law from antiquity to modern publicists, proposed a balancing approach, and held extradition sui generis rather than criminal. A postscript records that on October 17, 2000, one week after his printing deadline, the Court reversed itself by the same 9-6 margin, adopting essentially the two dissents' arguments after three justices changed their votes.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 19 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' recounts Veterans Federation Party v. Comelec, which CJP presents as a rare case in which the Supreme Court was unanimous on the constitutional and legal questions yet divided on mathematics. After the first party-list election of May 11, 1998, the Comelec proclaimed thirteen qualifying parties and then, on the petition of thirty-eight defeated groups, ignored the two percent threshold to fill all fifty-two seats; the qualified parties in turn sought three seats each. The Court held unanimously that the twenty percent constitutional allocation is a ceiling rather than a mandate, that the two percent threshold and three-seat limit of RA 7941 are constitutional, and that the Comelec, as a mere implementing body, gravely abused its discretion in circumventing the statute. The division came on how to compute additional seats. Justice Vicente V. Mendoza, who had researched European practice, urged the German Niemeyer formula; CJP objected during the September 2000 deliberations that Germany fills all its party-list seats and imposes no cap on a party, while the Philippine system has a ceiling and a three-seat limit, so the formula would again give every qualified party three seats and defeat proportional representation. The Court sustained him twelve to three and gave him the ponencia. His method ranked the parties, identified a 'first party,' fixed its seats by a six percent benchmark, and awarded the other qualified parties additional seats in proportion to the first party's, refusing to round off fractions because rounding could exceed the seats the law allows. Mendoza dissented on seven grounds, chiefly that a rule applied only to the first party is no formula at all and amounts to judicial legislation. CJP answered that the formula merely translated the statutory parameters into an equation and that the cure for any harshness lies with Congress, quoting Justice Puno's concurrence and closing with the Epilogue of his ponencia urging sectoral groups not to despair of the party-list system, Philippine style.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 21 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' recounts Pimentel v. Aguirre, in which Senator Aquilino Q. Pimentel Jr. challenged Administrative Order 372 for requiring local government units to cut non-personal-services expenditures by 25 percent and for withholding part of their internal revenue allotments. Writing the ponencia, CJP sustained Section 1 but struck down Section 4. He began with doctrine, included deliberately as part of the Court's teaching function: Article X, Section 4 confines the President to general supervision, which Mondano v. Silvosa, Taule v. Santos and Drilon v. Lim distinguish from control, because Cabinet members are alter egos while local officials are elected and directly accountable to their constituents. He then set out the Philippine concept of local autonomy as decentralization of administration rather than of power, citing Ganzon v. Court of Appeals and Limbona v. Mangelin, and described fiscal autonomy as the power to raise revenue, share in national taxes, allocate resources by local priorities and prepare local budgets, subject to national supervision exercised through consultation. Section 1 survived because, despite its commanding tone, it was merely advisory and carried no sanction -- its language 'does not amount to a command that emanates from a boss to a subaltern.' Section 4 fell because the Constitution and the Local Government Code mandate automatic release within five days of each quarter, free of any lien or holdback, so even a temporary retention is forbidden. He then refuted Justice Kapunan's dissent on three points: prematurity, which he called a novel theory that people must await the implementing evil, answered with Tanada v. Angara and Tatad; the President's role as chief fiscal officer, answered by noting that the cited powers were statutorily authorized while Section 4 was not; and the claimed implied power to withhold, answered by Section 284's consultation requirement, which was never satisfied. He closed by noting the resulting holding that even an abstract violation of the Constitution suffices to trigger judicial intervention.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 23 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' takes up Basher v. Comelec, which some would call an insignificant case, to show that the Supreme Court takes up such matters anyway when it cannot let an injustice pass. Hadji Rasul Batador Basher and Abulkair Ampatua contested the post of punong barangay in Maidan, Tugaya, Lanao del Sur; after two failed elections the exercise was reset to August 30, 1997, but according to the Comelec voting began only around nine that evening amid tension, threats from the town mayor and guns drawn between his followers and the election officer's military escorts. Ampatua was proclaimed with 250 votes to Basher's 15. Basher alleged that the candidates had agreed there would be no election, that the ballot box had been turned over to the police, and that the voting was later conducted at the former mayor's residence without announcement. The case was assigned to Justice Sabino R. De Leon Jr., who would have affirmed the Comelec, but CJP dissented during deliberations, the Court sided with him 11-2, and his Dissent became the ponencia. It held the exercise void on four grounds and a fifth that he called most significant. The situs was illegal, since Section 42 of the Omnibus Election Code requires a public building within the barangay and the designated Cagayan Elementary School was not used. The time was irregular, since voting runs from seven in the morning to three in the afternoon and the thirty-meter exception presupposes an election already begun. The date and the postponement were invalid, since only the Comelec may declare a failure of election and the election officer held no summary proceeding. Finally, the announcement over the mosque minutes before voting was no notice at all, a conclusion drawn a fortiori from Hassan v. Comelec. Justice De Leon dissented, urging deference to the Comelec's findings and caution in nullifying elections.

Tan, in which CJP's ponencia held that a judicial declaration of nullity of a previous marriage is necessary before another may be contracted, and that one who remarries without it commits bigamy. Vincent Paul G. Mercado married Thelma Oliva in 1976 and Consuelo Tan in 1991; Tan filed a bigamy complaint in October 1992, and only afterwards did Mercado sue to annul the first marriage for psychological incapacity, obtaining a decree in 1993. He argued before the Court that a void marriage is deemed never to have taken place, so there was no first marriage to speak of. CJP answered by first tracing what the Court itself had called conflicting jurisprudence: People v. Mendoza and People v. Aragon had acquitted on the theory that no declaration was needed, Vda. de Consuegra v. GSIS and Wiegel v. Sempio-Diy had stressed that one was, Tolentino v. Paras and Yap v. CA had gone the other way, and Domingo v. CA had declared that the Family Code settled the matter. Because Domingo was a civil case, he had to justify the requirement in a criminal prosecution, which he did by showing that Mendoza and Aragon rested on Section 29 of Act No. 3613, carried into Article 83 of the Civil Code and Article 41 of the Family Code, whereas Article 40 was a new provision expressly requiring a final judgment. That statutory mooring having been cast aside, remarriage without a decree exposes the party to conviction. Mercado's later decree was immaterial, since the crime was already consummated, and his position would encourage delay by letting accused persons invoke pending nullity suits as prejudicial questions. Justice Vitug urged a narrower reading limited to marriages that at least ostensibly occurred; CJP found the observation worth reflection but inapplicable. A postscript cites Bobis v. Bobis, decided almost the same day, holding such a civil action not a prejudicial question.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 6 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' reproduced an address to a Rotary District Conference. Justice Panganiban explained that Supreme Court justices keep a low profile and act quietly on matters brought by litigants, and that his workload had ended the perfect Rotary attendance he had enjoyed for 12 years from 1983 to 1995; he accepted the invitation only after District Governor Rudy Estrellado and Conference Chairman Boy Villareal sent his club president Ed Tumangan to his chambers. He justified the topic from Rotary's own creed, quoting Cliff Dochterman's 'ABCs of Rotary' that Rotarians encourage high ethical standards and that a world-minded Rotarian defends the rule of law, and observing that this common passion unites Rotarians with magistrates. He then updated them on the 'Davide Watch' begun when Hilario G. Davide Jr. took his oath on November 30, 1998, insisting it was not a collection of motherhood statements but a plan implemented day after day through the Action Program for Judicial Reforms, monitored by a full-time Program Management Office and supported by the Philippine government, local donors, UNDP, the World Bank, the Asia Foundation, UNICEF, the ADB and several bilateral donors. As proof of commitment he cited the Court's unprecedented discipline of its own, and as proof of reciprocity he asked for exemption from the Salary Standardization Law and a lump-sum budget. He then described four projects Rotarians might assist: Zero Backlog, which had cut the Court's dormant cases from about 2,000 in 1995 to fewer than 50 while lower-court inflow still outran outflow by thousands of cases a year; computerization, with 1,500 computers loaded with Lex Libris, a judiciary homepage, prospective e-courts and new Halls of Justice on the way to paperless courts by 2010; education, with updated Rules of Court, all-new rules on electronic evidence and other novel subjects, and live-in seminars on the new economy and the new biosciences; and Alternative Dispute Resolution, where Philippine Judicial Academy-trained mediators settled more than 80 percent of 1,000 referred cases in 2001. He recounted the Christchurch conference of October 2001, where a UN special rapporteur and a World Bank executive praised the program, and closed by inviting Rotarians to help implement it.

Robert Keyes supported the plea, and militant leaders announced they would march at 6:00 a.m. unless Estrada resigned.", "The grim scenario he foresaw: violence and bloodshed if the two groups clashed, a revolutionary government if Mrs. Arroyo acted while a legally recognized President remained, or a coup d'etat -- in any case the obliteration of the Constitution, the abolition of constitutional offices, economic collapse and civil strife.", "His conclusion after prayer and reflection that the only way to avert bloodshed and save the democratic system was to have Mrs. Arroyo sworn in, and his 5:30 a.m. call to Chief Justice Davide proposing the oath by noon.", "Why only the Supreme Court could act: the Court and its members are normally passive officials who act on petitions, but the situation was extraordinary, only the Court had the credibility and moral authority to avert catastrophe, and Davide's performance as presiding officer of the impeachment court had made him the most trusted Filipino in a scientific poll.", "Davide's immediate agreement, CJP's announcement over radio and television, a questioning call from another justice, and the emergency session at which all twelve justices present backed the swearing in provided GMA made a formal written request -- after which they went to the EDSA Shrine to witness it.", "The legal aftermath: the January 22, 2001 Resolution confirming the Chief Justice's authority to swear in GMA as President; the March 2, 2001 unanimous 13-0 Decision in Estrada v. one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 11 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' reproduced a symposium address at the University of Sto. Tomas Central Seminary. Justice Panganiban opened by having the audience rise for the Centennial Prayer for the Court, composed by the Centenary Executive Committee he chaired after consultations with Catholic, Protestant, Muslim, Born-again and other groups, and now recited at each Supreme Court session and in all courts. Answering the objection that an official prayer breaches the separation of church and state, he argued that the Philippines is theist, not atheist, not even agnostic, that the Constitution itself opens by imploring the aid of Almighty God, and that the doctrine requires only government neutrality among denominations -- forbidding public funds for one group's basilica, promotion of one group's tenets, salaries for religious duties, or religion as a condition of any right -- so that while there is separation of church and state, there is no separation of the state from God. Turning to the topic he had been given, and to the Inquirer's naming of the Court as 'Filipino of the Year 2001,' he recounted January 16-20, 2001: the Senate Impeachment Court's 11-10 refusal to open the second envelope said to link President Estrada to the 'Jose Velarde' deposit, the EDSA throng, mass resignations, and the withdrawal of AFP and PNP support on the afternoon of January 19, after which, he concluded, there was no effectively functioning government. Sleepless, he woke at 4:00 a.m., heard that militants would march on Mendiola by six, foresaw bloodshed, a revolutionary government or a coup -- each obliterating the Constitution -- and at 5:30 a.m. telephoned Chief Justice Davide to propose that he swear in Vice President Arroyo by noon. Davide agreed at once; an emergency session of the twelve justices present endorsed it subject to a written request. He then traced the aftermath: the January 22 Resolution, the 13-0 Decision of March 2, 2001 in Estrada v. Desierto and Estrada v. Arroyo with his and Davide's recusals, the 13-0 denial of reconsideration, and the four theories -- resignation, permanent disability, abandonment and reality -- behind the unanimous result. He closed by reading EDSA 2 as a confluence of events planned in heaven, citing Davide's Bible falling open to Isaiah 62 and the day's gospel from Mark.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 14 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' reproduced CJP's address contending that the public opinion poll is an emerging paradigm of free expression. He opened with the Gospel reading of August 25, 2002, in which Jesus asked his disciples who people said he was and then who they themselves said he was, calling it 'the first recorded opinion survey in history' and evidence that 'polling is rooted not only in law, but also in theology,' before confining himself to juridical grounds. Invoking the adage attributed to Voltaire, he set out the two aspects of free expression -- freedom from previous restraint under Section 4 of Article III and freedom from subsequent punishment under Section 18 -- and traced the widening modes of expression from sermons and slogans to yellow ribbons and silent picket lines to satellites and the Internet, whose constitutional protection he said he awaited. He argued that polls both reflect and shape opinion and arm voters with power, citing Mahar Mangahas's WAPOR keynote, and compared foreign regimes in Singapore, India, Mexico, France, the United Kingdom and the United States, including the premature Florida call. He then recounted ABS-CBN v. Comelec, the exit-poll decision he wrote, which held that Comelec could not prohibit exit polls, restating the Court's account of expression as a preferred right embracing 'the thought we hate, no less than the thought we agree with,' the clear and present danger rule of Holmes against the dangerous tendency rule of Cabansag v. Fernandez and People v. Perez, and the Court's rebuttals of Comelec's claims of confusion and unreliability. He then welcomed SWS v. Comelec, written by Justice Mendoza, which struck down Section 5.4 of the Fair Elections Act as a prior restraint beyond Comelec's Article IX-C powers and failing the third and fourth O'Brien criteria, and recalled his own Concurring Opinion that no substantive danger had been shown. He closed by conceding that polling may be reasonably regulated to safeguard it, endorsing the ABS-CBN recommendations on how exit polls should be conducted, and insisting that 'For every freedom, there is a corresponding responsibility,' with pollsters bound to disclose methodology and educate the public on the limits and abuses of polls.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 16 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' presented the Supreme Court's decision in Estrada v. Sandiganbayan upholding the Anti-Plunder Law. CJP supplied only the opening frame: he recalled that on March 2, 2001 the Court had unanimously upheld Gloria Macapagal Arroyo's ascension and denied Estrada immunity, that the Ombudsman then charged him with plunder under RA 7080, and that Estrada, 'in a bid to shortcut his detention and obtain immediate acquittal,' attacked the law's constitutionality; he then reprinted, with permission, former Senate President Jovito R. Salonga's Kilosbayan article as the chapter proper. Salonga, who had drafted the measure as Senate Bill No. 733 in August 1988 out of his PCGG experience, recounted its unanimous passage by the post-EDSA Senate -- including several affirmative votes by Senator Estrada himself -- and set out the charge of more than four billion pesos in illegal-gambling protection money, tobacco excise funds, Belle Corp. commissions and the 'Jose Velarde' deposits. He then explained the 10-4-1 Decision opinion by opinion. Justice Bellosillo held the law presumed constitutional, its standards ascertainable, its words 'combination' and 'series' plain on the legislative record, its Section 4 no dispensation from proof beyond reasonable doubt, and Estrada estopped from claiming ignorance of a law he had voted for. Justice Mendoza concurred that strict scrutiny, overbreadth and vagueness are tools for free speech cases and inapt for penal statutes, which must be judged as applied, and that plunder is a malum in se requiring mens rea. Justice Panganiban's own Separate Opinion answered the dissenters point by point: a penal law suffices if it answers 'What is the violation?'; 'simple statutory construction, not a declaration of unconstitutionality, is the key' to the undefined terms; 'pattern' is procedural rather than an essential element, so RA 7080 is not a copy of RICO; and the quantum of evidence was not lowered but raised. The article closed by noting that Estrada could now meet the charges on the merits, 'not by resorting to mere legalisms, but by showing the sheer falsity of the offenses attributed to him.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 18 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' recounted Lim v. Executive Secretary, the challenge to the Balikatan joint military exercise brought directly to the Supreme Court by Arthur D. Lim, a former president of the Integrated Bar, and Paulino P. Ersando as citizens, lawyers and taxpayers, joined by the party-list intervenors Sanlakas and Partido ng Manggagawa. The petitioners argued that the 1951 Mutual Defense Treaty permitted assistance only against an armed attack by an external aggressor and that the Visiting Forces Agreement did not authorize American combat operations on Philippine soil. By 10 to 3 the Court, through Justice Sabino R. De Leon Jr., dismissed the Petition on procedural grounds: no taxpayer standing, certiorari and prohibition being improper remedies on the facts alleged, prematurity because the claimed violation was merely speculative, and the Petition being in substance one for declaratory relief, which the Court has no jurisdiction to grant. The ponencia nonetheless discussed the VFA's deliberately ambiguous term 'activities,' concluded that combat-related activities as distinguished from combat itself were authorized, refused to take judicial notice of media coverage of events in Mindanao, and dismissed the case without prejudice to a sufficient petition in the proper Regional Trial Court. CJP agreed with the dismissal but wrote separately. He acknowledged that the 'transcendental importance' of the constitutional question could have justified relaxing procedure, but held that the Petition lacked 'enough factual moorings upon which to base an intelligent discussion and disposition of the legal issues': it never alleged that American troops had actually engaged in offensive combat, and its claim that a shooting war was unavoidable was conjectural, set against the Solicitor General's Terms of Reference limiting the exercise to six months and barring combat. He stressed that cases could not be decided on hypothetical assumptions, that courts may consider only facts alleged and proven, and that without firm findings no grave abuse of discretion could be imputed. He listed five questions that remained genuinely open, summarized Justice Kapunan's dissent, and concluded that the substantive constitutional issues were still unsettled.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 21 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' recounts Panganiban's ponencia in Government of the United States of America v. Hon. Guillermo G. Purganan, in which an eight-member majority answered 'in general... No' to two novel questions: whether Mark Jimenez was entitled to notice and hearing before a warrant for his arrest could issue, and whether he was entitled to bail while extradition proceedings were pending. After recalling Secretary of Justice v. Lantion, where the Court reversed itself 9-6 on reconsideration, he narrates how the United States sought Jimenez's extradition on Florida indictments for conspiracy to defraud, tax evasion, wire fraud, false statements and illegal campaign contributions, and how Judge Purganan instead held a hearing, issued the warrant and then fixed bail at one million pesos. The Decision first laid down 'five postulates of extradition': that extradition is a major instrument for the suppression of crime; that the requesting state will accord due process; that the proceedings are sui generis and summary; that compliance must be in good faith under pacta sunt servanda; and that 'persons to be extradited are presumed to be flight risks.' Reading Section 6 of PD 1069, the Court held that the words 'immediate' and 'if it appears' and the absence of 'hearing' dispense with prior notice, and it outlined the procedure judges must follow since the Rules of Court contain none. On bail it held the constitutional guarantee inapplicable, due process satisfied by a subsequent hearing, and bail available only as an exception on a clear and convincing showing of no flight risk and of 'special, humanitarian and compelling circumstances,' including reciprocity. Panganiban then reproduced Carpio's concurrence, the Puno and Bellosillo opinions urging a remand, and the Vitug and Santiago dissents, before rebutting the remand as 'a cop-out' and the charge of disregarding basic freedoms as 'baseless.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 22 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' continues the running survey of death penalty developments that Panganiban had included in each of his four previous books. He records that under RA 7659 only seven convicts have ever been lethally injected -- Leo Echegaray first, on February 5, 1999 -- and that although People v. Echegaray upheld the law 12-3 and the Court had affirmed 143 death impositions as of August 8, 2002, 'the executive branch of government has shown some reluctance in fully implementing' it: President Estrada's December 2000 moratorium was continued by President Arroyo, whose August 27, 2002 memorandum granted 90-day reprieves. Congress was again debating repeal through Senate Bill 2060, while Pagdayawon v. Secretary of Justice held that a pending bill cannot justify staying a final sentence and declined to revisit constitutionality. He restates that 'the international trend is unmistakably towards the abolition of legalized killing,' citing the Optional Protocol to the ICCPR. Against a PAO report that 107 convicts had been 'spared,' he supplies the fuller figures from the Judicial Records Office -- 483 cases reviewed, 143 affirmed, 46 acquitted, 294 modified or remanded -- so that only about a third of capital sentences survive, and argues that if trial courts can be wrong more often than right 'there is always a probability of an erroneous death being inflicted.' He then lists eight conditions barring a death sentence and nine new pronouncements of his seventh year: age and relationship cannot be stipulated; People v. Pruna's six guidelines on proving age; the suggestive show-up in People v. Escordial; sufficiency of the information in Quezada; the town mayor as a disqualified counsel in Velarde; the inadmissibility of unwritten confessions in Felixminia; the reliability of DNA testing in Vallejo; separate voting on guilt and penalty in Roque; and the retroactive effect of RA 8294 on illegal firearm possession.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 1 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' reproduced CJP's address on judicial activism, delivered to a rare assembly of all Philippine appellate jurists alongside an American and two Thai justices. He opened with Eisenhower's 1961 quip that his two great mistakes were still sitting on the Supreme Court, identified them as Earl Warren and William Brennan, and sketched the Warren Court's expansion of civil rights against the counsels of restraint from Felix Frankfurter and Robert Jackson, who accused the activists of entering the political thicket while the activists replied that the Harvard School had excised all heart out of the law. He then turned to the decisive textual difference: Section 1 of Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution not only grants ordinary judicial review but imposes on every judge the duty to determine whether any branch or instrumentality has gravely abused its discretion. Because that intervention is framed as a duty and not a mere power, he argued, Philippine judges are mandated to be activist and may not shirk, waver or equivocate, on pain of repeating the judicial cop-outs of martial law. He credited Chief Justice Roberto Concepcion, the provision's author, with tracing it to the dictatorship's use of the political-question defense, and warned, with Garcia v. Comelec and Father Bernas, against being beguiled by American jurisprudence written for a different constitutional setting. He then offered his own rule: courts may not limit a grant of absolute discretion, but where the Constitution imposes conditions, limitations or restrictions, their observance is a legal question -- as in Francisco v. House of Representatives, where the second impeachment complaint against Chief Justice Davide fell to the one-year bar, and unlike Lopez v. Senate of the Philippines, where the Court declined to disturb the canvassing Joint Committee. On jurisdiction he cited Santiago v. Guingona and Lopez for the rule that the allegations of the petition confer it. He defended the Court's economic rulings on Meralco rates, Manila Bay reclamation, NAIA Terminal III, poll computerization and online gambling against business criticism, saying Philippine judges are duty-bound to afflict the comfortable and comfort the afflicted; traced the widening definition of grave abuse from Rule 65's capricious-and-whimsical formula to any act contrary to the Constitution, the law or jurisprudence; enumerated the guarantees of judicial independence and the Court's added prerogatives over the lower courts, the bar and the rules of procedure; and closed by arguing that the weakest branch, lacking purse and sword, finds its strength in moral courage, for its might is in its being right.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 7 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' records CJP's address to the Fourth Asian Regional Conference of the World Association of Public Opinion Research, opened with a joke about a surgeon who assured a patient he would survive because nine of his last ten patients had already died. Thanking Mahar Mangahas and greeting WAPOR president Kathleen Francovic, he observed that polling had grown from a marketing research tool into a credible index of voter preference in the hands of organizations like Social Weather Stations, believed by Filipinos sometimes more than the official count. He surveyed how other countries treat election polls -- bans in Singapore and Mexico, judicial protection in India and Canada, voluntary restraint in Britain, and liberalization in South Africa and France -- noting that embargoes are evaded through foreign websites. He then explained two landmark Decisions. In ABS-CBN v. Comelec, which he wrote, the Court rejected as speculative Comelec's claim that exit polls posed a clear and present danger to the electoral process, holding that respondents were randomly chosen, that results were not meant to replace the official count, and that exit polls formed part of free expression. In Social Weather Stations v. Comelec, the Court voided Section 5.4 of the Fair Elections Act as prior restraint, beyond Comelec's powers, and an unreasonable regulation under United States v. O'Brien. He restated the doctrine that free speech is an indispensable condition of other freedoms and that debate should be uninhibited, robust and wide open, encompassing the thought we hate, while conceding that polling may be regulated to safeguard it through designated areas, professional pollsters and disclosure of margin of error and methodology. He closed on the Court's own standing: it decides with cold impartiality and resists mobs and lobbies, yet commanding neither army nor money it needs residual public trust, its real strength lying not in its might but in its being right -- which is why SWS surveys prompted its transparency reforms.

Electoral Commission to hold that judicial review is integral to checks and balances, reinforced by the expanded certiorari jurisdiction engraved in Section 1 of Article VIII.", "The tools of constitutional construction applied -- verba legis, ratio legis est anima, and ut magis valeat quam pereat -- and the line of cases (Santiago v. Guingona, Tanada v. Angara, Bondoc v. Pineda, Coseteng v. Mitra, Daza v. Singson, Tanada v. Cuenco) showing review of congressional action.", "The holdings on standing (relaxed, given expenditure of public funds and the transcendental issues), ripeness (the complaint had been filed and the rules enforced), justiciability (constitutionally imposed limits make the question examinable) and judicial restraint (adjudication could not be declined because no other tribunal could decide).", "The construction of 'initiate': amicus Florenz Regalado, who had sponsored Section 3(5) as a constitutional commissioner, affirmed that initiate meant to file and to take initial action, so Sections 16 and 17 of Rule V, deeming proceedings initiated in three other ways, contravened the Constitution -- and Arroyo v. De Venecia confirmed that House rules may not ignore constitutional restraints.", "The disposition: because the first Complaint was filed June 2 and referred August 5, 2003, the second Complaint of October 23, 2003 fell within the one-year bar; Sections 16 and 17 of Rule V were unconstitutional and the second Complaint barred.", "The Bellosillo Opinion: judicial restraint and reasoned hesitance, a harmonious blend of courtesy and caution, and remedies to be exhausted within the legislature -- yet he too found the second Complaint constitutionally infirm.", "The Puno Opinion: the issue was justiciable and impeachment sui generis, but under the 'coordinacy theory' the Court should defer until the House and Senate had acted, since wrong timing could negate the very jurisdiction claimed; he voted to dismiss.", "The Vitug Concurrence: impeachment is legal and political and sui generis, and where the House transgresses the detailed constitutional procedure the issue becomes constitutional; the Court, he wrote, was probably weak but did not have to be a weakling, and the keeper of the fundamental law could not be a bystander.", "His own Concurring Opinion: his initial inhibition because a petitioner was a former law partner, because amicus Salonga was a close friend, and because he was one of the eight justices charged in the first Complaint and had used JDF-funded facilities -- and the Court's October 28, 2003 Resolution directing him to participate.", "The authorities on participation despite interest, drawn from amicus Bernas at the Oral Argument -- Perfecto v. Desierto -- plus the practical point that if the seven charged justices all inhibited, the Court would lose its quorum and jurisdiction.", "His constitutional argument: unlike the 1935 and 1973 Constitutions and unlike the US Constitution, the 1987 charter commands the Court to strike down grave abuse of discretion by any branch, a provision authored by former Chief Justice Concepcion to remedy the judicial cop-outs of the Martial Law era, so that Philippine judges are mandated to be activists while US justices may choose between the Warren Court's activism and the Rehnquist Court's passivism.", "His due process point -- the House rules are also unconstitutional insofar as they do not give the charged official notice and an opportunity to be heard -- and his Epilogue rejecting the Salonga-Pangalangan deferential thesis as 'passing the buck,' with the closing claim that the judiciary's weakness becomes its strength and that its might is in its being right.", "The remaining opinions -- Santiago (defects real but resolution premature; endorsement is not filing), Gutierrez (the anti-harassment clause and the futility of misguided self-restraint), Callejo (six grounds rejecting restraint and a close parsing of 'file' versus 'initiate'), Azcuna (impeachment placed in Article XI on accountability, and proceedings occur in the House while the case is tried in the Senate) and Tinga (constitutional limits are mandatory, standing may be relaxed under Barrows v. one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 15 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' is CJP's account of Francisco v. House of Representatives, which he called the most controversial case decided by the Supreme Court during his ninth year in office. The Court effectively stopped the House from acting on the second impeachment Complaint against Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr., and on November 10, 2003, the day the Decision was promulgated, the House voted 115 to 77 to respect it, averting what he described as a constitutional crisis of googolplex proportions; he credited the Senate's restraint and President Arroyo's support for the outcome. He recounted the facts -- the 2002 House Resolution probing the Chief Justice's disbursement of the Judiciary Development Fund, Estrada's first impeachment Complaint of June 2, 2003 referred to the Committee on Justice on August 5 and dismissed as insufficient in substance on October 22, and the second Complaint filed the next day by Representatives Teodoro and Fuentebella -- and then the Court's ruling, delivered through Justice Carpio-Morales: judicial review extends to impeachment proceedings; standing was relaxed and the issue was ripe and justiciable; and, on the authority of amicus Florenz Regalado who had sponsored the provision, 'initiate' means to file a complaint and take initial action on it, so that Sections 16 and 17 of Rule V of the 2001 House Impeachment Rules contravened Section 3(5) of Article XI and the second Complaint was time-barred. He then summarized each Separate Opinion in order of seniority, from Bellosillo's and Puno's calls for restraint and Santiago's view that the process should first run its course, through Vitug's, Gutierrez's, Callejo's, Azcuna's and Tinga's concurrences. In his own Opinion he disclosed that he had inhibited because of a former law partner, a close friendship with amicus Salonga, and his own exposure in the first Complaint, but was directed to participate; citing Perfecto v. Meer, Nitafan, Abbas and Estrada v. Desierto, and noting that mass inhibition would strip the Court of a quorum, he argued that jurisdiction may not be declined. Because the 1987 Constitution, authored on this point by Chief Justice Concepcion to end Martial Law-era judicial cop-outs, commands judges to strike down grave abuse of discretion, he concluded that they are mandated to be activists, rejected the deferential Salonga-Pangalangan thesis as passing the buck, and closed that the judiciary's weakness becomes its strength, for its might is in its being right. The vote was 11-3-1, with Chief Justice Davide taking no part.

Comelec, the case in which the Supreme Court voided the Comelec contract for the automated counting and canvassing of the 2004 votes, a Decision he wrote after his Dissenting Opinion became the majority's ponencia.", "His narration of how Comelec gravely abused its discretion: awarding a billion-peso contract to a 'consortium' whose existence and eligibility were never documented, then executing the contract with MPEI alone, in violation of its own bidding rules and the Government Procurement Act.", "His account of the technical failures Comelec waived away -- counting machines that missed the 99.9995 percent accuracy rating, could not detect and block previously downloaded results, and lacked an incorporated audit trail -- and of the admission that the software evaluated was only a demo version.", "His Epilogue and the Court's disposition: the Resolution and Contract declared void, the payments ordered recovered, the Ombudsman directed to determine criminal liability, and the Motion for Reconsideration denied with finality."]
sub_topics: ["He opens with the decade of failed attempts to automate Philippine elections and a counting system unchanged in a hundred years -- still super-slow and fraud-prone -- and the nation's expectation that the May 10, 2004 presidential elections would be fully automated.", "He sets out Comelec's three-phase modernization -- voter list cleanup, automated counting and canvassing, and electronic transmission -- and notes that the first contract fell in Comelec v. Quijano-Padilla and Photokina and the third in Brilliantes v. Comelec.", "He discloses the case's internal history: it had been raffled to Justice Tinga, but during the deliberations from December 2003 the majority voted to uphold CJP's Dissenting Opinion, which became the new ponencia.", "The facts: RA 8436 of December 22, 1997 authorizing an automated election system; Comelec Resolution 02-0170 adopting the three phases; the January 28, 2003 Invitation to Apply for Eligibility and to Bid; Resolution 5929's eligibility criteria including the twenty-million-voter track record, the 10 percent equity requirement and the 20 percent performance bond.", "The bidding: the two-envelope, two-stage system; 57 bidders reduced to Mega Pacific Consortium and Total Information Management Corporation; the DOST technical evaluation that gave both failed marks; and Resolution 6074 of April 15, 2003 awarding the project to MPC anyway.", "Locus standi: because the nation's political and economic future hung on the 2004 elections, the subject matter was of paramount public interest and transcendental importance, justifying relaxation of the rule on standing.", "Prematurity: the Court held that Comelec en banc, by awarding the project on April 15 before the BAC issued its report on April 21, made it legally impossible for petitioners to use the protest mechanism of RA 9184 -- and in any case the May 29, 2003 letter to Chairman Abalos was a sufficient written protest.", "The first ground of grave abuse -- identity and eligibility: no joint venture, consortium or similar instrument was ever submitted, so Comelec had no basis to conclude that a consortium existed, was eligible, could deliver, or that its members were jointly and severally liable.", "What surfaced only after the bidding: four separate bilateral agreements instead of one multilateral pact -- MOAs with SK C&C and WeSolv limiting liability to each firm's own area of work, and Teaming Agreements making Election.com and ePLDT mere subcontractors not solidarily liable to Comelec.", "The contract itself: 'The Automated Counting and Canvassing Project Contract' was executed between Comelec and MPEI, signed by Willy U. Yu as president of MPEI, with no mention of any consortium, joint venture or joint and several liability -- measured against the definition of joint venture in Kilosbayan v. Guingona.", "The second ground -- technical failure: both bidders missed the mandatory 99.9995 percent accuracy rating, and the Court condemned the practice of setting unrealistic specifications only to water them down after the award as a sure indication of fraud that discourages bona fide bidders.", "Further technical deficiencies: the machines could not detect previously downloaded precinct, city, municipal and provincial results and prevent their re-entry, opening the way to massive fraud by a few keystrokes; and the audit trail, mandatory under Section 7 of RA 8436, was not yet incorporated into MPC's machines.", "The software admission: Commissioner Borra conceded at the Oral Argument that the software then in use was merely the demo version, with the final one still being developed, leaving the Court with the impression that Comelec was keeping its fingers crossed and hoping the final product would work.", "Remedial measures and further flaws: 100 percent testing could not cure the grave abuse already committed; the December 15, 2003 MIRDC-DOST letter that Comelec invoked in fact reported hardware testing, not software reprogramming; and permitting the winning bidder to change the software amounted to a substantive amendment without public bidding.", "The Epilogue: the Court at the crossroads of the nation's history; Comelec's failure to measure up to its historic task; the finding that it had shoddily accepted hardware and software that admittedly failed legally mandated requirements; the demand that public funds be recovered; and the closing maxims that the end never justifies the means and that penumbral contracting will not produce enlightened results.", "The disposition and the Separate Opinions: Resolution 6074 and the MPEI Contract declared null and void, with referrals to the Ombudsman and the Solicitor General; concurrences by Justices Santiago (eligibility, exhaustion, and the midstream change of the accuracy criterion) and Gutierrez (MPEI nonexistent at the time of the Invitation, and mandatory requirements that cannot be waived).", "The dissents: Chief Justice Davide on the destabilizing effect of voiding a partly performed contract with no time to re-bid and no suggestion of graft; Justice Vitug on the enormity of the factual disputes making certiorari inapt; and Justice Tinga's extended dissent on the writs invoked, exhaustion, the notarized consortium agreements, solidary liability, collective qualification and the DOST findings -- a 9-5 result with one vacancy.", "The Motion for Reconsideration: the same issues re-raised and rejected; the clarification that no criminal prejudgment had been made; the distinction from the Amari and Piatco cases, which were commercial and involved no irregular disbursement, whereas here nearly P850 million of the P1.3 billion had already been irregularly paid; and the denial with finality."]

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 16 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' is CJP's account of Information Technology Foundation v. Comelec, in which the Supreme Court voided the contract for automating the counting and canvassing of the 2004 votes. He began with the century-old Philippine counting system, still super-slow and fraud-prone, and with Comelec's three-phase modernization, noting that the first phase contract had already fallen in Comelec v. Quijano-Padilla and Photokina and the third in Brilliantes v. Comelec. He disclosed that the case had been raffled to Justice Tinga but that during deliberations from December 2003 the majority adopted his own dissent as the ponencia. Reviewing the facts -- RA 8436, Comelec's Resolutions, the two-envelope bidding, the fifty-seven bidders narrowed to Mega Pacific Consortium and TIMC, the DOST evaluation giving both failed marks, and the April 15, 2003 award by Resolution 6074 -- he upheld the petitioners' standing because the nation's future hung on the elections, and rejected the claim of prematurity because Comelec en banc had awarded the project six days before the BAC reported, making the statutory protest impossible. On the merits he found grave abuse of discretion on two grounds. First, no consortium agreement was ever submitted, so Comelec had no basis to find MPC existent, eligible, capable or solidarily liable; four bilateral agreements surfaced only after the bidding, limiting each firm's liability, and the Contract itself was signed with MPEI alone, with no mention of any consortium. Second, the counting machines failed the mandatory 99.9995 percent accuracy rating, could not block previously downloaded results -- opening the prospect of massive fraud by a few keystrokes -- and lacked the audit trail required by Section 7 of RA 8436, while Commissioner Borra admitted that the software evaluated was only a demo, leaving Comelec, in the Court's words, keeping its fingers crossed. Post-award testing could not cure the abuse, and allowing the software to be changed was a substantive amendment without bidding. His Epilogue declared that Comelec had failed to measure up to its historic task, ordered the recovery of public funds and referral to the Ombudsman, and closed that the end never justifies the means and that penumbral contracting will not produce enlightened results. He then summarized the concurrences of Justices Santiago and Gutierrez and the dissents of Chief Justice Davide, Justice Vitug and Justice Tinga, a 9-5 result, and the denial with finality of the Motion for Reconsideration.

unlawful aggression is the most essential element, and here a sufficient interval had passed, Marivic having withdrawn to the children's bedroom while Ben ceased his attack and went to bed.", "The Court's important qualification: had Ben still been awaiting her, the imminence of the threat would not have ceased, and where the brutalized person already suffers from the syndrome, further evidence of actual physical assault at the time of the killing is not required, since to make her await an obvious deadly attack would sentence her to murder by installments.", "Mitigating circumstances: the repeated severe beatings constituted cumulative provocation that broke down her psychological resistance and self-control, and this psychological paralysis diminished her will power under paragraphs 9 and 10 of Article 13 of the Revised Penal Code.", "Passion and obfuscation: Ben had threatened to kill her while dragging her by the neck toward the cabinet where he kept a gun, and she was eight months pregnant, so that the attempt was on her life and her fetus's; one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 17 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' is CJP's account of People v. Genosa, the first Philippine case to consider the viability of the battered woman syndrome as a defense to parricide, a Decision he could write, he said, only after immersing himself in medical and scientific study of the phenomenon and its treatment abroad. Marivic Genosa had been abused by her husband for more than eight of their twelve married years when, on the evening of November 15, 1995, eight months pregnant, she killed him; admitting the killing, she claimed the syndrome as self-defense. He set out the clinical background at length: the definition of a battered woman, who must have passed through the battering cycle at least twice; the traits of low self-esteem, emotional dependence, self-blame and false hope; and the three phases of the cycle of violence -- tension-building, in which her placatory behavior legitimizes the batterer's sense of entitlement; the acute battering incident, brutal and beyond her control; and the tranquil phase of remorseful reconciliation, in which she is most thoroughly tormented. He described the illusion of absolute interdependency and drew on Lenore Walker, Dr. Natividad Dayan and Dr. Alfredo Pajarillo on immobilization, learned helplessness and posttraumatic stress. The Court nevertheless held that the defense fell short, since only one full sequence was proved and the experts testified theoretically without the factual basis for their conclusion, and that self-defense failed because unlawful aggression, its most essential element, had ceased when Ben stopped attacking and went to bed. Yet it cautioned that where a brutalized person already suffers from the syndrome, no further proof of actual assault at the moment of killing is needed, for to make her await an obvious deadly attack would sentence her to murder by installments. Crediting cumulative provocation and psychological paralysis under paragraphs 9 and 10 of Article 13, and passion and obfuscation arising from the threat to her life and her fetus's, and rejecting treachery as unproven, the Court vacated her death sentence, reduced it to prision mayor to reclusion temporal and qualified her for parole. Justice Ynares-Santiago dissented for complete self-defense and acquittal, joined by three others, making the vote 10-4, and the chapter closes with Republic Act No. 9262, effective March 27, 2004, whose effect on the ruling he left an open question.
