one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 18 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' recounted Sanlakas v. Executive Secretary, the four consolidated Petitions that challenged President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo's Proclamation No. 427 and General Order No. 4, which declared a state of rebellion and called out the Armed Forces after some three hundred officers and enlisted men seized the Oakwood Premiere Apartments in Makati on July 27, 2003. CJP first recalled the precedent of the May 1, 2001 'EDSA 3' assault on Malacañang, where a similar declaration was lifted after five days and the challenge in Lacson v. Perez was dismissed as moot. Here the mutiny ended the same evening but the state of rebellion stood until August 1, 2003. Justice Dante O. Tinga, though agreeing the cases were moot, wrote on the merits because the question was 'capable of repetition yet evading review.' His ponencia held that Section 18 of Article VII grants the President 'a sequence of graduated powers,' that the conditions of actual invasion or rebellion and the demands of public safety attach only to the suspension of the writ and to martial law, and that the President's executive power, reinforced by the 'unstated residual powers' recognized in Marcos v. Manglapus, supported the declaration -- which was in any case 'an utter superfluity,' 'devoid of any legal significance' and 'deemed not written.' CJP, joined by Justices Quisumbing and Callejo, wrote separately to argue that the Petitions should be dismissed on mootness alone: nothing extant remained to be declared valid or void, the suits had become pleas for declaratory relief outside the Court's original jurisdiction, and the repetition theory may be invoked only where the Court has jurisdiction over the subject matter and the party remains directly prejudiced. He summarized Justice Vitug's concurrence, and the Santiago and Gutierrez opinions voting to grant the Petitions, then tallied the votes to conclude that, with only five justices expressly upholding constitutionality, the question had not been definitively laid to rest.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 19 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' explained Velarde v. Social Justice Party, the Decision CJP himself wrote, which arose from the Social Justice Society's Petition for Declaratory Relief asking whether religious leaders violate the separation of Church and State by endorsing candidates or urging their flock to vote for particular ones. The Regional Trial Court of Manila had ruled for SJS on June 12, 2003, and the Supreme Court, thinking the question transcendental and novel, gave the appeal priority and held Oral Argument on April 13, 2004 -- only to conclude that no decision on the merits was possible. The Petition, he recounted, alleged no existing controversy between the parties, no specific violated right and no ultimate facts; it rested on the speculation that Brother Mike Velarde and his co-respondents had endorsed or threatened to endorse candidates, and so sought only an advisory opinion, which courts are proscribed from rendering. It likewise stated no cause of action, since no breach was impending or threatened and no direct injury was shown, and SJS lacked legal standing, its claimed 'keen interest' being impersonal, vague and highly speculative -- though the Court observed that standing could be waived for an issue of paramount public interest. The proceedings below were tainted as well: the trial court did not hear the Motions to Dismiss, gave no reason for denying them, left the Motions for Reconsideration unresolved, and decided before answers were filed, acting with inexplicable haste and grave abuse of discretion. Because the assailed Decision contained no statement of facts and no final disposition, it violated the constitutional command that decisions express clearly and distinctly the facts and the law on which they rest, and was void and legally inexistent, leaving nothing to review. For the guidance of the bench and the bar, CJP then reproduced the Court's primer on the five essential parts of a good decision, closing with the standard that a decision be clear, concise, complete and correct.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 20 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' recounted how Romualdez v. Sandiganbayan gave the Supreme Court the occasion to settle a question that Estrada v. Sandiganbayan had left open: whether the void-for-vagueness doctrine may be used to invalidate penal laws. In Estrada the Court had upheld the Anti-Plunder Law by a 10-4-1 vote but had not met the 'on its face' challenge head on, merely citing Justice Mendoza's Separate Concurring Opinion that overbreadth and vagueness apply only to free-speech cases; CJP himself had written a Separate Concurring Opinion there. Romualdez, a brother-in-law of former President Marcos charged by the PCGG in 1989 with violating Section 5 of Republic Act 3019, attacked that provision as vague and overbroad after a long train of motions to dismiss and to quash. The Court first held those motions procedurally fatal -- a motion to dismiss was in substance a prohibited second motion to quash, the Rules abhor repetitive motions, and issues may not be raised by installment -- yet reached the merits because of the importance of the case in curtailing graft and corruption. It then held that the doctrines have special application only to free-speech cases, that a statute aimed at conduct is tested only as applied, that every statute is presumed valid, and that under Dans v. People the law adequately answered 'What is the violation?' through its two elements; the word 'intervene' meant simply 'to come between.' A vague Information called for a bill of particulars, not a quashal; the reinvestigation by the Ombudsman satisfied Cojuangco and Raro; prescription ran from discovery after the PCGG's work, so the 1989 Information was timely; and immunity failed because the 1981 amendment could not reach a 1975 act and, under Estrada v. Desierto, immunity attaches only during incumbency. CJP closed by reproducing Justice Tinga's Separate Opinion that the Estrada pronouncement was obiter and that a vagueness challenge is a proper due process claim.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 21 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' surveyed the Supreme Court's new jurisprudence on capital offenses for the period from October 10, 2003 to October 10, 2004, the year marking CJP's ninth on the Court. He opened with Judicial Records Office statistics and observed that less than one third of the capital cases reviewed since the Death Penalty Law took effect on December 31, 1993 had been affirmed, a figure he read as proof of the Court's special assiduousness. The year's most significant ruling was People v. Mateo, Justice Vitug's valedictory ponencia, which held it wise and compelling to have the Court of Appeals review all heinous-crime judgments before they reach the Supreme Court, and which the Court implemented through AM No. 00-5-03-SC amending Rules 122 and 124. Having voted for Mateo without writing separately, CJP set out six reasons in plain English: death convicts deserve the same multiple review that petty offenders enjoy; capital cases turn on facts and the Supreme Court is not a trier of facts while the Court of Appeals is; a decade of doctrine now guides the CA; automatic Supreme Court review survives by constitutional fiat and acquittals remain unappealable; the CA had been enlarged to 69 justices; and the High Court would gain time for novel disputes and its Judicial Reform Program. He then reviewed the year's other rulings -- DNA evidence in Vallejo and Yatar and the limits of the self-incrimination clause, the validity of routine airport searches in Suzuki, the rejection of a complex crime of robbery with homicide and assault in Otayde, the reading of an Information as one whole document in Villanueva, the strict scrutiny of waivers in Macarang and Beriber, the searching inquiry required in Besonia, the divided treatment of successive custodial investigations in Mojello, and the rulings on sexual assault, relationship, pretrial stipulations, proof of age and filiation, explosives, and the quorum question recalled and re-deliberated in People v. Ebio.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 7 of 'Judicial Renaissance' reproduces an address Justice Panganiban delivered at the XIX Biennial LAWASIA Conference in the Gold Coast, Queensland, at the invitation of chairperson Chief Justice David K. Malcolm, explaining how the integrity and independence of the Philippine judiciary are upheld. Although court decisions are not made on the basis of what is popular or newsworthy, he argued, the judiciary must continuously retain the trust of litigants and the public, and the Court's annual placement among the country's five most credible institutions is owed chiefly to its repeated demonstrations of independence. He then set out ten structural guarantees. The 1987 Constitution, written after the bloodless 1986 People Power Revolution toppled a dictatorship, reduced executive and legislative power and intensified judicial power, and no office may review the Supreme Court's decisions. The Court is uniquely mandated to nullify any act of any branch or official, including the President or Congress, done with grave abuse of discretion -- which he stressed is not just a power but a duty, since a power can be relinquished but a duty cannot be evaded -- and it has voided laws, executive orders, acts of cabinet secretaries and military and police officers, government contracts, and even a congressional impeachment of the Chief Justice barred by a constitutional time-bar. Doing so, he insisted, does not make the Court superior to the political branches but ensures that law overrides the desires and caprices of officials, so that the rule of law and not of men prevails. He further described the Court's role as sole judge of presidential and vice-presidential election contests, its power to review the factual basis of martial law or suspension of habeas corpus, the bar against laws diminishing its jurisdiction, security of tenure for judges until 70, the Judicial and Bar Council's limit on presidential appointments, fiscal autonomy, control of admission and discipline of lawyers, and its rule-making power. He closed on a paradox: the judiciary is still the weakest branch, yet its very weakness -- its lack of budget and police powers -- becomes its strength, its true power lying in moral courage born of competence, independence and integrity.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 18 of 'Judicial Renaissance' recounts Central Bank Employees Association v. Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, which Panganiban opens with its holding: an initially valid provision of law can become subsequently unconstitutional when its continued operation would violate the equal protection of the law. RA 7653 of July 3, 1993 abolished the old Central Bank and created the BSP; almost eight years later the employees association sought to stop the implementation of the last proviso of Section 15(c), Article II, which exempted officers at Salary Grade 20 and above from the Salary Standardization Law while leaving the rank-and-file covered. The BSP answered that the proviso must be read with the bank's fiscal and administrative autonomy and the Monetary Board's mandate, and the Solicitor General argued the classification rested on actual and real differentiation. Voting 9 to 4 through ponente Justice Reynato S. Puno, the Court held the proviso was not infirm on its face, but that later laws exempting the rank-and-file of seven other government financial institutions had worked an 'invidious discrimination' against the BSP's 2,994 rank-and-file employees. Puno invoked relative constitutionality, citing US cases and Rutter v. Esteban, and applied a two-tiered scrutiny: the proviso passed the rational basis test, since the officers' exemption addressed the BSP's lack of competitiveness, but failed strict scrutiny because a classification by salary grade is akin to one based on economic class. Panganiban dissented, arguing that relative constitutionality was inapplicable and had no express basis in positive law, that respect for Congress as a coequal branch and the absence of urgency counseled restraint, and that the proviso satisfies the three-tiered review because neither salary grade nor government employment is a fundamental right or suspect class. He reports Justice Carpio's dissent that the majority had effectively enacted a pending bill and had wrongly lumped the regulatory BSP with commercial GFIs, and Justice Carpio Morales's 145-page dissent attacking the ponencia's 'double standard,' urging that the statutes be read in pari materia, and concluding that with House Bill 123 pending, judicial restraint was mandatory.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 21 of 'Judicial Renaissance' recounts the sequel to the Court's January 13, 2004 Decision nullifying the Comelec's contract with Mega Pacific eSolutions for automated counting machines, a contract voided for clear violation of law and jurisprudence and reckless disregard of the poll body's own bidding rules, with the result that the machines went unused in the 2004 national elections. Although the Decision became final and was entered in the Book of Entries of Judgment on March 30, 2004, the Comelec moved for leave to use the 1,991 idle ACMs in the August 8, 2005 ARMM elections, pleading RA 9333's automation mandate, the absence of funds, the machines' deterioration, storage costs of P329,355.26 a month, and a certification by 'information technology experts' that the software met ISO/IEC 12207 standards. Panganiban, who wrote the unanimous Resolution of June 16, 2005, sets out the grounds for denial in order. First, a final and executory judgment can no longer be modified or reversed, and granting leave would have subverted the Decision; moreover, a check of the records showed that the experts' letter had already been filed as an annex to an earlier motion for reconsideration, and for all its technical jargon it did not alter the finding of grave abuse of discretion -- the Commission, he writes, seemed to think it could resurrect a dead case like a witch doctor muttering incantations over a corpse. Second, the concession would have jeopardized recovery of over a billion pesos improvidently paid and might even have abated the Ombudsman prosecutions and impeachment proceedings. Third, the machines and their nonexistent software had failed eight critical integrity requirements. Fourth, the Motion was too vague to say how many units the ARMM needed or how the machines would be protected for return. Fifth, the Comelec had ample time to bid anew or to manualize, as it had for the May 2004 elections. Finally, no justiciable controversy existed, making the request at best one for an advisory opinion; the Court closed by directing the Comelec to follow the Decision, return the machines, recover the funds, and devise a sound computerization plan.

Garcia, where revision and appreciation of ballots in all 881 precincts widened the protestee's margin from 803 to 1,417 votes.", "Angping v. sub_topics: ["The chapter's premise: having written in 'Leveling the Playing Field' that he enjoyed his role as HRET chairperson and saluted his brethren-lawmakers, CJP now redeems his commitment to report more extensively on the Tribunal.", "The HRET's composition under Section 17, Article VI -- nine members, three justices designated by the Chief Justice with the senior justice as chairperson and six representatives chosen by proportional representation -- and the roster as of press time on October 10, 2005.", "The distinction between an election protest, filed by a defeated candidate within ten days of proclamation on grounds of fraud or irregularities, and a quo warranto petition, filed by any voter of the district on the ground of disloyalty or ineligibility.", "The novelty of a challenge to 'returns': the HRET Rules have no express provision for it and the contest type had not been tested before his term, until Angping v. Roces.", "The five grounds for summary dismissal under Rule 21: insufficiency in form and substance, late filing under Rules 16 and 17, non-payment of the filing fee, non-payment of the cash deposit or its first P150,000, and illegibility of the petition and annexes.", "The procedural sequence after summons under Rule 22: answer and counter-protest within ten days, joinder of issues under Rule 54, preliminary conference for simplification of issues, stipulations, limits on witnesses, evidence aliunde, withdrawal of precincts and dates for evidence, then a preliminary conference resolution.", "The divergent tracks thereafter: a hearing commissioner receives evidence in quo warranto cases within twenty-day periods, while an election protest proceeds to collection of ballot boxes, revision under Rule 88 in pilot or all contested precincts, reception of evidence, and the Tribunal's appreciation of ballots.", "The docket at the start of the term and the eight protests plus three quo warranto petitions disposed of -- Roco v. Villafuerte (withdrawal, with the counter-protestant denied his damages claim), San Juan v. Cerilles (insufficient in form and substance and lack of jurisdiction for failing to allege the proclamation), and Cerbo Jr. v. Mangudadatu (failure to file a reply).", "Further dismissals: Calizo v. Cruz (failure to submit written arguments), and Andueza v. Bravo (filed beyond the period under Rule 16).", "San Miguel v. Dy: a challenge to Rep. Consuelo A. Dy's residence in Pasay City, where the address in her Certificate of Candidacy was alleged to be a cockpit arena; witnesses, school certifications and her political career as councilor and representative persuaded the Tribunal of her domicile of origin and animus revertendi.", "The doctrine applied there, citing Romualdez-Marcos v. Comelec: residence in election law is synonymous with domicile, an individual does not lose domicile by living and maintaining residences elsewhere, and a change requires actual and deliberate abandonment, with the burden on the petitioner.", "Samson v. Crisologo: Rep. Vincent Crisologo, convicted of arson and arson with homicide in 1972, conditionally pardoned in 1981 and granted an absolute and unconditional pardon in 1986 restoring full civil and political rights, was challenged under Article 36 of the Revised Penal Code.", "The Tribunal's two holdings in Crisologo: res judicata could not bar the case because jurisdiction shifts from the Comelec before proclamation to the HRET after it, and absolute pardon restoring full political rights removed all disabilities, including the rights to vote, to be voted for and to hold public office.", "Roman v. Garcia: a protest over the 2nd District of Bataan, where Garcia led by 803 votes, 479 precincts were protested and 881 counter-protested, and the Tribunal dispensed with pilot precincts and ordered revision and appreciation in all 881.", "The first issue there -- alleged massive frauds and illegal electoral practices -- failed for want of any evidence from either side, leaving the case to turn on revision and appreciation alone.", "The rules of appreciation recited: the cardinal objective of discovering and giving effect to the voter's intention, the presumption of validity, invalidity of ballots prepared by one person or filled by two distinct persons, the marked-ballot rules on repeated names, and the Neighborhood, Intent and Idem Sonans Rules for claimed ballots.", "The outcome in Bataan: final totals of 75,833 for Garcia and 74,416 for Roman, widening the margin to 1,417, and the unanimous dismissal on September 22, 2005 of both protest and counter-protest.", "Angping v. Roces: Zenaida Angping's substitution for her husband Harry, whose Certificate of Candidacy the Comelec First Division cancelled by a resolution 'deemed promulgated' on April 30, 2004, and Comelec Resolution No. 6823 denying due course to her substitute candidacy.", "The Tribunal's ruling through Rep. Mauricio G. Domogan: Miranda v. Abaya did not apply because the withdrawal and substitution preceded the actual issuance of the cancelling resolution, the substitution was allowed under Section 77 of the Omnibus Election Code, and Resolution No. 6823 was a mere administrative issuance void for want of the notice and hearing required for quasi-judicial action under Section 78.", "The vote of 6-2-1 holding the protestant a proper party, the affirmative finding of jurisdiction, the rejection of the forum-shopping charge, and the observation that the protestee had been proclaimed on a mere 6,347 votes amid the district's high voting population.", "CJP's Separate Opinion in Angping: the allegations sufficed to confer jurisdiction, the protestee's 'prejudicial questions' were no ground for immediate dismissal, review of Resolution No. 6823 was not dispositive, and the primordial duty of the Tribunal was to ascertain the true winner in the election.", "His jurisdictional checklist -- a protestant who duly filed a Certificate of Candidacy and was voted for, a proclaimed protestee, and filing within ten days -- and the basic rule that jurisdiction is determined by the allegations of the petition, regardless of entitlement to the relief sought.", "His reasons for finding no forum shopping: the certiorari petition in the Supreme Court sought only nullification of Resolution No. 6823 and could not have declared a winner, while the protest sought a re-canvassing to find the true and lawful winner.", "The subsequent proceedings: simultaneous revision and re-canvassing ordered, the protestee's withdrawal of revision in the unrevised precincts granted on June 22, 2005, suspension under the Supreme Court's TRO of June 28, 2005, and the Court's Decision of September 15, 2005 sustaining the HRET by a vote of 8-4-3 and lifting the TRO.", "The pending cases: seven protests already revised, with 100 percent revision ordered in Candazo v. one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 22 of 'Judicial Renaissance' is Panganiban's report on the House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal, written to redeem a promise made in 'Leveling the Playing Field' and timed to his first anniversary as chairperson on July 15, 2005. He sets out the HRET's constitutional charter under Section 17, Article VI -- sole judge of all contests relating to the election, returns and qualifications of representatives -- names its nine members as of October 10, 2005, and explains its practice: an election protest by a defeated candidate, a quo warranto petition by any voter, the five grounds for summary dismissal under Rule 21, summons and answer, the preliminary conference, and then either reception of evidence before a hearing commissioner or the collection of ballot boxes followed by revision and appreciation of ballots. Of the 15 protests, 3 quo warranto petitions and 1 petition to re-canvass returns filed after the May 10, 2004 elections, 8 protests and all 3 quo warranto cases had been disposed of, and he lists each dismissal with its resolution number and dates. He gives fuller accounts of San Miguel v. Dy, where evidence of domicile of origin and animus revertendi defeated a residence challenge under Romualdez-Marcos v. Comelec; of Samson v. Crisologo, where an absolute pardon restoring full civil and political rights was held to remove every disability, and where jurisdiction was said to pass from the Comelec to the HRET upon proclamation; and of Roman v. Garcia, where neither side proved the alleged massive fraud and revision of all 881 precincts widened Garcia's margin from 803 to 1,417 votes under the Neighborhood, Intent and Idem Sonans Rules and the principle that ballot appreciation exists to give effect to the voter's intention. The chapter's centerpiece is Angping v. Roces, a novel petition for re-canvassing alone, in which the Tribunal upheld the substitute candidacy and its own jurisdiction and Panganiban wrote separately that the Tribunal's primordial duty was to ascertain the true winner. He closes by praising the Tribunal's diligence, forecasting that it would finish its cases within two years, commending the Secretariat by name, and reproducing a poem an HRET lawyer had privately given him.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 18 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' reproduced Chief Justice Artemio V. Panganiban's address at a testimonial dinner tendered in his honor by the ASEAN Law Association, where he thanked chapter president Ave Cruz for refusing to accept a 'no,' acknowledged Justice Leo Quisumbing and ALA president Chao Hick Tin, and noted that he had driven five hours from Baguio City, where the Supreme Court was holding its summer sessions. Departing from the usual fellowship talk, he turned to recent Philippine judicial history, reporting that three days earlier the Court had promulgated a landmark Decision partially voiding Executive Order 464, which had barred executive officials from congressional inquiries without prior presidential approval; the Court held that Congress could compel their appearance because the power of legislative inquiry was as broad as the power to legislate, while directing Congress to state in its invitations the subject matter and related questions so that executive privilege could properly be invoked. He cited the ruling to illustrate the interplay of powers under the tripartite allocation of authority, in which the three branches are neither antagonistic nor subservient but coordinate and check one another. He described the judiciary as the people's refuge for every conceivable conflict, and argued that although the bench commands neither the armed forces nor the budget, its very weakness had become its strength, its authority resting on moral courage born of competence, independence and integrity. Likening the Court to constitutional monarchs who stabilize the ship of state by sheer presence, he said it anchors the Philippine ship of state on steady and calm waters. He recalled vowing, on assuming office on December 21, 2005, to lead a judiciary of four Ins battling the ACID problems, and restated his twin beacons of liberty and prosperity: the scales weighing heavily for the poor in liberty cases, deference to the political branches in matters of prosperity. He closed by leaving the Panganiban Court's record to the judgment of history.

sub_topics: ["The facts: on September 28, 2005 the President issued EO 464, effective immediately, requiring heads of departments to secure presidential consent before appearing before either House and defining the nature, scope and coverage of executive privilege.", "Section 2(b) enumerated who were covered -- senior executive officials, generals and flag officers, PNP officers of chief superintendent rank or higher, senior national security officials, and such others as the President might determine -- each by the judgment of their respective superiors.", "Invoking EO 464, executive and military officials declined to appear at Senate hearings in late 2005 and early 2006 on allegations of presidential electoral fraud, irregularities in the North Rail project, and the misuse of fertilizer funds.", "The senators claimed EO 464 virtually rendered the Senate inutile, and the Senate and several senators filed consolidated Petitions for Certiorari and Prohibition invoking Article VI, Sections 1, 21 and 22, and other provisions.", "The three synthesized issues: whether EO 464 contravened the congressional power of inquiry, whether it violated the right to information, and whether respondents gravely abused their discretion by implementing it before publication.", "Standing: the Senate and its individual members had a substantial and direct interest and could sue to keep their legislative prerogatives inviolate; party-list representatives Ocampo, Casiño, Virador, Beltran, Mariano and Maza, and the national party-list group Bayan Muna with its three House seats, likewise had standing.", "PDP-Laban, not a party-list group, had no standing: its claim that EO 464 hampered its legislative agenda was vague and uncertain and at best a 'generalized interest,' whereas concrete injury is an indispensable element of a justiciable dispute.", "Ripeness: EO 464 did not require a deliberate withholding of consent or an express prohibition, and since its implementation had already produced nonappearances it would have been sheer abandonment of duty for the Court to refrain from passing on its constitutionality.", "The Question Hour: the Constitutional Commission's framers treated Sections 21 and 22 as distinct, and the present Constitution removed the mandatory character of appearance during the Question Hour to conform to a presidential system -- so Sections 1 and 2(a) of EO 464, which referred only to Section 22, were upheld.", "Inquiries in aid of legislation: Sections 2(b) and 3 were invalidated because, per Arnault v. Nazareno, the power of inquiry is coextensive with the power to legislate and grounded on the necessity of information to the legislative process.", "Limits on the inquiry power: per Bengzon v. Senate Blue Ribbon Committee an inquiry may not usurp judicial functions, is subject to certiorari review, must follow duly published rules of procedure, must respect the Bill of Rights, and should indicate the subject and the questions involved.", "Executive privilege defined: Schwartz, Rozell and Black's Law Dictionary were quoted, U.S. v. Nixon was recounted as recognizing a constitutionally allowable but defeasible privilege, and Almonte vs. Vasquez was cited for the presumptive privilege for presidential communications.", "The principle that emerged: executive privilege is recognized only in relation to certain sensitive types of information, its validity depends on the ground invoked and the context, and its extraordinary character inclines heavily against executive secrecy and in favor of disclosure.", "Exemption from inquiry: only a valid claim of privilege exempts department heads, never their status as such; only the President is absolutely exempt, being reachable only through impeachment, and members of the Supreme Court are exempt on separation-of-powers, fiscal-autonomy and judicial-independence grounds, a point Senate counsel Joker Arroyo conceded upon the Chief Justice's interpellation at Oral Argument.", "How the claim must be made: clearly asserted with a statement of its specific basis, though Congress must not demand such particularity as to compel disclosure of the very information protected, the privilege against self-incrimination offering a useful analogy.", "Why Section 3 in relation to Section 2(b) was invalid per se: it virtually allowed the President to authorize claims of privilege by mere silence, leaving Congress woefully unable to judge whether withholding was justified; the power to invoke is limited to the President, or to the executive secretary acting 'By order of the President.'", "The reasonable-time rule: a summoned official must be given time to inform the President or executive secretary of a possible need to invoke, and if neither invokes after a reasonable time, Congress may compel the appearance.", "Right to information: EO 464 concerned only congressional demands, not citizens' demands, which lack the obligatory force of a subpoena duces tecum -- yet because legislative investigations are generally public, any issuance unduly limiting disclosure there denies citizens access to matters presumed of public concern.", "The Motions for Reconsideration: non-publication of the Senate's inquiry rules had no bearing on EO 464, which rested solely on executive privilege; the 'for practical purposes' tentative prevention was rejected as speculation; and PDP-Laban was distinguished from Bayan Muna on party-list representation and seat-forfeiture grounds, both Motions being denied with finality on July 14, 2006.", "Justice Tinga's Separate Opinion: EO 464 was really a set of instructions under the presidential power of executive control and valid on its face, since even without it the President could order officials not to appear; one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 19 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests The Senate v. Ermita, the challenge to Executive Order 464, which the President issued on September 28, 2005 requiring department heads and a broad class of senior executive, military, police and security officials to secure presidential consent before appearing before either House of Congress. Invoking it, officials declined to attend Senate hearings on alleged presidential electoral fraud, the North Rail project and the fertilizer funds, and the Senate and several senators sued, claiming the order had rendered the chamber inutile. In a unanimous 14-0 Decision written by Justice Conchita Carpio Morales, the Court first upheld the standing of the Senate, its members, the Bayan Muna, Anakpawis and Gabriela representatives and the Bayan Muna party-list group, while denying standing to PDP-Laban for asserting only a generalized interest, and held the case ripe because implementation had already produced nonappearances. On the merits it distinguished Section 22 of Article VI, the Question Hour, where appearance is discretionary under a presidential system, from Section 21, inquiries in aid of legislation, where attendance is compulsory because, per Arnault v. Nazareno, the power of inquiry is coextensive with the power to legislate. Sections 1 and 2(a) of EO 464 were therefore sustained, while Sections 2(b) and 3 were struck down. Drawing on Schwartz, Rozell, Black's Law Dictionary, U.S. v. Nixon and Almonte vs. Vasquez, the Court held that executive privilege covers only certain sensitive types of information, never officials by reason of office, and that its extraordinary character inclines heavily against secrecy and in favor of disclosure. A claim must be clearly asserted with its specific basis stated, may be invoked only by the President or the executive secretary 'By order of the President,' and cannot be made by mere silence; an official summoned must be given reasonable time to seek an invocation, failing which Congress may compel appearance. The Court also noted that unduly limiting disclosure in public legislative investigations denies citizens information presumed of public concern, denied both Motions for Reconsideration with finality on July 14, 2006, and recorded Justice Tinga's separate view that the order was valid on its face as an exercise of executive control though unconstitutional in its application.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 20 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests Bayan Muna v. Ermita, the consolidated challenge to Batas Pambansa 880, the Public Assembly Act of 1985, and to the Calibrated Preemptive Response policy that Malacanang announced in a press release of September 21, 2005 as being in force in lieu of maximum tolerance. Petitioners argued that BP 880 required a permit regardless of any clear and present danger, curtailed the choice of venue although time and place form part of the message, was not content-neutral, and violated international human rights instruments, and that CPR was preemptive, unsupported by statute, contrary to the maximum tolerance the law mandates, and chilling. In a unanimous 13-0 Decision written by Justice Adolfo S. Azcuna, the Court upheld petitioners' standing, affirmed the primacy of assembly, petition, speech, expression and the press as the very basis of a functional democratic polity, and held that BP 880 is not an absolute ban but a content-neutral regulation of the time, place and manner of assemblies, already so described in Osmena v. Comelec. A permit may be denied only on a showing of clear and present danger to public order, safety, convenience, morals or health -- a limitation recognized even under the Universal Declaration and the ICCPR -- so the law is neither overbroad nor a prior restraint, and the delegation to mayors is bounded by a precise and sufficient standard. Because the solicitor general could name only Cebu City's Fuente Osmena as a designated freedom park, the Court ruled that thirty days after finality no prior permit may be required in the public parks and plazas of any non-complying locality, since without an alternative forum to deny the permit is to deny the right. CPR, it held, served no valid purpose if it meant maximum tolerance and was illegal if it meant anything else, and it was struck down as a darkness that shrouds freedom that merely confused the people and was used by some police agents to justify abuses; the DILG was directed to secure compliance with Section 15 within thirty days.

sub_topics: ["The Decision opened with a paean to liberty quoting the Chief Justice's philosophy that in cases involving liberty the scales of justice should weigh heavily against the government and in favor of the poor, the oppressed, the marginalized, the dispossessed and the weak.", "The facts: on February 24, 2006, as the country marked the 20th Anniversary of EDSA People Power I, President Arroyo issued PP 1017 declaring a state of national emergency and GO 5 implementing it, lifting them a week later through PP 1021 after seven Petitions had been filed.", "Respondents justified the issuances by a conspiracy to unseat or assassinate the President allegedly hatched by some military officers, leftist insurgents and members of the political opposition.", "Malacanang cancelled all programs for the EDSA anniversary and revoked rally permits issued by local governments, and Presidential Chief of Staff Michael Defensor announced that warrantless arrests and the takeover of facilities, including media, could already be implemented.", "KMU and NAFLU-KMU members marched toward the EDSA shrine anyway; protesters were violently dispersed, and UP professor and columnist Randolf S. David and Akbayan president Ronald Llamas were arrested without warrant.", "On February 25, 2006 CIDG operatives raided the Daily Tribune offices and confiscated news stories, documents, pictures and mock-ups, with police stationed at the Tribune and at the pro-opposition papers Malaya and Abante.", "Mootness: by 11-3-1 the Court held that PP 1021 did not moot the Petitions, since illegal acts had been committed during the eight days PP 1017 was operative and an unconstitutional act confers no rights and imposes no duties.", "The four exceptions to mootness -- grave constitutional violation, exceptional character and paramount public interest, the need for controlling principles, and capability of repetition yet evading review -- were all present, reinforced by CJP's Separate Opinion in Sanlakas v. Executive Secretary.", "Standing: David, Llamas, Cacho-Olivares and the Tribune Publishing Co. had alleged direct injury from illegal arrests and unlawful searches, and the other petitioners were heard on the ground of transcendental importance; impleading the sitting President as respondent was improper.", "Review of factual bases: following Integrated Bar of the Philippines v. Zamora and Lansang v. Garcia, the standard is arbitrariness rather than correctness, and the burden lies on the petitioner to show the President's decision totally bereft of factual basis -- a burden petitioners failed to carry against the solicitor general's detailed narration.", "Facial challenge rejected: the overbreadth doctrine is a tool for testing statutes in free-speech cases, facial invalidation is a manifestly strong medicine to be used sparingly and only as a last resort, and a petitioner must establish that there can be no instance in which the assailed measure might be valid.", "Vagueness rejected as well, since the doctrine requires a showing that the measure is vague in all its possible applications and petitioners made no such attempt.", "First provision -- the calling-out power: per Sanlakas the Commander-in-Chief clause grants a sequence of graduated powers from the calling-out power through suspension of the writ to martial law, the sole criterion being necessity to prevent or suppress lawless violence, invasion or rebellion, with every act beyond it ultra vires.", "The Court distinguished a declaration of a 'state of rebellion,' which merely announces a condition of public moment under the Administrative Code, from a proclamation of national emergency invoking Section 17 of Article XII -- an awesome power that could not be dismissed as harmless, as Sanlakas had done.", "PP 1017 was emphatically not a declaration of martial law and could not justify warrantless arrests and seizures, a ban on public assemblies, press censorship or media takeover, or the issuance of presidential decrees.", "Second provision -- faithful execution: the President's ordinance power is limited by the Administrative Code of 1987, legislative power belongs to Congress under the present Constitution, and the military may be ordered to enforce only laws pertinent to suppressing lawless violence, not civil or customs laws.", "Third provision -- the state of national emergency: Section 17 of Article XII must be read with Section 23 of Article VI, so that the takeover of a private utility or business affected with public interest requires a delegation from Congress, the President being unable to decide alone whether the exceptional circumstances exist, when they cease, or which businesses to take over.", "Void-as-applied: courts are not at liberty to invalidate a measure merely because it has been abused or misabused, and nothing in PP 1017 allowed the police to conduct illegal arrests or searches.", "GO 5 and terrorism: 'lawless violence' is extant in the statutes and the Constitution, but Congress has yet to define and punish 'acts of terrorism,' so the President alone would decide what terrorism means -- a judgment absolute and without restriction, inviting indiscriminate arrests, raids, media takeovers and dispersals, and therefore unconstitutional as to that portion.", "The arrest of David was unjustified: the officers could invoke only their observation of rallyists wearing 'Oust Gloria Now' shirts and their erroneous assumption that he led the rally, and the inquest prosecutor ordered his release after seven hours for insufficiency of evidence.", "The dispersal and arrest of KMU members rested on Malacanang's arbitrary wholesale cancellation of permits, in disregard of the rule that freedom of assembly may be limited only upon a showing of clear and present danger, tolerance being the rule and limitation the exception, and of BP 880's requirement of notice and hearing before revocation.", "The Tribune raid violated Rule 126 of the Rules of Court and the freedom of the press: the seizure of materials for publication, the stationing of policemen and the arrogant warnings to media were plain censorship, and the Court invoked the motto Obsta principiis.", "The Court's reproduced summation held PP 1017 constitutional as a call to the AFP, its extraneous decree-issuing, law-enforcement-at-large and media-restraint provisions ultra vires, GO 5 valid except for 'acts of terrorism,' and the four enumerated acts unauthorized -- while refusing, on elementary due process, to impose sanctions on unidentified individual officers.", "CJP's Concurring Opinion regretted that unanimity had been impossible after the EO 464 and CPR rulings, disagreed with the Dissent that the President could lawfully reissue PP 1017 as worded, and warned that those testing the outer limits of presidential prerogative were playing with fire.", "Justice Ynares-Santiago concurred that the calling-out power authorizes neither decrees nor warrantless searches nor prior restraint, and argued that Section 17 of Article XII, sitting in the article on National Economy and Patrimony, presupposes an economic rather than a political emergency.", "Justice Tinga, joined by Justices Corona and Velasco, dissented from Sanlakas, which he had written: PP 1017 was valid on its face, the comma in the phrase 'to all the laws and to all decrees' showed the President had not arrogated the power to issue decrees, terrorism is already encompassed by extant penal laws, and the majority had adjudicated David's injuries with undue haste, without trial and without impleading the officers -- leaving the ruling, in his closing words, to be read as an extended advisory opinion."]

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 21 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests David v. Arroyo, the challenge to Presidential Proclamation 1017 and General Order No. 5, issued on February 24, 2006 as the country marked the 20th anniversary of EDSA People Power I and lifted eight days later by PP 1021. In that interval the EDSA celebrations were cancelled, rally permits were revoked wholesale, KMU and NAFLU-KMU marchers were violently dispersed, Randolf David and Ronald Llamas were arrested without warrant, and CIDG operatives raided the Daily Tribune. Writing for the Court, Justice Angelina Sandoval-Gutierrez held the Petitions not moot, since an unconstitutional act confers no rights and the case was capable of repetition yet evading review; upheld standing on direct injury and transcendental importance; and, applying the arbitrariness standard of Lansang and Integrated Bar of the Philippines v. Zamora, found the President justified in calling out the Armed Forces because petitioners had not shown the proclamation factually baseless. Facial challenges for overbreadth and vagueness failed, facial invalidation being a manifestly strong medicine. Dividing the operative text in three, the Court sustained the calling-out clause under Section 18 of Article VII, denied that the faithful-execution clause let the President issue decrees or direct the military to enforce unrelated laws, and held that a declared national emergency under Section 17 of Article XII confers no power to take over private utilities without a congressional delegation under Section 23 of Article VI. GO 5 was valid except for 'acts of terrorism,' undefined by Congress and therefore left to the President's absolute judgment. The warrantless arrests, the permit cancellations made without notice or hearing, and the Tribune raid and warnings to media were declared unauthorized and plain censorship, though due process barred sanctioning unnamed officers. The chapter reproduces in full CJP's Concurring Opinion, which the ponente treated as integral: regretting the loss of unanimity, he answered Justice Tinga's Dissent that PP 1017 might be a paper tiger but had nuclear teeth that must be defanged, warned that its drafters were testing the outer limits of presidential prerogatives and playing with fire, and recalled that an earlier Court's want of moral courage had let a past President fall into the precipice of authoritarianism. Justice Ynares-Santiago's concurrence and Justice Tinga's dissent, joined by Justices Corona and Velasco, close the chapter.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 22 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests KMU v. The Director General (NEDA), the challenge to Executive Order 420, which President Arroyo issued on April 13, 2005 directing all government agencies and government-owned and -controlled corporations to adopt a uniform data collection and format for their existing identification systems. Two issues were framed: whether the order usurped legislative power and whether it infringed the citizen's right to privacy. The Court held that because the GSIS, SSS, Philhealth, the Mayor's Office, the LTO and the PRC already recorded data and issued cards, unifying those systems was purely an administrative matter within the President's power of control under Section 17 of Article VII, which also obliges her to ensure that the laws be faithfully executed. Since that control does not extend to the judiciary or to the independent constitutional commissions such as the Comelec, EO 420 does not establish a national ID system; legislation would be needed for a special appropriation, for compulsory coverage of all branches and citizens, or for data beyond those routinely required. On privacy, the Court noted that agencies had issued IDs for years without complaint, that the data were limited to 14 items of which only eight appear on the card, and that the remainder were strictly confidential under Section 6(d) and therefore outside the right to information on matters of public concern. Measured against Whalen v. Roe, in which the U.S. Supreme Court upheld the centralized reporting of patients receiving controlled prescription drugs, the 14 routine items were far less sensitive and far more benign, while Ople v. Torres was distinguished as having annulled a broadly drawn issuance devoid of safeguards solely because its subject matter required legislation. Justice Ynares-Santiago, joined by Justice Azcuna, dissented: a multipurpose ID's scope of usage would be staggering and all-encompassing, no citizen could avoid it, Philippine privacy jurisprudence was at its infancy, and EO 420 supplied none of the safeguards, procedures, access limits or sanctions that had saved the statute in Whalen, so the parameters for such electronic files should be set by legislation rather than by a mere executive order.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 23 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests Lumanlaw v. Peralta, a unanimous ruling penned by the Chief Justice. Lumanlaw was charged with illegal possession of a dangerous drug in November 2002 and held in the Manila City Jail under a Commitment Order, yet his arraignment was postponed fourteen times between his arrest and the filing of his Petition in 2004 -- because his counsel de parte was absent, because the judge was unavailable, and above all because the jail wardens repeatedly failed to bring him to court -- leaving him detained almost two years without ever being arraigned, his two Motions to Dismiss both denied. He sought mandamus under Rule 65. The Court held his right to speedy trial violated, explaining that the 30-day period of the Speedy Trial Act is not absolute and that judicial proceedings must contend with the realities of everyday life, so the question is not a mathematical calculation of elapsed periods but whether the delays were vexatious, capricious, oppressive or unjustified. Reviewing the reasons for each postponement, it found the violation manifest and saw a lack of earnest effort to arraign the accused as soon as the calendar allowed. It observed that an arraignment takes at most ten minutes and entails no legal gymnastics, that the absence of private counsel was no reason to postpone when the accused himself had asked for a counsel de oficio, and that the wardens' failures could have been averted by efficient court management and proper supervision of the clerk of court. The judge had instead let the listlessness of the parties, his staff and the wardens dictate the pace, doing nothing even after two urgent Motions to Dismiss. On the remedy, the Court held that mandamus may issue to control discretion where undue delay amounts to grave abuse producing manifest injustice, and that the want of a prior motion for reconsideration and the hierarchy of courts would not bar the writ, since procedural rules are not strictly enforced when enforcement would cause a miscarriage of justice and the protection of the people's civil liberties overwhelms all rules of procedure.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 24 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests Silahis International Hotel, Inc. v. Soluta et al., in which the Court, through Justice Conchita Carpio Morales, once again upheld the inviolable right of persons against warrantless and unreasonable searches and seizures -- this time against private persons. Hotel management said it had searched the employees' union office in the basement after reports of marijuana, dollar smuggling, prostitution and a theft syndicate, following surveillance and with the permission of union officer Henry Babay. The union's account differed: on the morning of January 11, 1988 officer Soluta found the office door jammed, a laundrywoman reported having seen five men in barong tagalog forcing it open at dawn, and when a locksmith was fetched, club-wielding men in barong tagalog arrived and beat the employees. While police were awaited, Petitioner Panlilio ordered a security guard to force the door, searched over Babay's objection and his demand for a warrant, and found marijuana flowering tops, on which thirteen union officers were charged under the Dangerous Drugs Act. The trial court acquitted them, finding the specimen inadmissible and the confiscation suspicious, and the officers then sued for malicious prosecution and violation of their right against illegal search, winning damages in the trial court and the Court of Appeals. Before the Supreme Court the petitioners argued chiefly that the constitutional guarantee could not be invoked against private individuals. The Third Division denied the Petition, holding that such rights occupy a lofty position in every civilized and democratic community and that Article 32 of the Civil Code makes any public officer, employee or private individual who directly or indirectly impairs them liable for damages. Since the petitioners had surveilled the office since late 1987 and had ample time to secure a warrant, their course stank in illegality; ownership of the room did not deprive the lawful occupants of standing to object; consent could not be presumed absent clear and convincing proof of a knowing and voluntary waiver; and because the article reaches those indirectly responsible, the petitioners and the security personnel who orchestrated the search were held jointly and severally liable for actual, moral and exemplary damages.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 25 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests Estrada v. Escritor, in which the Court held that a court interpreter who lived with a man not her husband was not administratively liable, because she had made out a case for exemption based on her fundamental right to freedom of religion. Alejandro Estrada had asked the presiding judge of a Las Pinas trial court to investigate Soledad Escritor for an act he believed tarnished the image of the court, and she was charged with 'disgraceful and immoral conduct' under the Revised Administrative Code. Escritor testified that she had been widowed in 1998, that her arrangement with Luciano Quilapio Jr. had begun more than twenty years earlier while her own husband was living with another woman, and that as a member of Jehovah's Witnesses she had executed a 'Declaration of Pledging Faithfulness' approved by the elders and recorded in the Watch Tower Central Office, which made the union moral and binding within the congregation until legal impediments were lifted. An earlier Decision of August 4, 2003, which became the law of the case, had remanded the matter and ordered the solicitor general to intervene, and had settled that benevolent neutrality or accommodation was the framework for construing the religion clauses while the compelling-state-interest test governed the Free Exercise plea. The Court revisited the two opposing strains in American jurisprudence -- strict separation anchored on the Jeffersonian 'wall of separation' and benevolent neutrality -- and the Sherbert, Yoder and Smith line, distinguished mandatory, permissive and prohibited accommodation, and concluded that the Philippine Constitution gives accommodation more leeway, that criminal laws are not beyond the Free Exercise Clause, that accommodation protects minority religions from majoritarianism, and that the religion clauses are stated in absolute terms. Applying the three-step test, it noted that the solicitor general had conceded sincerity and centrality, shifting the burden to the government, which offered no evidence of paramount interests endangered and none at all on least intrusive means. Justice Carpio dissented, joined by the Chief Justice and Justices Morales and Callejo, arguing that Smith had overturned the Sherbert test and warning that 'today concubinage, tomorrow bigamy' would escape sanction; Justice Ynares-Santiago dissented separately, holding the issue legal rather than religious.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 30 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests Rufino v. Endriga, the quarrel over who may name the trustees of the Cultural Center of the Philippines. Trustees appointed by President Fidel V. Ramos in 1995, whose terms ran to December 31, 1998, were told by President Joseph Estrada on December 22, 1998 that seven new appointees led by Armita B. Rufino would replace them; the ousted Endriga group filed quo warranto, invoking Section 6(b) of Presidential Decree 15, under which the remaining trustees fill vacancies by election and the President may act only when the board is entirely vacant. The Court of Appeals granted the Petition, and on appeal the Rufino group attacked Section 6(b) as repugnant to Section 16 of Article VII, which allows the appointment only of officers lower in rank. Although the Rufino group's resignation and President Arroyo's appointment of new trustees could have mooted the case, the Court passed on the merits to prevent a repeat of the controversy and to protect the CCP from being periodically wracked by internecine politics. By 10-3 it held Section 6 (b and c) irreconcilable with the Constitution, since it authorized an appointing officer to appoint an officer equal in rank to himself. It then held that the word 'heads' in Section 16 refers to the chairpersons of commissions or boards and not to their members, reasoning from the different phrasing used in the 1935, 1973 and 1987 Constitutions when the power was granted to members of a collegial body, from the framers' deliberations, and from the fact that every board has a chief executive; since the CCP charter and rules made the board chairperson the head of the CCP, only the chairperson could be vested with the power to appoint lower-ranked officers. The provision also ran afoul of the President's power of control, for the CCP fell under the Executive Branch and the self-election of trustees made it a self-perpetuating entity virtually outside that control. Justice Tinga dissented, arguing that the board as a collegial body outranks its individual members, that the Appointments clause permitted Congress to vest the power in it, and that executive control reaches the acts of a subordinate and not the actor himself, so officials whose terms are fixed by law cannot be removed at the President's pleasure.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 32 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests Mirasol v. DPWH, the tollway-traffic case decided for the Court by Justice Antonio T. Carpio. Acting under Republic Act 2000, the Limited Access Highway Act of 1957, the DPWH had issued Department Order No. 215 in June 1998 declaring the Manila-Cavite (Coastal Road) Toll Expressway a limited-access facility, and petitioners sued in the Makati Regional Trial Court to nullify that order together with Administrative Order No. 1 of 1968, Department Order No. 74 of 1993 and the Revised Rules on Limited Access Facilities promulgated through the Toll Regulatory Board. After the trial court enjoined the total motorcycle ban in June 2001, the DPWH issued DO 123 admitting motorcycles of 400 cubic centimeters, and in 2003 the same court dismissed the petition while voiding DO 123 on equal-protection grounds. On appeal the Court partly granted the petition. It first held that the earlier injunction was a provisional remedy that merely served to preserve the status quo, an ancillary measure that Section 9 of Rule 58 required to be confirmed by a final injunction, so res judicata did not bar the dismissal. It then traced the old Department of Public Works and Communications through Presidential Decree 458, the 1973 renaming of departments as ministries, and Executive Orders 546 and 710, concluding that the authority to regulate limited-access highways devolved to the Department of Transportation and Communications; DO 74, DO 215, the TRB regulations and DO 123 were therefore void, and the equal-protection question was never reached. AO 1, however, had been issued in 1968 before the split, enjoyed the presumption of validity and merely set rules to ensure public safety and the uninhibited flow of traffic; the right to travel did not mean the right to choose any vehicle in traversing a tollway, there being no absolute right to drive. Justice Tinga, joined by three colleagues, dissented, tracing highway administration through the Bureau of Public Highways to the DPWH and urging deference to long-standing practice.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 33 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests Hernandez v. Napocor, decided unanimously through Justice Minita V. Chico-Nazario. From 1996 the National Power Corporation erected 29 steel poles, each 53.4 meters high, to carry the overhead cables of its 230-kilovolt Sucat-Araneta-Balintawak Power Transmission Project through Dasmarinas Village in Makati, where the petitioners lived. Trouble followed when residents found scientific studies linking the electromagnetic fields of high-voltage lines to illnesses ranging from cancer to leukemia; Representative Francis Joseph G. Escudero denounced Napocor's cavalier treatment of safety and consultation requirements in a privileged speech, Representative Arnulfo Fuentebella demanded an explanation, and Napocor's four options -- transferring the line, keeping a 12-meter distance, going underground, or rerouting along C-5 and the South Luzon Expressway -- ended in impasse. Petitioners sued for damages with a prayer for a restraining order in March 2000, Judge Francisco B. Ibay restrained the energizing of the line, and the Court of Appeals reversed, holding that Section 1 of Presidential Decree 1818 stripped courts of jurisdiction to enjoin government infrastructure projects. The Supreme Court granted the petition. It held that PD 1818 aimed only to avert the untimely frustration of government infrastructure projects and was never meant to be a blanket prohibition that would disregard the fundamental right to the health, safety and well-being of a community; the bar covered administrative acts involving facts or technical discretion, not questions of law, and this case raised questions of law -- the constitutional right to health and Napocor's compliance with the Local Government Code's prior-consultation requirement. The injunction also found support in Section 3 of Rule 58, which requires only a probable violation of rights, and the record -- the studies, Napocor's own brochure requiring safe distances from residences, and its documented relocation negotiations -- placed the risk within the realm of a scientific scale of probability, which was enough for a provisional remedy. The Court added that its circulars enjoined utmost caution, prudence and judiciousness rather than an unbridled prohibition, and closed by asking of what use modernization would be if it proved a scourge to an individual's fundamental right to life in all of its desired quality.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 20 of 'A Centenary of Justice' reported the Supreme Court's decision in Social Weather Stations v. Comelec, which struck down Section 5.4 of RA 9006, the Fair Elections Act, barring publication of election surveys fifteen days before a national and seven days before a local election. CJP opened by recalling ABS-CBN v. Comelec, the exit-poll case he had written for the Court and reported in an earlier book, where he had expressed elation at the 10-4 vote because it showed the Court could meet head-on new paradigms of free expression brought about by advances in science and technology; the survey case, he wrote, strengthened that confidence. He set out the challenged provision and the statutory definition of an election survey, then reproduced the 7-5-3 ponencia of Justice Vicente V. Mendoza holding the ban an unconstitutional abridgment of speech, expression and the press: it laid a prior restraint, the Comelec's constitutional powers over media reach only equal opportunity, time, space and the right to reply, and under the United States v. O'Brien test the provision failed criterion three, since it suppressed a whole class of expression while leaving columnists and commentators free to opine, and criterion four, since aims such as preventing last-minute pressure, the bandwagon effect and dagdag-bawas could be pursued by punishing unlawful acts rather than speech. He distinguished National Press Club and Osmena, where the ad ban had constitutional authorization and supplied Comelec space and Comelec hour as a substitute. He then summarized the concurrences of Justice Melo, who had dissented in ABS-CBN, and of Justice Puno, who invoked the clear and present danger rule and the overbreadth doctrine, and quoted his own concurrence treating freedom of expression as a preferred right limitable only upon a substantive danger. He reproduced Justice Kapunan's dissent on balancing free speech against equal access to public service, and closed by explaining that the earlier ABS-CBN dissents had rested only on mootness.

CJP's conclusion: since 'the most significant elements of intangible wealth are education and the rule of law,' the 'much more important focus' than natural resources or infrastructure is 'the primacy of education, the promotion of the rule of law, and the strengthening of our democratic institutions' -- 'the truly lasting legacies.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 11 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 7), CJP's August 26, 2007 Inquirer column, reviews Jose T. 'JoeAl' Almonte's book 'We Must Level the Playing Field' -- which CJP and President Ramos were invited to launch -- reading it as the key to 'the soul of the Ramos presidency.' CJP recalls first being 'wary' of the 'shadowy and enigmatic' national security adviser, picturing him as 'some sort of James Bond,' before the 'Wednesday Group' meetings revealed 'a true-blue ideologue, thinker, and strategist' whose ideas reinforced CJP's belief that 'the rule of law must not only safeguard liberty but must help eradicate poverty and nurture prosperity.' The book's central aim is to 'level the playing field of enterprise' by dismantling 'networks of collusion' -- a vision that led the Ramos government to break up monopolies in 'telecommunications, transportation, banking, insurance,' open strategic industries and attract investment against 'oligarchic interests.' Almonte, a retired general, also analyzed the military (the 'best organized' institution, hence 'a major player in post-independence politics,' whose dissident officers could only be kept in 'their barracks' by real reforms) and insurgencies ('wars of ideas... won or lost depending on which side gains the people's trust'). On social and political reform, he argued the poor 'need economic opportunities more than they need welfare,' that 'parliamentary government will not be a cure-all' and 'might... produce revolving-door governments,' and that democracy's future 'may lie outside the formal political arena' with a civil society building parties 'based on principles and programs, rather than... naked power.' The book, CJP concludes, confirms the Ramos government had 'a clear ideology' -- and that while FVR 'may have been the embodiment of Philippines 2000,' Almonte was its 'sentient' soul.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 15 of 'A Centenary of Justice' analyzes Cruz v. Secretary of Environment (GR 135385, December 6, 2000, per curiam), the constitutional challenge to the Indigenous Peoples' Rights Act of 1997 (IPRA, RA 8371), which a 7-7 deadlocked Court dismissed for want of a majority -- an 'indecisive Decision' petitioner Isagani Cruz himself lamented. Opening with Kalinga chieftain Macli-ing Dulag's cry ('How can you own that which will outlive you? Only the race owns the land'), CJP frames the question as 'social justice or reverse discrimination?': whether IPRA's grant to indigenous cultural communities/indigenous peoples of 'ownership' over ancestral domains and lands -- including waters, minerals and natural resources -- violates the Regalian doctrine of State ownership under Section 2, Article XII. Seven justices voted to uphold: Justice Kapunan (joined by Davide, Bellosillo, Quisumbing, Santiago) grounded native title in Cariño v. Insular Government as an exception to jura regalia (while conceding natural resources belong to the State), and Justice Puno described a 'distinct... private but community' indigenous ownership formalized in a CADT, with resource rights limited to stewardship and small-scale use plus priority in large-scale development under State control. Seven voted to strike down: CJP's own Separate Opinion argued IPRA unconstitutionally grants ownership and control over public-domain lands and natural resources that 'are owned by the State' and 'shall not be alienated,' defeating the State's required 'full control and supervision'; that native title (Cariño) reaches at most the land surface, not the resources beneath; and that concentrating roughly a third of Philippine territory and 80% of its minerals among about 12 million people (110 ICCs) against 60+ million other Filipinos is 'reverse discrimination' offending the constitutional aim of a 'more equitable distribution of opportunities, income, and wealth.' Crucially, he concedes the constitutionality of PRIORITY, preferential use and small-scale utilization (Section 57), objecting only to perpetual exclusive OWNERSHIP -- his conception of social justice being to 'empower and enable the poor to be equally able to compete with the rich,' not to 'permanently deprive the many in order to coddle the few.' Justice Vitug likewise voted to strike down key sections as 'an unacceptable abdication of State authority,' urging Congress to re-examine and codify the law, while Justice Mendoza would have dismissed on standing alone.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 16 of 'A Centenary of Justice' is CJP's account of his own ponencia in Ang Bagong Bayani-OFW Labor Party v. Comelec (GR 147589, June 26, 2001), which defined the Filipino party-list system as a 'social justice tool.' Building on Veterans Federation Party v. Comelec (which called the scheme 'party-list system, Philippine style'), the case asked who may participate after the Comelec, by Omnibus Resolution No. 3785, accredited 154 aspirants for the 2001 elections. The Court reached two holdings. First, political parties -- even major ones -- are not disqualified merely for being political parties, since neither the Constitution nor RA 7941 excludes them. Second, the system nonetheless exists to enable the 'marginalized and underrepresented' (RA 7941, Section 2) and cannot be appropriated by the non-marginalized: rejecting the Solicitor General's 'open to all' theory -- under which even 'the super rich of Forbes Park' could join -- CJP wrote that 'the law crafted to address the peculiar disadvantages of Payatas hovel dwellers cannot be appropriated by the mansion owners of Forbes Park,' since the mega-rich, though few, are overrepresented because 'their economic clout engenders political power.' Using a dormitory 'open house' analogy, he reasoned the system is for outsiders who cannot win regular district elections, so admitting the overrepresented would dilute and prejudice the marginalized. Justices Vitug and Mendoza dissented (vote 9-5), urging that the Constitutional Commission had voted down reserved sectoral seats and chosen proportional representation open to all, so reserving the system for the marginalized was judicial legislation. CJP refuted them on verba legis -- the plain language controls, the Charter leaves the mechanics to RA 7941, and deliberations are merely persuasive -- and laid down an 8-point screening guideline on remand (both party and nominees must represent the marginalized; the religious sector is barred; a retiree cannot represent youth, an industrialist the urban poor). His Epilogue grounds the ruling in the principle that 'those who have less in life should have more in law,' giving the masses 'genuine hope and genuine power' to become 'veritable lawmakers,' and answers critics that 'we did not change the Constitution' -- the Charter did not reserve the system, but neither did it prohibit reservation, and RA 7941's clear policy is the linchpin.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 3 of 'Justice and Faith' is CJP's primer on the Philippine legal framework for joint ventures, distilled from international and domestic authorities into a single working synthesis for bar and business audiences. The chapter opens with definitional reconciliation across four sources (International Trade Center Thesaurus, 46 Am Jur 2d, Black's Law Dictionary 5th ed., and Philippine Law Dictionary 3rd ed.), producing a common three-feature core: (a) association of persons or companies established to undertake jointly some commercial enterprise or achieve a common purpose; (b) contribution of money, property, industry, knowledge, skill or other identifiable asset; and (c) community of interest in performance, right to direct and govern management, and an agreement (express or implied) to share in profits, risks and losses. CJP then distinguishes joint ventures from partnerships along three axes -- JVs lack distinct legal personality, JVs typically have an ad-hoc / single-enterprise object versus a partnership's continuing business, and corporations may join JVs but are statutorily ineligible for partnerships. He maps a two-mode structural taxonomy (equity JVs by formation of a new company or by equity participation in an existing company; contractual JVs that are technology-oriented or marketing-oriented), and overlays this with the regulatory architecture: 1987 Constitution Article XII (National Economy and Patrimony) and Article XVI Section 11 (Mass Media), the Foreign Investments Act of 1991 (RA 7042), and the Negative List enumerating eight sectoral reservations (mass media; licensed professions; retail trade under RA 1180; cooperatives under RA 6938; private security agencies under RA 5487; small-scale mining under RA 7076; marine resources except deep-sea fishing; rice and corn industry under RA 3018 and PD 194), plus PNP- and DND-clearance products, dangerous drugs, sauna/massage establishments, racetrack and gambling activities, and US$500,000 paid-in-equity thresholds for domestic and export enterprises. On rights and liabilities inter se, CJP notes that partnership principles serve as gap-fillers when the JV agreement is silent, and that stockholders' agreements may supplement (or operate independently of) the corporation's articles and by-laws. He closes with two specially regulated JV regimes -- construction projects under PD 929 (May 4, 1976) and petroleum/coal/geothermal operations under operating or consortium agreements with the government under PD 1862.

Panganiban presented before the 16th World Law Conference of the World Jurist Association at the Philippine International Convention Center on October 27, 1993. He begins from the post-Cold War setting -- the Soviet Union dissolved, the balance of terror dismantled, 'Pax Americana' arrived -- in which leaders now rivet their attention on economic pre-eminence and states compete for trade through tax havens, incentives, foreign trade zones and free ports. That competition, he says, has outgrown single-country effort and produced trade blocs, which he defines through Foreign Affairs Secretary Roberto R. Romulo and illustrates through the European Community's 'Europhoria' over the Single European Market of December 1992 (set back by the tumultuous Maastricht ratification, the monetary crisis, German unification, recession and Balkan strife) and NAFTA, signed December 17, 1992 and effective January 1, 1994. Asean's answer was AFTA, built on the three documents adopted at the 4th Asean Summit of January 27-28, 1992, whose nine features he sets out in detail: establishment within fifteen years by 2008, the CEPT scheme as the main mechanism, a fast track of fifteen products to 0-5 percent within seven to ten years and a normal track over ten to fifteen, temporary and permanent exclusion lists, a 40 percent origin rule, elimination of quantitative restrictions, and removal of other non-tariff barriers within five years. He then names the resulting harms -- trade diversion and investment diversion -- and devotes the body of the paper to seven legal problems: the absence of any judicial or quasi-judicial dispute-settlement mechanism (and none at all for private producers), the absence of an institutional implementing authority, double taxation in its juridical and economic forms, dumping through free ports such as Singapore's and Subic's, non-tariff barriers phased out faster than the tariffs, CEPT's narrow scope compared with the EC's and NAFTA's opening of goods, services, capital and people, and the unresolved question whether the three documents require Senate concurrence under the 1987 Constitution, which he argues deserves a second look despite the government's contrary practice. He concludes that trade liberalization is the wave of the future but that developing governments cannot open their borders unprotected; regional blocs are only an intermediate step, and AFTA will fail unless the laws, regulations and adjudicatory systems of the member-countries are reviewed, updated and harmonized concurrently with the bloc itself.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 13 of 'Love God, Serve Man' is the short acceptance speech CJP delivered on November 15, 1985 at the closing session of the 55th ASTA World Travel Congress in Rome, after his election as chairman of the International Council of Governors of the American Society of Travel Agents. He thanked the international members and his fellow governors for giving him 'the highest position within their authority,' confessed that he felt inadequate and overwhelmed by the responsibility, and insisted that the honor was 'not only for me personally but is, in fact, a tribute to my country and to my people.' He read his election as 'a triumph of the American dream' in which even the lowliest may aspire to lead, serve and succeed -- the dream he attributed to Thomas Jefferson writing that all men are equal, to Abraham Lincoln telling the lowliest 'Chin up, for you are free forever,' and to Lee Iacocca, who had invoked 'the American religion of fairness' in his keynote earlier that week. Granting that ASTA had served its American members well, whether through political action in the US Congress or educational seminars at the World Travel Congress, he defined his own mission as pleading that same religion of fairness so that international members would receive equal benefits, modified to their specific objectives -- beginning with seminars retooled for the 14th International Conference in Athens that February, to which he invited all delegates. He closed by pledging the international members' cooperation and support under his incumbency, arguing that this mixture of the American dream of equality, freedom and fairness with international solidarity would build the greatest international society of travel professionals in the world, and saluted the congress from the Philippines and from Baron Travel Corporation: 'Mabuhay ASTA!'
