one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 16 of 'Love God, Serve Man' is the reaction paper CJP delivered on March 15, 1994 at the UP Law Center, at the Phi Kappa Phi 60th anniversary roundtable on Dr. F. Landa Jocano's thesis that traditional values have positive roles in stimulating industrialization and that the lack of appreciation of those roles impedes rapid growth. He accepted the first half but attacked 'the rather absolutist and exclusivistic implication of the second,' and answered from three perspectives. As a Catholic layman he reported PCP II's inquiry into why a country so rich in potential is so poor in reality, quoting its finding that 'it is not our values so much that are at fault as the exaggeration and the wrong uses we have put them to,' its insistence on an inculturated faith, its verdict that 'our society remains a sick society' despite full churches, its diagnosis of dichotomized Christians, and its prescriptions of re-evangelization and total integral development. As a businessman he challenged Jocano's century-long frame, recalling that until the late '60s the Philippines was the show window of democracy in Asia -- under four pesos to the dollar, single-digit inflation, public schools as good as the best universities -- so that the study should cover only the last 25-30 years; and he argued that the Filipino is productive, diligent and law-abiding abroad yet not at home, which points to reward systems rather than native values. He illustrated the malaise with Kardo, the taxi driver who escapes every ticket by LUSOT, LAKAS and finally LAGAY, the dead presidents in his wallet serving as his lawyers, and asked whether Jocano's core values were not basically Tagalog. As a lawyer of 33 years he showed that Philippine law has been calibrated to local custom, that the 1987 Constitution encodes pananagutan, malasakit, balikatan and bayanihan, and that the Supreme Court decides with an eye to contemporaneous conditions, closing with Roscoe Pound's 'Law must be stable, but it cannot stand still.'

Secretary of Energy and its companion case, in which the Court through Justice Puno invalidated RA 8180, the Oil Deregulation Law, by 9 to 2 for allowing Petron, Shell and Caltex to act as an oligopoly and for erecting barriers against new players through its tariff differential, minimum inventory and predatory pricing provisions. Because he had come from the business community, he took it upon himself to explain the ruling to the Rotary Club of Makati on January 6, 1998, and included that speech in full as a postscript. In it he summarized the proceedings in five steps, listed five criticisms and answered each: economic policy must conform to a Charter that uniquely guarantees economic rights; the demand for outside expert advice misunderstands the adversarial system, in which justice is not administered by plebiscite; the Court knew that voiding a new law revives the old but cannot itself amend; striking only three provisions would have left the cartel intact; and partial deregulation, though wise, would have required the Court to legislate. He closed with the doctrine from his own Tanada v. Angara that only unconstitutionality or grave abuse of discretion may void an economic act, and with the reasons the Court cannot prejudge a pending bill.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 8 of 'Battles in the Supreme Court' sets out Justice Panganiban's long-running objection to what he calls the 'indemnity only' doctrine in labor cases. He begins with the settled rule that a lawful dismissal requires both a just or authorized cause under Articles 282, 283 and 284 of the Labor Code and observance of due process through the twin requirements of notice and hearing, and notes the asymmetry that follows: absence of cause makes the dismissal illegal and brings reinstatement and back wages, while absence of due process leaves the dismissal legal and yields only indemnity of P1,000 to P10,000. That practice began in 1989 with Wenphil v. NLRC, from which he says he has 'quite vehemently and continuously dissented,' first in a footnote to his own ponencia in MGG Marine Services and then at full length in his dissent in Better Buildings v. NLRC, which the chapter reproduces under his original subheadings. He argues that Wenphil rested on facts making compliance impractical -- a violent-tempered fast-food employee who brandished an ice scooper and shouted profanities -- while later cases presented no such exigency, so that 'indemnity became an easy substitute for due process.' In Better Buildings the employer gave no notice at all, ignoring more than twenty years of service and merely instructing the guard to bar the worker from the premises. Pointing out that Kwikway and Pepsi-Cola had called such dismissals violations of the Constitution and the resulting judgments void, he condemns a penalty 'too insignificant, too niggardly, and sometimes even too late a sanction for the violation of a sacred right,' one that permits 'a virtual purchase of a fundamental right by the rich and powerful.' He therefore proposes that a dismissal without due process be branded illegal even with valid cause, with separation pay plus indemnity but no reinstatement or back wages, citing Worldwide Papermills as precedent and Fabella v. Court of Appeals as proof that strict compliance is demanded elsewhere. He concedes an exception where compliance was impossible or gravely adverse, places the burden of proof on the employer, and closes on the constitutional stakes -- 'Denial of due process is thus no less than a denial of justice itself' -- predicting that the issue will soon reach the Court en banc.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 9 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' used Phimco Industries v. Brillantes to show that justices do change their minds when persuaded, since practice allows a vote to change at any time before promulgation. Justice Panganiban recounted the facts: after a deadlocked collective bargaining negotiation, the Phimco Industries Labor Association filed a Notice of Strike in March 1995 and its 352 members struck; at the union's own petition the acting Secretary of Labor assumed jurisdiction in July and ordered the strikers back to work within 24 hours; and the match manufacturer challenged the order as grave abuse of discretion. Justice Purisima, to whom the case was assigned, first recommended dismissing the petition, but CJP's Dissent -- arguing that a match factory could hardly be indispensable to the national interest -- convinced the whole Third Division, and Purisima, in what CJP called a gallant show of humility, changed his mind and wrote the contrary ponencia, holding that grounding assumption on obtaining circumstances rather than the legislated standard would let the secretary intervene in any dispute at his pleasure. Asked by his colleagues to convert the Dissent into a Concurring Opinion, CJP reproduced it in full. He quoted Article 263 (g), concluded that assumption is meant to be used sparingly and that the secretary must respect labor's paramount right to concerted activities, and surveyed the cases: national interest had been found in school administration, a major exporter, drugs and pharmaceuticals, a domestic airline and a large tire producer, but denied most eloquently in GTE Directories, involving a telephone-directory publisher. He catalogued the broad powers that follow assumption and argued that their breadth calls for caution and strict judicial scrutiny. Tracing the power to its martial law vintage in General Order No. 5 and Letter of Instructions No. 368, which enumerated the vital industries covered, he observed that even then no blanket authority existed. He read Article 263 (g) as police power requiring public necessity, noted that intervention often favors management rather than labor, and rebutted the secretary's rationale, pointing out that Phimco's exports were negligible and that the secretary himself had admitted the case fell outside the strict categorization. Noble intentions, he concluded, do not confer jurisdiction; the case began as a battle but ended in a unanimous vote.

He began by quoting the present Civil Service Law -- Secs. 47, 51 and 52 of Book V, Title I, Subtitle A of the Administrative Code of 1987 (EO 292) -- and distilled from it two kinds of preventive suspension: suspension pending investigation, which runs up to ninety days and ends in automatic reinstatement if the case is not decided, and suspension pending appeal, which entitles the respondent to compensation if he is eventually exonerated. He then reported Gloria v. Court of Appeals, where a divided Court speaking through Justice Vicente V. Mendoza allowed pay only for the appeal period, reasoning that EO 292 had deleted the old RA 2260 grant of 'full pay for the period of suspension' and that, per Mechem, exoneration is not enough because the suspension must also have been 'unjustified.' CJP recounted arguing the contrary in the Court's deliberations -- that the majority was being too literal and unfair to government employees and was in effect reversing earlier rulings awarding back salaries 'without any qualification or deduction' -- and reproduced his Separate Opinion. There he argued that since the majority itself conceded that preventive suspension pending investigation is not a penalty but only a means to an unhampered investigation, withholding pay would transform it into a penalty unauthorized by law and offensive to due process; that 'no-work-no-pay' cannot apply to employees who are willing to work but forbidden to report; that baseless charges make a suspension unjustified ab initio; that the silence of EO 292, a law issued by President Corazon Aquino under the Freedom Constitution with no recorded deliberations, cannot be read as a denial of the right; and that the constitutional mandate to afford full protection to labor, which has no United States counterpart, resolves any doubt for the employee. He distinguished the Ombudsman Act, which expressly makes suspension run without pay, as in Callanta v. Ombudsman, and closed by hoping the Court would reverse Gloria so that government could set the example in giving labor its due.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 7 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' paired CJP's recollection of joining the Supreme Court with a digest of Ty v. Trampe, the decision he chose as his first ponencia. He explained that new appointees are greeted with a mixture of genuine welcome and cautious evaluation, unobtrusively scrutinized in how they converse, write and conduct themselves, with their first ponencias, dissents and questions at oral argument watched most closely; he himself was briefed on the Court's processes by Justice Jose A.R. Melo. Knowing this, he prepared his first decision carefully, choosing a case that would be jurisprudentially significant yet written well enough to win concurrence, and regarded the enthusiastic unanimous concurrence of the full Court as proof that he had passed his first major test. The case arose from a January 6, 1994 Notice of Assessment issued by the municipal assessor of Pasig on a new Schedule of Market Values, which raised real estate taxes by 418 to 570 percent; the petitioners argued the assessor had ignored Presidential Decree 921, and Judge Aurelio C. Trampe dismissed their petition on the ground that the Local Government Code of 1991 had repealed the Decree. The Court held that it had not. Section 534 of RA 7160 enumerated the statutes it revoked without naming PD 921, leaving only a general repealing clause, and it is a basic rule of construction that repeals by implication are not favored unless two laws are so clearly repugnant that they cannot coexist, since a court's function is to harmonize conflicts rather than take the place of Congress. Comparing the statutes, the Court found PD 921 limited to financial services in Metropolitan Manila while RA 7160 covered nearly all local government functions nationwide, so that harmony between Section 9 and Section 212 was not only possible but desirable. Its Epilogue chided the trial judge for consigning a statute and three unanimous decisions to the statutes' graveyard and admonished him to be more judicious in setting aside established laws, doctrines and precedents.

Court of Appeals, which CJP called the most significant of the sixteen decisions he wrote in the month after his unanimously supported first ponencia. Buyers Demetrio Demetria and Jose O. one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 9 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' collected five unanimous decisions CJP wrote on the Presidential Commission on Good Government and its crusade to recover the alleged ill-gotten wealth of former President Marcos, his family, nominees and cronies. In First Philippine Holdings he held that a company claiming ownership of 6,299,177 sequestered PCIBank shares had to be allowed to intervene before the Sandiganbayan, since intervention settles the whole controversy in one action and the shares were in the custody of the court, and that the Sandiganbayan's jurisdiction over ill-gotten wealth is exclusive, plenary and all-embracing, reaching every related incident. Three sequestration cases turned on the PCGG's own Rules: the writ against Dio Island Resort was void because it was issued by a regional representative rather than a commissioner, and no later ratifying resolution could cure it; the writ against Provident International Resources, though signed by only one commissioner, survived because it predated the Rules of April 11, 1986 and no rule is given retroactive effect unless explicitly decreed; and the writs against Prime Holdings and its PTIC shares, signed after the Rules took effect by a single commissioner, were void because two signatures are the best evidence of the Commission's approval, while the amended complaint impleading the Cojuangcos three years later could not satisfy the six-month requirement of Section 26, Article XVIII. The chapter closed with Chavez v. PCGG, where the Court upheld a citizen's standing and its own venue, held that the State must disclose matters of public concern including the negotiating terms of any settlement, and voided the December 1993 General and Supplemental Agreements splitting $356 million in Swiss deposits: the PCGG could not grant criminal immunity to principal defendants, could not grant tax exemptions vested in Congress, could not promise the dismissal of pending cases, and could not waive future claims -- a waiver the Court called a dangerous precedent effectively ensconcing the Marcoses beyond the reach of the law.

superpower remained.", "He described the shift in attention from government control to deregulation, from government ownership to privatization, and from national sovereignty to globalization and petitioned the Supreme Court to challenge the constitutionality of Philippine adherence, and listed the five main issues.", "On jurisdiction the Decision held that where a legislative act is seriously alleged to have infringed the Constitution it becomes the duty of the judiciary to settle the dispute, certiorari, prohibition and mandamus being appropriate remedies for constitutional issues.", "It stressed at the same time that the Court would not review the wisdom of enlisting in the WTO, nor pass on trade liberalization as policy, nor rule on tariff reduction, but only determine whether the Senate gravely abused its discretion.", "On economic nationalism it held the Article II Declaration of Principles and State Policies not self-executing but merely guides, denying a cause of action for one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 10 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' recounted Tañada v. Angara, the unanimous decision CJP penned upholding Philippine membership in the World Trade Organization. He opened with a survey of the century -- the collapse of Fascism, Nazism and Stalinism, the last gasps of colonialism, the end of the Cold War and the emergence of a single superpower -- and argued that the arena for world preeminence had shifted from brute force to economic and intellectual dominance, with attention moving from government control to deregulation, from government ownership to privatization, and from national sovereignty to globalization and liberalization, all institutionalized in the WTO the Ramos government joined to widen market access for Philippine exports. Days after the Senate concurred through Resolution No. 97, Senators Tañada and Coseteng, Representatives Andolana and Arroyo and others challenged the adherence, raising five issues. The Court held that it had jurisdiction, since a legislative act seriously alleged to infringe the Constitution makes it the judiciary's duty to settle the dispute, while stressing that it would not review the wisdom of joining or the merits of trade liberalization. It held that the Article II Declaration of Principles is not self-executing and creates no cause of action, that the Constitution favors Filipino goods and labor yet permits exchange on the bases of equality and reciprocity and never intended an isolationist policy, and that charters must be interpreted to cover future and unknown circumstances, as the 1935 Constitution's silence on the United Nations showed. It held that treaty obligations do not impair legislative power, since sovereignty is restricted by membership in the family of nations and by pacta sunt servanda; that the TRIPS presumption shifts only the burden of evidence; and that concurrence in the WTO Agreement alone conformed exactly to what the one-page Final Act required. Its Epilogue found no patent and gross arbitrariness in the Senate's overwhelming consent, warned that striking it down on policy grounds would itself be grave abuse, and left the choice to the people through their elected officers.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 11 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' gathered the labor rulings Artemio V. Panganiban wrote in his first three years on the Supreme Court (October 10, 1995 to October 10, 1998), all unanimously supported, as his answer to how a judge finds the right balance between labor and management -- a search he called contentious even though the Constitution guarantees full protection to labor and, in case of doubt, the law favors labor. In San Pedro Hospital v. Secretary of Labor he held a six-month suspension of operations invalid because the hospital's unexplained failure to submit financial statements left its claimed crisis unproven, and upheld the labor secretary's power to order a new CBA with a union security clause and to grant back wages without first ruling on the strike's legality. In North Davao Mining v. APT he denied separation benefits to workers of a company killed by over P20 billion in losses, distinguishing BISSI on the ground that when a business dies its cashflow 'literally dries up' and 'one cannot squeeze blood out of a dry stone.' Philippines Today treated Felix Alegre's abrasive memorandum to the Star's chairman, read with his clearing of his desk and his acceptance of a senator's job, as voluntary resignation, its Epilogue insisting that 'General principles do not decide specific cases' and that each case 'has its own flesh and blood.' Naguiat awarded regular separation pay to Clark taxi drivers displaced by the bases phase-out and held the actively managing owner solidarily liable for the corporate tort; Caurdanetaan applied the 'four fold' test to declare cargadores regular employees and refused the NLRC's remand, invoking the duty to leave 'no root or branch to bear the seeds of future litigation'; Somerville rejected a lone year's financial statement as proof of retrenchment-justifying losses; and Pascua awarded moral damages and attorney's fees for dismissals marked by precipitate dispatch and utter disregard of due process.

primary_topics: ["Chapter 17 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' -- CJP's account of Serrano v. NLRC, promulgated January 27, 2000, in which the en banc Court, through Justice Mendoza, held that an employer's failure to give the required notice before a dismissal for an authorized cause is not a denial of due process but merely makes the termination 'ineffectual,' with back wages and no reinstatement, over the Dissents of Justice Puno and himself.", "The background he supplies from his own earlier book: how the Court for ten years granted only an indemnity of P1,000 to P10,000 where just or authorized cause existed but due process was ignored, and how he had rankled at that cavalier treatment in MGG Marine Services, Better Buildings and Del Val and hoped the Court en banc would one day review the proper sanction.", "The majority's three reasons, quoted at length -- that the Due Process Clause limits governmental and not private power, that notice under Article 283 is not an adversary proceeding but a chance to prepare for job loss and to let DOLE verify the economic cause, and that the requirement descends from the mesada of the 1882 Spanish Code of Commerce and the Termination Pay Law rather than from the Constitution -- plus the analogy to notarial rescission under Articles 1592 and 1191 of the Civil Code.", "CJP's Dissent in three theses: the notice requirement rests on the Constitution and not merely the Labor Code; a dismissal without due process is illegal, so the remedy is reinstatement plus full back wages and a return to the status quo ante; and even the Labor Code, in Article 277(b), grants not only notice but 'ample opportunity to be heard,' with a single exception where due process would be impractical or futile.", "Justice Puno's Dissent, reproduced at length, from the rule of audi alteram partem through his four numbered objections to his closing plea that 'to many employees, dismissal is their lethal injection.'", "The separate positions of Justices Bellosillo ('disturbance compensation' of P10,000) and Vitug (unpaid wages, proportionate 13th month pay and P10,000 nominal damages), and CJP's Epilogue that the majority bought labor a larger monetary award at the price of a vital right, an issue he expects to be debated again."]
sub_topics: ["The frame: in Serrano the Court answered in the negative the question whether workers are entitled to due process prior to dismissal, over the separate Dissents of Justice Puno and CJP himself.", "The prior law: an employer had to prove both just or authorized cause and due process; dismissals without cause were illegal and drew reinstatement with back wages, but where cause was proven and due process ignored the employee got only an indemnity or nominal damages of P1,000 to P10,000.", "CJP recalls Chapter VIII of 'Battles in the Supreme Court' -- 'Battles Over the Rights of Labor' -- where in MGG Marine Services, Better Buildings and Del Val he rankled at the Court's cavalier treatment of due process and hoped for an en banc review of the proper sanction.", "The facts: Isetann Department Store phased out its entire Security Section as a cost-cutting measure and engaged an outside agency; Ruben Serrano, head of the Security Checkers Section, was terminated on October 11, 1991, the very day he received the notice.", "The majority's holding: the lay-off was for redundancy, an authorized cause under Article 283, so separation pay of one month per year of service was due, management being entitled to determine what units are essential and whether work should be contracted out; the same-day notice denied him written notice, making the termination merely 'ineffectual' and compensable by back wages, not reinstatement.", "Majority reason one: the Due Process Clause limits governmental power and does not apply to the exercise of private power, since only the State can take life, liberty or property.", "Majority reason two: notice and hearing are required before organized society's powers are brought to bear; an Article 283 lay-off involves no charge and no adversary system, the 30-day notice serving to let the employee prepare for job loss and DOLE determine whether economic causes exist, while the time for notice and hearing under Article 282 is the trial stage before the NLRC.", "Majority reason three and the history: the notice requirement traces to Article 302 of the Spanish Code of Commerce of 1882 and the mesada, through Article 2270 of the Civil Code, RA 1052 and RA 1787, to the 1981 implementing rules of BP 130 and the 1989 amendment of Article 277(b) by RA 6715 -- so the earlier regime cannot be said to have denied due process; and an employer cannot be an entirely impartial judge of his own cause.", "The Justinian analogy: not all notice requirements are due process requirements, some being applications of the precept to act with justice and observe honesty and good faith, whose breach makes a party liable in damages rather than voiding his act -- as with notarial rescission under Articles 1592 and 1191 of the Civil Code.", "CJP's Dissent opens with gratitude that the Court reexamined the ten-year doctrine and raised the award from a nominal indemnity to full back wages, before taking issue with the majority's legal basis.", "His first thesis: the notice requirement finds basis not only in the Labor Code but, more importantly, in the due process clause of the Constitution, whose provisions are deemed written into every statute, contract and undertaking, employment being a property right.", "His second thesis, supported by a long line of authority: where procedural due process is violated the proceedings are voided and the parties returned to the status quo ante -- Pepsi-Cola Bottling ('void and nonexistent'), People v. Bocar on courts being ousted of jurisdiction, Bacus v. Ople and Ang Tibay, PNB v. Apalisok, Fabella v. Court of Appeals reinstating schoolteachers, the bail cases, People v. Sevilleno on searching inquiry, People v. Parazo on a deaf-mute retardate denied a sign language expert, and a Comelec nickname resolution set aside for want of notice and hearing.", "His third thesis: it is inaccurate to say the Labor Code grants notice alone, since Article 277(b) subjects termination to security of tenure and requires the employer to furnish a written statement of causes and to afford 'ample opportunity to be heard' -- a requirement he reads as applying to Articles 282, 283 and 284 alike.", "He presses the internal contradiction: 'ineffectual' means having no legal force, so a dismissal with no legal effect should produce reinstatement plus full back wages, and limiting the consequence to back wages has no statutory basis.", "The exception he preserves: where the employer can prove that compliance was impossible, impractical or gravely adverse -- as in Wenphil, where the employee was caught virtually in flagrante delicto after brandishing an ice scooper and shouting profanities -- the dismissal is not illegal, though a nominal sum may be given as a measure of compassion under Article 2221 of the Civil Code.", "His critique of Wenphil's afterlife: it was applied perfunctorily to cases with no exigency at all, including Serrano's own same-day dismissal, so that 'Indemnity or damages has become an easy substitute for due process.'", "His constitutional argument for private due process: traditional doctrine confined constitutional rights to claims against the State because only the State could violate them, but with liberalization, deregulation and privatization corporate behemoths and individuals may now abuse human rights, so the doctrine must be modified.", "His moral close: due process begins with the employer, not the labor tribunals; the administration of justice begins with each of us in everyday dealings; and denial of due process is no less than a denial of justice itself.", "Justice Puno's Dissent: audi alteram partem as the essence of procedural due process; the Wenphil-bred 'dismiss now, pay later' strategy; the pre-dismissal notice as the linchpin of an employee's defense; the greater need for scrutiny in Article 283 cases where the facts lie with the employer and DOLE is the equalizer; the Constitution's placement of labor rights in Article XIII; Kingsize Manufacturing and Batangas Laguna Tayabas Bus as proof of long-adopted private due process; the rejection of the vendor-vendee analogy because labor is 'neither a chattel nor a commodity'; and his plea that 'to many employees, dismissal is their lethal injection.'", "The other opinions: Justice Bellosillo would sustain the termination as valid but irregular and give P10,000 as 'disturbance compensation'; Justice Vitug would award unpaid wages, proportionate 13th month pay and P10,000 in nominal damages.", "The Epilogue: the majority gave labor a larger monetary award -- from indemnity to full back wages -- but deprived the working force of a vital right, a shift so fundamental that CJP predicts he and Justice Puno, and perhaps others, will see the issue debated again."]

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 17 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' recounted Serrano v. NLRC, promulgated January 27, 2000 after more than a year of internal debate, in which the en banc Court answered in the negative the question whether workers are entitled to due process before dismissal. Isetann Department Store had phased out its Security Section and terminated Ruben Serrano on the very day he received notice; Justice Mendoza, for the majority, held the lay-off a valid redundancy under Article 283, awarded separation pay, and characterized the defective notice as making the termination merely 'ineffectual,' compensable by full back wages rather than reinstatement. His reasons were that the Due Process Clause limits governmental and not private power, that an Article 283 notice serves to let the worker prepare and DOLE verify the economic cause rather than to answer a charge, that the requirement descends from the mesada of the 1882 Spanish Code of Commerce and the Termination Pay Law, and that failure to give it is like failing to make a notarial demand before rescinding a sale. Artemio V. Panganiban dissented, first thanking the Court for reexamining a ten-year doctrine under which he had long rankled at indemnities of P1,000 to P10,000, then arguing three theses: the notice requirement rests on the Constitution and not merely the Labor Code, since employment is a property right and constitutional provisions are written into every statute; a violation of procedural due process voids the proceeding and restores the status quo ante, as a long line of labor, administrative, criminal and election cases showed, so the remedy is reinstatement plus full back wages; and Article 277(b) itself grants ample opportunity to be heard. He preserved one exception, for cases like Wenphil where compliance was impractical or the employee was caught in flagrante delicto, and warned that indemnity had become an easy substitute for due process, letting the rich purchase a constitutional right granted to the poor. He reproduced Justice Puno's dissent at length and closed with his own creed -- due process begins with the employer, the administration of justice begins with each of us, and denial of due process is a denial of justice itself -- noting in the Epilogue that the majority had bought labor money at the price of a vital right.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 22 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' explains how the Supreme Court divides its work and then recounts CJP's dissent from an 8-7 en banc takeover of a case already decided by a Division. He first sets out the structure: Article VIII, Section 4 permits the Court to sit en banc or in divisions, and the Court then sat as a Banc of fifteen and three Divisions of five, whose judgments are coequal, so that some people say there are really four Supreme Courts. About 85 to 90 percent of decisions come from the Divisions. Referral to the Banc is governed by the constitutional enumeration and by Circular 2-89 as amended in 1993, whose Item 8 allows three members of a Division to seek referral. In Firestone Ceramics v. Court of Appeals and its companion Republic case, the Third Division unanimously ruled for private respondents on September 2, 1999 in a ponencia by Justice Gonzaga-Reyes and then refused referral 4-1, with Justice Purisima alone dissenting. At his instance the Banc, on June 28, 2000, took the cases over anyway, invoking paragraph 9 of the Circular, the land's 99-hectare size and the cases' sufficient importance. Justice Reyes dissented on five grounds, including that the Banc is not an appellate court and that the pending Motion for Reconsideration belonged to her Division; Justice Puno urged deferral. CJP argued that the majority gave no cogent or compelling reason and merely pontificated. What disturbed him most was the contrast with the Sumilao farmers' case, where a genuine 2-2 deadlock had not persuaded the Banc to intervene, with only he and Justice Vitug supporting Justice Melo's proposal. He demanded consistency: take both cases or neither, for sauce for the poor goose should be the same sauce for the rich gander. A postscript notes that the Resolution contravened the unanimous AM No. 99-8-06-SC of February 15, 2000, which assigned motions for reconsideration to the deciding Division.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 17 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' presented Republic v. Cocofed, which CJP identified as one of the most important decisions of his seventh year on the Court and which he 'had the honor of writing.' The ruling held that the controlling sequestered shares in the United Coconut Planters Bank should be voted by the government, because they had been bought with coconut levy funds exacted from more than a million farmers during the Marcos regime -- funds the Court declared 'not only affected with public interest' but 'in fact, prima facie public funds.' Rather than restate the case himself, CJP reprinted with permission the Kilosbayan summation written by former Senate President Jovito R. Salonga, the first PCGG chair, who had sequestered the shares. Salonga defined prima facie for lay readers, recounted the PCGG's 1986 recovery mission and his own Los Angeles meeting with Eduardo Cojuangco, and traced fifteen years of litigation from the 1987 reconveyance suit through the 1990 lifting of sequestration, the 1993 resolution, the 1995 Narvasa decision, and the 2001 demand for a stockholders' meeting that produced the assailed Sandiganbayan order. He then laid out the reasoning step by step: registered owners normally vote, the PCGG is a mere conservator, sequestered shares alleged to be ill-gotten are tested by the two-tiered test of prima facie ill-gotten character and imminent dissipation, but shares shown to be originally governmental or bought with public funds fall instead under the public character exceptions of BASECO and Cojuangco-Roxas, on the principle that 'legal fiction must yield to truth.' Since respondents' counsel had judicially admitted the shares came from the Coconut Consumers Stabilization Fund, the Court itemized six reasons the levies were public -- the police and taxing powers, the purpose of the levy, the admission, COA review, BIR treatment and the decrees themselves, with Marcos's own deletion of the words calling the fund private. The Court added a caveat limiting the ruling to the voting question and ordered the Sandiganbayan to decide the main cases within six months. Salonga then reprinted Justice Melo's dissent and Justice Vitug's partial dissent.

sub_topics: ["CJP opens by quoting the preface of his own Decision, paraphrasing Justice Oliver Wendeel Holmes Jr.: general propositions do not decide specific cases; laws are interpreted 'in the context of the peculiar factual situation of each proceeding.'", "He states the petitioner's theory -- that a rescissible contract of sale is valid until actually rescinded, so the buyer could collect rentals in the interim -- and concedes it would have been 'theoretically correct' but for the absence of delivery.", "The facts: Carmelo & Bauermann leased land and two buildings to Mayfair Theater for 20 years under contracts granting Mayfair a right of first refusal, then sold the properties to Equatorial for P11,300,000 without first offering them to Mayfair.", "The 1996 mother case (GR No. 106063) rescinded that sale and ordered Carmelo to return the price and let Mayfair buy at P11,300,000; execution stalled because Carmelo could no longer be located, so Mayfair deposited the money with the Manila Clerk of Court and stayed on the premises.", "After the leases expired, Equatorial sued to collect rentals; the trial court dismissed the claim and wrongly called the Deed of Sale 'void at its inception,' and Equatorial elevated the rental claim to the Supreme Court.", "By a vote of 10 to 5, in a ponencia CJP 'had the honor of writing,' the Court held that 'no right of ownership was transferred from Carmelo to Equatorial in view of a patent failure to deliver the property to the buyer.'", "The basic parameters of the law on sales: rent is a civil fruit belonging to the owner by right of accession; ownership is a real right acquired only upon delivery, 'not by contract alone, but by tradition or delivery' -- Non nudis pactis sed traditione dominia rerum transferantur.", "Delivery is 'a composite act, a thing in which both parties must join and the minds of both parties concur,' and both actual and constructive delivery require the vendor's absolute giving up of control and the vendee's assumption of it.", "Applied to the facts: execution of a public instrument is only a legal fiction of delivery that holds 'only when there is no impediment'; Mayfair's court action impugning the sale was 'a legally sufficient impediment,' so 'fiction yields to reality - the delivery has not been effected.'", "Article 1164 is answered by Article 1385: rescission obliges the return of the things sold 'together with their fruits, and the price with its interest,' so rentals paid would have had to be returned anyway.", "CJP confronts the awkward record -- the mother case, Justice Padilla's Separate Opinion and even his own Separate Concurring Opinion all said Equatorial received rentals -- and answers that these do not concede actual delivery.", "The explanation: Equatorial had filed two ejectment suits (Civil Case No. 121570 in 1987 and Civil Case No. 131944 in 1990) which Mayfair won; Mayfair paid rentals only to keep physical possession under the Rules of Court, 'merely to avoid imminent eviction,' not in recognition of Equatorial's title.", "The bottom line: a rescissible contract may theoretically be valid until rescinded, but that general principle 'is not decisive'; what is decisive is that ownership is acquired by tradition, and the sale 'was judicially rescinded before it could be consummated.'", "A second, independent ground -- bad faith: the mother case, final and executory, found Equatorial a buyer in bad faith whose lawyers had studied the lease contracts, so it is entitled 'solely to the return of the purchase price it paid to Carmelo; no more, no less.'", "Since the mother case had categorically denied interest, 'another fruit of ownership,' rentals cannot be granted 'without mocking this Court's en banc Decision'; if petitioner suffered loss it 'must bear it in silence,' else 'bad faith would be rewarded instead of punished.'", "The Melo concurrence: the issue was already squarely resolved in 1996; petitioner's submissions are 'deceiving'; granting the petition would reward bad faith after 23 years of deprivation and the 'fantastic and groundless' claim of P115,947,867.00 -- and Mayfair, were it a natural person, could have asked for moral damages.", "The Vitug dissent: rescissible contracts are the least infirm of defective contracts, 'valid, binding and effective until rescinded'; rescission under Article 1381 is prospective and unlike resolution under Article 1191, so ownership passed to Equatorial from July 30, 1978 until finality on March 17, 1997, and 'ownership... is never described as being either in good faith or in bad faith.'", "The Sandoval-Gutierrez dissent: the mother case ordered Equatorial to execute deeds 'to return ownership to Carmelo,' which presupposes transfer; receiving rentals is an exercise of possession through another; Mayfair as lessee held only as a mere holder and so was no impediment; and under Guzman v. Court of Appeals and Article 1658 the lessee owed rent to the new owner."]

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 19 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' recounts Panganiban's ponencia in Equatorial Realty Development v. Mayfair Theater, which he prefaced by paraphrasing Justice Oliver Wendeel Holmes Jr.: 'General propositions do not decide specific cases,' since laws are read in the peculiar factual situation of each proceeding and each case 'has its own flesh and blood.' Carmelo & Bauermann had leased land and two buildings to Mayfair for twenty years under contracts giving Mayfair a right of first refusal, then sold the properties to Equatorial for P11,300,000 without offering them to Mayfair; in the 1996 'mother case' (GR No. 106063) the Court rescinded that sale, but execution stalled because Carmelo could not be found, so Mayfair deposited the price and stayed on. When Equatorial later sued for rentals, arguing that a rescissible contract is valid until actually rescinded, the Court held by 10-5 that 'no right of ownership was transferred from Carmelo to Equatorial in view of a patent failure to deliver the property to the buyer.' Panganiban laid down the basic parameters -- rent is a civil fruit of ownership, and ownership is a real right transferred 'not by contract alone, but by tradition or delivery' -- and reasoned that execution of a public instrument is only a legal fiction of delivery that holds when no impediment exists; Mayfair's timely court objection was such an impediment, so 'fiction yields to reality.' He explained that Mayfair's rental payments, made while two ejectment suits were pending, were 'paid merely to avoid imminent eviction' and conceded nothing. As an independent ground he invoked the final finding of Equatorial's bad faith: it is entitled 'solely to the return of the purchase price... no more, no less,' and must bear its loss 'in silence,' lest 'bad faith would be rewarded instead of punished.' He then reproduced Justice Melo's concurrence, Justice Vitug's dissent on the nature of rescissible contracts, and Justice Sandoval-Gutierrez's dissent arguing that ownership and possession had in fact passed.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 20 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' sets out Panganiban's dissent in City Government of Makati v. Civil Service Commission and Eugenia Galzote, which asked whether a civil servant detained on a non-bailable charge must still file a leave application and may be dropped from the rolls if she does not. Galzote, a Makati clerk charged with kidnapping for ransom with physical injuries, was suspended from September 9, 1991, dropped from the rolls effective January 21, 1993, acquitted in September 1994, and ordered reinstated with back wages by the CSC, which the Court of Appeals sustained. Writing for a divided Court, Justice Bellosillo held that the employer's own suspension order was the equivalent of prior approval of leave, that notice sent to her house was insufficient, and that the CSC could reasonably read an 'automatic leave of absence' into its rules for events of force majeure akin to illness; Justices Kapunan and Vitug concurred. Panganiban dissented. He argued that neither the Civil Service Law (EO 292) nor the CSC Rules provides for automatic leave; Section 35 makes thirty days' absence without approved leave AWOL regardless of reason, and Section 20 makes approval contingent on the needs of the service, so it 'cannot be presumed.' Detention was no excuse, since 'there was nothing to stop her from writing' to her employer, and 'the government cannot be left in the lurch.' An application, he insisted, 'is not a mere formality; it is not a useless ceremony,' else public efficiency would 'depend on the whim of the individual employee.' Her acquittal was beside the point: 'she was dropped from the rolls because she was AWOL.' He distinguished Gonzales and his own UP v. CSC, held her void suspension excused nothing beyond ninety days, and closed on public service and the rule of law: 'No work, no pay. No application, no approval. No leave, no benefits.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 2 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' reproduced CJP's address to the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas on the Supreme Court's role in creating a favorable investment climate. After an opening joke about an investor bargaining with God over a cent, he divided his subject into the Court's powers and duties and the jurisprudence affecting investments. He described the Philippine separation of powers, defined judicial independence as the finality of the Court's decisions and their freedom from extraneous influence, called the Court the last bulwark of democracy, and noted that unlike countries with separate constitutional courts and arbitration tribunals the Philippines vests all judicial power in one tribunal. He enumerated five functions: ordinary review of appeals, extraordinary certiorari review for grave abuse of discretion in its two forms, administrative supervision of all lower courts, control of admission to and discipline of the bar, and rule-making including rules protecting the Bill of Rights. He then took up the rulings that had angered business. The first Oil Deregulation Law, voided in Tatad v. Secretary of Energy, had provoked calls to impeach the justices and to amend the Constitution, yet it was struck down precisely because it was anti-business, perpetuating the monopoly of Shell, Petron and Caltex against the constitutional mandate of free trade; Congress then passed a cleaner law and Total, Flying A and Seaoil entered the market. The voided mega contracts for NAIA Terminal III and the Manila Bay reclamation raised the sanctity-of-contract objection, which he answered with the rule that an agreement violating the Constitution or the law is not a contract at all, illustrated by analogies about a purchased gun and a stolen car. He reassured investors that trial courts are barred from restraining government infrastructure projects, disclosed his own assignment to review the foreclosure injunction rules at the Bankers Association's request, and defended preliminary injunctions as tools of justice and equity. Turning to the plagues of corruption, inefficiency and delay, he described the Action Program for Judicial Reform, the Court's disciplinary firsts and its penalties on more than 350 judges in three years, and the support of the World Bank, the ADB, the UNDP, the Asia Foundation and several foreign governments. He closed with six requests to his audience -- suggestions, reports of victimization, refusal to bribe judges, early legal advice, no dubious shortcuts, and attention to decisions like Tañada v. Angara -- and the assurance that the Court would continue to uphold the rule of law and stable jurisprudence.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 4 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' presents CJP's address to the Employers Confederation of the Philippines on why the Supreme Court had voided three mega-contracts. He opened with the courtesy call of the US-ASEAN Business Council on September 11, 2003, when visiting American investors asked what advice would safeguard their investments and he replied that justices normally do not render advisory opinions, since under the adversarial system judges are passive participants who speak through decisions tied to their peculiar facts. He read that polite question as the familiar criticism that the Court was interfering inordinately in economic matters, and took up the AMARI, PIATCO and MEGA PACIFIC Decisions, setting aside the Western Mining case as sub judice because he had written the main dissent. His premise was that the Constitution gives the judiciary the duty, not merely the power, to strike down any act tainted with grave abuse of discretion, defined as action contrary to the Constitution, the law or jurisprudence or done whimsically, capriciously or arbitrarily. In AMARI, a unanimous Court through Justice Carpio held that reclaimed public land could be leased but not sold to a private corporation and submerged areas were inalienable, later finding a P140.16 billion price gap and calling the deal the grandmother of all scams. In PIATCO, written by Justice Puno, the Court found five defects, among them an award to a financially unqualified bidder, an amended agreement that destroyed the fair competition essence of bidding, prohibited government guarantees, and an exclusive Luzon terminal amounting to a monopoly. In MEGA PACIFIC, which he wrote, the contract went to an entity that had not bid, the machines flunked the DOST accuracy and audit-trail tests, the software could not prevent repeated downloads, and Comelec admitted testing only a demo version. He concluded that the Court had upheld the rule of law and the leveling of the playing field, advancing business in general even where particular contractors lost.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 5 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' collects CJP's keynote address on how Supreme Court Decisions protect consumers, delivered after his compañero, former Comelec Commissioner Chino Marquinez, insisted the Court should explain its economic rulings from the consumer's side. He began with three phenomena that changed social behavior in the twentieth century -- the automobile, television and the personal computer -- and observed that through all of them the consumer had remained at the center, quoting Lyndon Johnson and John Kennedy's 1962 message that consumers include us all yet are the only important economic group not effectively organized. He then diagnosed four Filipino vulnerabilities: the hold of caveat emptor, the habit of buying the cheaper unwarranted good and absorbing the loss, the cultural restraints of pakikisama and pakikipagkapwa that delay legal action until a merchant is judged walang kapwa-tao, and ignorance of remedies coupled with the cost of suing, all aggravated by standardized contracts dictated by the stronger party. Against that background he surveyed the Court's consumer jurisprudence: Tañada v. Angara holding that the Constitution favors consumers rather than industries; Tatad v. Secretary of Energy striking down the oil deregulation law because the statute as cobbled by Congress offended the Constitution; Republic v. Meralco excluding income tax from operating expenses and ordering refunds; Freedom from Debt Coalition v. ERC voiding a provisional rate increase for want of publication and consultation; Quisumbing and Macrotextile on disconnection and utility delay; the credit-card cases of Olalia, Ermitaño and Mandarin Villa; DBP and Segovia on reducing iniquitous interest; and New Sampaguita Builders, which he wrote, giving teeth to the Truth in Lending Act by voiding undisclosed and unilaterally adjustable charges. He closed with sales-warranty and airline cases, including China Airlines v. Chiok, and the thesis that caveat emptor no longer strictly applies and that the seller must equally beware.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 8 of 'Judicial Renaissance' reproduces the keynote address Justice Panganiban delivered at an Asian Development Bank symposium on judicial reforms, on the theme of enhancing the effectiveness and accountability of the judiciary. He began by recalling the 9th Conference of Chief Justices in Christchurch in October 2001, where UN and World Bank speakers praised the Philippine Supreme Court, and listed the endorsements that followed: the World Bank posting the Action Program for Judicial Reform on its website as a model, assistance from USAID, CIDA and AusAID, advanced negotiations for a Japanese grant to build the Philippine Judicial Academy complex in Tagaytay, a 2.3-million-euro European Union grant for Access to Justice for the Poor, and ADB TA No. 3693-PHI on strengthening independence and defining accountability. He described the highest court of the past as a fortress, a Mount Olympus whose gods were unapproachable, and argued that transparency requirements of the Constitution, the Ethical Standards Law and the judicial conduct codes, together with the information revolution and a persistent media, had partly opened its doors -- a development he accepted, since people no longer accept doctrines they do not understand. Answering ADB General Counsel Arthur M. Mitchell's invitation to show how an accountable judiciary reduces poverty, he made a three-tier case: the 1987 Constitution is pro-poor, pro-labor and pro-human rights and guarantees legal assistance that shall not be denied by reason of poverty; Congress has passed implementing laws on arrest rights, domestic violence, child protection, barangay dispute settlement, housing, agriculture and labor; and the Court itself exempts indigents from fees, grants free counsel, works with the IBP and FLAG, and authorized the Shari'ah Appellate Court. He cited his own ponencia in Ang Bagong Bayani reserving the party-list system for the marginalized, the labor line running from Calalang v. Williams through eight settled doctrines, human-rights safeguards in criminal procedure, and strict death-penalty review culminating in People v. Mateo, noting his own opinion that the death penalty was unconstitutional. Conceding criticism from businessmen and a foreign diplomat, he insisted the social justice orientation must remain, lest the marginalized take the law into their own hands, and closed by quoting his book 'Leveling the Playing Field' on the Court safeguarding not only food but also freedom.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 14 of 'Judicial Renaissance' reproduces Justice Panganiban's address to an international gathering of mining investors, delivered weeks after the Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of the Mining Law. He began with a primer on the Philippine system: a republican, presidential government whose three branches are coequal and coindependent, coordinating and checking one another, and a judiciary constitutionally bound to nullify any act done with grave abuse of discretion -- a duty, he stressed, not merely a power, since a power can be relinquished but a duty cannot be evaded. He assured his audience that despite this authority the Court is not superior to the political branches, upholds their acts in case of doubt, and offers investors a final, independent recourse when their rights are trampled, adding practical advice to follow the rules honestly, hire credible counsel before contracting and avoid bribery. Turning to La Bugal-B'laan Tribal Association v. Ramos, which had become final on February 1, 2005 when the Motion for Reconsideration was denied 10-4 with one abstention, he outlined ten features of the ruling: FTAAs may be entered only by the President and only with corporations; they cover only minerals, petroleum and other mineral oils; EDU remains under the State's full control and supervision, exercised through the President and the DENR secretary as alter ego; FTAAs must conform to RA 7942 and its rules; foreign-owned companies bear all the risk and may be granted reasonable managerial and marketing prerogatives while the State retains board-like residual control; the President may set the fiscal regime; and the Court will not inordinately interfere absent grave abuse. He explained that the entire Court agreed FTAAs were permissible and that the dispute concerned executive discretion over the government's share, rejecting the four dissenters' demand for a 60 percent minimum because no constitutional provision empowered the Court to fix it, and quoting the ruling that the Constitution should be read in broad, life-giving strokes. He then addressed the petitioners' OXFAM and World Bank evidence on mining-dependent communities and environmental degradation with the Court's answer that priority for mining is a policy question for the President and Congress, while noting the residual controls, the mandated distribution of benefits among national, provincial, municipal and barangay levels, and the exhortation to prevent irreversible ecological damage. He closed by citing the Decision's record 246 pages, its call for an appropriate balancing of interests and needs, and his own plea that investors help develop not just the mining industry but the whole country and its people's prosperity.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 15 of 'Judicial Renaissance' is Justice Panganiban's technical summary of La Bugal-B'laan Tribal Association v. Ramos, the companion to the preceding chapter's lay account. He traced the facts from President Aquino's Executive Order 279, through President Ramos's approval of RA 7942 and DENR Administrative Order 96-40, to the 1995 FTAA with Western Mining Corporation Philippines covering 99,387 hectares and the 1997 Petition alleging that fully foreign-owned corporations were being allowed to exploit minerals contrary to Section 2 of Article XII. He then set out the original Decision of January 27, 2004, which read the constitutional history from the Regalian doctrine through the concession and service-contract systems, held that FTAAs were confined to technical or financial assistance and could not extend to foreign management -- 'precisely the evil' the framers sought to eradicate -- and struck down the Section 3(aq) proviso, Sections 23, 33 to 41, 56, parts of Section 81 and Section 90, along with the WMCP FTAA for conveying beneficial ownership. He reproduced Justice Vitug's Separate Opinion and his own Dissent, in which he urged dismissal for mootness after WMC's shares and the FTAA passed to Filipino-owned Sagittarius, argued that 'involving' signified inclusion rather than exclusion, observed that the Constitutional Commission had used 'service contracts' and 'technical or financial assistance' interchangeably, and proposed an oral argument on international lending practices lest the Court make the country an economic isolationist. The reversing Resolution, which he penned, rested on the non-interference doctrine, held the case moot yet resolved it for paramount public interest, stratified Section 2 into five propositions, applied a reality check to the implausibility of State-run large-scale mining, and redefined full control and supervision as macro-level control less than dictatorial but sufficient to direct, restrain, regulate and govern the enterprises. It upheld foreign-held exploration permits, found no conveyance of beneficial ownership, excised Sections 7.9 and 7.8(e) of the WMCP FTAA as separable, and compared FTAAs favorably with co-production, joint venture and production-sharing agreements. He refuted the Morales Dissent's either-or construction and its timber-license analogy as a well-nigh confiscatory stance, defended the DENR secretary's authority against the Carpio Dissent, and quoted the Epilogue's insistence on unanimity over full State control and on justice for present and future Filipinos. He closed with the Carpio, Morales, Tinga and Nazario opinions and the denial with finality of the second Motion for Reconsideration.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 16 of 'Judicial Renaissance' reports Abakada Guro Partylist v. Ermita, in which the Supreme Court, through a Decision penned by Justice Ma. Alicia Austria-Martinez, dismissed all five Petitions and upheld RA 9337, the Expanded Value-Added Tax Law, as constitutional in its entirety, while unanimously holding former Finance Secretary Cesar V. Purisima in indirect contempt and fining him P20,000 for statements that placed the Court into dishonor, disrepute and discredit. Justice Panganiban narrated the passage of the three bills, the Bicameral Conference Committee that reconciled them, the signing of the enrolled bill on May 24, 2005 and the TRO issued on July 1, the law's effectivity date. The petitioners attacked the standby authority in Sections 4, 5 and 6 allowing the President, on the finance secretary's recommendation, to raise the rate to 12 percent once VAT collections or the deficit crossed the specified fractions of GDP; the 70 percent cap on creditable input tax, the 60-month amortization and the 5 percent withholding VAT; and the BCC's deletion of the no-pass-on provisions and insertion of Senate-only sections contrary to exclusive origination. The Court refused to go behind the enrolled bill, reiterated Tolentino on the no-amendment and origination rules, applied the completeness-and-standard test to find only a delegation of fact-ascertainment, held that entitlement to input tax credit is a statutory privilege carrying no vested right, and ruled the law uniform, equitable and unaffected by the progressivity principle, which it said has no relation to VAT. Chief Justice Davide, and Justices Puno, Ynares-Santiago, Sandoval-Gutierrez, Callejo, Azcuna and Tinga wrote separately, variously arguing that the BCC cannot act as a third house of Congress, that the germaneness test is overbroad, that the no-pass-on deletion was invalid, and that the input-tax cap would exterminate small and medium enterprises. In his own Separate Opinion, Panganiban voted to void Sections 1, 2 and 3 as not germane to the House bills, treated the enrolled bill doctrine as non-absolute, accepted the standby authority as a complete delegation making the President's role administrative rather than legislative, disagreed with the majority's view of the finance secretary as an agent of Congress by insisting the secretary remains the President's alter ego, and concluded that the law's economic advantages and long-term effects lie beyond the reach of judicial review.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 17 of 'Judicial Renaissance' reports Southern Cross Cement Corporation v. Philippine Cement Manufacturers Corporation, which clarified Republic Act 8800, the Safeguard Measures Act. Justice Panganiban traced the dispute from Philcemcor's 2001 application for a definitive safeguard measure on gray Portland cement, through the DTI's provisional P20.60 duty, to the Tariff Commission's March 2002 report finding no serious injury; DTI Secretary Manuel Roxas II disagreed with that finding but, relying on a DOJ Opinion that Section 13 barred his review, denied the application, whereupon Philcemcor obtained a Court of Appeals decision setting aside his ruling, the secretary imposed the duty anyway in June 2003, and Southern Cross pursued parallel remedies before the Supreme Court and the Court of Tax Appeals. The Second Division found no proven forum shopping and held that the CTA, not the CA, had jurisdiction, because certiorari lies only absent a plain, speedy and adequate remedy, Section 29 of the SMA supplies one, split jurisdiction is abhorred, and the phrase 'in connection with the imposition of a safeguard measure' reaches a negative ruling as well; the CA Decision was therefore an absolute nullity and the DTI Decision drawn from it void, since the spring cannot rise higher than its source. On the merits the Court held that a positive final determination by the Tariff Commission is a condition precedent to imposition, though the secretary may still decline in the public interest and is never bound to adopt the Commission's recommendations, and it described the scheme as a check and balance between agencies of disparate specializations. The en banc upheld the Decision in toto on August 2, 2005 by an 8-5-2 vote. Panganiban concurred on jurisdiction but dissented on the merits, arguing that the taxing power may be delegated only to the President, that the alter ego principle is the sole constitutional basis for the secretary's power, that the President's control over the Executive Department cannot be curtailed by Congress, that the Commission's determination is not among the Section 5 conditions, that public interest is indubitably a political question for an official answerable to the people, and that the implementing rules, the Commission's own order and its chairman's statements confirm that its role is merely fact-finding and recommendatory. He added that binding the secretary to a negative determination while letting him reject a positive one was apparently illogical, that his decision should be appealable to the President, and that courts should adopt a hands-off approach to policy, intervening only for blatant illegality or grave abuse of discretion.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 19 of 'Judicial Renaissance' recounts Agabon v. NLRC, promulgated November 14, 2004 during Panganiban's tenth year on the Court, in which an 8-to-6 majority abandoned Serrano v. NLRC and reverted to the Wenphil doctrine. Riviera Home Improvements had hired Virgilio and Jenny Agabon in January 1992 as cornice and gypsum board installers and dismissed them in February 1999 without any termination notice for abandoning work; the labor arbiter ruled for them, but the NLRC found abandonment and the Court of Appeals agreed. Writing for the majority, Mme. Justice Consuelo Ynares-Santiago held there was a just cause but that the employer had breached the twin-notice requirement of the Omnibus Rules, and so owed each petitioner nominal damages of P30,000. Panganiban traces the doctrinal line: before 1989 a dismissal without notice was illegal; Wenphil made it valid with a P1,000 indemnity; Serrano in 2000 made it ineffectual and required full back wages to deter employers wont to 'dismiss now and pay later'; Agabon returned to indemnity, stiffened, reasoning that under Article 279 a termination is illegal only if it is not for a just or authorized cause. He dissented, calling the ruling an 'inexplicable turnaround' that set back labor's rights and diminished respect for due process, and restated the position he had taken in Serrano: illegal dismissal results not only from the absence of a just or authorized cause but also from the failure to observe due process, so the sanction is full back wages plus reinstatement and a return to the status quo ante, the only exception being a Wenphil-like case where observing the procedure was impractical and futile, where compassion may supply a nominal sum under Article 2221 of the Civil Code. He reports Justice Puno's dissent grounding notice in constitutional social justice and security of tenure, and Justice Tinga's concurrence treating the breach as merely statutory and relocating the remedy in the Civil Code, with four proposed standards for nominal, actual, temperate and moral or exemplary damages.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 9 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' reproduced Chief Justice Panganiban's lecture to the Asian Institute of Management Policy Center's 51st Globalization Lecture Series, an invitation he said he could not decline because of his wife Leni's 32-year stint on the AIM faculty. It was, he noted, the first time he had been asked to correlate his judicial philosophy with civil society's role in economic development, and he divided the lecture into a disquisition on Liberty and Prosperity, civil society's stake in it, and the specific ways it could contribute. He restated the vow he made on December 21, 2005 -- a judiciary of four Ins, impervious to the plague of 'ships,' battling the four ACID problems -- and the Supreme Court's supervision of the bar, 'the vineyard from which our judges take root,' with both directed to safeguarding liberty and nurturing prosperity. Observing that lawyers' mastery of civil liberties has not been matched by attention to prosperity, he cited the Constitution's prosperity mandates and quoted his own book Leveling the Playing Field, and argued that the redefinition of poverty as a deprivation of essential assets elevates the right to prosperity to a universal human right. Turning to civil society, he traced its long Philippine tradition, credited it with People Power and with services, organizing and training beyond politics, and called it a pillar of democracy that precedes the judiciary as vanguard of freedoms -- while insisting its participation is bounded by the same Constitution that sustains it, since anarchy destroys both liberty and prosperity. He reported a round-table with Professor William Easterly and Philippine economic officials that found no single formula for growth, yet maintained that Martial Law had proved authoritarianism barren and that Filipinos would not trade freedom for food. He surveyed the reorientation of UNDP, World Bank, ADB, Asia Foundation and USAID programs toward access to justice and anti-corruption, cited Cardoso's panel on participatory democracy, and closed by naming three roles for civil society: initiating cases, pushing legal empowerment of the poor, and advocating collective solutions to poverty.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 15 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' reproduces Chief Justice Panganiban's address on the judiciary and the economy, delivered to an audience that included delegates to the 6th Mining Conference. He began with the constitutional setting: a charter crafted after the bloodless 1986 People Power Revolution, a republican and presidential government whose powers are shared among Congress, the President and a single, unitary Supreme Court, with the branches coordinating and checking one another. He stressed the courts' express mandate to nullify any act of any branch or official done with grave abuse of discretion -- a duty written in after the Martial Law years to make the courts 'activists' capable of checking the political branches -- and argued that a well-functioning judiciary is indispensable to a sound business climate because investor confidence is tied to a stable and predictable justice system. He then answered three recurring business complaints. To the charge of undue interference he replied that commercial transactions have been litigated for more than a century and now include patents, copyright, genetically modified organisms and cloning, and asked who else would decide such questions or protect the public from economic tyrannies; citing his book 'Leveling the Playing Field,' he maintained that the Court is 'a friend rather than a foe of legitimate business' and that nullifications of contracts are exceptions. To the charge of reviewing the wisdom of other branches he answered no, quoting the Mining Act of 1995 ruling that the Court 'refrains from delving into matters of policy,' and noted the same laissez-faire posture toward purely private contracts. On public contracts he said the Court is extra vigilant where public funds or corruption are involved, because a power can be relinquished but a duty cannot be evaded, while insisting that nullification asserts the rule of law rather than judicial supremacy. He advised investors to obey the law, hire ethical counsel before contracting, and avoid bribery under RA 9160, then explained FTAAs, CPAs, JVAs, MPSAs and exploration permits, the reservation of small-scale mining to Filipinos, and the State's full control and supervision. Quoting World Bank counsel Anthony Gerald Toft, he closed on a judiciary that espouses justice and jobs, freedom and food, integrity and investments.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 26 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests Abacus v. Ampil, in which the Court divided the loss between a stock market investor and his broker. The petitioner, a broker and dealer of securities at the Philippine Stock Exchange Center, opened a cash account for the respondent on April 8, 1997; he began trading on April 10 and by the end of the month owed P6,617,036.22. After he failed to settle within the required period and an extension, the broker sold his securities on May 6, 1997, leaving him still owing P3,364,313.56. The trial court and the Court of Appeals held both parties in pari delicto and without recourse against each other, because the broker had violated Sections 23 and 25 of the Revised Securities Act and Rule 25-1 by failing to require payment within three or four days of trading and to seek an extension. The Court agreed that the so-called mandatory close-out rule imposed an obligation and not merely a right -- to cancel or liquidate an unpaid order and thereafter to require cash deposits before executing further purchases, so that no undue credit would be extended to a cash customer -- but held that those margin requirements bore only on the trades made after the initial purchases of April 10 and 11, 1997. Those first transactions were valid when made, so the broker could still collect on them under the general law on obligations and contracts; the margin rules existed to protect the general economy, not to give the customer a free ride at the broker's expense. For the later trades the broker had unclean hands, having effectively converted a cash account into a credit account, but the investor was equally guilty: the Court rejected his claim to be an innocent victim, found that he had knowingly speculated by asking for extensions and withholding sell orders, and denied his counterclaim. His remaining obligation was to be computed from the closing prices at T+14. On the second issue the Court held that the suit was an ordinary civil case to enforce the parties' Agreement, and that deciding it did not deprive the SEC of its authority to punish willful violations.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 27 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests Didipio v. Gozun, a reprise of the mining-law controversy, in which the Court through Justice Minita V. Chico-Nazario brushed aside the procedural objections and answered all the substantive questions in the negative. On June 20, 1994, before the Philippine Mining Act of 1995 was passed, President Fidel V. Ramos executed a Financial and Technical Assistance Agreement with Arimco Mining Corporation covering some 37,000 hectares in Nueva Vizcaya and Quirino, including Barangay Didipio in Kasibu; Arimco later consolidated with Climax Mining Limited into a company 99 percent of whose controlling stockholders were Australian nationals. After a demand letter to the DENR secretary was referred to and rejected by the Mines and Geosciences Bureau panel of arbitrators, residents petitioned for prohibition and mandamus to have Republic Act 7942 and DAO 96-40 declared unconstitutional and the FTAA cancelled. The Court held the controversy ripe, since the law had been enacted, the order approved and agreements entered into, with petitioners in danger of being ousted from their landholdings; actual eviction did not have to happen before it would intervene, and their standing was likewise affirmed. On the merits it held that Section 76 was a taking provision, the eminent domain authority of qualified operators under PD 512 being deemed incorporated in it, but that the taking was valid because the mining industry was pivotal to economic development and yielded public benefit, and because just compensation was provided for. The claim that the agreement contractually reduced the State's discretion was rejected, the FTAA merely facilitating the government's voluntary acquisition of surface areas for a contractor disqualified from owning land. The Mining Act did not encroach on the courts' power over just compensation, since an arbitral determination is only preliminary unless accepted by all parties. Citing La Bugal-B'laan, the Court held that the State retained more than sufficient control over mining operations, that 'agreements involving either technical or financial assistance' were not limited to mere assistance, and that service contracts were not eradicated by the 1987 Constitution but continue under full State control with safety measures against past abuses.

being a public utility, it was organized to operate the Manila airports for public use.", "MIAA was instead a government instrumentality vested with corporate powers, able to exercise eminent domain, police authority and the levying of fees and charges, and thus fell under Section 133(o) of the Local Government Code, which bars local taxes, fees or charges of any kind on the National Government, its agencies and instrumentalities.", "The Court restated the canons of taxation at work: a tax is never presumed, the law imposing it must be expressed in clear language, doubt about taxability is resolved against taxation, exemptions are strictly construed against the taxpayer but an exemption granted by Congress to a national government instrumentality is construed liberally in its favor.", "There was no reason for local governments to tax national instrumentalities rendering essential public services, the only exception being where the legislature clearly intended it for sound and compelling policy considerations, in language that must be explicit.", "The airport land and buildings were properties of public dominion under Article 420 of the Civil Code, the term 'ports' covering airports as well as seaports, and they were devoted to public use for international and domestic travel; one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 28 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests Manila International Airport Authority v. City of Parañaque, in which the Court through Justice Antonio T. Carpio held the real properties of MIAA exempt from local real estate tax. Created under Executive Order 903 to operate the NAIA Complex, MIAA had received from the city Final Notices of Real Estate Tax Delinquency totalling P624,506,725.42 for 1992 to 2001 and then warrants of levy, after the Office of the Government Corporate Counsel first opined that the Local Government Code had withdrawn its exemption and later reversed itself; the Court of Appeals dismissed its Petition as filed out of time, and only a temporary restraining order issued on February 7, 2003 stopped the scheduled auction of the airport. Following Oral Argument, the Court held that MIAA was not a government-owned or -controlled corporation, having no capital stock divided into shares, no stockholders and no members, and not being organized for any purpose the Corporation Code assigns to nonstock corporations, but a government instrumentality vested with corporate powers and therefore covered by Section 133(o), which bars local taxes on the National Government, its agencies and instrumentalities. A tax is never presumed, the Court said; doubt about taxability is resolved against taxation, and an exemption granted by Congress to a national instrumentality is construed liberally in its favor. It further held that the airport land and buildings were properties of public dominion under Article 420 of the Civil Code, devoted to public use, outside human commerce and therefore beyond levy or auction sale, with MIAA holding title merely in trust for the Republic and the President alone able to withdraw them from public use. Since MIAA was not a taxable person, Section 234(a) exempted the Republic's property, except for portions leased to private entities, whose beneficial use had been granted for consideration. The assessments, notices and auction sale were declared void. Justice Tinga, joined by Justices Martinez and Callejo, dissented, accusing the majority of overturning Mactan and a dozen precedents to protect 'the precious Ming vase that is the Manila International Airport Authority', arguing that MIAA is a GOCC performing proprietary functions and taxable, but agreeing that its charter bars any sale of its properties, leaving the city only a limited lien.
