one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 31 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests Yuchengco v. Sandiganbayan, the fight over sequestered PLDT shares. The Republic, through the PCGG, had sued in Civil Case No. 0002 to recover the ill-gotten wealth of the late President Ferdinand E. Marcos, including PTIC shares held by Ramon and Imelda Cojuangco and by Prime Holdings, Inc.; PTIC was PLDT's biggest stockholder, holding some 28 percent of its outstanding shares. Alfonso T. Yuchengco and Y Realty intervened as claimants to PHI's 46 percent of PTIC. After the Sandiganbayan severed the ownership issue for separate trial and, with no restraining order in force, promulgated a Partial Decision on May 6, 2002 dismissing both the Republic's Complaint and the Complaint-in-Intervention, five consolidated Petitions reached the Court, which denied the interlocutory ones for mootness or absence of grave abuse and the Yuchengcos' for lack of reversible error, leaving only whether the Partial Decision conformed to the evidence and the law. Holding that Executive Order No. 14-A required only preponderance of evidence, the Court through Justice Conchita Carpio Morales found that the preponderance clearly lay with the Republic and that the Sandiganbayan had grossly misappreciated the facts. Jose Yao Campos testified that he had organized PHI for Marcos with stockholders who held no financial interest; Rolando C. Gapud called it a dummy corporation of the Marcoses; and Francisco de Guzman confirmed that Campos's associates had organized it, that its office sat inside United Laboratories, and that it issued only deeds of assignment. From these the Court concluded that Marcos owned PHI, that Cojuangco managed a Marcos-controlled corporation for at least two years, and that the 1983 divestment to his relatives was authorized by Marcos, so the 111,415 PTIC shares were ill-gotten in whosever hands. Justice Callejo concurred separately on the conclusiveness of Campos's admissions against interest, while Justices Garcia and Sandoval-Gutierrez dissented, holding the Republic's proof insufficient and reasoning that because the deeds named the Cojuangcos rather than being indorsed in blank, the familiar Marcos modus operandi was absent and Cojuangco had been the beneficial owner from the start.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 34 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests Coastal Pacific Trading v. Southern Rolling Mills, a unanimous decision granting the petition of a defrauded creditor. VISCO, a steel processor, had mortgaged its land, machinery and equipment to the Development Bank of the Philippines in 1961 and again, by an unrecorded second mortgage, to respondent banks in 1963; under a processing agreement it received 3,000 metric tons of steel coils from Coastal Pacific and returned only 1,600. After VISCO defaulted, the banks converted their loan into more than 90 percent of its equity, formed a consortium and took over management, filling nine of the ten board seats. The chapter then traces the transactions the Court found fraudulent: the quiet renaming of the FEBTC account to drop the word VISCO as a precautionary measure and to avoid a government takeover; the 1974 sale of the generator sets whose proceeds, instead of going directly to DBP, were routed through the consortium so that it could be subrogated to DBP's recorded primary lien; and the 1980 foreclosure and 1985 sale that ended with the properties in the hands of National Steel Corporation. The Court first held that the Court of Appeals erred in treating the earlier Southern Industrial Projects case as a bar, since several creditors of one debtor cannot be considered as identical parties, do not become privies by assailing the same transactions, and hold distinct rights giving rise to distinct causes of action. On the merits it found more than a preponderance of evidence of a deliberate plan to defraud: as trustees, the consortium's directors should have managed VISCO's assets with strict regard for all the creditors' interests, yet miserably failed in their duty of fidelity, and the assignment of the DBP mortgage bore the earmarks of fraud. Because NSC was a buyer in good faith and restitution was impossible, the Court awarded Coastal actual damages measured by its unsatisfied judgment credit, plus P250,000 in exemplary damages as a warning to other creditors not to abuse their rights.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 35 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests Nasecore v. Energy Regulatory Commission, decided unanimously by the Supreme Court en banc through Justice Romeo S. Callejo Sr. on February 2, 2006. Under the EPIRA of 2001 the ERC had approved Meralco's unbundled rates and ordered it to recover changes in purchased-power cost through a new Generation Rate Adjustment Mechanism, adopted with the ICERA in a February 2003 Order, in place of the old Purchased Power Adjustment. When Meralco applied under the GRAM to raise its generation charge and the ERC approved an increase from P3.1886 to P3.3213 per kWh effective immediately, consumer groups led by Nasecore sought certiorari, arguing that the amended application had never been published as Section 4(e), Rule 3 of the IRR of the EPIRA required. Meralco and the ERC answered that the GRAM rules radically differed from the IRR and required no publication, the GRAM being an adjustment mechanism rather than an independent rate application. The Court held that the ERC had gravely abused its discretion. The IRR spoke of any application or petition for rate adjustment or for any relief affecting the consumers without distinction, so it reached anything that would raise the retail rate; recalling the six requirements outlined in Freedom from Debt Coalition v. ERC, the Court stressed that the application itself, not merely the notice of hearing, had to be published, and that consumer and LGU comments had to be considered -- requirements aimed at protecting the consumers and diminishing the disparity or imbalance between them and the utility. The failure to publish was fatal, depriving consumers of the right to comment. A second ground was independent: the GRAM rules had themselves never been published under Executive Order No. 200 nor filed with the ONAR, and under Tanada v. Tuvera were ineffective. Justice Tinga concurred separately, calling publication both jurisdictional and a due-process component. On August 16, 2006 the en banc denied reconsideration with finality, rejecting American authorities on escalator clauses and holding that the Constitution recognized higher values than administrative economy, efficiency and efficacy.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 4 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 7), CJP's July 5, 2009 Inquirer column, reflects on the Catholic Church's 'awesome gathering power,' shown when -- 'defying the influenza A(H1N1) contagion' -- more than 12,000 lay faithful filled the SMX for the Congress on Parish Liturgical Life. CJP, who cut short an Alaska vacation to attend, arrived as Gaudencio Cardinal Rosales concluded a keynote met with 'adulating love.' Though the theme was 'religious, not political,' he sensed the 'disciplined disciples' (lay leaders of the Archdiocese's 13 vicariates and 92 parishes) 'could have been swayed to any direction,' and was 'convinced that Cardinal Rosales could easily produce more than enough warm bodies to change the course of our history, just as Jaime Cardinal Sin did in 1986 and 2001,' summoning 'an army of faithful' able to 'topple authoritarian and corrupt regimes' -- as the prelate had shown by resisting Charter change amid the NBN-ZTE scandal. The 'secret weapon,' he writes, is 'the lethal combination of parishes and Catholic schools in Metro Manila.' Recalling his own sharing at the Congress, he tells how, on becoming Chief Justice, he chose to remain 'an ordinary parishioner' and extraordinary minister at the Santuario de San Antonio 'without extra arrangements or protocols,' because 'in serving our Lord... we, the people of God, are all equal' -- and, invoking Matthew 25, that at the 'pearly gates' the Lord will ask not about 'bank accounts' or 'doctoral degrees' but 'whether we shared our resources with the poor.' He closes with a tribute to Washington Sycip at 88, whose birthday gathering of 500 business titans made him the commercial counterpart to the archbishop's pull -- 'wisdom and strength over the ages.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 6 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 7), CJP's April 12, 2009 Easter Sunday Inquirer column, is 'a story of faith' about his 1996 heart scare and what he believes was a miraculous healing. Accompanying his wife Leni to cardiologist Dr. Dante Morales that March, he consulted about 'dizzy spells, cold sweat, and chest pains'; an ECG and a treadmill test came back 'positive for myocardial ischemia,' and Morales -- after a 2-d echo -- advised an angiogram, quipping that the tests were like courts: 'the ECG... the Municipal Trial Court; the treadmill... the Regional Trial Court; the 2-d echo... the Court of Appeals; and the angiogram... the Supreme Court,' so 'since we lost in the three lower courts of medicine, we should appeal to the highest.' With the angiogram postponed, his friend Pat Garcia arranged a second opinion from US-based surgeon Dr. Jorge Garcia, who suspected coronary ischemia. Meanwhile his ailing colleague Justice Ricardo Francisco asked Fr. Pascual Adorable to say a private 'Healing Mass' on March 22, during which CJP 'prayed ardently for Justice Francisco' and forgot his own looming procedure, before Fr. Adorable 'prayed over' each justice and spouse. Anticipating bypass surgery, he entered Makati Medical Center reading the Yale 'Heart Book' -- but during the April 13 angiogram, as the dye spread, 'Dr. Morales exclaimed, "Your coronary arteries are all clear!"', a complete clearance later confirmed by Dr. Garcia ('when you die, it will not be due to any heart problem'). Medical 'buffs' and 'agnostics' might call it coincidence, but 'as a believer' CJP holds that 'the praying over and the healing Mass made all the difference' -- and that, having prayed only for Francisco, 'the Lord remembered' him too, proof that 'for man it may not be possible but for God nothing is impossible.'

He recalls meeting Pat in 1987 as counsel to the 'Excel Group,' being 'ushered... to the Philippine Daily Inquirer and to Marixi... Prieto,' who 'enticed' him to become president of 'the most widely read broadsheet' -- fulfilling the 'impossible dream' of 'a poor boy hawking newspapers in the streets of Sampaloc.' Pat was 'gentle, genteel... and always fair,' yet 'resolute in his convictions,' kept a 'low profile' and felt 'uneasy when publicly acclaimed,' embodying 'whoever exalts himself will be humbled; but whoever humbles himself will be exalted.' He 'never used... highfalutin words,' was never heard 'erupt in anger,' and let his actions speak, so 'what you see is what you get with Pat.' Loyal and caring, he helped friends 'neither counting the cost nor expecting anything in return' -- in 1996 'voluntarily' arranging CJP's heart consult with his surgeon cousin Dr. Jorge Garcia, and in 2004 having Print Town publish CJP's 'Leveling the Playing Field,' which 'sold out' within a year. Bidding 'adieu,' CJP is 'certain that [Pat] is now with our Father in heaven,' invoking John 14's promise -- 'where I am, you also shall be' -- for one who, 'like our Lord, was meek and humble of heart.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 8 of 'A Centenary of Justice' reproduces the 'Inspirational Message' CJP delivered on January 27, 2001 at the Waterfront Hotel in Cebu City during Region VII's 'Culmination Night' -- fittingly the first region to celebrate, since CJ Hilario G. Davide Jr. hails from there. Defining inspiration (after Webster) as 'an act or power of moving the intellect or emotion' and quoting Longfellow that 'lives of great men all remind us we can make our life sublime,' CJP argues that 'true leadership is sourced from example and inspiration, not from force and domination,' and offers Davide as the judiciary's model in four virtues. First, integrity and moral courage: in a decade as jurist (and earlier as legislator, constitution-maker and elections chairman) no corruption ever touched him -- 'no business cronies, no favored friends, no officious relatives' -- and 'what political will is to a sovereign head, moral courage is to a magistrate,' so that a judge who has memorized the Constitution and the UDHR but lacks the courage to stand against the establishment 'is really nothing.' Second, simple, frugal, transparent living: Davide 'does not drink, does not smoke, does not gamble,' wakes near 3:30 a.m. to pray, and is soft-spoken yet self-actualized. Third, dedication: he reports at 5:30 a.m., writes exhaustively 'dissecting issues with a surgeon's scalpel,' and ran his CJ duties while brilliantly presiding over the Impeachment Court. Fourth, faith: his practice of cutting the Bible each morning for the day's instruction yielded two providential readings -- 2 Maccabees 10 ('Purification of the Temple') on his November 30, 1998 appointment, inspiring his mission to cleanse the judiciary and reward the competent and ethical, and Isaiah 62 ('Restoration of Zion') on January 20, 2001, the day he resolved to swear in Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo as the 14th President at the EDSA Shrine. CJP closes by urging the judiciary to follow this example -- a Chief whom the 'normally critical' Philippine Daily Inquirer had named 'Filipino of the Year' and polls rated the most admired citizen -- 'not only for the here and now, but also for the hereafter and forever.'

one_paragraph_summary: Appendix A of 'A Centenary of Justice' reproduces CJP's tribute 'A Salute to My Mentor,' delivered June 17, 2001 at the launch of former Senate President Jovito R. Salonga's autobiography 'A Journey of Struggle and Hope.' CJP recounts the moment in 1956 when, a freshman amid a thousand striking Far Eastern University law students, he watched the new 36-year-old dean Salonga -- a Yale and Harvard graduate and bar topnotcher -- walk alone to the microphone and, 'in thirty minutes flat,' turn the hostile crowd back to their classrooms, the moment he found 'the guru who would become my role model not only in my chosen career but... in my life as a whole.' He traces Salonga's mentorship through his own student leadership (president of the FEU council and the National Union of Students), the insistence on academics that won him Latin honors, and the 1960 bar he nearly quit -- sick and wading floodwaters -- but passed sixth-highest at Salonga's urging. He joined Salonga's firm (with partners Ordoñez, Yap and Gonzales), absorbing 'integrity, prudence and fairness,' and describes Salonga as a man who 'taught by example,' lived 'an almost ascetic life,' and never traded principle for 'friendship, kinship, relationship, wealth or power'; their cross-faith friendship (Protestant mentor, Catholic protege) endured four decades because 'we never discuss what separates us, but only what truly binds us.' Most movingly, CJP discloses the seven Judicial and Bar Council rejections he suffered from 1992 to 1995 -- for 'alleged insufficiency of... competence' and 'alleged transgressions and sins' -- through which Salonga sustained him with Romans 8:28 until his appointment by President Ramos. He closes with Salonga's treasured teaching that 'law cannot be separated from life' and that, beyond the things money can buy, it is far more important to aspire for 'the things that money cannot buy, like excellence, integrity, honor, dignity and a reverential regard and love for God.'

After warmly describing a Philja invitation from the 'respected and loved' Chancellor Ameurfina Melencio Herrera as 'a summons... which cannot be refused,' CJP recalls his own 1995 entry 'direct to the Supreme Court' and the 'spiritual soul-searching' it prompted. Against the Lord's core teaching of love (love God, neighbor and even one's enemies), he poses a hard question: if God is love, why does He punish, and why is a judge called to impose penalties? He answers with a parable -- a traffic-court judge fines a repentant young woman, then removes his robe and pays the fine himself, because she is his daughter, so that 'justice was served, and so was love.' The judge, CJP says, is Christ, who, because justice is in God's nature, could not waive the sanction of His own law, yet, being love personified, sent His Son to atone for and 'own the punishment meant for us' -- fulfilling both justice and love. He closes by charging the new judges that the rendition of justice is 'not only a human necessity; it is a divine essentiality': when they give people their due 'fairly and speedily, without fear or favor,' they do the work of the Lord, for 'to dispense quality justice is to do God's work.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chief Justice Andres R. Narvasa's Foreword to 'Justice and Faith' frames the book around CJP's own self-chosen title -- the 'twin beacons that have guided the professional and personal life of Mr. Justice Artemio Panganiban': Justice and Faith. The collection, Narvasa writes, is 'modest in volume though not in quality' but suffices to give the serious reader insight into that twin-beacon thesis. He singles out as 'particularly impressive' the chapter in which CJP acknowledges with 'frankness and humility' his 'much-cherished ambition for a seat in the High Court' and the 'long and difficult road to its fulfillment'; that culmination, when it came, CJP celebrated with 'exemplary industry' -- 'no less than 230 ponencias in the two years following his elevation,' by his own reckoning. Narvasa commends two chapters in particular as 'absorbing reading' that should 'prove useful to those who aspire for the profession': CJP's account of how he developed his decision-writing style, and his advice to would-be lawyers. The Foreword also notes that CJP 'does not forget the sitting judge' -- expounding the 'mental skills and disciplines' a judge should possess in 'seeking out crucial issues, analyzing the evidence and arguments, determining the applicable law and, finally, expressing his conclusions in clear, precise and logical manner' -- 'pithy advice that judges would do well to follow.' Narvasa closes with the compliment that 'the book leaves the reader looking for more in the same vein' and the hope that 'the author will not disappoint him.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 5 of 'Justice and Faith' reproduces CJP's master-of-ceremonies introductions of the then-sitting members of the Supreme Court at Justice Justo P. Torres Jr.'s retirement rites on October 22, 1997 -- each delivered as the named justice rose, per a 'hallowed tradition,' to present the honoree with a memento of his term. Only ten justices are introduced because Padilla and Hermosisima had retired and Narvasa and Regalado were abroad on official business. The vignettes are deliberately plural: Puno is 'a trained surgeon' wielding 'laser-like precision' and waging Holmes-like lonely dissents; Vitug is 'an icon of the academe' whose restrained language renders law in 'cadenced expression'; Romero, 'the gracious and precious gem of the Court, its only lady member,' tenaciously battles 'sometimes chauvinistic colleagues'; Francisco is 'the essential magistrate' guided solely by 'the quiet comfort of a disciplined conscience'; Mendoza is 'molded in the ivy-league traditions of Yale,' scholarly and impeccable; Kapunan is 'the perfect gentleman of the bench,' firm but never imperious; Melo is 'the consensus builder' and 'the living barometer' of the Court; Bellosillo is 'the paragon, the pith and soul of the career magistrate,' diligent and methodical; and at the rhetorical climax CJP shifts into Tagalog to name Davide 'the epitome of the Filipino jurist -- makabayan, maginoo, marangal, matapang, masipag, mapagkakatiwalaan.' The longest introduction is reserved for the honoree, Justice Torres, whose March 13, 1996 Ramos appointment is woven into a 'lucky 13' running joke (CA seniority 13, SC seniority 13, his father Justo Sr. 13th in the 1925 bar), softened only by Rose's heart, where 'he is Number One and only'; the closing invites the audience to rise for Torres's valedictory.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 6 of 'Justice and Faith' is CJP's BLD prayer-meeting reflection a week after he took his October 10, 1995 oath as Justice of the Supreme Court, recounting how Scripture and prayer guided him through three years of frustration and seven JBC bypassings 1992-1995 (alleged insufficiency of competence, a former client surfacing with a 25-year-old complaint, the 'career CA justice' priority, the 'others are even more qualified' formula) -- sustained throughout by Romans 8:28. In January 1995 CJP surrendered: 'Take, O Lord, all that I am, all that I will ever be.' When Justice Quiason retired in July, a close-friend justice nudged him; on Saturday July 29 at 1 a.m. CJP could not sleep and prayed for two hours, asleep at 4 a.m. awaiting a sign. The sign came at Mass the next morning -- Luke 11:1-11, 'Ask, seek, knock' -- with cold perspiration and hair on end. He asked for confirmation; on Sunday August 6, the transfiguration gospel (Luke 9:28-36) supplied 'Listen to Him.' He resubmitted his name to the JBC. On Wednesday August 9, with wife Leni as co-prayer-leader at the BLD South Sector meeting at St. James School in Sucat, Parañaque, CJP boldly proclaimed the discernment publicly -- at the risk of ridicule if it proved false -- quoting the Jesuit maxim 'I will work as if everything depended on me, and I will pray as if everything depended on God.' At the JBC's September 13 meeting an exclusion attempt was deferred when one member (CJP believes guided by the Holy Spirit) pleaded for a postponement; on September 20 'no one, by some mysterious reason, objected,' and CJP passed the screening for the first time. Two weeks of intercession by the BLD community, the Carmelites and the Pink Sisters followed, then the appointment call. President Ramos asked, 'How did you do it?' -- CJP replied, 'I did not do it. The Lord did it!' He closes by pledging before the assembly that 'all my actions and all my decisions will only be in accordance with His commandments and His gospel. I hold office by God's grace and I pledge to serve Him and our people with fortitude, integrity, competence and prudence.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 7 of 'Justice and Faith' is CJP's commencement address at the University of Iloilo on March 21, 1997, accepting the LL.D. honoris causa conferred by his long-time friend Congressman Alberto J. Lopez. Rather than 'a pompous lecture,' CJP tells the graduates his story -- Sampaloc poverty, newsboy, bootblack, peddling cigarettes and bibles; Mapa High honors and a UP scholarship he could not take up because his father lacked the 15-centavo bus fare from Cataluña St. to Diliman, so he enrolled at FEU instead 'walking distance from our house'; the youngest FEUCSO presidency and NUSP co-founding where he met Leni Carpio of St. Scholastica's; Salonga's mentorship and the top-ten bar in 1960; an admission to Yale Law that he could not take up for the same fare reason; his Hong Kong wealth years swept away in the 1982 stock-market crash; the 1983 Rotary Manila induction at which he met then-PC chief Gen. Fidel V. Ramos who, twelve years later, appointed him to the Supreme Court after seven JBC bypassings. From this arc CJP distills three lessons. First, adversities are preludes to greater victories -- FEU instead of UP brought Salonga; the denied Yale fare produced Baron Travel and funded five children's overseas master's degrees; the Hong Kong crash freed him to return home and reach the Supreme Court ('an achievement that money cannot buy nor can any stock market crash take away'). Second, do not lose heart -- Anthony Robbins's tabulated age-list of Abraham Lincoln's defeats (31, 32, 34, 35, 36, 43, 46, 48, 55, 56, 58) ends with the US presidency at 60. Third, have faith in God -- Isaiah 55:8-9 ('my thoughts are not your thoughts...my ways are not your ways') and Romans 8:28 ('God makes all things work for the good of those who love Him'). He closes with the four-act farmer's-horse parable ('good luck, bad luck, who knows? Only God knows!') and the synthesizing maxim: 'We will work as if everything depended on us. And we will pray as if everything depended on God.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 9 of 'Justice and Faith' is CJP's BLD reflection on John 10:27-30 (the Good Shepherd discourse), delivered the night before the 1995 Philippine elections and offered to newly elected officials -- senators, congressmen, governors, mayors -- as the leadership measure. He opens with an unusual-leader catalogue (wooden cross, thorns crown, reed scepter, rusty-nail ring, 'Crucify Him' constituents) before naming the only King who resurrected from the dead, then expounds five leadership qualities of Jesus as the chapter's spine. First, clear vision and mission -- the Sermon on the Mount as 'the greatest teaching of all time,' preference for the poor and peacemakers, parables designed to make listeners 'discover something for themselves' (Lk 10:36, 7:42, 20:16). Second, courage and conviction -- Albert Nolan's 'Jesus Before Christianity' on the courage to question tradition, sinners-and-tax-collectors company, the searing Mt 23:25-27 woes against Pharisees as 'whitewashed tombs.' Third, servant-leadership -- Mk 10:42-45 ('Anyone among you who aspires to greatness must serve the rest') is set against Filipino patronage politics in which leaders 'arrogate unto themselves power...allocate huge discretionary funds...dispense patronage and favors'; the foot-washing (Jn 13:14-16) is the example. Fourth, prayer and faith -- the mountain retreat (Mt 14:23-24), the Gethsemane sweat 'like drops of blood' (Lk 22:44), 'Father, forgive them' and 'into Your hands I commend my spirit' from the cross, the Lord's Prayer as the model. Fifth, justice and love -- Romans 14:17, Mt 26:35-40, Isaiah 42, the adulteress in Jn 8:1-11 ('Let the man among you who is sinless be the first to cast a stone'), and St. Paul's hymn to love (1 Cor 13). He closes with a judge-pays-the-fine analogy -- the speeding lady-driver case in which the judge imposes a P500 fine then removes his robe, walks to the court cashier and pays it himself because the law-breaker is his daughter ('Justice was served -- and so was love') -- and reads the atonement as the cosmic instance of this convergence: Jesus the judge imposed the law of God for sin, then bore the guilt and paid the penalty Himself. 'Such is the Leader in Jesus. Such is the Shepherd that is Jesus. Such is the Shepherd of my soul.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 10 of 'Justice and Faith' is CJP's Holy Friday reflection on Luke 23:46 ('Father, into your hands, I commend my spirit'), the last words of Jesus on the cross, framed as a paradigm of perfect obedience that every disciple is invited to imitate in daily work and decisions. He opens with a vignette of his six-year-old grandson Miggy, who told him he earned a preschool outstanding-pupil award at Southridge School by studying hard, watching no TV except during holidays, waking early, and doing his homework every day -- then placed the certificate at the home altar, a child's complete sacrifice-and-offering. CJP then catalogues the plural Christian imitations of Christ -- contemplative hermits, priests and nuns, missionaries who 'sail the seven seas,' even flagellants -- before turning to the most ordinary form, citing Mother Teresa: 'We are all called to be Christ to others so that others may become Christ to still many others.' He develops this with a litany of ordinary vocations: a student offering his grades, a policeman patrolling honestly, a housewife preparing meals lovingly, a husband working faithfully, a businessman selling quality at reasonable prices, a government functionary discharging duties in integrity -- each lifts work to the Lord as Christ did on the cross. Augustine's 'our hearts are restless until they rest in God' anchors a walking-wounded image of humanity; CJP supplies his own confession -- a restless young man chasing fame, fortune, power, position and possession that produced no peace and no fulfillment ('Who am I? Why was I born? Where am I headed for?'). Only when he committed to the Father, acknowledged the Holy Spirit, and proclaimed Jesus as 'Lord and Savior, Healer and Friend' did the dual-citizenship orientation arrive: a resident of earth, truly a citizen of heaven. He closes with a dedicatory pledge in oath form -- 'I hold my present office -- as indeed my life and my time -- by God's grace' -- and a closing prayer: 'O, Heavenly Father, into Your hands we commend our work, our minds, our lives and our spirits. Amen.'

one_paragraph_summary: Appendix A of 'Justice and Faith,' titled 'A Man of God and of the Law,' is the book-jacket-style biographical profile that organizes CJP's pre-bench identity around six topical headings -- Top-Notch Catholic Lay Leader, Well-Known Civic Leader, Former Business Leader, Popular Youth Leader, Outstanding Family Man, and Legal Philosophy -- and closes with five press blurbs from 1995-1997. The Catholic-lay spine names CJP's 1996 appointment by Pope John Paul II to the Pontifical Council for the Laity (the only Filipino among 30 international members), his national vice chairmanship of PPCRV, secretaryship of the Council of the Laity of the Philippines, servant-leadership of the Bukas Loob sa Diyos Covenant Community, lay delegation to PCP II (Jan-Feb 1991), and parish ministry as special minister of Holy Communion. The civic-and-business sections record CJP as founder of NUSP, president of FEU Central Student Organization, 'most illustrious knight' of Kappa Gamma Phi, president of the Rotary Club of Manila (1990-1991, the largest in Asia), president of Philippine Daily Inquirer (1991-1992), vice president of PCCI, international chairman of ASTA (first Asian to head it), president of the Organization for Tourism of the Philippines for ten years, governor of MAP for four, chief legal counsel to PPCRV, MAPSA, and the Liberal Party, and chair of the Multi-Sectoral Conference on the Administration of Justice (June 13 and October 17, 1992) that drew up the first-1,000-days program for President Ramos. The academic record -- FEU Bachelor of Laws cum laude (1960), Most Outstanding Student (1959), Associate in Arts 'With Highest Honors' (1956), ten years as a professor of law and political science at FEU/Assumption Convent/San Sebastian (1961-1970), and the Doctor of Laws honoris causa from the University of Iloilo (March 21, 1997, the C07 honoris-causa occasion) -- sits alongside the family section noting wife Elenita 'Leni' Carpio-Panganiban (AIM professor) and five children, all with master's degrees from leading universities abroad (Maria Elena, UC MBA, Baron Travel president; Jose Artemio III, UP music summa cum laude, Stanford MS 'with distinction'; Maria Jocelyn, Chicago MBA; Maria Theresa, Michigan MBA; Maria Evelyn, Harvard MPP). The Legal Philosophy section then states CJP's divestiture-on-elevation (resigning business and most civic posts on SC appointment, keeping only PCL, Rotary Manila, and the Bantayog ng mga Bayani Foundation), his two-year productivity ledger (230+ ponencias, 11 separate opinions, 140 extended resolutions, 675 minute resolutions), and the substantial-justice creed in his own words: 'Each case has its own flesh and blood ... ' and 'the real essence of justice does not emanate from patchwork legal technicality ... but from the spirit's gut consciousness of the dynamic role of law in the ultimate development of the social edifice.' The appendix closes with the Rotary inaugural pledge -- 'Upon this creed, LOVE GOD SERVE MAN, I shall be judged ... in my whole unworthy life here on earth' -- and a reception dossier of five press blurbs triangulating the man-of-God-and-of-the-law thesis from independent vantage points: Bas's 'a man of prayer' (Manila Standard, Oct 26, 1997), Farolan's confidence in the High Court's deliberations (Philippine Star, Nov 3, 1997), Sison's 'the first justice ... who has openly advocated the use of simple and non-legal terms' (Philippine Star, Oct 29, 1997), PDI's 'former newsboy and bootblack who rose to become a prominent lawyer' (Oct 14, 1995), and Manila Bulletin's 'he will do justice to every man' (editorial, Oct 7, 1995).

one_paragraph_summary: The back matter of 'Justice and Faith,' titled 'From the Men of Justice and Faith,' is a short anthology of accolades from six named figures across ecclesiastical, judicial, academic, and legal-press vantage points -- Chief Justice Andres R. Narvasa (Foreword excerpt reprinted, naming the 'twin beacons' that have guided CJP's professional and personal life); Jaime L. Cardinal Sin (Oct 20, 1995 dinner speech in CJP's honor, calling him 'a very dear friend and lay collaborator ... a truly Catholic lawyer, faithful to the magisterium and loyal to the Lord Jesus Christ'); Bishop Edmundo M. Abaya, then-recent former Vice President of the CBCP (Sept 8, 1995, saying he is 'above all, a man of God and of our Church'); retired Justice Isagani A. Cruz (Oct 15, 1997 letter, 'proving to be one of the most competent members of the Supreme Court today'); Dr. Enrique P. Syquia, publisher of The Lawyers Review (Oct 31, 1997, attesting that CJP is 'the most prolific decision writer in the Supreme Court; but despite the quantity of his decisions, they are also 'quality' as well as clear and readable'); and Dr. Benjamin G. Tayabas, President of Pamantasan ng Lungsod ng Maynila (Nov 2, 1995, naming CJP as 'an exemplary model for the students and faculty of Pamantasan ng Lungsod ng Maynila'). The composition is itself the argument: by closing the book with six independent institutional voices -- Cardinal Archbishop of Manila, former CBCP Vice President, Chief Justice, retired Justice, legal-press publisher, and public-university president -- the back matter triangulates the man-of-God-and-of-the-law identity that the Appendix has just stated as fact, and brackets CJP's first two SC years between two clusters of endorsements (September-November 1995 around his oath; October-November 1997 around the book's publication and his second anniversary). Reprinting Narvasa's 'twin beacons' formula at the back matter closes the volume on the same integrative frame with which it opened -- a deliberate compositional move that makes Justice and Faith the keystone of CJP's self-presentation as a debut author.

Romulo; and the Club, at 455 members, is the oldest in Asia and the largest outside the United States, which he says has loaded a heavy burden upon his lean and unworthy shoulders. Elected as early as December 1989, he spent seven months planning with his team and produced a printed Program of Action built on a three-point VISION, structured like a triad and a pyramid: Manila Rotary is for its members, colleagues and guests; for excellence in the professions, business, education and government; and mostly and most importantly for the poor, the afflicted and the weak. He enumerates the programs under each point -- weekly meetings and membership targets, the 4-way test and journalism and scholarship programs, and a long list of charitable projects from medico-surgical missions and a new eye bank to immunization drives, Save A Heart, Save A Life, Sagip Kabataan, newsboys' Mini-Olympics and shoeshine stands -- and states the budget frankly: P10 million needed against a previous high of P5 million, with dues unchanged and P7 million to be raised. He then grounds Rotary's maxims theologically in Christ's threefold command to Peter to feed My sheep, defines peace as the fruit of social justice, and closes by submitting to be judged upon the credo and inviting all to recite the Prayer of St. Francis of Assisi.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 3 of 'Love God, Serve Man' is the address CJP delivered at the Manila Hotel launching the RCM Eyebank Foundation, and it is first of all a thanksgiving. Speaking on behalf of the Foundation and of all the blind people who will soon see the color, movement and wonders of the world, he thanks President Fidel V. Ramos for gracing the launching and dedicating his double Paul Harris contribution of P50,000 to the Eyebank; the Foundation of Rotary International for a $50,000 grant secured over two years by former RI President Mat Caparas and former RI Director Benny Santos; the sister clubs of Tokyo South, Kowloon East, Taipei, Taipei Central and Taipei Fu-Jung; the Paul Harris fellows and local donors listed in the Balita; and Rotarian Andre Simard, the Canadian ambassador, for laboratory equipment from his government. Contributions stood at P2,735,800, which the dreaded finemaster Santi Dumlao was expected to round up to a neat P3 million within the hour, enough for the Eyebank to be operationalized. He thanks the volunteer Rotarian ophthalmologists led by Dr. Ed Caparas and his son Victor, who have full practices yet cut down their leisure time to serve the poor. He then places the Eyebank in the Rotary Club of Manila's 74-year line of institutions, alongside the Philippine Tuberculosis Society, the Philippine Cancer Society, the Community Chest, the Boy Scouts and Sagip Kabataan, calling it the only facility of its kind in the country and possibly in Asean, and explains that it was set up to concretize the biblical gift of sight in our technological age by collecting and preserving corneas for implantation. Of the three things it needs -- equipment, surgeons and tissue donors -- only the third remains, and since he is neither philanthropist nor surgeon but only a poor but talkative lawyer, he supplies it by asking everyone to fill out donor forms, then calls for those unwilling to stand, finds none, and claims the whole hall. He closes by pledging, in keeping with President Ramos' Philippines 2000, to reduce curable blindness by at least 30 percent by the year 2000.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 8 of 'Love God, Serve Man' reprints the article Atty. Artemio V. Panganiban, national vice chairman and chief legal counsel of the Parish Pastoral Council For Responsible Voting, published on the front page of the Philippine Daily Inquirer on March 11, 1992 as a summary of speeches he had delivered around the country. He opens with the objections he kept hearing -- politics is dirty, the Church will be smeared by its mud, and involvement violates the separation of Church and State -- and answers them under three heads: why the PPCRV was organized, what it is, and how it will achieve its goals. Church involvement, he explains, was largely unheard of before 1965, but grew through the 1986 snap election, when the CBCP under Ricardo Cardinal Vidal exhorted the faithful and then condemned the poll's unparalleled fraud; for 1992 the Church moved from endorsing NAMFREL to directly sponsoring the PPCRV, a step he traces to three sources. Vatican II taught man's total or integral development, redefined 'church' to include the laity, recognized the laity's equality with the clergy in dignity and mission, and through Christifideles Laici charged the lay faithful never to relinquish participation in public life. PCP II directed that, politics having become an obstacle to integral development, the laity must participate with competence and integrity, while its Resolution 28 barred bishops, priests and religious from partisan politics. Three CBCP pastoral letters then demanded a formed electorate rejecting payoffs, patronage and personalities, conditions free of guns, goons and gold, and organization down to the precinct -- to which the PPCRV answered with principles, platforms and performance, with 'the glory, grace and gospel of God,' and with a pledge to poll-watch. Defining the movement as a lawyer would, he describes it as a national, parish-based, political but non-partisan lay movement supported by the hierarchy, covering 2,300 parishes in 78 dioceses with a projected 2.3 million members, accredited by the Comelec on February 18, 1992 as its national citizen's arm, devoted to voter education through five seminar modules with special emphasis on the youth, and running a trimedia campaign, Qualification Standards, a research committee and parish-level fora. He concludes that the PPCRV cannot be violating the separation of Church and State because it is lay-led, non-partisan and forbidden by no law, and that with eight presidential candidates and a likely plurality winner, its members could be the rock upon which the state may build its foundation.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 9 of 'Love God, Serve Man' records the reflection Atty. Artemio V. Panganiban delivered on February 23, 1994 before a prayer meeting of the Bukas Loob Sa Diyos Catholic Covenant Community at the Philippine International Convention Center, where he served on the Council of Servant Leaders and chaired the BLD Foundation. Taking Mark 1:15 as his text, he opens with the parable of Pancracio, a hard-working young man who became a multi-millionaire at 35, crashed his new BMW, and in a coma begged Mr. Death for more time, confessing he had never prayed and did not know the Commandments; granted a reprieve and the promise of warning, he relapsed into wealth, women and wine, and at 45 was told that the eyeglasses, the dentures, the soaring uric acid and cholesterol and the blood sugar above 300 had been warning enough. Since a part of Pancracio lurks in everyone, he says, the Lord's command to reform is not a warning but an order. He then sets out his three Cs of reformation. Contrition means being sincerely sorry, facing the consequences and confessing before a forgiving God; it is a daily practice for the renewed, since prayer without repentance is without power; and it means hating sin itself, as one driver stops at a red light from conviction and another only from fear of the policeman. It also requires restitution, as Zacchaeus repaid fourfold. Conversion is the firm commitment never to sin again and the vow to follow Jesus -- a call to metanoia usually lifelong but sometimes instant, as with St. Paul, St. Augustine and the repentant thief. Evangelization follows as the converted begin to glow and become unconscious witnesses, the lamp that cannot be hidden; and because we cannot go to heaven alone, it reaches to human development, the yoke of the poor, injustice and peace, judged at the last by what was done for the least of our brethren. Quoting PCP II that evangelization must transform the whole fabric of society because 'our society remains a sick society,' he reads four signs of the times for BLD -- four of its members drafted into PCP II, Sonny de los Reyes's election to head the Council of the Laity, the community's new vision-charism-mission, and his own reluctant call after two years of hiding, answered at last with 'Here I am Lord.' He closes on the statistics of the unchurched: only about a million of 56 million Filipino Catholics are active, 88 percent being the 'invisible laity,' so the Lord's reward for BLD's past work is more hard work under the Great Commission.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 10 of 'Love God, Serve Man' prints for the first time the personal 'sharing' in which Atty. Artemio V. Panganiban narrates his own reconversion to the ways of Jesus Christ. He begins with St. Augustine's line that our hearts are restless until they rest in God, and argues that all of us, having been injured, insulted, afflicted, broken or crushed, belong to a ragtag army of walking wounded pretending to be whole and healthy. In his own case, he says, he tried to quiet that restlessness outside God's way: an angry young man, he vowed a generous slice of worldly wealth, power and fame. He recounts a childhood of poverty -- parents who both died before he finished schooling, sleeping on cold sidewalks, selling newspapers, shining shoes, peddling textbooks to classmates so he could own one, educated in public schools and a non-sectarian university and, though baptized a Catholic, with no idea of the Christian faith. Voracious study brought Latin honors, acclaim as Most Outstanding Student, a place at the top of the bar, the presidency of the University Central Student Council and the leadership of the National Union of Students of the Philippines; but he learned right after graduation that honors and student leadership did not satisfy his thirst for life and love, and he vowed instead to become super rich. In Hong Kong in the early '80s he was counsel in transactions involving billions of Hong Kong dollars and enjoyed private jets, yachts, Rolls-Royce limousines and Patek Philippe watches, only to watch such wealth vanish in the 1982 crash and to find that the lavish life-style merely increased his appetite for more; fame in the society columns likewise brought no peace and alienated him from his wife and children. The turning point came in 1986, when he was baptized in the Holy Spirit at a Life in the Spirit seminar sponsored by Bukas Loob Sa Diyos, proclaimed Jesus his Lord and Savior, and became 'a new creation.' Understanding life in Christ as a recurring cycle of passion, death and resurrection, he had to die to his pride and ambitions; and because his resurrection would be incomplete if he alone found God, he took up the shepherd's walking stick, read the Bible cover to cover and made Scripture his guide in law, business, home and leisure. He closes by ascribing his happy home, professional advancement and 'evangelical prosperity' to surrender, confessing himself still a sinner thoroughly unworthy of God's blessings, and quoting St. Paul's First Letter to Timothy, where the former blasphemer and persecutor is made a servant and judged faithful.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 11 of 'Love God, Serve Man' records CJP's November 27, 1992 speech at Siena College, Quezon City, before the National Convention of Dominican and Siena Schools, on 'Lay Empowerment in Building a Community of Believers' as decreed by PCP II and Vatican II. He opened by confessing that he rarely addressed educators, nuns and priests, since a survey ranked them highest in credibility while lawyers stood second to last -- a point he illustrated with the joke of the lost balloonists told their exact position 'accurate but entirely useless,' and the epitaph 'Here lies lawyer John Quill; he lies still.' Defining the laity from Lumen Gentium as all the baptized outside Holy Orders and the religious state, he noted that in a Church now called the 'People of God' they form 99 percent of the membership. He then set out PCP II's two fundamental aspects of the lay vocation: full belonging, so that lay people are 'not second-class members' but co-workers equal in dignity and mission, the remaining hierarchy being 'a hierarchy of service and not of excellence'; and secular character, so that lawyers stay lawyers, teachers find holiness in teaching, and 'Christians cannot shun politics because it is dirty' -- a point he illustrated with his daughter Mabel's call to be an Opus Dei numerary, which he first misunderstood. Empowerment, he explained, comes directly from Christ through baptism and confirmation, giving the laity a share in His 'priestly, prophetic and kingly office'; but possessing it is not using it, and its effective exercise requires four things together -- genuine conversion of mind and heart, renewed catechesis (Christo-centric, biblical, authentically Filipino, systematic), renewed worship, and renewed social apostolate -- since each is deficient without the others. He listed the four areas of the lay calling, insisted that 'bait-Pinoy' must become 'buting-Pinoy,' and closed with CBCP figures showing 88 percent of Catholics 'unchurched, uninvolved and untouched by the parish,' challenging the teachers before him, 'the successors in the profession of Christ,' to answer God's challenge.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 12 of 'Love God, Serve Man' is the transcript of CJP's extemporaneous, mostly Tagalog talk of May 19, 1991, delivered to some 5,000 people of Smokey Mountain gathered at the Folk Arts Theater as the General Assembly of the Sambayanang Kristiano, and meant to carry the message of the Second Plenary Council of the Philippines to the masses. He opened with a riddle -- the theme song of those in hell is 'SANA,' of those in heaven 'Osana,' the difference being the 'O' for the Ostia -- then set three questions: what a Plenary Council is, what two aspirations of PCP II mattered most, and how they could be lived. He explained that a plenary council makes church law once approved by the Holy See; that the first Philippine council of 1953 admitted only bishops and priests; and that PCP II, convened at the instance of the CBCP, gathered 489 participants including 156 lay people, the first time in 2,000 years that laymen shared in the Church's lawmaking -- an experience he called humbling and unforgettable, admitting he felt unworthy and spoke only after the bishops encouraged him. He then gave PCP II's twin aspirations. RENEWAL, or pagbabago, demanded conversion of heart and mind from a people Christian inside church yet violent and corrupt outside it, and required a faith that is Christ-centered, rooted in the Word of God, inculturated as authentically Filipino, and others-oriented, since 'A self-seeking, self-oriented faith is no faith.' SOCIAL TRANSFORMATION meant the proclamation of a 'Church of the Poor' -- not a Church wanting people poor but one lifting them from poverty through livelihood and solidarity rather than dole-outs -- which he read, following Bro. Sonny de los Reyes, as a declaration of identity, mission, constituency and commitment. Because 'Church' now means all the faithful, PCP II recognizes lay empowerment, the people power begun in Mendiola and EDSA. He closed with Justice Hugo Gutierrez's parable of the wounded healer at the pool of Bethesda.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 17 of 'Love God, Serve Man' is the keynote address CJP gave on November 17, 1988 to the National Student Congress of the National Union of Students of the Philippines in Cebu City, 30 years after he founded the organization. He opened in recollection of his own student days -- his search for identity, singleminded pursuit of excellence and formation of enduring values -- when 'I was very poor; I had nothing' and was therefore truly free, having been elected FEU Central Student Organization president in 1957 as a second-year law student and then organizing the NUSP, and later the Institute of Student Affairs. He named three decades of NUSP leaders, restated its founding proposition that the best in man and society is attained 'only in freedom, dignity, equality and responsibility,' and congratulated the union for outgrowing purely student concerns to fight dictatorship, corruption and now poverty and oppression. Turning to the next 30 years, he posed one question: why, alone among the peoples of the Pacific, have the Filipinos remained poor? He rejected dictatorship as the answer, since Korea, Taiwan and Singapore had dictators too, 'without meaning to mitigate the guilt of the man in Hawaii'; rejected foreign exploitation, poor education and professional inferiority, since the Filipino excels abroad and 'is praised everywhere, except when he is in his own country.' His own answer was the 'godfather mentality' and the dole-out syndrome, which have made LAKAS, LUSOT and LAGAY -- influence, chicanery and bribery -- replace honest work, as in his favorite taxi driver's three-stage escape from every traffic violation. Twenty years of Marcosian dictatorship had trained people to look to government for everything, so that 'Nothing works without a lobby,' and 1986 had brought 'a change of leaders, not a change in values.' Having failed to move his elders, he brought the plea to the youth and challenged the NUSP to lead a crusade for honesty, hard work and self-discipline.

By His resurrection, he wrote, Jesus 'triumphed over evil, saved man from sin and erased all doubts that, indeed, He is God,' and without that resurrection 'Christianity would be meaningless.' He then read the passion as a demonstration of 'the Christian ethic of active non-violence': though innocent of the mob's charge of 'blasphemy,' Christ endured public ridicule, whip-lashings, cross-carrying and death, and in rising triumphed over 'mob emotionalism, false charges, human suffering and sin.' Turning the feast into a personal demand, he argued that believers too must pass through 'our own passion and death' before they can rise, asking 'how can there be resurrection without crucifixion?' -- and clarifying that this death need not be physical but may be the renunciation of 'attachment to sin, to worldliness, to lust,' a reform of life 'in accord with the basic Christian doctrine of love (love for God and neighbor).' He gave his fellow Rotarians four concrete tests of cross-carrying: choosing spouse and children over lust and self-gratification; paying honest taxes 'particularly where evasion has little risk of discovery'; refusing to take advantage of another despite superior talent or resources; and rolling up their sleeves to serve 'the least of our brethren' rather than 'luxuriating in our air-conditioned offices.' He quoted Christ's warning that 'He who will not take up his cross and come after me is not worthy of me' (Matt. 10:38), and closed on daily practice: Easter is celebrated 'in our lives daily as we choose honesty over deceit, hard work over easy money, virtue over vice, love over vengeance.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 19 of 'Love God, Serve Man' reprints Artemio V. Panganiban's New Year message for 1991, published in the Rotary Balita of January 3, 1991. He opened with stacked admissions of surprise: that the Soviet Union, 'while embracing and professing communism,' would reconcile with Christianity; that Mikhail Gorbachev would visit the Pope and call the suppression of Czechoslovakia and the invasion of Afghanistan mistakes; and, most of all, that Gorbachev would tell the Pope 'it was a mistake to exclude religion from the life of the Russian people.' Perestroika and glasnost, he wrote, 'were just the beginning of the thaw,' with free enterprise and economic liberalism now sweeping 'that once-upon-a-time caged empire' -- and even Rotary making history with the first Rotary Club of Moscow. He contrasted this with his earlier picture of the Soviets as 'heartless men who were constantly chasing James Bond,' and, with the Iron Curtain lifted, generalized that man is everywhere the same, his spirit created in God's image 'be he Russian, American or Filipino,' hungering and thirsting for fulfillment. Some try to satisfy that hunger with 'drugs, women, wine and wealth,' some with 'a madding lust for power,' some by bathing in 'the sunshine of mob adulation'; but such greed is 'self-destructive and at best, temporary,' pleasing 'the human in man' while never satisfying 'the more overwhelming spirit in man.' Quoting St. Augustine that 'man is restless till he rests in God,' he said he 'did not have to be a Russian' to discover that he could not separate religion from daily life, could not 'dichotomize my work from my faith,' and that 'my Christianity and my humanity are one inseparable whole.' He confessed a 'restless past' in which God seemed 'apart and unreachable' and prayer unnecessary, and described his present practice of speaking with Jesus in his thoughts each morning, holding that 'it is not what I ask of Him that really matters; it is what He tells me I should do that truly matters,' for 'I am but a servant of God. Nothing more.' His one wish for 1991 was to become more open to God's word so that daily he might do only what God willed -- 'Thy will be done' in his life, family, career, the Rotary Club of Manila and his country.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 20 of 'Love God, Serve Man' collects four public prayers and invocations Artemio V. Panganiban delivered between December 1991 and June 1994, introduced by an editor's note observing that he was often invited to pray at retreats and prayer meetings and to give invocations before civic and professional organizations. The first, at the country's first National Day of Prayer and Renewal at the Rizal Park grandstand on December 14, 1991, addressed 'God and Father of all families on earth' and asked that families grasp the need to pray 'in unity as one people and one nation,' see 'the pivotal role of strong families in shaping a strong society,' and recognize peace in the home as 'the lasting basis of genuine peace and harmony in the world,' ending on the image that 'when families pray together, they stay together and become living stones in building a society.' The second, before the Rotary Club of Manila at the Manila Hotel on June 9, 1994, asked forgiveness for dwelling on weakness rather than on God's healing power, blessed guest speaker Salvador H. Laurel, and then ran a fourfold antithesis: thanks for electric power at last, but a greater plea for 'divine power to free our minds from the darkness of ignorance, sophistry and self-righteousness'; thanks for the freedoms used for the people of East Timor, but a greater plea for zeal for Filipinos' own liberation from hunger and poverty; thanks for what money buys, but a greater plea for 'integrity, discipline, honor, hard work and faith in God'; thanks for prosperity, but a longing for eternal peace hereafter. The third, at the launching of Bishop Teodoro C. Bacani Jr.'s 'Church in Politics' at Villa San Miguel on January 16, 1992, thanked God for the book that would let the Parish Pastoral Council for Responsible Voting transform political life, and asked courage 'to combat the evils of guns, goons and gold' and uphold 'grace, gospel and God,' to defeat the 'politics of patronage, payoff and personalities' in favor of 'principles, platform and prayers,' and to elect leaders who are 'Maka-Diyos, Maka-Bayan, Maka-Tao at Maka-Mahirap.' The fourth, again before the Rotary Club of Manila on July 29, 1993, proclaimed God's presence molding, teaching, inspiring, empowering and healing those gathered, asked for 'sagacity and integrity for our leaders' and a community 'where the weak shall be strong and the strong shall be just and the just shall be compassionate,' and sought a special outpouring of grace on guest speaker Executive Secretary Teofisto Guingona Jr. All four close through Jesus, who 'lives and rules with You in the unity of the Holy Spirit, one God forever and ever.'

Panganiban was asked to write on the gospel reading John 13:31-35 for the fifth Sunday of Lent in 1992, printed in BLD Counsels on May 19, 1992. He began with the thesis that 'Love is the distinguishing mark of a Christian disciple,' drawn from 'our Lord's new and most important commandment, "Love one another"' -- noting that it was addressed to the disciples gathered at the cenacle, 'excluding Judas.' He then set the synoptic parallels beside it (Matt. 22, Mark 12, Luke 10), where the Pharisees ask which commandment is 'the greatest' and Jesus answers first 'You shall love the Lord your God' and second 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself.' Both John and the synoptics make love supreme, he granted, but the degree demanded of one disciple toward another is 'far greater' than that owed a 'mere "neighbor"': a non-disciple -- 'Pharisee,' 'scribe' or 'lawyer' -- is told to love his neighbor as himself, while disciples are commanded to love one another as much as 'my love has been for you.' Hence neighbor-love is human, being equal to a man's love for himself, while love for a fellow disciple is divine, being equivalent to God's love for His followers. For the measure of that divine love he turned to St. Paul (Phil. 2:5-11): Christ's humility and obedience to the Father's will, 'accepting even death, death on a cross.' To love like a man is to preserve life; to love like God 'goes beyond preserving life' and 'consists in being Christ' -- offering one's life so that fellow disciples may be saved. Translating the command into Bukas Loob sa Diyos, he wrote that love for those outside the community is human and quantifiable while love for fellow BLD members should be divine and therefore immeasurable, 'to love without counting the cost, as St. Francis says,' since BLD disciples are bound 'not just by common faith and worship, but by a solemn written covenant to love one another as He loves us.' Accordingly, praying for healing, tending the lambs, worshipping at prayer meetings, sacrificing for the BYOP and serving in apostolates must all be done more intensely inside the community than outside. He closed with the day's other readings -- Paul and Barnabas encouraging the disciples 'to persevere in the faith,' and the promise that God will dwell among His people and 'wipe every tear from (our) eyes' -- concluding that the everlasting kingdom of divine love 'shall begin in us and with us.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 22 of 'Love God, Serve Man' collects three speaker introductions Artemio V. Panganiban delivered between 1989 and 1993, prefaced by an editor's note calling him as sought after an introducer as he was a main speaker. The first, for Senate President Jovito R. Salonga at the Century Park Sheraton on March 15, 1989, opened on national history -- in every crisis 'men of integrity, wisdom and courage rise up undaunted and unafraid,' Rizal and Mabini, then Laurel and Recto, and now, after 'an epic battle against a corrupt and decadent dictatorship,' the guest. Declining to read the distributed curriculum vitae, CJP introduced Salonga as he personally knew him: his law professor and dean 30 years earlier, his first boss, and the man whose Far Eastern University teaching he took over. He described a 'forceful tremolo' that spellbinds hearers, listed the firsts -- topping the 1943 bar, Yale's Ambrose Gherini Prize, and topping the senatorial elections in 1965, 1971 and 1987 -- and noted that at the Presidential Commission on Good Government 'the vaunted money, men and machines of Marcos and his cronies' failed to defile a reputation that 'remained unblemished and ever immaculate.' He sketched an ascetic private life -- a man who does not smoke, drink or gamble and does not even own his house in Pasig -- and retold the 1971 Plaza Miranda grenade attack that left Salonga with a thousand shrapnel wounds, who woke asking, 'There must be a reason why God spared my life.' The second, for Maximo V. Soliven on September 30, 1992, called him 'a legend of our time' with a 'many-splendored career,' each superlative conceded as 'only a partial truth. But a truth nonetheless': the longest English-language column six days a week, work for Newsweek and the New York Times, the Philippine Star, the founding of the Philippine Daily Inquirer in 1985 to fight the dictatorship, and, at 27, the pre-martial law Evening News. After the awards, the French knighthood, the interviews with world leaders and the expulsions by Ngo Dinh Diem, Ne Win and Lee Kuan Yew, CJP located the real heroism in Soliven's maximum-security detention as Ninoy Aquino's cellmate and the seven-year writing ban that pained him most. The third, for Dr. Jesus P. Estanislao before the 19th Philippine Business Conference on December 14, 1993, presented him as 'the epitome of a God-loving person and model public servant' and living proof that 'one can be a saint in the midst of the noise and banging of the world,' before running his degrees, his term as secretary of finance and his academic posts, and concluding that nothing in his career had ever placed his integrity or judgment in doubt.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 4 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' reproduced the speech with which Justice Panganiban introduced Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr. as guest of honor. He began by listing the six biographical facts the broadcast and print media had already heralded -- Davide's Cebu schooling and law degree from the University of the Philippines; his election as an opposition member of the Batasang Pambansa during the Marcos years; his membership in both the 1971 Constitutional Convention and the 1986 Constitutional Commission, making him a seasoned constitutionalist; his service as Comelec chair and as head of the commission that investigated the almost-successful 1989 coup attempt; his marriage to Virginia Jimenea-Perez and their five children; and the tears of joy of his 95-year old father -- and then declined to repeat them, choosing instead to introduce the speaker as he had known him during three years together in the Court, in en banc meetings and in the Third and First Divisions Davide chaired. He described a man who lives simply and transparently, who does not drink, smoke or gamble, rarely attends social occasions outside official functions, walks briskly in the early morning, and is humble and soft-spoken yet self-actualized, with no craving for money because he is rich in integrity, wisdom, humility, patriotism and a sense of righteousness. Two things, he said, stood out in Davide's character as a jurist. The first was thoroughness: ponencias loaded with relevant detail, fast and avid reading, a day begun at 3:30 a.m. and an arrival at the Court by 6:30 a.m., an elephantine memory that once quoted back footnotes from CJP's own ponencias, and a pen of laser-like precision. The second was moral courage, which he defined as being to a magistrate what political will is to a sovereign head -- the willingness to battle the establishment, to be a beacon for the weak, and to stand by conviction against all odds -- and which he traced to purity of spirit and clarity of conscience. He closed by saying that the guest had not merely challenged the gods but had become the loftiest of the Olympian gods of Padre Faura.

He opened by thanking UE president Josefina R. Cortes and Law Dean Carlos M. Ortega, recalling that although he studied law at FEU, UE was the site of the 1960 bar examinations in which he placed among the topnotchers, and that he had nearly missed those examinations after falling ill, walking through knee-deep floodwater from the FEU Hospital at the urging of his dean, Jovito R. Salonga. He then catalogued the new e-age fortunes -- Gates, Morgridge and Chambers, Moore and Noyce, Bezos, Case, Dell and Schwab -- and, drawing on Gates's 'The Road Ahead,' described a wallet-sized computer that would replace money, camera, phone and map. He warned that the shift would reshape the graduates' careers: rules of evidence and court procedure would be radically amended, electronic commerce and deregulation would require new doctrines, DNA and cloning would alter civil and criminal law, dentistry would be transformed, and 1.6 million new infotech jobs were opening. His advice, he conceded, would sound strange: to meet new paradigms the graduates should retain, practise and internalize old values, because paradigms change but values endure. He summarized these as three Es under the acronym ExEE -- excellence, illustrated by the 3M employee Art Fry whose Post It note grew from a choir problem; ethics, rooted in character ethic and requiring a change in men rather than a change of men; and eternity, the life after death where our final destiny lies -- closing with Isaiah and an imagined graduate crediting his success decades later to that day's message.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 6 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' reproduced CJP's address to a CAP forum honoring President Sergio Osmena, which he began by insisting the speaker should have been his host, Dr. Alejandro R. Roces -- his FEU mentor, the adviser he recruited for the National Union of Students in 1957, his wedding sponsor in 1961, and the education secretary who made him his legal counsel a year after he passed the bar. He then recounted a televised biography of Aristotle Onassis, who commanded wealth, heads of state and famous women yet died a broken man in 1975 because he never answered the questions Who am I? Why was I born? Where am I headed for? How do I get there? Humans, he argued, share animal appetites but find fulfillment only in their rational and divine natures, and what we call values are the traits that lift us from mere existence to life on high. He then set out three: excellence, defined as competence, dedication to duty and hard work, illustrated by his blind masseur Larry, his barber and his tailor, by Edison's line on perspiration and by Dado Banatao's counting of 100 or 200 failures for every success, and taught by the parable of the farmer who met every turn of fortune with 'Good luck? Bad luck? Who knows?'; ethics, rooted in integrity as honesty and truth regardless of personal consequences, codified for officials in RA 6713 and betrayed by leaders' double standards, double speak and spin doctors, which he blamed, with the Catholic Church's diagnosis of dichotomized Christian lives, for the country's poverty, graft and violence; and eternity, where spiritual laws carry consequences as civil and physical laws do, a plea he extended to Muslim, Jewish and other God-loving listeners, supported by Havel on the common elements beneath religions. He added transparency as a fourth value for public servants, and closed by calling excellence, ethics and eternity the immutable e-values for the e-age and beyond.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 12 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' reproduced CJP's Far Eastern University commencement address, delivered as the university conferred on him the degree of Doctor of Laws, honoris causa. He opened with thanks to President Edilberto C. de Jesus and board chair Dr. Lourdes Reyes Montinola and with a joke that this second honorary doctorate finally made him 'the academic equal of my wife and children,' since he had been 'suffering from a venial inferiority complex' as the only one in his family without a graduate degree. Turning serious, he recalled his own 1960 graduation from the FEU Institute of Law, a father who was 'an underpaid but overworked government employee' supporting four children and seven siblings but who insisted 'education was the key to success and fulfillment in life,' and the deaths of both parents before he could finish -- a course rescued by an FEU scholarship and by his selling bibles to professors and textbooks to classmates. He then set out the four things FEU taught him. First, academic excellence: unable to afford 'the then 15-centavo bus fare' to UP, he enrolled grudgingly at FEU, found the faculty strict and demanding, and was driven by Dean Jovito R. Salonga -- who monitored his grades and called on him to recite at the height of his FEUCSO and NUSP leadership -- to graduate with honors and place among the bar topnotchers. Second, a well-rounded education, learned from Dean Alejandro R. Roces's 'Education for Culture' and President Teodoro Evangelista, from which he drew the legal corollary that 'excellence in law is not enough; a lawyer must also have a good grasp of the arts and sciences.' Third, his Catholic faith, given him by chaplain Fr. Michael Nolan, who 'introduced me to God,' and Fr. James Sheehy, and elaborated into a parallel between human, physical and spiritual laws. Fourth, a hunger for leadership, encouraged by Don Angel Palanca and 'Mang Etoy' del Rosario. He surveyed present FEU policies approvingly and closed with Salonga's teaching that 'it is far more important to aspire for the things that money cannot buy, like integrity, honor, dignity and a reverential regard and love for God.'

Ong as a demonstration of the Rotary motto 'Service above self: he profits most who serves best,' then identified himself with the honorees by recalling his own graduation from Mapa High School some 45 years earlier, a poor but honest government-employee father supporting four children and seven siblings, and his own hawking of newspapers, shining of shoes and peddling of cigarettes on the sidewalks of Espana and Cataluna Streets, along with selling bibles to teachers and textbooks to classmates. Though he had reached 'the dream of every lawyer' in the Supreme Court, he told them he envied them, since 'Honor graduate lang po ako, hindi valedictorian.' His thesis was that 'academic excellence, by itself, is not enough': it must be joined to three other traits, the three Ps. On patience, he warned that brilliant people become impetuous, overbearing and dismissive, confessed that he himself had always been in a hurry and had grown angry when others could not keep up, likened haste to overspeeding, and advised his listeners to 'make haste slowly.' On perseverance, he cited Edison's motto on perspiration, the entrepreneur Diosdado Banatao's report to Asiaweek that 'For every success, there are 100 or 200 failures,' the long chain of defeats that preceded Abraham Lincoln's election at sixty, and the medieval parable of the farmer whose every turn of fortune drew the reply 'Good luck? Bad luck? Who knows? I will just keep doing my best,' concluding that adversities are often preludes to greater victory. On prayer, he quoted Isaiah on God's higher thoughts and ways, testified that God had never abandoned him, noted that the courts, Senate, House and Cabinet all open with prayer, and urged a daily, sincere prayer of any length or language, since God answers 'in His own way, not our way; in His own time, not at the time we demand.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 13 of 'Judicial Renaissance' collects Justice Panganiban's remarks at the launch of Jovito R. Salonga's book 'The Task of Building a Better Nation.' He opened with the 13th International Judicial Conference in Kiev, which he attended with Chief Justice Davide alongside chief justices from former Soviet republics and allies, and whose theme -- judicial independence and the courts' role in safeguarding elections -- honored the Ukrainian Supreme Court for annulling a fraud-ridden presidential election and clearing the way for the balloting that brought Viktor Yushchenko to power. What struck him more than the sessions were the 'corridor conversations' about life after the USSR's collapse: under authoritarian rule everyone had a job but nobody was working, while privatization, deregulation and globalization brought efficiency together with unemployment and inflation. He argued that the Philippines, freed from twenty years of Marcos rule only in 1986, was comparable to those states, and that the yellow People Power revolution had presaged the velvet revolutions of 1989 and Ukraine's orange revolution. Turning to Salonga's book, he set out its diagnosis of three interrelated maladies -- massive poverty, rampant corruption and uncontrolled criminality -- traced to the concentration of wealth in an elite and to a double standard of justice, and its address to the youth, supported by a roll of young leaders from Rizal and Bonifacio to Quezon and Roxas, to which he added the young Salonga himself. He endorsed the book's treatment of the judiciary as guarantor of civil, political and economic rights, repeated his own conviction that those with less in life should have a better chance at competing with those who have more in law, and noted Salonga's defence of Chief Justice Davide against impeachment charges pursued in ruthless, cold-blooded haste. Salonga's prescription -- an open, pluralistic and free society resting on human dignity as the first article of faith -- is distinguished from politicians' copycat incantations, he said, by Salonga's insistence after Confucius that government must be government by example: dissolving his law firm on appointment to the PCGG, living austerely in a rented house with a small car and cotton barongs, authoring the ethics, anti-plunder and anti-coup laws, and forsaking wealth for service. He closed with the 1971 Plaza Miranda grenade attack that left Salonga briefly clinically dead, answering the honoree's question about God's purpose in sparing him: to be a beacon in a darkened country.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 1 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' is the brief statement in which CJP accepted his appointment as the 21st Chief Justice of the Philippines, taking office, as he noted, in the 21st century. He said he accepted with deep humility and a great sense of responsibility, thanked President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo for naming him to what he called the highest nonpolitical office in the land, and offered as his measure of thanks a vow to uphold at all times the constitutional ideals of competence, integrity, probity and independence, which he assumed she had weighed in choosing him. He read the timing of the appointment against the season celebrating the birth of the One who came down to earth to serve and not to be served and who embodies truth, justice and peace, and so saw the office as an opportunity for even greater service to God and country. He named his predecessor, Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr., as his model, citing the aim in The Davide Watch of a judiciary that is independent, effective and efficient, and worthy of public trust and confidence, and Davide's parting confidence that the judiciary could do better still, which he pledged to fulfill. Reflecting on the heavy burden ahead, he took consolation in Pope Benedict XVI, the self-described simple, humble worker in God's vineyard, that the Lord knows how to work through imperfect instruments to bring about great things. He closed by pledging, with the support of his colleagues and of the approximately 2,000 judges and 26,000 court personnel nationwide, to safeguard the liberty of the people and nurture their prosperity while upholding the rule of law and the independence of the judiciary, in an atmosphere of transparency and accountability.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 2 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' answered friends' testimonials with two stories, one fictional and one true. The first was a medieval parable of a farmer whose runaway horse, unexpected windfall of eleven horses, son's broken leg and consequent exemption from a fatal conscription each drew the same reply: 'Good news, bad news, who knows? I will just keep on doing my best and God will do the rest.' The second was CJP's own life. Born poor, the youngest of four children of a father who had left school to support seven siblings, he hawked newspapers, sold cigarettes and shone shoes in postwar Sampaloc, sleeping on sidewalks to wait for the dawn delivery, and received a purely secular education in public schools without catechism. His ambition to be a chemical engineer gave way to his father's insistence on law; a UP scholarship went unused because the family could not afford the bus fare to Diliman, so he enrolled at Far Eastern University nearby, funding his studies by peddling textbooks and selling bibles. A Yale scholarship won on Dean Salonga's recommendation was lost for want of plane fare. Each frustration, he recounted, proved a blessing in disguise: poverty taught him hard work, yielding a cum laude degree and sixth place in the 1960 bar; big dreams carried him to the presidency of a leading newspaper; the lost Yale trip produced Baron Travel Corporation; and his five children earned the Ivy League graduate degrees he had missed. FEU gave him demanding professors, the ideal of knowing everything about something and something about everything, lay Catholic faith through Columban priests, student leadership, and his wife Leni. He declined early government offers and a Cabinet post from President Ramos, accepting instead a Supreme Court seat in 1995, and learned of his appointment as Chief Justice mid-speech at a hotel dinner, freezing before the microphone for the first time in his life.
