one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 8 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' gathered three addresses Chief Justice Panganiban delivered to the youth in 2006 -- the University of Cebu commencement on April 1, the Ateneo de Manila law school graduation on April 23, and the new lawyers' oath-taking at the Philippine International Convention Center on May 9 -- into a single compendium organized around what he called the Three E's of A Life Worth Living: Excellence, Ethics and Eternity. He explained that his workload and judicial propriety forced him to decline most invitations but that these rites returned him to his own youth and gave him, near retirement, an elder's duty to pass on timeless values. Recalling his graduation from the Far Eastern University Institute of Law, he credited his dean Jovito R. Salonga with insisting that academics outranked his student-council and NUSP offices and with refusing to let him abandon the bar examinations when flu and gastroenteritis put him in hospital during the first week. Excellence, he argued, means choosing what one wants most and mastering it, embodied in St. Ignatius of Loyola's magis, and is not the goal but the tool that opens windows of opportunity -- only the first stage of winnowing. Ethics, the second E, rests on old-fashioned principles no code can exhaustively specify, and he rejected the quick fixes of motivational speaking and consumerism, observing that money still cannot buy peace of mind, dignity or respect in a society where the vile deride the upright. For the third E he offered personal testimony: reared poor and schooled without religion, he came to faith late, and he set out the 3 Rs of repentance, restitution and reformation together with the prayer he composed as an associate justice and published in Justice and Faith. He closed by counselling that failure is a detour rather than a dead end, that success should not intoxicate, and with Phillips Brooks's verse on praying for powers equal to one's tasks.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 3 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 2), CJP's June 21, 2009 Inquirer column, is 'a primer on how the Court decides cases in the normal course,' prompted by the Court's unusual signed resolution throwing out the petitions against House Resolution 1109 -- special treatment, he notes, compared with the one-sentence dismissals reserved for 'utterly unmeritorious and cerebrally deficient' petitions. He explains that the Court is a 'review court' that does not take initial cognizance of controversies but mainly affirms, modifies or reverses lower-court rulings and polices jurisdiction and grave abuse, and that it is a 'passive branch' whose authority 'must be triggered by the filing of a petition by a proper party.' Unlike open trial courts, its internal deliberations are confidential -- only the net results (decisions, resolutions, and concurring, dissenting and separate opinions) are released -- and he quotes Justice Regalado that 'in trial courts, the rule is transparency; but in the Supreme Court, it is confidentiality.' The justices decide collegially: they debate and vote independently but bind the Court only in session, with no justice acting alone, and the 'backbreaking job' is done in chambers and at home through study, reflection and writing -- 'they do not talk too much; rather, they write a lot,' the CJ steering discussion to written opinions once it exceeds five minutes. Oral arguments are rare, held in the Padre Faura hearing hall for difficult cases at about 20 minutes a side (often extended), sometimes aided by amici curiae invited as a 'rare privilege,' and followed by written memoranda. Finally he lays out the structure: the Court sits en banc or in three five-member divisions (a division ruling being as final as an en banc one), deciding by a majority of those taking part, with the CJ assigning justices and a strict seniority rule governing seating and the 'working chairman' who runs the CJ's division.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 5 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 2), CJP's December 27, 2009 Inquirer column, catalogues the eight functions of the Chief Justice, written as a turmoil-weary public looked to the Court -- for though they should turn to elected leaders, the abuses they complain of 'come mainly from executive officials.' First, the CJ is 'primus inter pares,' presiding over and shaping the Court's work yet holding 'only one vote,' so he leads by 'moral ascendancy and persuasive skill, not a boss-subordinate relationship.' Second, he is the chief executive of the entire judiciary -- 2,000 judges and 26,000 employees -- who must both honor precedent and 'innovate, re-engineer' the branch. Third, he is a passionate reformer driving speedy justice and automation, interacting even with foreign institutions in a 'sensitive balancing act' that demands public trust in his integrity and independence. Fourth, as the Court supervises the practice of law, he is leader of the bar; fifth, as ex-officio chair of the Philippine Judicial Academy, he is the academic 'maestro' of judicial education; sixth, as JBC chair he is the 'mover and shaker' of judicial selection, since 'the need for quality judgments begins with quality judges'; and seventh, he is the 'administrator, manager, and financial wizard' who, under the Constitution, the Administrative Code, the GAA, the JDF Law (PD 1949) and the SAJ Law (RA 9227), wields 'exclusive sole power' to disburse the judiciary's funds. Eighth, under the 'minute scrutiny' of an inquisitive media, he is a role model and exemplar of public service whose 'quiet persona' draws civic groups in times of political wrangling. In sum, leading 'the last bulwark of democracy' while carrying leadership duties 'to the farthest corners of the country,' the CJ is, CJP argues, 'more accurately addressed' as Chief Justice of the Philippines, not just of the Supreme Court.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 7 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 2), CJP's July 4, 2010 Inquirer column, sets out to demystify 'the most mysterious among major government agencies' -- the Supreme Court, whose processes stay hidden because, unlike trial courts, 'the public discovers a case only after a judgment is issued.' He recalls making it his 'self-imposed duty' to write a book each year to explain the Court's work, and notes that the Court itself did better on May 4, 2010 by codifying its processes as 'The Internal Rules of the Supreme Court' (A.M. No. 10-4-20-SC) -- rules that, by their own caveat, cannot limit the Court's constitutional powers and may be 'amended, revised, deleted, suspended or dispensed with' as the en banc finds 'just, fair and proper.' He explains that the Court sits en banc or in three five-member divisions, that 'a decision rendered by any of the three divisions is deemed a decision of the Court itself,' and that the most important cases (constitutionality of a treaty, law or EO; the death penalty; novel questions; reversals of jurisprudence; huge financial impact) are reserved to the banc. He lays out the 'controversial but well settled' rule that the banc does not exercise appellate jurisdiction over the divisions -- a division's denial of a referral motion is 'final and not appealable' -- while candidly noting that the banc has at times still reviewed and reversed division judgments under its power to suspend the Rules. On workload, he contrasts the Court's roughly 6,000 new cases and 1,200-1,500 full decisions a year with the US Court's ~10,000 petitions and ~100 acceptances, and describes the raffle system (about 30 cases a month per justice) and the new 'Member-in-Charge' role, which oversees a case but may not become its ponente -- so that if a draft ponencia loses the vote, the main dissenter writes the decision and the old draft becomes a dissent.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 1 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 3), CJP's May 27, 2007 Inquirer column, makes the case for mediation as a tool to unclog court dockets, opening with a crisis: fewer than 2,000 judges carry about a million pending cases -- over 500 each, unevenly spread, some buried under 6,000 -- and the backlog worsens daily as new filings outpace judgments that often merely shift the burden to appellate courts. Through its Action Program for Judicial Reform (APJR), he writes, the Court is appointing more judges, computerizing, streamlining the Rules of Court and promoting alternative dispute resolution, of which he singles out mediation. Full-blown litigation is 'tedious, time-consuming, stressful, expensive,' breeding 'broken relationships' and even 'new cycles of violence'; mediation, by contrast, is speedy, peaceful, cheaper and 'win-win,' suited to 'the Filipino way of ending problems sans loss of face,' and usable before or during a case. Once 'frowned upon' for ousting courts of jurisdiction, mediation proved itself in a 2001 pilot in which Philja-trained mediators settled '80 percent of the 1,000 cases referred to them' in under two weeks -- some more than 10 years old -- prompting the Court to institutionalize court-annexed mediation, with a Philja curriculum, the nationwide Philippine Mediation Center, a per-case mediation fee, and mandatory mediation at pretrial (save 'non-mediatable' cases). A 'phase two,' Judicial Dispute Resolution (JDR) -- an innovation from the National Judicial Institute of Canada, piloted in the San Fernando and Bacolod RTCs and pioneered by Executive Judge Adelaida Ala-Medina -- lets the pretrial judge act as conciliator and 'neutral evaluator,' with strict confidentiality if it fails and the case is re-raffled. Mediation has become 'a new profession' of accredited court 'officers,' and CJP closes by recalling the November 2006 National Conference on Court-Annexed ADR Mechanisms (USAID- and Asia Foundation-funded), which reported settling about 24,983 of 35,223 cases mediated from 2002 to 2006 -- a 71-percent success rate.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 3 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 3), CJP's September 9, 2007 Inquirer column, explains the role of the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) in securing a credible judiciary. He begins with why independence matters: where Congress makes laws and the President enforces them, 'unelected judges' decide legal questions by applying law to facts, so a court that upholds a citizen's rights becomes 'a majority of one against the whole government' -- a power obeyed because of constitutional authority and 'implicit trust' in the courts' fairness. Magistrates must therefore be chosen for the four 'nis' (independence, integrity, industry, intelligence) and be immune to 'the plague of ships' (kinship, relationship, friendship, fellowship), with independence and integrity most vital -- 'a judge who does not possess independence and integrity... has no place' on the bench, 'in the same manner that a biased basketball referee has no place in the game.' Under the old system, he recalls, the President had wide latitude but appointees faced Commission on Appointments confirmation that subjected them to 'intensive questioning' and 'personal demands for favors,' diminishing their independence -- so the 1987 Constitution, at Chief Justice Concepcion's suggestion, created the JBC to recommend appointees, limiting the President to a list of at least three per vacancy and abolishing CA confirmation. He details the JBC's seven seats (three ex-officio, four regular) and the practical wrinkle that two members of Congress sit, giving the legislature two of eight votes and raising the approval threshold to five. Yet the reform is incomplete: appointees are shielded from Congress, but JBC members are not, and 'nothing except the highest form of statesmanship' stops a President from steering the Council -- so a President 'could still pack the courts.' He closes by listing the JBC's standing criticisms -- opacity and a 'lackluster' process, unfilled vacancies that aggravate delay, and 'unworthy nominees' who get appointed and 'taint the whole judiciary' -- setting up his follow-up column on reforming it.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 4 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 3), CJP's September 16, 2007 Inquirer column, answers critics who would abolish the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) and revert to Commission-on-Appointments confirmation. He resists: the regular JBC members, who need CA confirmation and may seek reappointment, are themselves 'vulnerable to the same political pressures,' and judges as presidential appointees still feel executive influence -- so the answer is to 'strengthen the anti-political shield of the judiciary, not... shove it back to the partisan mud.' His structural proposal: let the Supreme Court appoint the three regular members representing the retired justices, the Integrated Bar and the legal academe, while the President names only the private-sector representative without CA confirmation -- giving the Court four seats to the President's and Congress's two each, to 'further depoliticize' selection. He sets this in global context: the JBC, then 20 years old, reflects a worldwide reform adopted 'in more than 25 countries,' and, citing Judge Sandra Oxner's study, notes councils abroad average about 20 members, actually appoint judges in France and Italy, are usually chaired by the chief justice, and in Japan are simply done by the Supreme Court. Because systemic change needs a constitutional amendment, he reviews the JBC's interim process reforms -- its October 10, 2000 Rules (implementing 'proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence,' amended at Senator Pimentel's instance to allow a single-member veto for 'questionable integrity'), full-time members and staff (from late 2005), media-opened interviews, and the JBC website he launched on April 21, 2006. He closes with three 'humble suggestions': make public the votes of JBC members for listed candidates (as justices' votes are known), have regular members observe the judges' code of ethics by analogy (no socializing with candidates), and hold those full-time members to the same 'proven competence, integrity, probity and independence' demanded of judges.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 5 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 3), CJP's April 20, 2008 Inquirer column, is a practical guide on how to pass -- 'nay, top' -- the bar exams, following up his earlier piece on the 'dismal' 2007 results and the need for the Supreme Court, the President and law schools to 'collaborate to produce better lawyers.' Feeling 'inadequate' because he 'placed only sixth' long ago, he hands the advice to three recent topnotchers -- Joan de Venecia (2005, UP), Arlene Maneja (2002, UST) and Mercedita Ona (2007, Ateneo) -- and relays their common tips. On mindset: believe you deserve to be there, forget past failures, cultivate composure, and do not compare yourself with others, since 'preparation is an individual task' and understanding beats rote memorization. On planning: make time for 'serious self-evaluation,' budget days by subject, keep a realistic plan, and organize materials (even 'eight separate boxes' by subject) so no time is lost. On self-care: be 'kind to yourself,' allow rest, and stay physically fit -- exercise, sleep, nourishing meals, vitamins and stress management -- lest the body give out. On time: attend review classes for subjects you know but read up first on those you do not, and save 'bar tips' for the pre-week, while abandoning emotional baggage and distractions. On craft: 'perfect your handwriting and grammar,' since examiners are 'only human' and reward readable, logical answers (a point all three topnotchers credit), and write out notes if you learn visually. On substance: 'study smartly' from streamlined materials (codal provisions, a good reviewer, jurisprudence updates), master the basics and their application (even via 'audio codals' on the road), ask for updates since doctrines change and questions are facts-based, and 'Pray. Pray. Pray.' His final reminder: 'there is no shortcut to passing the bar' -- put in the hours, ignore what you cannot control like 'examiners' or 'kinds of questions,' and devote your energy to studying and 'positive thinking.'

Because the President may appoint only from the JBC's list of at least three per vacancy and judicial appointments no longer pass through the Commission on Appointments, 'the primary responsibility... falls squarely on the JBC': if it nominates only the most qualified, every appointment is 'unquestionable,' but 'even if just one undeserving candidate is smuggled into the list, the whole selection process tumbles' -- so its three 's' functions (search, screen, select) 'cannot afford a single mistake.' Conrado Castro's proposal to record and publish the JBC's votes, now cast by secret ballot. Reasoning that since 'the votes of individual justices... are made known,' open JBC voting would 'pinpoint responsibility' when 'magistrates misbehave' and 'breed public confidence,' he endorses it. The JBC, he concludes, must nominate 'only... the most eminent' and 'will be praised or condemned by the quality of all their choices' -- naming the members so readers know who is accountable: 'Will they pass the test?'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 10 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 3), CJP's December 12, 2010 Inquirer column, hails the Supreme Court's small-claims reform as a remedy for the poor, 'to [whom] justice is elusive, distant, and expensive' -- deterred by 'intimidating technicalities,' 'bottomless lawyers' fees' and 'inexplicable delays,' so that they 'simply bear the injustice' and risk becoming 'prey to the importuning of extremists and rebels' who promise 'instant vindication without... due process.' The Court, he writes, 'turned a page in judicial reform' with a system that needs 'no lawyers, no formal pleadings, and no strict legal rules of evidence,' with the judge encouraged to decide 'after just one hearing' -- 'the dream of the legally illiterate.' No new courts or judges were created: 'The Rule on Small Claims Cases' lets the first-level courts (MeTC, MTCC, MTC, MCTC) sit concurrently as Small Claims Courts -- 'the Poor Man's Courts' -- for money claims not exceeding P100,000 (purely civil cases, the civil aspect of criminal actions, or the enforcement of barangay settlements and arbitration awards), begun by a ready-made 'Statement of Claim' and answered within 10 days by a verified 'Response,' with court-staff help. To keep things summary and final, the Rule bars most motions and 'even petitions for certiorari, mandamus, and prohibition,' and forbids lawyers from appearing at the hearing (though parties may consult counsel before or after). The hearing has two phases: the judge first conducts 'Judicial Dispute Resolution' (mediation, conciliation, neutral evaluation) and, failing settlement, a 'Judicial Decision Phase' in which -- unlike a passive ordinary-case judge -- he takes an 'interventionist role,' 'actively eliciting evidence' while staying 'strictly neutral,' ensuring 'a level playing field while protecting the weak.' The hearing must end in one day, with a same-day, 'final and unappealable' judgment immediately furnished to the parties -- a reform meant to 'substantially declog court dockets' and, 'more important, dispense swifter justice to the poor and powerless.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 1 of 'A Centenary of Justice' reproduces the Closing Statement Justice Panganiban delivered on June 11, 2001 -- the Supreme Court's exact 100th birthday -- at the final lecture of Phase I of the Centenary Lecture Series, which he calls 'the fulcrum of the celebrations' among the Court's 50-plus centenary activities. He surveys the series begun July 11, 2000: former CJ Andres R. Narvasa opened it with 'The Chief Justices in Philippine History'; retired CJ Enrique M. Fernando spoke on a century of constitutionalism; Justice Ameurfina A. Melencio Herrera honored the women of the bench in 'Feminine Grace, the High Court and Jurisprudence' ('though outnumbered, the lady justices were never out-written, out-argued or out-achieved by the men'); Prof. Michael O. Mastura addressed 'Shari'ah Law and the Philippine Legal System'; and foreign luminaries Justice Dorit Beinisch of Israel and Dr. Pal Solt of Hungary spoke on civil liberties and the role of supreme courts, illustrating the universality of human-rights principles. Four lectures treated current jurisprudential trends -- including 'Old Doctrines and New Paradigms' by 'an incumbent member of the Court whose name need not be mentioned' (CJP himself, the book's Chapter 2). CJP frames the series as a deliberate past-present-future arc, closed by the incumbent Chief Justice's reform vision. He extols the 'Davide Watch' -- the judiciary-at-the-new-millennium program announced on CJ Davide's assumption on November 30, 1998, 'inspired by Scripture, born of idealism, but grounded on the reality of the possible' -- stressing that it is not 'merely a broad statement of intent' but is 'complemented by a definite development plan implemented day by day' through the Action Program for Judicial Reform (APJR), backed by the UN Development Fund, World Bank, Asia Foundation, UNICEF, ADB, and bilateral aid from Japan, Canada, Australia, the US and the Netherlands. His governing thesis: a centenary 'cannot be justified by a mere rehash of past successes or by an overextended gloating over the present' but must 'set forth our collective dreams of the future.' He closes on the song line 'the trouble with hello is goodbye,' insisting that while the lecture series must end, its influence will endure as 'a well-remembered renaissance in the judiciary.'

First, the Foundation for the Enhancement of Legal Education (chaired by Atty. Ricardo J. Romulo): the Court seeds P10 million and the Foundation raises P40 million for a P50-million endowment funding national professorial chairs and scholarships for poor law students, paying full-time professors at rates comparable to the Asian Institute of Management so under-resourced schools can 'teach law in a grand manner' as Ateneo and Silliman do. Second, a Special Committee on Legal Education under Justice Jose C. Vitug reviewing the curriculum, with a corollary group under retired Justice Ameurfina Melencio A. Herrera reforming the bar examinations. Third, a national moot court competition under former UP Law Dean Merlin M. Magallona. Fourth, a National Speech Festival of debates, oratorical and essay contests co-sponsored by the Philippine Association of Law Schools and supervised by Justice Secretary Hernando B. Perez, with 75 law schools from 9 regions participating (an editorial bracket records the winners: UP's Claude Albert Morales in oratory, Xavier University in debate, and FEU's Margarita Victorino in the essay contest). His governing thesis is that mastery of language is the most basic requirement of lawyering -- 'a student who does not have a singular command of communication skills has no place in the noble profession of law' -- because 'language is a time binder' that let Mendel and Einstein transmit lifetimes of discovery 'in just a matter of hours.' He closes wishing the debaters to 'become the competent and ethical lawyers that you aspire to be.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 5 of 'A Centenary of Justice' reproduces CJP's speech at the 'Advocates' Forum for Media' (March 16, 2001, Linden Suites, Ortigas), explaining the Supreme Court's centenary push for mediation as a remedy for clogged dockets and delayed justice -- a problem he had earlier addressed in 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' (2000). He opens with a civilizational arc: ancient disputes were settled by 'superior muscles, swords or guns' where 'Might dictated right,' until gentility taught that 'right is better than might; the pen, more powerful than the sword; and reason, more reliable than aggression,' giving rise to constitutions, codes and courts. But litigation, he notes, is 'tedious, time-consuming, stressful, expensive,' and often ends in 'broken relationships and permanent animosities,' sometimes inflicting 'deeper wounds' and 'new cycles of violence.' The e-age alternative is Alternative Dispute Resolution (negotiation, conciliation, mediation and arbitration) -- 'old methods with a new twist,' some older than litigation, now refined into an integral part of judicial reform. He cites their institutional anchoring (Rule 18 of the Rules of Court at pretrial, the Interim Rules on Corporate Rehabilitation, the E-Commerce Act and the Retail Trade Liberalization Law) and the cautionary case of Purefoods Corporation v. CA, where a dispute over generators bought to ease the 1992 power crisis was decided only in 2000, 'when the crisis was already over.' Focusing on mediation, he describes Asia Foundation-funded PhilJA training directed by Boston- and Harvard-trained Filipino mediator Annabelle T. Abaya, and argues mediation's distinctive value: it resolves disputes 'speedily, conveniently and peacefully,' conforms to 'the Asian and Filipino ways of solving problems without loss of face,' and is especially apt for continuing relationships (family, labor, tenancy, commercial, consumer and barangay-level). He announces 'Settlement Week' (March 26-April 6), when over 300 regional trial courts in Metro Manila, Cebu and Davao would simultaneously refer actual cases to 300 trained mediators, and closes by asking media to help PhilJA and the Court popularize 'this old method with a new Philja twist.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 12 of 'A Centenary of Justice' reproduces CJP's keynote at the PRSP Anvil Awards (February 23, 2001, Hotel Intercontinental, Makati), included in the book because it lays out the Supreme Court's transparency policy. After congratulating the Grand Anvil winner (the Intel Philippines Science Fair) as a model of corporate selflessness, CJP gives three reasons for speaking. Carpio Sr., founder and first president of the PRSP and 'Dean of Filipino PR Practitioners,' who once nearly recruited CJP into his PR firm. Khan Jr. His governing thesis is that the once-'inscrutable' Court -- 'a fortress, a Mount Olympus' -- must embrace transparency because, though its rulings are nonpolitical, it 'can be effective only insofar as it retains the long-term support of the public,' which is possible only if the institution is understood; hence the PIO's objective is simply 'to tell others the truth about the Supreme Court and its work,' not to 'sanitize,' 'angle,' 'proselytize' or 'propagandize.' He notes the reform program's broad support (World Bank, UNDP, USAID, CIDA, the Dutch and Belgian governments, AusAID, ADB, the Asia Foundation) and closes with a call for PR practitioners to help, since 'public relations and judicial dispensation have a basic commonality -- the search for truth.' He now reports the sequel: on January 30, 2001 the full Court UNANIMOUSLY denied the movants' Motion for Reconsideration and upheld the Third Division's own unanimous original decision. On the merits, the Court reaffirmed that the Court of Appeals correctly refused to annul the title -- res judicata applied through the Margolles case because 'absolute identity of parties is not required but only substantial identity,' Firestone and the Margolles losing parties having raised the same argument against OCT No. 4216 (that it covered forest land so the 1929 registration court lacked jurisdiction over the Gana spouses), making them 'privy in law'; the burden of proving a 70-year-old decree void rests on the petitioner; and the State faced no real loss of patrimony, since reverted land 'would not be devoted to public use' but reserved for disposition to private persons, including Firestone itself -- 'a simple matter of equity and good sense.' CJP's purpose in including the piece is institutional: the unanimous outcome showed 'the folly' of ignoring the maxim that 'Sauce for the poor goose should be the same sauce for the rich gander,' since the banc's needless takeover 'merely resulted in a waste of precious time' and 'uselessly and imprudently clogged the Court's dockets.'

He then turns to the provocative idea of eliminating paper from 'the most paper-dependent discipline in the world,' where 'Put it in writing' assumes paper and rules like parol evidence, the statute of frauds and best evidence carry 'a definite bias in favor of documentation.' CJP closes with measured restraint, noting there is 'as yet no intention... to eliminate paper as the primary medium,' and welcoming the lecture as 'the epochal prelude to paperless legal proceedings in our country.'

His first Dissent (Imelda Marcos v. Comelec, 15 days after oath) and first ponencia (Ty v. Trampe, 52 days after, nullifying an unreasonable real-estate-tax increase) anchor the chronology; Tañada v. Angara (WTO, 72 pages) is the longest ponencia. The thesis: 'simple English comprehensible as much as possible to a high-school graduate' so the Constitution is read 'in the sense understood by the ordinary men and women who place their lives on the line in its defense' (Marcos Dissent). 'More than lingual elegance and even legal pugnacity, I strive for simplicity, clarity and precision in nuances and shades of meanings.' Part I lays out a six-part ponencia anatomy (introduction → statement of the case → statement of facts → issues → Court ruling → disposition, with optional epilogue), distinguishes criminal from noncriminal cases, codifies the present-tense convention ('the drama of each case becomes more vivid... as if the parties or their counsel are actually and presently arguing'), and demands disciplined penalty designation and an acquittal-clause RELEASE language. The Epilogue records the monastic discipline of chambered work -- completely sold his law-firm interests, resigned all business, cut civic memberships with three exceptions (Pontifical Council for the Laity, Rotary Club of Manila, Bantayog ng mga Bayani Foundation), bars visitors and personal phone calls, and includes letters marked 'personal' in the Court agenda because 'there is nothing personal about matters pending before the Court.' He closes with a Lord's-Prayer echo: 'Your will be done, oh Lord, not mine.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 4 of 'Justice and Faith' is CJP's FEU Institute of Law commencement address (c. 1995), introduced by his former FEUCSO predecessor Judge Clemente M. Soriano and hosted by Dean Justice Oscar R. Victoriano. CJP returns to 'the green and gold portals' thirty-five years after his own 1960 graduation, recounting his Salonga-tutored bar-prep, hospitalization on day one of the 1960 exams, and the FEU-bar-topnotcher pedigree that later produced his Panganiban-Benitez-Parlade-Africa-Barinaga law firm. The body of the speech diagnoses the Philippine justice system's deepest grievance -- clogged dockets and lawyerly delay tactics -- quoting Chief Justices Marcelo B. Fernan and Andres R. Narvasa's UP self-assessments and the Multi-Sectoral Conference on the Administration of Justice CJP chaired at De La Salle on October 17, 1992; the 'anak na pinag-awayan' courtroom joke supplies the popular face of that delay, while the Flor Contemplacion outrage (decoded against a SWS finding that 1 in 3 Metro Manila households had a member abroad) supplies the moral. CJP then gives the graduates a seven-point advice: improve bar preparation; embrace ADRs (arbitration and mediation, including the ICC's international rules); cooperate with judges through pre-trial admissions; use law to promote justice not to delay it (anchored in retired Justice Isagani R. Cruz's 'conscience of the government' ponencia); volunteer free legal services for the poor (IBP, PPCRV, NAMFREL); develop a personal philosophy of law (S × P = D realism, with Holmes/Pound/Concepcion as exemplars); and finally, surrender to God. He closes by collapsing the six secular advices into the seventh through Philippians 3:8-9 ('not by the letter that killeth but by the spirit that giveth life') and Matthew 25 -- the ultimate question we will be asked at judgment is whether we used possession and profession to defend the weak and the poor, not how many bar honors, millions or titles we collected.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 4 of 'Love God, Serve Man' transcribes the extemporaneous report Atty. Artemio V. Panganiban rendered to President Fidel V. Ramos on October 17, 1992 at De La Salle University, Greenhills, as chairman of the Workshop on Administration of Justice of the Multi-Sectoral Conference convened by the Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry to propose a program of government for the next 1,000 days. He opened at the Cenacle, where the risen Lord twice greeted the demoralized disciples with 'Peace be with you!', and used that bequest to frame the report: the workshop had chosen the government's single-minded pursuit of peace as the major achievement of Ramos's first 100 days (June 30 to October 8, 1992), seeing 'the bright dawn of PAX RAMOS in our troubled land of the morning.' His premise was that there can be no genuine peace -- one that solves the root causes of violence rather than merely halting hostilities -- without justice first: justice that is speedy, efficient and objective, based on solidarity with the oppressed and meaning development for the poor. He noted the Supreme Court's constitutional powers of administrative supervision and of review for grave abuse of discretion, credited its on-the-job training of judges, continuous hearings within 90 days and desk books, but recorded persisting complaints of delay and of poor decision quality. Because the President's own role in adjudication is limited to appointments, supervision of prosecutors and police, and review of quasi-judicial agencies, he argued that no meaningful reform is possible unless the President, Congress and the Supreme Court join in a 'National Covenant of Justice and Peace'; since judges are barred from non-judicial activity, the workshop instead addressed a written appeal to all three. He then summarized eleven recommendations drawn from resource speakers Irene R. Cortes and Eduardo de los Angeles and resource persons Franklin M. Drilon and Antonio T. Carpio -- supporting the peace process, a JUDGEWATCH formed by 188 NGOs, citizen awareness, upgraded legal education, barangay police visibility and the revived foot patrol, gun control, and docket-unclogging through small claims courts, mandatory commercial arbitration, jurisdictional pruning, strict time limits, discovery and judicial mediation, plus coordination of executive law functions, free legal aid for indigents, continuing review of rules, and review of overseas contract worker cases. Noting that more cases are filed than resolved, he closed by paraphrasing John F. Kennedy -- negotiate to remove fear -- and by invoking the love, justice and peace of Jesus.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 1 of 'Battles in the Supreme Court' opened what CJP called a little window on how the Court works, written to mark his third anniversary as a justice on October 10, 1998. He began with Chief Justice Andres R. Narvasa's March 1998 farewell to the Manila Overseas Press Club, where Narvasa said he was proudest of the Court's independence in deciding cases affecting the President, and answered the charge that appointees of President Fidel V. Ramos had lined up their votes for him: in three years, CJP wrote, he had perceived no improper political, ideological or partisan alignment, no power blocs, cliques, coteries or factions, and no justice, not even the primus inter pares, had asked him to vote a particular way. Promising not to violate the confidentiality of deliberations, he described instead the Court's unwritten practices. The Court is basically a review court, passive until a petition is filed, deciding whether a lower court or any branch of government committed reversible error or grave abuse of discretion. Its work is collegial: no justice can bind the Court alone, agendas run to 150 to 250 items, discussion is brief and argument is written rather than spoken, and oral arguments with amici curiae are rare. He set out the seniority protocol, the divisions, robes and sessions, then traced the three rounds a case passes through, listing twenty-one grounds for dismissal by minute resolution in the first, the comment-and-reply exchange in the second, and memoranda, deliberation, a ponencia and nominal voting from the most junior justice upward in the third. Turning to delay, he used three years of Annual Reports to show output matching input and blamed an inherited backlog of about 2,000 cases, welcoming the transfer of NLRC review to the Court of Appeals. He closed with how cases are raffled and assigned, his reservation about per curiam anonymity, and the observation that the real battles occur in the banc.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 2 of 'Battles in the Supreme Court' served as CJP's prologue to the case accounts that follow. Covering his first three years on the Court, from October 10, 1995 to October 10, 1998, he described debating questions with almost every member of the Court and receiving dissenting, concurring and separate opinions on his ponencias. He recounted his own development: in his first months he was awed by the consuming presence of colleagues whose lucidity, legal wisdom and analytical skill he admired, and he tended to adhere to precedents and conventional doctrines, until he realized that being with the majority was not as fulfilling as expressing his thoughts openly and freely according to his best light. He quoted Justice Isagani A. Cruz's April 1998 column, which noted his dissent in People v. Montilla and hoped he would see that dissenting would not diminish the dissenter's cause or his integrity, and gave his reply that jurists are never diminished by their dissents, only by their reckless or thoughtless concurrences. As evidence that he would not be a fence-sitter or bench warmer, he cited his output of 115 to 120 ponencias a year and the doubling of his separate opinions to thirteen in his third year, pledging to concur most of the time but to dissent steadfastly, even if alone, when the need arose. He then catalogued his disagreements colleague by colleague -- with Narvasa on the Death Penalty Law, Regalado on searches and arrests, Davide on charter change, Romero on illegitimate children, Bellosillo on Filipino First, Puno on privacy, Vitug on the right of first refusal, Kapunan on residence, Mendoza on political advertising, Francisco on obedience to superiors, Purisima on the Marcos acquittal -- then listed the dissents and concurrences his own ponencias drew, and the cases that ended unanimous. He closed by noting that constitutional cases imbued with public interest sparked the most debate, and that his summaries were written from his own viewpoint.

one_paragraph_summary: The Epilogue to 'Battles in the Supreme Court' opens with a private exchange during deliberations: a fellow justice, torn between upholding his earlier vote and changing it on a Motion for Reconsideration, asked Justice Panganiban how he made up his mind and wrote his opinions, and received the reply, 'I study, I reflect, I pray and stick to my conscience.' Pressing further, CJP reminded his colleague that fifty years hence their decisions would still be discussed and dissected by lawyers, law students and the public, and that beyond that audience they would have to account for their actions at the pearly gates before a Lord and Supreme Judge who might apply the very standards by which they had judged others. He confesses that during the early months of his incumbency he struggled to conform to precedent and conventional judicial wisdom, but learned over the years that he found greater fulfillment in expressing himself openly and decisively even when in the minority or alone, repeating his conviction that jurists are never diminished by their dissents, only by their reckless and thoughtless concurrences. He salutes the colleagues who likewise deliberated actively and wrote voraciously, wishes that their tribe increase, and surveys the departures around him -- Feliciano and Padilla already gone, Regalado, Narvasa and Romero reaching compulsory retirement, and the short-tenured Hermosisima, Torres, Francisco and Martinez who nonetheless left their imprints -- while finding consolation in the probity and fearlessness of their younger successors. His closing thesis is institutional: the mission of a jurist and of the Court does not depend on the number of unanimous decisions, for a free and thinking Court cannot be expected to speak with a uniform and hackneyed voice; the people's rights are best served by a divided Court that is a veritable marketplace of free ideas. The real victory of jurists, he concludes, lies not in conforming to conventional wisdom but in the courage to express their deepest thoughts and to pursue lonely causes, caring nothing for the fortunes of individual litigants and everything for principles, causes and philosophies. He ends personally, with over eight years still ahead of him and three already immensely enjoyed.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 1 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' reproduces Panganiban's tribute at the retirement of Mr. Justice Antonio M. Martinez, opening with Chief Justice Andres R. Narvasa's image of a justice returning to the land of the living after being judicially entombed, and listing the ordinary liberties the retiring magistrate regains, including release from the silence every member of the Court is pledged to observe. From that occasion he turns to the nature of the office: no university on earth teaches a course on how to be a Supreme Court justice, and, quoting Anthony Lewis's 'Gideon's Trumpet,' a justice brings only his character, intellect, education, experience, human understanding and imagination, relying thereafter on creativity, innovation, reflection and prayers. He notes that career jurists adjust more easily than those picked straight from private practice, the academe or the nonjudicial branches, yet all feel at once the god-like finality of decisions no other agency may review. Where elected officials answer to current popular sentiment, magistrates must live in a world of reason where logic, evidence and conscience are their only yardsticks, a discipline made possible by the permanency of tenure and the independence the Constitution grants. The search for principles and doctrines, he argues, is the essence and bedrock of a jurist's work, and cases are won by reasoned argument rather than by popularity, compromise, friendship or vote-trading. Conceding that the Court is effective only while it keeps the public's faith, since it commands neither army, police nor money, he distinguishes the shifting winds of public emotion from long-term institutional trust and insists that the Court's function is not to mirror popular ideas but to teach and open vistas to enlightened opinion. Invoking Frankfurter's phrase that the Court is 'the conscience of society,' he defines the test of a magistrate's mettle as standing by convictions when the mob rages, and closes by mourning Martinez's too-brief stint and praising his scholarly ponencias and passion for truth and fairness.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 2 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' is Panganiban's brief welcome at the ceremonies honoring the retiring Chief Justice, and it turns on a single contrast. Court watchers, he observes, have compared the Supreme Court to an unsolvable puzzle contained in a riddle shrouded in mystery and imbedded in an enigma: they may appreciate its role as protector of the Constitution and defender of the people's liberties, but they find its mystic ways impenetrable and often picture its members as a collection of grumpy old men with failing eyesights, so low-profile that they cannot be picked out in a tapestry of common mortals. Yet ordinary mortals they are not, he says, because their decisions speak of precedence and continuity bordering on eternity, as though their authors had been with the Court since its birth almost a century earlier. Even to lawyers the Court is distant, impregnable and impersonal, an abstraction on Mt. Olympus that receives petitions, supplications and prayers and, after an unpredictable lapse, issues promulgations and commandments; in the one percent of the time it emerges from its hidden fortress for oral arguments, it mystifies counsel with hostile and perplexing questions before their valued clients. Retirement ceremonies are the exception. The justices exchange their dull all-black working robes for scarlet-lined ceremonial togas, discard their impatient frowns, nod and wave in recognition of friendly faces, and come down from their Olympian thrones to speak at microphones normally reserved for mere lawyers. The day's proceedings, he adds, are unusual because they honor the Chief himself but traditional because they follow familiar numbered sequences culled from a century of usage, and the Court has every reason to be friendly because it is proclaiming both its leader's virtues and the collective achievements of the seven years he headed it. He welcomes the guests in Tagalog and closes by inviting them to sit easy, relax, smile, and for once even applaud.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 3 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' reproduced a short inspirational message Justice Panganiban delivered to trial judges. He opened with an apocryphal story: a lawyer with a multi-billion-peso case pending visited a newly inducted judge and, accused of bribery for parking a brand-new Mercedes Benz in the driveway, explained that he was not giving but selling the car for one thousand pesos -- at which the pacified jurist said he was buying two. The joke, he said, demonstrated the temptations pressed on the bench, some brazen and some subtle: blackmail, political pressure, friendship, kinship and even religious relationships, with lawyers often retained for their judicial connections rather than their skill, so that the ultimate question litigants ask is not whether the case is meritorious but whether counsel knows the judge. Because judges must finally rely on themselves, he set out what he called the four "Ins" of a good judge. Integrity meant not merely honesty toward others but intellectual decency and personal honor, judged by intentions known only to oneself and to God. Independence meant freedom from intellectual, mental and emotional bias, illustrated by Earl Warren, mocked on appointment as a mere politician but remembered as the personification of an independent judiciary. Industry meant a passion for work extending into evenings and early mornings, when a judge has the solitude to wrestle with conscience. Intelligence meant organized thought, grammatical expression and current knowledge of law, since law is a jealous mistress. He described the renunciations the black robes require -- of business, associations and social life -- and then recommended three daily practices: rereading the Canons of Judicial Ethics and Code of Professional Responsibility one provision at a time, interpreting them strictly and resolving all doubts against oneself; keeping a Bible or other book of faith at hand, as Chief Justice Davide did in cutting the Bible at random each morning; and saying a short daily prayer of praise as well as petition. He closed by reciting the prayer he had composed on October 10, 1995, his first day in the Court.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 5 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' assessed the first year of Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr., whose elevation on November 30, 1998 Justice Panganiban reported as universally acclaimed -- even by the President's critics, and reflected in Pulse Asia surveys showing the Supreme Court topping approval ratings, though he cautioned that the Court does not thrive on popularity but must keep enough residual public respect for its decisions to be obeyed. He traced the program's origin to Davide's habit of cutting the Bible at random: on the morning of his oath-taking it opened on 2 Maccabees 10, "Purification of Temple and City," which Davide read as a commission to cleanse the judicial stables and, in his Knights of Columbus speech, as a call to metanoia before any institutional change. CJP then reproduced "The Davide Watch" in full -- its policy statement, its vision of a judiciary independent, effective, efficient and worthy of public trust and of a legal profession that is ethical and accessible, and its mission items -- and summarized its core values as IIEE for the bench and EP for the bar, noting the SC-UNDP-funded Blueprint of Action then forthcoming under Justice Bellosillo. He inventoried the first-year measures: lump-sum appropriations won from Congress against a judiciary budget of only 1.12 percent of the national total; a more transparent Judicial and Bar Council; the new Committee on Public Information he was asked to chair and a Public Information Office under Atty. Khan; a long list of administrative cases ending in dismissals and forfeitures; PHILJA's strengthening, computerization and the Court's new web page; rulings such as St. Martin Funeral Home and Fabian that redirected appeals to the Court of Appeals; reorganized Divisions; the first regional judicial dialogs, including the Cagayan de Oro sortie he joined; and a reform program for the bar built on mandatory continuing legal education and accelerated discipline. He closed with an essay on Davide's decision-writing and juridical thought -- pro-environment in Oposa and Tano, a stickler for the rule of law in Quijada and Regala, conventional yet capable of the innovation CJP had opposed in the PIRMA case, and deeply spiritual -- all sewn together, he argued, by the credo Leadership by Example, which he traced to the Gospel of Mark.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 1 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' reproduces the substantive part of Panganiban's paper 'Speeding up Quality Justice,' written as chairman of the Supreme Court Committee on Public Information. He opens with the grounds on which judges have been disciplined -- arrogance, ignorance, incompetence, dishonesty, delay, corruption, partiality and 'pesky' illegal TROs -- and argues that sanctions alone cannot raise standards. Refusing to deny or excuse delay, he sets out the statistics: from 1995 to 1999 the Supreme Court disposed of more cases than were filed, reducing a post-EDSA backlog of about 6,000 to roughly 1,000, so that 'zero backlog' could fittingly mark its centenary on June 11, 2001. The lower courts run the other way, the first-level courts alone growing by 'a humongous total of 324,174,' with Court Administrator Benipayo reporting a disposition rate falling to 25.50 percent and a caseload of 801,625. Endorsing Chief Justice Davide's aim of fair, impartial and swift justice, he insists speed without evenhandedness 'would be railroading tyranny to our hapless people.' He classifies causes as systemic -- the adversarial system's due-process mechanics, an open-ended appellate system, BP 22 collection cases, thousands of automatic capital appeals, review of constitutional bodies, and supervision of all courts and lawyers -- and man-made, from unfamiliar or corrupt judges and 33 percent vacant salas to lawyers who abuse the Rules and dilatory court personnel. His solutions run in three lines: reforming law schools, bar examinations, JBC screening, Philja education and the RA 8557 pre-judicature course, plus rationalized compensation through exemption from the Salary Standardization Law and real fiscal independence; upgrading Halls of Justice, computers and the Court's website, and professionalizing judicial administration; and systemic measures from ADR and discovery to small claims courts, continuous trial, decriminalized bouncing checks and filtered capital appeals. The common denominator, he concludes, is transparency and accountability.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 2 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' is Panganiban's address to the Management Association of the Philippines, opening with personal tributes to MAP's Ric Pascua and Johnny Santos and an apology to old friends for the seclusion of a justice 'entombed in judicial cloisters,' since jurists must not only be impartial but appear so. He then poses three questions: the main complaints against the judiciary, the reforms that answer them, and what business can do. Through three apocryphal stories about 'Hukom Juan Suplado' -- a lawyer offering to sell the judge a Mercedes for a thousand pesos, a garbled court translation, and a 75-year-old man who turns out to be the infant two women once fought over -- he identifies corruption, incompetence and delay, or CID. Corruption, he says, includes the 'three ships' of friendship, relationship and kinship, and he cites the World Bank's 'Combating Corruption in the Philippines' and a February 2000 SWS survey in which 62 percent perceived significant judicial corruption. He then surveys the Court's reform program under its Centenary Executive Committee: upgrading law schools through a Committee on Legal Education, the new Board of Legal Education and the Foundation for the Enhancement of Legal Education; reforming recruitment through the JBC and RA 8557's pre-judicature course; rationalizing compensation through fiscal independence and exemption from the Salary Standardization Law; improving the disciplinary process; building Halls of Justice, distributing 1,500 computers and opening the Court's website; professionalizing judicial administration; and easing dockets through ADR, discovery, alternatives to BP 22 cases and filtered capital appeals. Because stability requires predictable justice, 'judicial reform becomes also the business of business,' and he asks four things: never bribe a judge, fund private reform efforts, send good lawyers to the bench, and pray -- closing with Bishop Benny Tudtud's 'Disturb Us O Lord.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 3 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' is Panganiban's lecture asking how microchips, modems and media have affected life on Mount Olympus, organized around three impacts of cyber technology. Invoking Alvin Toffler's The Third Wave, he argues that the information phase is transforming everything, citing the $162-billion AOL absorption of Time Warner, Amazon.com and its Person-of-the-Year founder Jeff Bezos, and Bill Gates's fortune built on compressing knowledge into microchips. Angara, Tatad v. Secretary of Energy and Garcia v. Corona; and the media rulings in ABS-CBN v. Comelec, protecting exit polls, and Vasquez v. Court of Appeals, importing actual malice. Second, he inventories the Court's response: a Committee on Computerization and the MISO, the Case Administration System, Computer-Assisted Legal Research covering decisions from 1901, computerized administrative processes, the Court's website, 1,500 computers for trial courts, and planned speech recognition, electronic data interchange, information kiosks and video teleconferencing. Third, he describes how a once-sacrosanct bench, whose justices were 'treated like little deities,' now faces a questioning post-EDSA generation and an invasive press. Of four options -- surrender, silence, combat or professional help -- the Court chose the fourth, creating the Committee on Public Information he chairs. He closes on transparency and accountability, welcoming fair scrutiny but pleading for discreet restraint, since 'the media and the judiciary are natural partners.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 1 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' is Artemio V. Panganiban's short introduction to the Action Program for Judicial Reform, followed by the verbatim reprint of that program's Executive Summary. He began by naming the 'Davide Watch' -- announced by Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr. immediately after he assumed office on November 30, 1998 -- as the centerpiece of Davide's stewardship, noting that he had already written extensively about that vision in his earlier book 'Leadership by Example' and that this volume would instead focus on 'the implementing effort,' detailed in the 156-page 'Action Program for Judicial Reform 2001-2006.' He described the APJR as 'comprehensive, pervasive and wide-ranging,' taking its bearing from past initiatives, especially the 'Blueprint of Action for the Judiciary,' and from consultations with stakeholders across the country held during Chief Justice Andres R. Narvasa's term and funded by a United Nations Development Program grant. Approved by the Supreme Court on December 8, 2000, the program is superintended by an Executive Committee whose full membership he lists, from Davide as chairman and Justice Josue N. Bellosillo as vice chairman through Justices Puno and Panganiban, Philja Chancellor Melencio Herrera, Court Administrator Velasco and the Integrated Bar of the Philippines president, with a technical staff named as well. He stressed that the APJR is 'the only standing committee in the Supreme Court that is directly headed by the Chief Justice,' with a full-time Program Management Office under Evelyn Toledo-Dumdum handling implementation, and, unable to reproduce the full text, reprinted the Executive Summary as background for the book. That summary concedes that earlier efforts, 'though numerous, have been sporadic'; restates the Davide Watch vision of a judiciary 'independent, effective and efficient, and worthy of public trust and confidence' and its six mission goals; sets out nine guiding principles and a four-pronged sectoral program addressing seven critical issues, from case congestion and budget deficiencies to politicized appointments and deficient court technology; costs the 2001-2006 program at PhP 4.3 billion, 53.45 percent domestic and 46.55 percent from official development assistance, with 75.47 percent going to institutions development, 18.33 percent to human resources, 5.83 percent to judicial systems and procedures and about PhP 16 million to reform support systems; anticipates external financing peaking early and declining as domestic funding sustains implementation; and describes the management arrangements -- phasing, sequencing, monitoring and evaluation, an inter-agency steering committee and an institutionalized program management office -- while calling the APJR 'an evolving document' that must remain responsive to the judiciary's and the country's needs.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 3 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' reproduces Artemio V. Panganiban's speech before 'this elite group representing American business in our country', delivered after weeks of criticism of how the judiciary had reached its recent decisions. Declining to discuss personalities or specific litigations, he said the Supreme Court had long recognized its problems and had embarked on the Action Program for Judicial Reform, begun in 2001 and due for full implementation by 2006. He named three: corruption, incompetence and delay -- 'the "CID" of our judicial system.' At the May 2002 political summit at the Manila Hotel, he reported, there was a common perception of 'two types of law -- one for the rich and one for the poor,' and corruption extends beyond bribery to 'the three "ships" that plague public service: friendship, relationship and kinship.' Incompetence showed in incomprehensible pleadings and in jurists whose grasp of elementary law 'appalls even high school graduates'; delay came from antiquated procedures, rising caseloads, vacant judgeships and litigants who win by 'confusing, outwitting or bankrupting their opponents.' On discipline, the Court had for the first time in its century admonished one of its own members, dismissed a Court of Appeals justice and suspended the Sandiganbayan's presiding magistrate, penalizing about 350 lower-court judges between January 1999 and April 2002. On recruitment, a third of trial courts stood vacant because a regional trial court judge earned about P25,333 -- 'a measly $500' -- less than half a comparable Makati lawyer's pay; the Court therefore sought a fixed share of the national budget, cut by Congress from two percent to under one, and exemption from the Salary Standardization Law. On competence, he cited Philja's 92 training programs in 2001, updated Rules of Court and new rules on electronic evidence, and the Benchbooks now called 'the bibles of judges.' On delay, he defined quality justice as 'not the rushing of kangaroo justice, but of justice based on truth,' reported that Zero Backlog had cut the Court's dormant cases from about 2,000 in 1995 to under 50 while lower-court filings still outran dispositions by thousands a year, described 1,500 computers loaded with Lex Libris, and promoted mediation. Domestic honors and donor support from the World Bank, CIDA, USAID and others, he said, proved that the APJR was 'not a hodgepodge of uncoordinated and poorly planned projects.' He closed by asking his audience for suggestions, for reports of wrongdoing to the Chief Justice or Court Administrator, and above all never to bribe a judge, since 'corruption will take place only if litigants consent to or abet it' -- assuring them that 'while there are a few hoodlums in robes,' the vast majority are 'men and women of integrity and competence.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 4 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' set out the ten prerequisites or key factors that the Supreme Court took into account in initiating the Action Program for Judicial Reform (APJR), which Justice Panganiban described as the most comprehensive judicial reform project ever undertaken by the Court, adding that its viability had to rest on a thorough understanding of the many variables affecting both the problems and the possible solutions. He listed them in order. First, a comprehensive diagnosis: with in-house officials and external experts, the Court reviewed the present state of the judicial system and assessed its environment and institutional capacity through a SWOT analysis, establishing a baseline from which goals and activities could be identified. Second, a review of all past Philippine judicial reform efforts so that their successes and failures could instruct the new program, with a number of their recommendations adopted. Third, involvement of stakeholders -- judges, court personnel, litigants, practicing lawyers, law professors and law students -- through nationwide workshops and dialogues, so that all affected parties had substantive involvement in setting objectives, prioritizing projects and fixing time frames. Fourth, facts versus perception: he maintained that the key to a sound reform program was the ability to distinguish the two, so perception surveys of judges, court personnel and external stakeholders were run alongside the factual diagnostics and also gauged public confidence in the system. Fifth, a global perspective, drawing lessons from successful foreign reform programs while recognizing that the Philippine system had cultural peculiarities that might not fit methodologies used elsewhere. Sixth, a holistic approach treating institution, policy procedure and resources as interdependent components. Seventh, proper sequencing, time frames and targets to avoid backtracking, delay and waste. Eighth, working within available resources, with a public investment program to schedule activities and calibrate funding and so avoid duplication. Ninth, a clear institutional framework: an independent Program Management Office under the Office of the Chief Justice. Tenth, a monitoring and evaluation system run by that office on performance indicators and milestone targets over a multi-year time frame. He closed by conceding that the responsibilities had been great and the challenges daunting, but reported that harnessed internal and external expertise and sustained top management commitment had produced a smooth flowing reform process, with prospects for success not too far ahead.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 5 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' reproduced an address on ethics and good governance that opened lightly and turned grave. Justice Panganiban quoted Joan A. de Venecia, a 21-year-old UP College of Law freshman, whose 'YoungBlood' column of May 16, 2002 in the Philippine Daily Inquirer noted that lawyers are depicted as 'guns for hire' and that the standard answer to 'What do you call 10,000 lawyers drowned in the sea?' is 'a good start'; he added a joke about a lawyer who denied under oath kicking his wife because 'She is not my wife!' He then cited the World Bank report 'Combating Corruption in the Philippines,' which reported a February 2000 Social Weather Stations survey finding that 62 percent of respondents believed there were significant levels of corruption in the judiciary, 65 percent that many or most lawyers could be bribed and 57 percent the same of judges, alongside accusations of deliberate delay, incompetence, arrogance, neglect of duty, partiality and immorality. He offered two assurances: that while there are some undesirable judges and lawyers the vast majority are honest, competent, hardworking and God-fearing, and that the Supreme Court had instituted a wide-ranging reform program. He described the 'Davide Watch' announced on November 30, 1998 and its day-to-day Action Program for Judicial Reform, supported by the national government, local donors, UNDP, the World Bank, ADB, UNICEF, the Asia Foundation and several bilateral donors, and covering law-school curricula, the bar examinations, aid to poor students, screening of appointees, continuing legal education and performance monitoring. Its central theme, he said, was a clarion call to ethics: the Court enforced the Code of Judicial Conduct and the Code of Professional Responsibility more strictly than RA 6713 required of officials generally, and for the first time in its 100-year history had censured one of its own members, dismissed a Court of Appeals justice, suspended the Sandiganbayan presiding magistrate, and disrobed, fined or disciplined hundreds of lower-court judges. But discipline was not enough. With more than a third of trial courts vacant and judges paid less than some Makati clerks, he argued that compensation had to be rationalized through real fiscal independence -- a lump-sum appropriation of about two percent of the national budget -- and exemption from the Salary Standardization Law, while rejecting both LGU allowances and a corporate fundraising offer as threats to independence. He closed on the four 'ins' of a good judge: integrity, independence, intelligence and industry.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 8 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' reproduced Justice Panganiban's remarks at the finals of the First National Moot Court Competition. He set the occasion in its centenary frame: the Supreme Court had celebrated its 100th birthday on June 11, 2001 and had appointed a Centenary Executive Committee that lined up more than fifty projects under the theme 'Katarungan at Bayan, Magpakailanman,' emphasizing allegiance to one cause, justice, and to one entity, the nation. The celebrations, he said, ran across intellectual, cultural, historical, educational, physical and structural activities in all regions, with two goals: to communicate the judiciary's role in nation building and to encourage participation in the ongoing judicial reform program. Originally scheduled for one year, they had been extended to June 11, 2002; the National Speech Festival, comprising oratorical, debate and essay contests, had been the major activity of the first year, and the moot court was the centerpiece of the second. He distinguished the two. The speech festival promoted forensic competition and mastery of language, but the moot court had more specific objectives and went beyond mere eloquence or rhetoric, seeking to enhance research, pleading preparation, knowledge of law, mastery of specific facts, teamwork and advocacy. Unlike debates and oratories, he explained, moot courts involve live, unrehearsed interaction between the speakers and the judges, so that the magistrates are themselves judged on their preparation, expertise and readiness to ask relevant questions. The contest was national in scope, with school eliminations, regional winners meeting in quarterfinals and semifinals, and two finalists competing for the championship; regional trial court judges sat in the regional rounds, Court of Appeals justices in the national rounds, and incumbent and retired Supreme Court justices in the final. He called it the nearest thing to actual appellate practice -- a virtual legal reality in which the facts are hypothetical but the issues, arguments and authorities are real, and which, being neither a drama nor a movie, has no script. He thanked the subcommittee under Merlin M. Magallona, the brief graders, the regional organizers, the twenty appellate justices, the simulated High Tribunal under Justice Vicente V. Mendoza, and Dean Pacifico Agabin for authoring the hypothetical DNA case, and hoped the contest would continue annually and enter law school curricula.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 9 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' reproduced Justice Panganiban's closing report and toast as chairman of the Centenary Executive Committee, delivered on June 11, 2002, as the Supreme Court's two-year jubilee -- launched June 9, 2000, meant to culminate on the Court's exact 100th birthday of June 11, 2001, and then extended a year -- came to a formal close. He restated the celebrations' two goals, to communicate the judiciary's role in nation-building over a century and to focus participation on the ongoing reform program, under the theme 'Katarungan at Bayan Magpakailanman,' and insisted that their success belonged not to the Execom chairman but to the hundreds who implemented each project. He then summarized thirteen activities: the fourteen-lecture Centenary Lecture Series led by Justice Ameurfina A. Melencio Herrera, spanning constitutionalism, biotechnology, paperless courts, Shari'a law, People Power and foreign judiciaries; the National Speech Festival run by the law deans; the First National Moot Court Competition under Undersecretary Merlin M. Magallona, which the law schools, IBP and student association agreed to continue biennially; public-information work including the three-volume Centenary Reader produced at no cost to the Court, books on past Chief Justices, and the award-winning video 'A Celebration of Justice'; regional celebrations under the court administrators; awards and an exhibit for retired magistrates; ecumenical services and the Centennial Prayer for the Courts now recited nationwide; judiciary and employee sportsfests; a cultural program for Supreme Court employees; the Centennial Awards for Judicial Excellence, whose top trial-court awardee had just been promoted; commissioned statues of Chief Justices Arellano and Abad Santos and murals of the Court's history; the Australian- and Asia Foundation-funded Benchbooks now called the bibles of judges; and the Settlement Week mediation pilot, which settled 1,469 of 1,816 referred cases and led to the Philippine Mediation Center. He then listed ten continuing reform projects -- Zero Backlog, new procedural rules under Justice Puno, the MCLE Board, 1,500 computers with Lex Libris, a legal-education foundation, building renovations, the new Centennial Building and Halls of Justice, Baguio cottages, employee mass housing, and the P500-million Philja Center in Tagaytay -- before accepting personal responsibility for any imperfections, crediting the Court and Execom for the successes, thanking the Lord Jesus Christ, and toasting the Court as the bulwark of justice and its justices as pillars of integrity, independence, intelligence and industry.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 15 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' was CJP's postscript to his previous book, 'A Centenary of Justice.' He reported being overwhelmed by close to a hundred congratulatory letters from members of the judiciary, foreign Chief Justices and magistrates, officials, legislators, diplomats, educators, churchmen, lawyers, NGO leaders and librarians, singling out a letter from President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo and an entirely handwritten one from former President Fidel V. Ramos, as well as Brother Willy Nakar's note praising his habit of beginning each book with the Word of God. He explained the practice behind the books: since being sworn into the Supreme Court in 1995 he had recognized that, like all government servants, he was accountable to the public and should adhere to transparency, owing readers the certainty that he had worked conscientiously, 'letting only truth, the law, reason and my conscience dictate my actions.' He listed the resulting series from 'Justice and Faith' in 1997 through the present volume, noted that the Supreme Court Press issued them in limited runs for libraries, law schools, NGOs and media, and observed with amusement that people wrote asking for all five even though the books were no 'literary potboilers.' He attributed the demand to a wider public appetite for transparency, quoting CHED Chairperson Ester Albano Garcia, and linked it to the Court's reform program under Chief Justice Davide, which is why the present book concentrated on the Action Program for Judicial Reform 2001-2006. He then described the books as a 'window to the Court,' citing Mahar Mangahas's Manila Standard column on his chapter about the SWS survey-ban case and his chapter on Perez v. Estrada, where the Court denied live coverage of the Estrada plunder trial 8-6 and he dissented, arguing it was already technologically possible to serve the people's right to information without violating the accused's due process -- a view Beth Day Romulo relayed in the Manila Bulletin as the Court 'turning its back' on technology. He closed with his chairmanship of the Centenary Executive Committee, a letter from Justice Dorit Beinisch of Israel's Supreme Court, and thanks to his readers and reviewers.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 6 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' is CJP's compilation of the questions and answers from the Supreme Court's 'Chamber-to-Chamber' Dialogues with the business community, prefaced by his own framing essay. He acknowledged that business leaders had long accused judges of dampening business by deciding economic issues over which they had no expertise, and conceded that deregulation, privatization, globalization, devaluation, oil taxation and whether to build an airport or reclaim Manila Bay were questions for policymakers. But when officials violated the Constitution or gravely abused their discretion, he wrote, the judiciary was duty-bound to step in; judicial decisions might affect the economy, yet the courts decided constitutional and legal rather than economic questions and merely championed the rule of law. The Dialogues, assisted by a grant from The Asia Foundation, were held in eleven key areas and in special sessions for ECOP, the LMCP and the Bangko Sentral's Investor Services Unit, with answers given in non-legal language by a panel of justices and court administrators. The compiled answers covered the 710 vacancies among 2,214 judicial positions as of December 2003 and their causes in low pay and the three-nominee rule; the JBC-and-President appointment process and PhilJA's pre-judicature program; constitutional periods for deciding cases and remedies for delay through alternative dispute resolution, a new ADR office, and a piloted two-judge system; mediation's 81 percent pilot success rate and the DOJ's 93 percent; computerized case-flow management, transcription and legal research; courthouse funding, model courthouses and proposed mobile courts; discipline of lawyers through the IBP and of judges through monthly reports and OCA investigation; and jurisdictional questions on the ARMM, labor cases, DARAB appeals, jails, tribal justice and commercial courts. On contracts he reported that only about 2 percent are voided, that the mega-contracts fell on the principle of leveling the playing field, and that entrepreneurs should consult counsel early, avoid shortcuts and never bribe judges.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 8 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' gathers CJP's short remarks to a gathering of journalists convened by Dr. Florangel Rosario-Braid of the Asian Institute of Journalism and Communication. He began by observing that in an age of information and transparency it had become increasingly common for magistrates to join such seminars, and contrasted that with the distant past, when the Supreme Court was a fortress, high-walled, forbidding and impenetrable, likened to a Mount Olympus where the gods of Padre Faura resided in lofty perches far above the valley dwellers, mysterious and untouchable, speaking only in guarded legalese that nonetheless determined the freedom, fame and fortune of the multitude below. That fortress, he said, had since been unlocked and slightly opened, punctured by the transparency requirements of the Constitution, the Ethical Standards Law and the Canons of Judicial Ethics, and by media practitioners who persistently knocked at its ramparts until their invasive power penetrated its thick walls. In response the Court had created a Public Information Office under its Committee on Public Information, opened a web page, issued more reader-friendly decisions, allowed its members to commune with media, published the bulletins Benchmark and Court News, and authorized an interactive radio program. He added a caveat: unlike the political departments, whose actions face endless debate and periodic popular judgment, the Court issues decisions not reversible by elections or referendums, and its job is to decide legal disputes with finality, so while it is not averse to fair criticism it will not join debates meant to overturn its judgments. He closed by naming the commonalities between judges and journalists -- the search for truth, the protection of basic rights, the defense of society's fundamental norms, and dependence on public confidence -- and asked the seminar to foster informed appreciation of the Court as the last bulwark of democracy and the final recourse of the damned.
