one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 12 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' is CJP's lecture to the judges of Chile on how Philippine trial courts manage bio-litigation. He defined case management strictly as the handling of a case from its filing to its disposition, a strategy for early disposition achieved by organizing case events, adding those the rules permit, eliminating those that cause undue delay, determining how many witnesses each cause requires, rationalizing objective and testimonial evidence, and keeping firm judicial control of the calendar -- all without running roughshod over the substantial and procedural requirements of due process. He described the Philippine sequence: a case is referred to mediation whenever appropriate and, if mediation fails, proceeds to mandatory pretrial, where civil cases are narrowed by simplifying issues, amending pleadings, obtaining stipulations, limiting witnesses and referring technical matters to a commissioner, and criminal cases by plea bargaining, stipulations, marking exhibits and waiving objections, subject always to the rights of the accused. Bio-cases, he explained, are managed along the same lines, the only difference being that extensive judicial intervention is required because of the novelty of the scientific issues. Because scientific evidence is the essential component of such cases, expert testimony becomes the primary means of establishing or disproving a cause of action, and he urged that the number, qualifications and relevancy of experts be settled at pretrial, noting a proposal that the court appoint the expert while the parties bear the cost, so as to forestall a clash of hired opinions. He recounted Philippine courts' early reluctance to accept DNA profiles and then People v. Vallejo, which settled their admissibility and listed the factors bearing on probative value, and situated that ruling in the relevancy test of the Rules of Court, more liberal than the Frye rule. He conceded frankly that the dearth and expense of DNA experts raise due process and equal protection problems, since an accused who cannot hire his own expert is denied a level playing field, and he canvassed the trial rights at stake -- self-incrimination, unreasonable searches, privacy -- along with calendaring discipline, a strict no-continuance policy, and the pilot testing of fast, standard, complex and holding tracks in one Metro Manila city, closing with the hope that Chile might adapt some of it.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 1 of 'Judicial Renaissance' is the tenth lecture of the Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr. Distinguished Lecture Series, delivered by Justice Panganiban at the Far Eastern University, where he had given his inaugural address as student council president 48 years earlier. He predicts that Davide will be remembered as one of the greatest Chief Justices in the Asia-Pacific, recalls dedicating his 1999 book 'Leadership by Example' to him, and measures him against the four Ins of an ideal magistrate -- Integrity, Independence, Industry and Intelligence -- before making his central distinction: the Chief Justice has only one vote as primus inter pares, but as chief executive officer of the entire judicial department, spending more than 60 percent of his time on the concerns of 28,000 judicial employees, he is a paradox who is detached as a jurist yet transparent and accountable as a leader. Davide's true legacy, he argues, is the reform program begun on his assumption of office: the Davide Watch announced at a Kilosbayan forum on December 11, 1998, with its vision of a judiciary worthy of public trust, and the Action Program for Judicial Reform approved on December 8, 2000, which grew out of the UNDP-funded Blueprint and an 18-month consultation under Chief Justice Narvasa. Regrouping the APJR's six technical components into three plain headings, CJP inventories the reforms in detail: bar examination and legal education reform, the Legal Education Board, the Judicial Apprenticeship Program, MCLE, a restructured Judicial and Bar Council, Philja's training and e-learning, court-annexed mediation and the JURIS Project with their success rates, the New Code of Judicial Conduct patterned on the Bangalore Principles, the sanctioning of 463 lawyers and 660 magistrates, the Judicial Excellence Awards and a doubling of judicial pay; then computerization through CFM and CAMIS, a computer in every courtroom, installment laptops, the e-library launched in November 2004 as 'the first of its kind in Asia,' the Benchbook, model electronic courts and new rules of procedure; and finally the opening of the judicial fortress through the Public Information Office, Chamber-to-Chamber and Judge-to-Judge Dialogues, jail decongestion, the PERLAS school program and Justice on Wheels. Citing the World Bank's Anthony Gerald Toft and a roster of donors, he calls the program a model, previews the International Conference and Showcase of November 28-30, 2005 that he chairs, and closes by promising that the APJR, the work of the whole judiciary rather than one man, will continue after Davide's retirement.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 2 of 'Judicial Renaissance' is a talk Justice Panganiban gave to a Rotary audience, offering what he calls an executive summary of the Supreme Court's Action Program for Judicial Reform. After thanking his hosts and explaining that his friend Mike Varela would not accept his refusal, he describes the APJR as a comprehensive program with six components -- Judicial Systems and Procedures, Institutions Development, Human Resource Development, Integrity Infrastructure Development, Access to Justice by the Poor, and Reform Support Systems -- so numerous in its projects that the Court created a separate Program Management Office. Having no time for over a hundred projects, he reorganizes them under three headings. The transformation of judges begins in law school, with the Court using its constitutional power over admission to the practice of law to steer the bar examinations, the coming Legal Education Board, a piloted Judicial Apprenticeship Program, strengthened MCLE and strict enforcement of the lawyer's oath that has seen 463 lawyers sanctioned in six years; it continues with the Judicial and Bar Council as a filter against partisan appointments, PHILJA's classroom and e-learning programs and the P600 million Japanese grant for a training center in Tagaytay, the New Code of Judicial Conduct patterned on the Bangalore Principles, 660 justices and judges disciplined from 1999 to 2004, the Judicial Excellence Awards, Judge-to-Judge Dialogues, Australian scholarships and a doubling of judicial compensation. The second heading covers tools: the USAID-backed Case Flow Management pilot and the CIDA-backed CAMIS, a computer literacy program for 28,000 personnel, computers in every courtroom and installment laptops, the e-library and Benchbook, new rules of procedure, model electronic courts financed by a World Bank loan, the old GSIS building converted into a Hall of Justice, and alternative dispute resolution. The third covers publics: a Public Information Office that exists to tell 'the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth' rather than to sanitize or propagandize, Chamber-to-Chamber Dialogues answering business criticism, and Justice on Wheels. He cites the World Bank's Anthony Gerald Toft that the APJR is 'fundamentally well-rooted' and that others have much to learn from it, previews the November 28-30, 2005 conference and showcase at the Makati Shangrila with its planned Asia-Pacific Judicial Reform Network, and closes with the answer he gave in Davao City: the program will continue after Davide's retirement because it is not his personal project but the work of the entire judiciary.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 3 of 'Judicial Renaissance' reproduces a luncheon address Justice Panganiban gave to the Consular Corps of the Philippines, whose dean, Her Majesty's Consul John Fielder, had asked him to speak on the Supreme Court's judicial reforms and the coming International Conference and Showcase; he opened by noting that he had himself once been consul ad honorem of the Republic of Honduras, making the occasion a reunion. He traced the reform effort to the 'Davide Watch' that Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr. enunciated on assuming office on November 30, 1998, and to the Action Program for Judicial Reform the Court approved on December 8, 2000, which addresses nine problems ranging from case congestion and budget deficiency to perceived corruption and limited access to justice by the poor, and which he compressed into a three-letter memory guide, the 'CID' targets -- corruption, incompetence and delay -- pursued through more than 100 projects coordinated by the Court's Program Management Office. He grounded the program in the proposition that stability and predictability in the dispensation of justice are indispensable requirements of good governance and hence a prerequisite of economic development, since speedy justice, democracy and the economy are intertwined into one tapestry of governance. The bulk of the speech was a donor-by-donor inventory: UNDP's Blueprint of Action and access-to-justice studies; the World Bank's Judicial Reform Support Program, e-library, computer-aided transcription, model electronic courts, 'Justice on Wheels' and the GSIS-building Hall of Justice; the ADB's million-dollar independence-and-accountability study; some thirty USAID activities; The Asia Foundation's Chamber-to-Chamber dialogues and PERLAS; CIDA's CAMIS grant and JURIS project; AusAID's Benchbook and Justice Link; the EU's 2.73-million-euro access-to-justice grant; and Japanese, British and Dutch support. He closed by saying he knew of no other country enjoying a similar degree of global assistance, vowing to pursue the reforms to completion, and inviting the consuls to bring their own judiciaries to the November 28-30, 2005 conference, which was expected to establish an Asia-Pacific Judicial Reform Network.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 5 of 'Judicial Renaissance' collects the remarks Justice Panganiban delivered at the ninth session of the Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr. Distinguished Lecture Series, a monthly series begun on February 9, 2005 to mark the aspirations and achievements of the Court during Davide's seven-year term. He recapped the lectures already given -- Jose C. Vitug on the legal profession in the digital age, Reynato S. Puno on legislative investigations and privacy, Raul C. Pangalangan on Davide's judicial philosophy, Fr. Joaquin G. Bernas on his role in drafting the 1987 Constitution, and Jovito R. Salonga, whom he called his esteemed guru and whom Senator Joker Arroyo had called the 'Last Titan of the 20th Century,' on maintaining public faith in the judiciary -- along with three international lecturers, Australia's Michael Donald Kirby, Guatemala's Rodolfo de Leon Molina and the World Bank's Anthony Gerald Toft, and noted that Justice Anthony Kennedy's scheduled September 12 lecture had been cancelled by the death of Chief Justice Rehnquist. He then introduced the day's nine-speaker panel on 'The Commitment to Judicial Education,' the first of three lectures on what Davide called the centerpiece of his stewardship, the Action Program for Judicial Reforms. The bulk of the address was a numbered inventory of fourteen valedictory activities collectively styled a 'Celebration of Thanksgiving': publication of Davide's speeches and opinions, a TV documentary, a coffee-table book, a concert and dance festival, CJP's own book 'Judicial Renaissance,' a traveling exhibit, Open Houses of Halls of Justice, a law-student essay contest, three sets of awards, the PERLAS rule-of-law education project, the ASEAN Law Association Conference and the International Conference and Showcase on Judicial Reforms of November 28-30, 2005. He publicly named the Valedictory Executive Committee's members, their assignments and its support staff, praising their unpaid labor, and closed by insisting that although Davide's stewardship ended at the mandatory retirement age of 70 on December 20, 2005, the reforms would endure as the cornerstones of the judicial renaissance he had stewarded.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 6 of 'Judicial Renaissance' reproduces a keynote address to the Philippine Business Forum / Economist Corporate Network that Justice Panganiban built around a chance encounter three weeks earlier at a concert in Makati, where he sat beside Richard Holmes of American Express International, who quoted a line displayed in his office and attributed to Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr.: do not put your trust in your money, but rather put your money in trust. Business, CJP said, is about honestly earned money; the Supreme Court needs trust, because it has no army or police to enforce its decisions, no money to exact loyalty, and no inclination to mount rallies. Decisions are won or lost on reasoned arguments flowing from legal principles and precedents, not on popular palatability, yet the Court must retain the long-term trust of the public as distinct from the shifting winds of public emotion. He then answered the charge that the Court interferes inordinately with economic policy, quoting at length his own 246-page Mining Law decision -- the Constitution should be read in broad, life-giving strokes, not used to strangulate economic growth, and the Court must restrain itself from intruding into policy matters -- and his 1997 ponencia in Tanada v. Angara, which refused to annul the Senate's concurrence in the WTO Treaty because the wisdom of that choice lay outside judicial review. The AMARI, PIATCO and MEGA-PACIFIC annulments, he argued, involved contracts that violated the Constitution, bidding laws and the agencies' own regulations and reeked of corruption, one being called the grandmother of all scams. He cited Makati Business Club and Social Weather Stations surveys ranking the Court among the five most trusted institutions, and Congress's reluctant obedience to the ruling voiding the second impeachment complaint against Chief Justice Davide, clarifying that this showed the supremacy of the Constitution and not of the Court. He then surveyed the Action Program for Judicial Reform -- judge selection, education, ethics, doubled compensation, discipline and awards, courthouse construction, e-courts, computerization, the e-library, alternative dispute resolution, new rules and information campaigns -- and closed by assuring his audience that they could put their trust in the Supreme Court.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 9 of 'Judicial Renaissance' collects an address Justice Panganiban gave at the fifth anniversary of Bantay Katarungan and the monthly forum of Kilosbayan, opening with the tradition that justices live in fortress-like isolation as gods of Mt. Olympus, better read than heard, and explaining that he broke it in obedience to his revered guru Jovito R. Salonga, whose foremost teaching was to aspire more ardently for the things money cannot buy. Noting that the judiciary was being transformed by the Action Program for Judicial Reform against what he abbreviates as CID -- corruption, incompetence and delay -- he argued that computers and courtrooms can be bought but upright, credible and competent judges cannot, and encapsulated the Constitution's and the New Code's lists of judicial qualities into four Ins: integrity, independence, industry and intelligence. Integrity, he said, exceeds honesty and requires the moral courage to denounce wrong, distinguishing martial-law officials who merely kept themselves pure from those who risked everything, among them Chief Justices Concepcion and Teehankee and Justice Zaldivar on the Bantayog Wall of Remembrance; it also demands impartiality and the appearance of propriety, which he illustrated by his refusal to meet Juan Frivaldo in 1996 -- prompting Frivaldo to tell Max Soliven he would flee to the jungles of Sorsogon -- before penning the decision that recognized his citizenship, and by his later explanation to Frivaldo that the victory was sweeter for not being the result of lakad. Independence, the second In, requires freedom from the 'ships' that plague public service -- kinships, relationships, friendships and fellowship -- and from gratitude to the appointing authority, as Earl Warren showed by becoming Eisenhower's conscience. Industry he documented with caseload figures: some 6,000 cases pending in the Supreme Court, about 400 per justice, and 343,875 and 445,999 cases in the RTCs and first-level courts as of July 31, 2004. Intelligence he equated with excellence, knowing everything about something and something about everything, listing eight rulings that demanded mining, marine, economic, mathematical, genetic, psychological, canonical and accounting knowledge. He urged Bantay Katarungan to score judges on the four Ins, and coupled that with a plea for exemption from the Salary Standardization Law and a lump-sum judicial appropriation, closing on the refrain of 'Impossible Dream.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 10 of 'Judicial Renaissance' reproduces a fifteen-minute keynote Justice Panganiban delivered to a conference of judicial awardees convened by the Supreme Court Committee on Judicial Excellence, which he chaired. He began with a memory from the Court's centenary four years earlier, when Israeli Justice Dorit Beinisch congratulated him for reporting in his book 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' the Court's effort to dismiss, suspend and fine many misfits; when he asked whether the Israeli Supreme Court also disciplined errant judges, she replied that in half a century it had received only one complaint, and the judge resigned when privately confronted -- a reply that turned his pleasure into embarrassment and led him to resolve to emphasize the positive. Because hundreds of Philippine magistrates had been sanctioned, he said, some sectors had formed the impression that the judiciary was inhabited by the inept and the corrupt, when in truth the competent and honest far exceeded them. The Conference gathered every awardee since the Foundation for Judicial Excellence began the search in 1991, with a threefold purpose: to encourage awardees, to inspire others, and to formulate an action plan for excellence, veering the focus from the errant to the exalted. He then set out the qualities to look for. Excellence demands mastery of law plus a working knowledge of every other field, since judges cannot merely be walking databases of the Constitution, the law and jurisprudence; he illustrated this with six rulings -- Tanada v. Angara, in which he had to read the 36-volume WTO Treaty; Veterans Federation Party v. Comelec and its mathematical formula; Santos and Molina on Canon Law and psychological incapacity; Vallejo and Yatar on DNA; Genosa on the battered woman syndrome; and La Bugal-B'laan on the 1995 Mining Law. Ethics, he argued, is indispensable, since knowledgeable judges without it are dangerous and reform requires not a change of men but a change in men. Finally he urged an eternal perspective, comparing spiritual laws to civil, criminal and physical ones, and closed by exhorting his audience to live the 3 Es -- Excellence, Ethics and Eternity.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 11 of 'Judicial Renaissance' reproduces the address Justice Panganiban delivered to the Integrated Bar of the Philippines' 10th National Convention of Lawyers in Baguio City, hosted by Atty. Angelica Y. Santiago and IBP president Atty. Jose Anselmo I. Cadiz, whose inaugural speech and 'psychedelic choice of heroes' -- the Kennedys, Ho Chi Minh, Nelson Mandela and Jose Abad Santos -- he praised by his old teacher's maxim that one is known by one's friends. Recalling Justice J. B. L. Reyes's lament that some attorneys behaved as 'hired guns' for their moneyed clients, he read the convention theme, 'Alleviating Poverty and Resolving the Fiscal Crisis,' as the profession's pledge to free the people not only from fear but from want, and aligned it with the Church's Eucharistic Prayer for a wounded people. He argued that law maintains social order and that development agencies now treat legal and judicial reform as a prerequisite to growth, quoting Dr. Ibrahim F. I. Shihata's 1995 World Bank report and describing the Asian Development Bank's law and policy reform work and its redefinition of poverty as a deprivation of assets and opportunities; the 1987 Constitution, he added, already supplied ample authority through its directives on social justice, human rights, ecology, labor and indigenous communities, as the Court's rulings in Department of Agrarian Reform v. Cuenca and Sta. Rosa Realty v. Amante showed. Drawing on his book Leveling the Playing Field, he set out the Court's laissez-faire posture -- deference to the economic agencies except where grave abuse of discretion appears, as Tanada v. Angara illustrates -- and reported that the 246-page La Bugal-B'laan Decision, the longest in the Court's 104-year history, had produced a 'sunshine effect' on investment, the stock market, the peso and the Manila Water and SM Investments offerings. He then charged the bar with six tasks: initiating development-promoting cases, enforcing accountability and transparency in public funds, reporting and refusing corruption, pursuing legal empowerment of the poor along ADB-recommended lines, building mechanisms for 'social sharing' after Jeffrey D. Sachs and the Ateneo's 10-Point Agenda, and leading lives of rectitude. He closed by commending the IBP's theme and urging concrete measures toward the twin goals of safeguarding liberty and nurturing prosperity.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 12 of 'Judicial Renaissance' reproduces the address Justice Panganiban gave at the induction of the IBP-Pampanga Chapter's officers, opening with thanks to Judge Irin Zenaida S. Buan, who introduced him by analyzing his legal philosophy from his decisions rather than reciting his biography. He praised the new breed of Pampango magistrates, recalled the province's place in a century of judicial history through Chief Justices Jose Abad Santos and Cayetano Arellano, and remembered that when he joined the Court in 1995 all five members of his Third Division were cabalens -- the 'Lahar Division,' of which he is now the only survivor. Amid what he called a national crisis of confidence and credibility, he sounded a call to ethics built on three virtues. Fairness, he said, means refusing to take undue advantage of the other side, which he illustrated with the 1960 hearing where, standing in for an indisposed Dean Jovito R. Salonga, he was spared cross-examination because opposing counsel Jose W. Diokno moved to postpone the case in fairness to a young compañero. Candor means admitting error and conceding when a passage is a mere obiter, and never misquoting a decision, since eagle-eyed magistrates detect misquotation. Integrity means acting on what is true and honest regardless of consequences; he asked lawyers to denounce corrupt and incompetent judges, to defend decent ones from scurrilous attacks and baseless administrative complaints that stall promotions, and to condemn lawyers who collect money from clients ostensibly to pay off magistrates, insisting that corruption survives only where the bar abets or tolerates it. He then reported the Office of the Bar Confidant's figures for 1999 to 2004 -- 463 lawyers disciplined, 23 of them disbarred -- and summarized three recent cases of estate fraud, obstinate immorality and deliberate deception of a trial court. Quoting Justice J. B. L. Reyes on keeping one's soul attuned to morality and honor, he developed the figure of a mariner's compass permanently calibrated to the north, warned against technicians who invert the hierarchy of loyalties, and closed by urging cabalen attorneys to keep no compass but ethics, no master but law, no guide but honor and no aim but justice.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 20 of 'Judicial Renaissance' recounts Presidential Commission on Good Government v. Sandiganbayan, which Panganiban presents as a case of first impression forcing the Court to balance its drive to upgrade the ethics of lawyers in government service against the government's right to recruit competent counsel. The PCGG had moved to disqualify Atty. Estelito P. Mendoza, solicitor general when the Central Bank declared GenBank insolvent in March 1977, from representing Lucio Tan and others in the sequestration cases over Allied Banking Corporation, invoking Rule 6.03 of the Code of Professional Responsibility against accepting engagement in any matter in which a lawyer had intervened while in government service. The Sandiganbayan denied the Motion, and by a majority of eleven, with two dissents and two non-participations, the Court denied the PCGG's certiorari Petition. Justice Puno's ponencia traced the Rule to the ABA's 1924 concern with the 'revolving door,' distinguished adverse-interest from congruent-interest conflicts, and held that advising the Central Bank on liquidation procedure was not the 'matter' the Rule contemplates and that Mendoza's participation -- signing an initiatory pleading -- was insignificant and insubstantial; it also warned against chilling government recruitment and against disqualification used as a harassment tactic. Panganiban wrote separately to dismiss the Petition only on conclusiveness of judgment and prescription, arguing that the Sandiganbayan's final April 22, 1991 Resolution on the identical ground had become immutable, that identity of parties and issues alone suffices for estoppel, and that the congruent-interest restriction should expire five years after separation from government, since a perpetual and absolute ban would be unduly harsh, unreasonable and unfair. He reports Justice Sandoval-Gutierrez's concurrence condemning the PCGG's 'scattershot' motions, Justice Carpio Morales's dissent rejecting both conclusiveness of judgment and the five-year cap, Justice Callejo's dissent urging strict application as an ethical compass, and Justice Tinga's view that applying a rule promulgated after Mendoza entered government would violate his right to due process.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 3 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' is CJP's Philconsa Constitution Day address, delivered soon after he took his oath on December 21, 2005 at 2:56 p.m. as the 21st Chief Justice, the first sworn in during the 21st century. He organized the speech around the Chief Justice's two roles. As primus inter pares he presides over en banc sessions, shapes the agenda, opens discussion and summarizes arguments, yet holds only one vote, and even Chief Justices from Arellano to Davide have found themselves in the minority. Pointing to published reports, the Court's e-library and the ten books he wrote over ten years, he summarized his judicial philosophy in a sentence: to safeguard the liberty and nurture the prosperity of the people while upholding the rule of law and the independence of the judiciary. On liberty he stressed that the 1987 Constitution protects social justice, labor, women, indigenous communities and human rights, invoked his own ruling in Ang Bagong Bayani that those who have less in life should have more in law, and traced a line of free-expression cases -- ABS-CBN, Social Weather Stations, and United States v. Bustos -- in which the Court leans in favor of freedom. On prosperity he urged deference to the political branches, citing Tañada v. Angara and La Bugal-B'laan, while reserving the power to strike down acts that clearly violate the Constitution or are arbitrary. Turning to his second role as leader of some 2,000 judges and 26,000 personnel, he set out the four Ins -- integrity, independence, intelligence and industry -- describing independence as freedom from kinship, relationship, friendship and fellowship, and declaring that the judiciary's might is in its being right. He named ACID as his reform agenda, reported the international standing won by the Action Program for Judicial Reform, and closed by answering doubts about his short term with the statues of Arellano and Abad Santos.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 4 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' set out Chief Justice Panganiban's core judicial philosophy in full. He opened with the program he announced on assuming the chief justiceship: a judiciary marked by four Ins -- independence, integrity, industry and intelligence -- morally courageous against influence, interference, indifference and insolence, and impervious to the plague of 'ships,' namely kinship, relationship, friendship and fellowship. He recalled the Supreme Court's supervision of the bar, 'the vineyard from which our judges take root,' his pledge to revitalize the Action Program for Judicial Reform around the four ACID problems of limited access to justice by the poor, corruption, incompetence and delay, and the DHL bargain he offered 26,000 judicial employees. These, he said, were only means; the end goals were safeguarding liberty and nurturing prosperity. He distinguished three ways of relating the two -- disjunctive, causal, and mutually inclusive -- and aligned himself with the third, insisting it was 'not liberty or prosperity but liberty and prosperity.' From this he derived a double standard of review: heightened or strict scrutiny weighing heavily against government in civil-liberties litigation, and deference to the political branches on economic and developmental questions. He illustrated the first with the new right to conduct and publish opinion polls upheld in ABS-CBN v. Comelec and echoed in Social Weather Stations v. Comelec, a decision he penned freeing an accused detained almost two years without arraignment, and three recent rulings on legislative inquiries, peaceful assembly and a state of national emergency. He grounded the second in Tanada v. Angara on the WTO Agreement and La Bugal-B'laan v. Ramos on the Mining Law, while preserving justiciability and the duty to strike down gravely abusive acts. Four developments -- constitutional commands on wealth distribution, Sachs's End of Poverty and the Gates-Bono philanthropy, the UNDP, World Bank and ADB insistence on a well-functioning judiciary, and PBSP-led Philippine corporate responsibility -- convinced him that prosperity now needs as much nurturing as liberty once did. He closed by offering the philosophy as a possible framework rather than an absolute prescription for other jurisdictions.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 5 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' recorded how Chief Justice Panganiban, as ex-officio chairperson of the Judicial and Bar Council, set out to reform judicial entry. He began by recalling the February 11, 2005 occasion when his revered guru, former Senate President Jovito R. Salonga, summoned him to address Bantay Katarungan and Kilosbayan on 'Judging the Judges,' where he compressed the Constitution's four attributes of a magistrate and the seven attributes of the 2004 New Code of Judicial Conduct into four Ins: integrity, independence, industry and intelligence. Those standards, he argued, matter even more at entry than in discipline, since the water of the judicial reservoir will always be murky if the inflow carries the germs of incompetence, indifference, influence and indolence. On his first official days in January 2006 he convened the Council to review its mission, effectiveness and public criticisms, and framed its work as three Ss -- search for, screen and select. The JBC had previously done only the last two; on his initiative it added an activist search through nationwide dialogues with the bar, justice agencies, the academe, NGOs, media and the public, radio and television announcements, and a website launched April 21, 2006. Constitutional deadlines for the Supreme Court vacancy left by Chief Justice Davide's retirement compressed that program, so dialogues were limited to the IBP, PBA, Wiloci, the Society for Judicial Excellence and the media. He detailed the incentives the Council would advertise -- doubled judicial pay, a new Security Committee, better halls of justice -- and the vacancy statistics driving the urgency, along with a new practice of announcing vacancies three months before retirements. Screening, he reported, now included background investigations, psychological and psychiatric examinations and public interviews, with selection by secret ballot subject to the integrity vote under Rule 10. He closed by defending the JBC against calls for its abolition while conceding it must become more proactive, transparent, assertive and accountable.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 6 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' reproduced the address Chief Justice Panganiban delivered at a testimonial dinner jointly tendered by twelve Philippine bar and legal organizations, an occasion he noted was rare in bringing them all under one roof. He opened with the Proclamation No. 1017 petitions, in which IBP President Jose Anselmo Cadiz and other IBP officers were petitioners and had endured a nine-hour Oral Argument on March 7, 2006 that ran to 10:00 p.m.; invoking the Court's confidentiality rule, he declined to discuss the case and used it only to show how much the nation's destiny depends on how lawyers advocate public-interest causes, noting the IBP's activity as well in the Executive Order No. 464 and Oakwood mutiny cases. He restated the twin visions announced at the start of his chief justiceship: a judiciary of four Ins -- integrity, independence, industry and intelligence -- impervious to the plague of 'ships,' and a revitalized legal profession that is responsible, dependable and morally upright and whose members stand for their convictions against all odds. Both, he said, serve the loftier goals of safeguarding liberty and nurturing prosperity, grounded in the Bill of Rights and in Article XII's mandate of a more equitable distribution of opportunities, income and wealth. He criticized lawyers who had become technicians of the law, inverting their duties so that justice came a far third, and argued that because rules of conduct can never cover the myriad situations of practice, an internalized ethical compass is required, recalling how his firm had declined a sizeable retainer from a businessman who asked whether they knew the judge. He then enlisted the bar against the four ACID problems, since the battle would be only half won without them, listing reforms from the January 12, 2006 strategic planning workshop: pro bono incentives, the April 21 e-payment system through Land Bank, a stricter nomination process, more halls of justice, and computerization, exemplified by the Sandiganbayan's digitized 2,700 cases.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 7 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' recounted what Chief Justice Panganiban called a chronicle of faith: the long and tortuous journey to build the Philippine Judicial Academy's Center in Tagaytay. He traced it from July 19, 1995, when President Fidel V. Ramos turned over the 3.3-hectare property to the Supreme Court through the free transfer of 51 percent of a sequestered corporation's shares on the initiative of then Presidential Legal Counsel Antonio T. Carpio, through the cornerstone laid on November 23, 1998 under Chief Justice Narvasa, to the funding detour in which Chief Justice Davide's June 2000 application under Japan's Grant Assistance Program was overtaken by that program's suspension in 2004 and had to be recoursed through the Non-Project Grant Assistance Counter Value Fund. The P300 million grant was finally handed over by Ambassador Ryuichiro Yamazaki on January 26, 2006, during his own term. He reported the preparations already made -- a Project Implementation Committee from the February 22, 2006 Action Planning Workshop, approved terms of reference, budget and timelines for the architectural design, referral to the APJR Bids and Awards Committee, and 12 prospective bidders -- with construction expected to begin the following year. He then set out the ambition: to raise the first and only training school for the Philippine judiciary into a national and ASEAN regional hub for continuing legal education, pre-judicature training, career enhancement and specialized programs, supported by cooperation agreements with Spain and, in prospect, France and the United Kingdom, and by regional moves toward a common judicial curriculum. He proposed as well a special school for aspiring career judges modeled on the Foreign Service Institute, entered by competitive examination but open to poor applicants through scholarships. He closed by tying the project to his ACID agenda, arguing the campaign against corrosive judicial incompetence could be waged faster if begun at the foundations of judicial training.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 10 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' set out Chief Justice Panganiban's full programmatic report on the Action Program for Judicial Reform, arranged by the four ACID problems he had made his priority. He restated his December 21, 2005 vow of a judiciary marked by four Ins -- independence, integrity, industry and intelligence -- impervious to the plague of 'ships,' his vision of a revitalized legal profession, and the DHL bargain with 26,000 judicial employees, all converging on the twin beacons of Liberty and Prosperity. He described the six-component APJR his predecessor Chief Justice Davide had begun in 2000 and the international and private support behind it, resting the whole enterprise on the proposition that speedy justice, democracy and the economy are intertwined in one tapestry of governance. On access, he called the Constitution pro-poor, pro-labor and pro-human rights, catalogued the Court's exemptions and free counsel for indigents, quoted Ang Bagong Bayani-OFW Labor Party v. Comelec on the party-list system as a social justice vehicle, invoked the labor line from Calalang v. Williams, and reported jail studies, the IBP decongestion project, the EU project for internally displaced persons and the Justice on Wheels mobile courts. On corruption, he described it as hiding behind kinship and friendship and answered it with entry standards, ethical education, discipline and Republic Act 9227's doubling of judicial pay, while asking Congress for a lump-sum appropriation of about two percent of the national budget and exemption from the Salary Standardization Law. On incompetence, he reported the June 2004 bar reforms, the MCLE, the JBC's three S tasks and 29.49 percent vacancy rate, PhilJA and the P300 million Japanese grant, the New Code of Judicial Conduct patterned on the Bangalore Principles, and the sanctioning of 463 lawyers and 660 judges. On delay, he described the Committee on Zero Backlog and a broad computerization program, from case flow management and CAMIS to the Sandiganbayan's paperless docket, the e-library, model electronic courts, e-payment and broadband connectivity.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 11 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' reproduces the address Chief Justice Panganiban gave to launch the Supreme Court's electronic library simultaneously in eight law schools and universities -- Arellano University School of Law, with a live simulcast to Aquinas University in Legazpi, Saint Louis University in Baguio, Silliman in Dumaguete, the University of San Carlos in Cebu, Xavier in Cagayan de Oro, Ateneo de Davao and Mindanao State University in Marawi. He noted that the e-library was the first of its kind in Asia and one of the few in the world, conceived and developed in less than a year for only US$10,000 granted by the World Bank, and that sharing it with the schools was meant to make the study of law easier, more convenient and more systematic. He contrasted the study of law in his own time, when students waited for barely readable mimeographed copies of decisions and wrote their own digests, with a present in which a few keystrokes bring a case onto the screen. He then tied the project to his program: on assuming office on December 21, 2005 he had pledged to continue Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr.'s Action Program for Judicial Reform, to lead a judiciary marked by four Ins -- integrity, independence, industry and intelligence -- and to attack the ACID problems of limited access to justice by the poor, corruption, incompetence and delay. Citing the Court's discipline of six lawyers and six judges in a single month, including a judge found grossly ignorant of the law in two child-rape cases, he presented the e-library, developed under Justice Antonio T. Carpio and launched on November 19, 2004, as the remedy for incompetence: cheap, updated within 48 hours, always open, space-free and fully searchable. He described computer orientation courses reaching 2,000 judges and 26,000 employees, easy-term laptop purchases, home DSL, the P300 million Japanese-funded PhilJA Development Center in Tagaytay, and the Sandiganbayan's full computerization as the model for the judiciary. Conceding that new technologies 'can only be as good as the people who use them,' he argued that law schools, not the courts, are the first line of defense against injustice, and exhorted professors and students to digitize their law schools.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 12 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' reproduces the closing address Chief Justice Panganiban delivered at a two-day Conference on Arbitration for the Judiciary, which he said he would not miss despite a hectic schedule because of his special affinity with the cause of arbitration. He restated the four acute problems he wanted to focus on as Chief Justice -- limited access to justice by the poor, corruption, incompetence, and delay in the delivery of quality judgments -- which he called the ACID problems that corrode justice, and located alternative dispute resolution as one of the ways of avoiding delay: an out-of-court settlement usually works well for the parties and the courts, is fast and efficient, decongests dockets, and allows judges to concentrate on the bigger issues of national interest. He thanked Justice Ameurfina A. Melencio Herrera for her tireless work through the Philippine Judicial Academy and acknowledged the conference co-sponsors -- the Chartered Institute of Arbitrators, the Kuala Lumpur Regional Centre for Arbitration, the Philippine Dispute Resolution Center, USAID and The Asia Foundation. He reported the Court's concrete steps to institutionalize ADR: court-annexed mediation integrated as a mandatory component of pretrial at the trial level, mediation recently approved at the appellate level, deference to contractual provisions referring disputes to arbitral bodies, and judge-to-judge dialogues stressing arbitration's role in de-clogging dockets. He surveyed the conference papers on national arbitration laws, the Uncitral Model Law, the arbitration agreement and party autonomy, arbitrability and the enforceability of awards, and acknowledged the conflicts that arise from the diversity of arbitration laws across jurisdictions. Quoting PhilJA's ADR Department, he described ADR as restoring the judiciary as the forum of last recourse. He listed five ways courts may support arbitration -- settling jurisdiction, granting interim relief, taking evidence, enforcing or repudiating awards, and keeping courts out through anti-suit injunctions or stays -- citing Professor Mario B. Valderrama and PDRCI President Eduardo Ceniza and Sections 28 and 29 of the Philippine ADR Law, conceded the difficulty of balancing the roles of courts and arbitrators, praised international forums for solving such problems, and promised to act on the conference report within his competence.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 13 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' reproduces Chief Justice Panganiban's address to an International Conference and Showcase on Judicial Reforms. He opened with the Code of Lipit-Ishtar, handed down by the ruler of Isin about 150 years before Hammurabi, whose graduated damages for injuring a rented ox showed what Sumerians valued; from this he argued that future generations would read a people's character in the laws, decisions and reforms it produced, and that judicial reforms 'provide a glimpse of our lofty aspirations.' Rather than recount more than 100 reform projects, he referred delegates to his newly launched 536-page book 'Judicial Renaissance' and summarized the program's four targets by the acronym ACID -- access to justice by the poor, corruption, incompetence and delay -- alongside Chief Justice Davide's goal of a judiciary independent, effective, efficient and worthy of public trust, to which he added a court system that safeguards liberty and nurtures prosperity. He listed the reforms underway and the unusual breadth of the program's backing from UNDP, the World Bank, the EU and ADB, from national aid agencies of Australia, Canada, Great Britain, Japan, the Netherlands and the United States, and from private donors. He then set out ten factors ensuring the program's success: constitutional guarantees of judicial independence, including the duty to strike down grave abuse of discretion, security of tenure, fiscal autonomy and the Court's rule-making and disciplinary powers; a comprehensive diagnosis using SWOT analysis and perception surveys; a review of past reform efforts; involvement of all stakeholders through nationwide workshops; a global perspective adapted to local peculiarities; a holistic approach linking institution, policy, procedure and resources; chronological sequencing of components; realistic goals within available resources, with donor-assisted planning and pilot projects; a separate Program Management Office staffed by management, reform and finance experts rather than judges; and clear, measurable standards monitored against milestone targets. He proposed a shared website, JRN21, and an Asia-Pacific Judicial Reform Forum, closing on the principle that good governance and sustained economic development are impossible without a stable, credible, independent, accountable, transparent and competent judiciary.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 14 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' reproduces Chief Justice Panganiban's Women's Month address, delivered days after the Court's March 8 exhibit honoring its female justices under the theme 'Gender-Responsive Philippine Judiciary: KKK (Kamalayan, Katarungan, Kababaihan).' He traced how quickly women had reshaped a once predominantly male profession: more than half the graduating classes of three leading law colleges over five years were female, prompting old professors to joke that male law students might become an endangered species; only 287 women against 7,846 men were admitted to the bar from 1901 to 1945, but 4,430 women against 6,493 men passed between 1996 and 2005, lifting the female share from 3.5 percent to 40.6 percent. He gave the counts on the bench -- five of fifteen Supreme Court justices, 17 in the Court of Appeals, three in a Sandiganbayan led by a woman presiding justice, two in the Court of Tax Appeals, and 419 lower-court judges -- and cited a Court study with UNDP and the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation showing more female lawyers in academe and NGOs. He described the Court's Strategic Gender and Development Mainstreaming Plan, its Committee on Gender Responsiveness (the first in Asia), the rules on violence against women and on harassment, the work-decorum guidelines, the codes of conduct, a proposed audit of issuances for gender-insensitive language, and the new Manual of Judicial Writing. Observing that the English language is not gender-friendly, he quoted masculine pronouns in the Bill of Rights, the qualifications for Senator, President and Supreme Court member, Article 1305 of the Civil Code and Rule 126 on arraignment, rejected the 'convenient excuse' that the masculine includes all genders, and showed how he had long pluralized or recast his own sentences to avoid sexist language. He then enlisted women judges in his agenda of the four Ins, the plague of 'ships' and the ACID problems, holding up Justices Cecilia Muñoz-Palma, Ameurfina A. Melencio Herrera and Carolina C. Griño-Aquino as models, and closed by praising those who had taken the less traveled road toward a judicial renaissance.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 16 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' reproduces the address Chief Justice Panganiban delivered on June 21, 2006, his sixth month in office, to the heads of Supreme Court offices and the leaders of the judiciary's employee organizations. He recalled taking his oath as the 21st Chief Justice on December 21, 2005, and delivering his first address to the rank and file at the flag ceremony of January 2, 2006, when, still in pain from surgery three days earlier and profusely perspiring, he hid his affliction and announced his policy of giving employees the maximum benefits allowed by law and within his discretion. He then set out the four ways a Chief Justice can grant benefits: the 'sole exclusive power' under PD 1949 to distribute 80 percent of the Judiciary Development Fund; realignment of the judiciary budget under the Appropriations Law and CFAG Joint Resolutions 1 and 90; additional allowances from surplus collections of the Special Allowance for Justices and Judges under RA 9227, which doubled judicial pay in four annual 25 percent increments from November 2003; and the regular benefits carried in the General Appropriations Act. He accounted for the first half of 2006 month by month -- P2,500 each in January, February and March, P3,800 in April, P2,900 in May and P3,400 in June, totaling P17,600 -- explained that he had set a P2,500 monthly floor because JDF collections fluctuated, and described the three-tier classification recommended by the Fiscal Management and Budget Office that gave the largest shares to those earning P7,000 or less. He estimated that about P57,000 had been released to each employee since December, effectively doubling many basic salaries, and listed increased SC Praise awards, a perfect-attendance award, retirement cash awards and service wristwatches, plus planned housing, health and laptop-acquisition programs. He gave two reasons: compassion, having been very poor himself, hawking newspapers, shining shoes and peddling cigarettes as a boy; and, more importantly, fairness, since a government demanding total loyalty must compensate properly. In exchange he asked for dedication, honesty and loyalty -- the DHL norms -- and written feedback within a month.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 17 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' reproduces Chief Justice Panganiban's first major policy address before a private organization, given to the Rotary Club of Manila forty-two days after he assumed office on December 21, 2005. He explained that he chose Rotary because it had initiated him into government: on June 17, 1992 then President-elect Fidel V. Ramos, a Manila Rotarian, offered him the justice portfolio, which he declined for not having campaigned; Ramos answered that this was immaterial, having observed him closely during his 1990-1991 Rotary presidency, and later offered the associate justiceship he accepted in 1995 -- an appointment, he noted, for which Ramos never asked a favor. He pledged a judiciary of four Ins -- integrity, independence, industry and intelligence -- morally courageous against influence, interference, insolence and indifference and closed to the plague of 'ships,' and a legal profession owing fidelity to truth and justice above clients' interests. His objectives were to safeguard the people's liberty and nurture their prosperity, pursued through two standards of judicial review: in civil-liberties cases the scales weigh heavily for the people, especially the poor and marginalized, invoking the Bill of Rights and Magsaysay's line that those with less in life should have more in law; in conflicts affecting prosperity and development, deference is owed the political departments, as he had argued in 'Leveling the Playing Field.' He committed to continuing Chief Justice Davide's reform program and to the ACID agenda. Answering the objection that this was too much for one year, he cited Rotary, whose presidents serve twelve months yet are remembered for great deeds, and his own decade of preparation on the Court. He then listed what he had done: a press conference and a televised interview with Korina Sanchez; a JDF advisory committee created for transparency after the 2003 controversy, plus disbursement of 2005 JDF funds to some 28,000 employees; an all-day Strategic Planning Workshop on January 12, 2006; and four concrete results -- the P300 million Japanese grant for the PhilJA Development Center, the second and third Justice on Wheels mobile courts, the e-payment pilot for court fees, and the USAID-funded computerization of the Sandiganbayan -- closing with a pledge that his 'RENAISSANCE COURT' of one year would be a model judiciary in the region.

sub_topics: ["In AC No. 6697 complainant Zoilo Antonio Velez sought the suspension or disbarment of Atty. Leonard de Vera for concealing a suspension order rendered against him by the State Bar of California and for violating the rotation rule of Administrative Matter No. 491.", "The California matter arose from an insurance case for Julius Wills III, injured in a 1986 automobile accident: de Vera received a $12,000 settlement check on his client's behalf and deposited it in his personal account, for which a hearing referee recommended a three-year suspension; the case was never decided on the merits because he resigned from the California Bar.", "On the rotation ground, the complainant alleged that de Vera's transfer of membership from the PPLM chapter to the Agusan del Sur chapter -- where he neither resided nor held office -- was a circumvention made solely to become IBP national president.", "Two companion matters were consolidated: Bar Matter No. 1227, de Vera's request that the Court schedule his oath-taking as IBP national president, and AM No. 05-5-15-SC, the letter-report of National President Jose Anselmo I. Cadiz on the IBP Resolution removing him for acts inimical to the board and the IBP.", "The dispute began when the IBP board approved the withdrawal of its Petition in Integrated Bar of the Philippines et al. v. Senate of the Philippines et al., after which de Vera allegedly made untruthful statements, innuendos and blatant lies about that Resolution during the plenary session of the 10th National IBP Convention.", "Governor Romulo A. Rivera wrote on May 12, 2005 seeking his removal, and the next day the board resolved by a two-thirds vote to remove him as board member and executive vice-president; Governor Pura Angelica Y. Santiago was elected EVP on June 13, relinquished the post on June 20, and Governor Jose Vicente B. Salazar was elected in her stead on June 25.", "President Cadiz then asked the Court to approve Salazar's election and assumption as national president should de Vera be disbarred or suspended or his removal approved, while de Vera protested both elections and claimed he had been removed without notice or due process.", "On the first issue, the Court unanimously held that AC No. 6052 was no bar to AC No. 6697: the earlier case concerned his qualification to run for governor for Eastern Mindanao under the IBP bylaws, the present one his privilege to practice law under the Lawyer's Oath and the Code of Professional Responsibility, and the two sought different relief.", "On the second issue, citing Maquera, the Court held that a foreign judgment of suspension transmutes into a Philippine one only if its basis included a ground for disbarment or suspension here, and that by insisting he was authorized by his client's father to use the funds, de Vera impliedly admitted using them for himself.", "Canon 16 being emphatic on the point, holding a client's money without acquiescence was indicative of lack of integrity and propriety, and depositing the check in his own account made him guilty of malpractice, gross misconduct and unethical behavior in violation of his oath of fidelity to his client.", "Because disbarment should not be decreed where a lesser penalty would accomplish the end desired, and considering the amount involved, the Court imposed suspension for two years.", "The transfer of chapter membership, however, was within his rights: neither the Code nor the Lawyer's Oath punishes a lawyer for aspiring to the IBP presidency or forbids perfectly legal acts to accomplish that goal.", "On the third issue, the Court held that the EVP position is not property in the constitutional sense and carries no security of tenure, removal for cause requiring only a resolution of two thirds of the remaining board members.", "Due process was satisfied: in administrative proceedings its essence is the opportunity to explain one's side, cross-examination is not indispensable and an actual hearing is not always essential; de Vera received a copy of the Complaint, was present at the meeting, and the transcript showed he had a fair opportunity to answer Atty. Rivera's accusations.", "The arithmetic also held: 'remaining members' excluded the complainant and the respondent, and of the seven qualified to vote, five voted for expulsion and two against, satisfying the two-thirds requirement.", "On removal for cause, the Court observed that conflicts are inherent in the internal life of any organization but that the IBP's effectiveness would be diluted if they were brought outside its governing body, diminishing its prestige with lawyers and the public; expelling a governor who insisted on publicizing his disagreement with a duly approved policy was therefore a legal cause.", "On the fourth issue, removal from the board ipso facto removed him as EVP, and the board's own rules and bylaws governed the filling of the vacancies; under Section 47 of Article VII the EVP automatically becomes president for the next succeeding term, which implied that the successor had to come from the 2003-2005 board.", "Bar Matter 491 was read to mean that it is the EVP position that is rotated among the nine regional governors, the rotation of the presidency being merely a consequence of automatic succession -- and the bylaws' intrinsic principle is that whoever assumes the highest position must first have been exposed to the demands of national leadership."]

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 29 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests Velez v. De Vera, a per curiam ruling consolidating a disciplinary complaint with two companion matters over the succession to the presidency of the Integrated Bar of the Philippines. Zoilo Antonio Velez sought Atty. Leonard de Vera's suspension or disbarment for concealing a California suspension order and for circumventing the rotation rule by transferring his chapter membership to Agusan del Sur; meanwhile the IBP board, after de Vera publicly attacked its withdrawal of a Petition against the Senate at the 10th National Convention, voted on May 13, 2005 by two thirds of its remaining members to remove him as governor and executive vice-president, and then elected Governor Santiago and, after she relinquished the post, Governor Salazar as EVP. The Court held first that an earlier case on his qualification to run as governor was no bar to the present complaint, since the two differed in subject matter, cause of action and relief. On the merits, citing Maquera, it held that a foreign suspension transmutes into a Philippine one only if its basis is also a ground here, and found that by insisting he had been authorized to use his client's money de Vera impliedly admitted using the $12,000 settlement check he had deposited in his own account -- conduct indicative of lack of integrity and propriety and amounting to malpractice, gross misconduct and unethical behavior. Because a lesser penalty could accomplish the end desired, it imposed suspension for two years rather than disbarment, while holding that his transfer of chapter membership was within his rights, since nothing punishes a lawyer for aspiring to the IBP presidency. It upheld his removal, ruling that the EVP position is not property in the constitutional sense and carries no security of tenure, that due process in administrative proceedings is simply the opportunity to explain one's side, which the record showed he had, and that publicizing his disagreement with a duly approved resolution was legal cause because an organization's effectiveness is diluted when internal conflicts are brought outside its governing body. Finally, reading Bar Matter 491 and the bylaws together, it held that the rotation rule attaches to the EVP office while the presidency passes by automatic succession, so the replacement had to come from the 2003-2005 board, and the elections of Santiago and Salazar were valid.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 1 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 1) is CJP's August 12, 2007 Inquirer column asking how President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo (GMA) will be remembered, and whether her State of the Nation Address legacy -- infrastructure, a wider social safety net, and peace in Mindanao -- is achievable. Granting that her aspirations are hard to fault, he reframes the debate: the critics ask where she will find 'the trillions' to fund them, but the real first priority, he argues, is to earn the people's trust, 'for without trust, no leader can succeed.' Citing Cardinal Rosales ('it is treason to lead without a vision, supported by core values') and paraphrasing Salonga, he insists that beyond the things money can buy (roads, bridges, schools), it is 'the things that money cannot buy' -- integrity, public esteem, character, moral ascendancy and credibility -- that matter most, and GMA's record-low ratings stem from her credibility deficit. He offers two prescriptions that 'require no funding': first, lead an internal transformation by holding relatives, officials and cronies strictly to the Constitution and the anti-graft, ethics and procurement laws, wielding presidential strength to be 'transformational, no longer transactional'; second, fortify democratic institutions by naming trustworthy -- not 'loyalist' -- appointees to the Supreme Court and the Comelec, since between 2007 and 2010 she would fill all fifteen Court seats (eight justices retiring, plus Chief Justice Puno) and all seven Comelec posts. He warns that court-packing backfires, recalling that Eisenhower's appointees Warren and Brennan voted against him and that Marcos's compliant Court 'aggravated the discontent that eventually toppled and disgraced him,' and assures her that 'with prudent legal advice, goals can be attained under the rule of law.' Such selfless acts, he concludes, would be a lasting legacy that costs nothing and would itself lift her credibility -- the key to making her SONA dreams a 2010 reality.

GMA's worst failing, he says, is the collapse of transparent and accountable governance, which has wrecked her credibility -- a 'dismal minus 11' SWS trust rating and the country's fall from 121st to 131st of 180 on Transparency International's corruption index -- and his standing remedies are to hold her circle to the anti-graft and ethics laws and to fortify the Supreme Court and Comelec. To critics who call the recovery a myth the poor cannot feel, he replies with 'the first of a thousand steps' (Korea, Singapore and China needed years), and closes with his cancer-patient analogy: a people who trust their leader will bear 'transitory torment' as a patient trusts a physician through chemotherapy, while a distrusted leader is mocked even for the pain of the cure -- as India's reformers found when they were voted out and their opponents reaped the prosperity. The moral: 'aspire for credibility, first and foremost.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 3 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 1), CJP's March 2, 2008 Inquirer column, confronts the deepening crisis of confidence in the Arroyo government as corruption scandals escalate. He surveys five ways out and finds each unlikely or unpalatable: voluntary resignation (which GMA rejected -- 'I am President and no one else'); a snap election (impossible, since there is no vacancy and the Vice-President would succeed); impeachment (hopeless in a House that had just 'defrocked' Speaker de Venecia); a coup d'etat (a 'Burma-type junta' 'far worse than GMA'); and emergency rule (which would make her a dictator in the company of Marcos, Suharto or Idi Amin), noting that 'martial law under the present Constitution is toothless.' Ermita' ruling, Neri's plea for silence cannot be granted, and CJP trusts the justices to resist reported pressure to reverse it. The truth, he insists, 'cannot be hidden forever,' so it is better it shine forth now while GMA can still contain the damage.

Turning to the present, he maps the field arrayed against a GMA constituent-assembly push: the presidential 'wannabes' (Estrada, Lacson, Legarda, Roxas, Villar) and oppositionists, the militants, civil society, business and media 'political noise,' and -- the decisive 'swing group' -- the 'middle forces' (bishops, Catholic laity, El Shaddai) who, mobilized by 'bread and butter' issues, become 'a march of the hungry and the angry' that 'would be invincible.' Against this he weighs GMA's 'weapons' -- the Lakas-Kampi machinery, her grip on the House and local officials, and a perfected patronage that dispenses the budget, PAGCOR/PCSO funds, infrastructure and VAT 'katas,' even a 'P3-billion largesse for the judiciary' pledged at a JELAC meeting in the Court's 'inner sanctum.' But, he argues, Marcos too had sycophants, friendly justices and compliant officials; the crucial difference is that the 1987 Charter 'extracted the teeth of martial law' -- allowing it only for 'invasion or rebellion,' for 'not exceeding 60 days,' and without suspending the writ of habeas corpus or the operation of the Constitution, the Court and Congress -- so martial law 'may not help GMA the way it did Marcos.' Quoting Ermita's 'Let the people be the judge' (provided the Comelec counts accurately), he concludes that if the enraged middle forces fill the streets during the Con-ass debates, the 'Cha-cha express' may never reach the Court, the Comelec and the plebiscite, and GMA's allies 'may just bugle an early retreat.'

Echoing the CBCP's plea (via new president Bishop Odchimar) for Comelec 'fallback positions,' he urges the commission to 'prepare for manual polls now,' arguing it can 'no longer perfect its automation system in time' for the May 10 polls: the PCOS machines were tested only in small, unrepresentative numbers -- not the 82,200 to be deployed -- and never made 'precinct specific,' calibrated to the actual ballots for each of the 1,630 towns, for which 'Comelec has no more time.' He then builds the 'no proc' scenario: the Comelec admitted possible problems in 'about 30 percent of the country,' and even a 15-percent failure would leave roughly six million votes uncounted -- in a tight race (Villar closing on Aquino) with a winning margin under four million, those votes would be 'determinative,' so no one could be proclaimed president, vice-president or senator. Meanwhile, with the other 85 percent unaffected, local winners -- including 'putative Rep. Gloria M. Arroyo' -- would be proclaimed, and the House could elect a speaker; with the presidency, vice-presidency, Senate presidency and speakership all expiring June 30, 2010, GMA could claim to be 'holdover' president and, once elected speaker, continue as 'acting' president under the constitutional succession, the depleted Senate lacking a quorum to intervene. Such a vacancy, he warns, could dovetail with a Senate-less parliamentary Cha-cha that makes her prime minister -- all destined for the Supreme Court, which is why 'political maneuverings abound' over the selection of the new chief justice. Confronting the alternatives -- martial law, military takeover, people power, civil strife -- he ends not with a forecast but with a prayer: 'Heaven help our country.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 9 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 2), CJP's September 5, 2010 Inquirer column, grows out of a conversation among judiciary retirees 'mulling how we could help revive or regain public esteem for the Supreme Court we all love.' While criticism and dissent are healthy, he argues, 'the whole Court must enjoy residual credibility at all times,' distinguishing 'the shifting winds of public emotion' from 'long-term trust' -- and the stakes are high, for if the Court loses its place as 'the last bulwark of democracy,' then, paraphrasing JFK, 'if peaceful resolution of disputes becomes impossible, violent revolution would be inevitable.' He rejects a colleague's proposal to 'stop criticizing and just heedlessly defend the Court' as 'unacceptable, impractical, and illogical': to defend effectively one must be 'objective, truthful, and credible,' since 'false hosannas would skew the institution's integrity' and 'undeserved praise is disguised ridicule.' Much of the damage, he says, is self-inflicted -- from Marites Vitug's 'Shadow of Doubt' and the 'bludgeoning' of the decision letting GMA appoint the new chief justice, to the 'dismaying flip-flop' in League of Cities v. Comelec, which he reconstructs step by step: unconstitutional in November 2008 (6-5, Carpio), motions denied through 2009, constitutional in December 2009 (6-4, Velasco), then unconstitutional again in August 2010 (7-6, Carpio). A change in the Court's composition might explain it, but 'some incumbents also changed sides,' and -- citing retired Justice Mendoza that the US Court never reconsiders -- he urges that 'one consideration... should be the limit,' because switching votes 'with nary an explanation' invites suspicion of inadequate study or 'succumbing to pressures.' He likewise faults justices who still write 'No part' or 'In the result' without explanation, in 'stark violation of the Rules.' His remedy: justices must be 'more prudent, more precise, and more decisive,' for 'transparency, accountability, and integrity' -- not PR hype or 'blind faith to defend the indefensible' -- are the Court's 'best antidotes' to distrust.

First, prompted by a 17-year-old reader's email asking whether Chief Justice Reynato Puno 'has what it takes to be Philippine president,' he gives a 'jurist, not politician' verdict: he is 'glad' Puno 'said he would not run,' because Puno has 'so much to do' leading 'the judiciary... in defending the Constitution and our democracy,' and any presidential interest would drag him and the Court 'to the gutter' -- the judiciary must be 'insulate[d]... from politics.' Talent does not transfer: 'one may be a good referee' without being 'a boxing champion.' Both the impeachment talk and the 'spidery enticements to lure him to the presidential web' share a 'common denominator -- both will cut short his term,' since running would force him to 'resign pronto,' leaving no one to 'save the people from constitutional machinations'; with the rule of law 'the bedrock of our democracy' guarded by the Court under the Chief Justice, the country 'cannot afford to lose the anchor of the Supreme Court' -- 'Puno for president? No.' Second, after drug-enforcement officers alleged bribery against some DOJ prosecutors, Executive Secretary Ermita twice phoned to invite him onto an 'independent... citizens' committee' to investigate, which he 'respectfully declined': the Office of the Ombudsman was 'precisely conceived by the Constitution' to 'investigate on its own... any act or omission of any public official,' and Ombudsman Merceditas Gutierrez holds the 'plenary power to stop, prevent and correct any abuse' with fiscal autonomy and independence 'like the judiciary.' A citizens' committee, by contrast, lacks autonomy and coercive powers, 'duplicates the functions of a constitutional agency' (so its orders 'may be challenged in court,' causing 'needless complications and delays'), would embarrass the self-styled anti-drug 'czarina' President, and is 'an affront to the Ombudsman.' His conclusion: 'No, thank you. Let the Ombudsman perform her constitutional duty. Let her show her mettle and credibility.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 8 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 3), CJP's August 2, 2009 Inquirer column, is a sharp protest -- written 'as a retired Chief Justice and ex-officio chair of the Judicial and Bar Council' -- against 'Malacañang's assault on the JBC's integrity and independence.' The trigger was a 'jolting letter' signed by Executive Secretary Eduardo Ermita that returned, 'without any legal justification,' the council's nominee list for two Supreme Court vacancies. CJP recalls the constitutional mandate: justices are appointed by the President 'from a list of at least three nominees prepared by the Judicial and Bar Council for every vacancy,' and 'any vacancy shall be filled within 90 days.' The JBC, after 'a protracted screening process,' had sent six nominees -- three each for the seats vacated by Justices Austria-Martinez and Tinga -- a slate of 'no pushovers' (four senior jurists and two private lawyers, including a 1967 bar topnotcher), so it had plainly 'done its constitutional duty.' Ermita's move, he argues, was a double blow: rejecting all six 'virtually accused the JBC of not doing its job,' and demanding names 'acceptable to the Palace' 'challenged its independence' -- even though the Constitution places the JBC 'under the supervision of the Supreme Court, not... the President.' By returning the list, Malacañang also breached its duty to fill the vacancies within 90 days (Martinez retired April 30, Tinga May 11), and CJP warns that a JBC which revised and resubmitted beyond that window would itself violate the Constitution. Because the council exists as 'a check on... the appointing power,' it 'must refuse to add more names'; to 'capitulate now' would 'completely erode' its raison d'être. Long faulted for 'timidity' and 'subservience to the Palace,' the JBC now had its chance to 'prove its critics wrong' and 'assert its independence and integrity by refusing to buckle' -- and he names every member so readers know who must hold the line.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 9 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 3), the August 9, 2009 Inquirer column 'Like Cory or Like Ferdie' -- curated here from the JBC-focused excerpt provided -- is a short, celebratory sequel to 'Jolting Assault on JBC,' reporting that the council did exactly what CJP had urged a week earlier. He opens by saluting the Judicial and Bar Council for 'resisting Malacañang's jolting assault on its integrity and independence': it 'unanimously rejected' Executive Secretary Ermita's letter asking for more nominees to fill the two Supreme Court vacancies. He quotes the council's chair, Chief Justice Reynato Puno, that the decision whether to include more names belongs exclusively to the JBC and cannot be compromised in the slightest without impairing 'the delicate check and balance' in the appointment of justices -- adding, 'Well said and well done.' In a notably even-handed turn, CJP also extends 'kudos... to the President for accepting the JBC's decision,' rather than forcing the issue, and for appointing 'without further ado' Court of Appeals Justice Mariano C. del Castillo and Dean Roberto A. Abad -- 'both... on the original list of six JBC nominees.' The column's title frames the episode as a test of the recurring choice between governing in the institution-respecting mold of Corazon Aquino or the authoritarian mold of Ferdinand Marcos, here resolved, on the JBC question, in favor of institutional integrity. (As noted, the source supplied is an excerpt limited to the JBC portion of the essay, so this entry captures that segment; the full column ranges more widely under the same 'Cory or Ferdie' frame.) Taken with the preceding chapter, it closes the two-vacancy standoff opened by the retirements of Justices Austria-Martinez and Tinga and the returned nominee list -- a rare, satisfying vindication of the JBC's constitutional role as an independent check on the appointing power.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 2 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 4), CJP's November 25, 2007 Inquirer column, attacks the Palace's bid to suppress former NEDA chief Romulo Neri's Senate testimony in the $329-million national broadband network (NBN) scandal through a 'nebulous claim of executive privilege.' Neri had testified that resigned Comelec Chair Benjamin Abalos offered him a P200-million bribe ('Sec, may 200 ka dito') but 'clammed up' on President Arroyo's involvement; Presidential Legal Counsel Sergio Apostol then 'sneered, "Bring the case to the Supreme Court,"' apparently calculating that a court loss would damage GMA less than 'a media feast' on Neri's revelations. Measuring the Palace's chances against the parameters set in Senate v. Ermita (2006, by Justice Carpio Morales), CJP lays out a six-point primer on executive privilege: Congress, 'in aid of legislation,' has a right to information and officials a duty to provide it; the President may withhold only three categories (state secrets, informer's privilege, and internal deliberations); 'disclosure is the rule and secrecy is the exception,' requiring a showing of 'the superiority of the public interest'; only the President may invoke it (or the Executive Secretary 'By order of the President'); it covers information, not officials (even 'a waiter' who overheard Cabinet secrets); and both the subpoena and any exemption request must be detailed enough for Congress to judge, with the Supreme Court resolving disputes. On that basis the Palace had not justified secrecy or followed the process, so its chances were poor. But CJP's sharper point is political: earlier inquiries -- the fertilizer scam (Joc-Joc Bolante), North Rail, 'Hello Garci' and the Venable contract -- remained 'in limbo,' and the 'Palace strategy' of muddling issues, delaying resolution and tiptoeing 'from crisis to crisis' had worked because public outrage was never 'enough... to rattle and shoo away GMA.' 'Kawawa naman tayong mga Pinoy!'
