one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 5 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 4), CJP's June 8, 2008 Inquirer column, previews three pending 'presidential secrecy' (executive privilege) cases as the Supreme Court resumed sessions, framing them as a test of whether it would 'serve or check President Arroyo.' The first, on 'secrecy of conversations,' is the Senate's motion for reconsideration of Neri v. Senate Committee on Accountability, which had 'sealed the lips' of former NEDA chief Romulo Neri; CJP declines to rehash the merits but warns that the ruling will shape both 'the contours of existing jurisprudence' and 'the public esteem for the Court.' Quoting his earlier column, he observes that a great Court is 'endearingly named after its chief, like the Davide Court or the Teehankee Court,' but a servile one 'is derisively named after the president it serves, like the Marcos Supreme Court' -- hoping the Neri ruling is 'a mere aberration' and not enough to brand the present bench 'the Arroyo Supreme Court,' since 'by its judgment, the tribunal itself will be judged.' The second, on 'secrecy of documents,' is Roxas v. Ermita, where Senators Roxas and Aquino sought to compel NEDA's Augusto Santos to surrender the NBN-ZTE meeting minutes; CJP notes Ermita invoked privilege 'without any justification at all,' merely directing Santos to snub the Senate, while the NEDA employees' group (ONE) publicly demanded disclosure -- so the question is whether the Court will 'find the courage to enforce the constitutional mandate of transparency and accountability.' The third, on 'secrecy of diplomatic negotiations,' is Akbayan v. Aquino, seeking disclosure of the JPEPA negotiations (the treaty signed by GMA and PM Koizumi in Helsinki but not yet effective for want of Senate concurrence); here the government warns that exposing negotiations would make the country 'a pariah' no nation would negotiate with -- so CJP leaves genuinely open whether 'confidentiality... be validly upheld as an exception to our stringent transparency rule. Abangan.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 8 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 5), CJP's January 10, 2010 Inquirer column, charges that the Melo-led Comelec had 'regretfully been squandering the people's trust' just months before the country's first automated polls. Melo's appointment had once 'restored credibility' despite objections over his age and 'closeness to the Macapagal family,' and CJP had backed him and his automation drive -- reminding him that 'beyond the appointing authority' lie 'media... history... a grateful nation... and an all-knowing God to judge him.' But recent events, he writes, had shaken his confidence: Melo admitted 'unnerving delays' in 'physical' preparations (ballot boxes, ballot condition, the candidate list, election-day substitutions) and teacher training was 'on hold'; only 30 of 600 sample ballots were read at the Smartmatic warehouse (blamed on a 'high shading threshold'); a 24-by-8.5-inch ballot had room for only 259 slots against 583 filed candidates, leaving about 324 'eased out'; and with 1,630 towns each having a distinct slate, there would be 'at least 1,630 types of ballots' and machines to deliver -- 'an untested logistical nightmare,' worsened because the Comelec had not posted the ballots online as he urged, having 'not finished cleaning up the candidates' list.' He then faults the body's 'inexplicable' decisions -- citing a 'stinging' Inquirer editorial on its 'partisanship' -- the 'monstrosity' unseating Gov. Grace Padaca (so flimsy GMA's lawyer Macalintal safely bragged he'd quit if the Court affirmed it), the ouster of Ang Ladlad on 'wobbly religious and gender grounds,' and the disqualification of Brig. Gen. Danilo Lim while accepting Col. Ariel Querubin though both were detained for breaking their military oaths -- 'a violation of his right to equal protection.' The Comelec, he concludes, 'has come up short in both its automation work and quasi-judicial decisions' and 'must work seven times more'; though he does 'not doubt the noble intentions' of Melo and Sarmiento, 'the time for automation is running out,' so 'it is time to prepare for manual elections.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 9 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 5), CJP's April 18, 2010 Inquirer column, attacks the Comelec's plan to manually count 30 percent of the ballots if the PCOS machines 'snag,' insisting 'hindi puede ang puede na' -- what is merely passable will not do. Defense Secretary Norberto Gonzales had affirmed the plan, and both 'confidently bragged' a failure of elections 'would not happen' (though Gonzales had earlier proposed an 'unconstitutional transition government' for just that). The plan, CJP argues, rests on the 'faulty assumption' that the precinct-specific automated ballots and machines will all be 'correctly delivered to the correct polling places' -- even as the Comelec handpicked Smartmatic to deliver the ballots 'without bidding' despite 'no track record in the courier trade,' and after the avoidable PCOS 'humidity problem' in Hong Kong. Because ballots and machines are 'precinct specific,' misdelivery causes 'a failure of election in both towns'; and the vaunted manual count is of the shaded automated ballots, not old 'generic' ones, so 'if no automated... ballots were delivered, there would be nothing to vote on and nothing to count.' Even assuming correct delivery, he lists four problems: the Boards of Election Inspectors are untrained on the still-printing new forms; voters may not endure the two-hour wait for standby machines, risking 'massive disenfranchisement'; the PCOS cannot transmit a manual count, so one manualized precinct delays the whole result; and there is a 'lack of safeguards,' since shaded ballots hide fraud that handwriting would reveal. A 30-percent manual count, he concludes, is 'not good enough... in fact, it is not good at all,' risking 'delayed... suspect and fraud-prone' results and a 'failure to proclaim the winners.' 'Am I being unduly strict? Not at all' -- the people set a '99.995 percent' standard and spent 'P7.2 billion,' so they 'have the right to demand and expect excellence.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 10 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 5), CJP's January 2, 2011 Inquirer column, urges President Aquino to 'start electoral reforms now.' Unlike the Court -- where in six years he can name only four of 15 justices, 'not enough to sway a new judicial philosophy' -- Aquino can reshape the Commission on Elections through a 'sweeping revamp': with Chairman Melo resigning and Commissioners Ferrer and Larrazabal retiring, he could 'appoint immediately three of the seven' members (including the chair) and two more in 2013, enough to 'dominate the poll body.' The 2010 polls, CJP allows, were held 'in relative peace,' and the results -- 'especially of the presidential contest' -- were 'accepted,' though more protests were filed than under manual elections. He sets the new Comelec three challenges. First, whether to automate at all: weighing speed against 'humongous expense,' he cites former Chair Christian Monsod's doubts about the 'non-transparent and secretive' P16.5-billion PCOS that 'did not address the traditional problems' of cheating, command votes and disenfranchisement -- so 'the country may not need an expensive automation system.' Second, if automation continues, which system: Monsod 'trashed' the PCOS as 'mass-produced in one step' and under-tested; the watchdog Lente found that 'peaceful and expedient elections did not translate to honest and credible elections,' with vote-buying 'most prevalent'; and the Comelec Advisory Council urged against buying the PCOS machines. Third, time: with May 2013 'just two and a half years' away and the PCOS perhaps to be jettisoned, the body is 'really pressed.' Recalling that Melo had about a two-year runway for 2010 yet the Comelec was 'almost always tardy' (with 'horrifying delays' in printing, delivery and calibration), and that Roque v. Comelec had settled the contract's legality 'but not the technical, administrative, and logistical issues,' he concludes that 'only two years and a few months remain' -- 'barely enough' -- so Aquino, Congress, the Comelec and the watchdogs 'should now carefully plan for the 2013 elections.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 3 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 6), CJP's February 7, 2010 Inquirer column, asks whether the Senate can stop a Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo 'holdover' presidency. He had argued that a failed election in 15 percent of the country could let GMA hold over, since the constitutional successors -- VP de Castro, Senate President Enrile, and Speaker Nograles -- would all 'end their terms... on June 30, 2010.' Readers near-unanimously proposed electing a Senate president whose term runs to 2013 to act as president, but CJP warns 'it is not' that simple: the fix assumes the Senate is a 'continuing body,' a notion rooted in earlier Constitutions that staggered 24 senators 'eight every two years' (leaving 16 in office), whereas under the present charter only 12 remain after an election -- 'who do not constitute a majority' -- so GMA's partisans could argue the Senate has 'ceased to be a continuing body.' That question would fall to the Supreme Court, and CJP reads the rushed JBC push to name a Chief Justice before Puno's May 17 retirement (during the March 11-June 30 appointment ban) as an attempt to control the holdover ruling -- though the Palace kept it an 'option,' since a 'credible' and 'non-controversial' Court would be needed to make any holdover publicly acceptable. He then warns that eight months could not perfect a nationwide PCOS system: ATMs, credit cards and even the Court's own decade-old computerization took years; PCOS field-test transmissions ran 'several hours' against a credit card's seconds; and with 82,200 machines, 47 million voters, and 'many other dangers' (printing delays, miscalibration, misdelivery, hacking, weak training), a 'no-proc' gridlock could arise from glitches in just five percent of votes -- about two million ballots. His conclusion: 'the closer the presidential race is, the more [likely] holdover becomes.'

Comelec) to deter manipulation; fifth, deploy watchdogs, since automation 'will not stop guns, goons, and gold'; and sixth, guard against 'massive disenfranchisement' by waiting out the long queues (clustered precincts now packing 'as many as 1,000 electors') and machine failures. Above all, he reframes the vote as 'not just a personal contest... [but] a battle for democracy,' since 'more important than the election of any particular candidate is the triumph of democracy over the dark forces of status quo' -- 'our sacrifice for democracy.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 6 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 6), CJP's May 16, 2010 Inquirer column, hails the Noynoy Aquino landslide as a 'thunderous triumph of People Power' that survived 'sweltering kilometric queues, technical glitches... and other booboos of Comelec and Smartmatic.' The first nationwide automated election, he writes, was 'People Power of the strict constitutional genre' -- the people choosing a peaceful transition 'no longer by staging mammoth street rallies, but by pouring a massive electoral mandate.' He sets it among three: the 'extra constitutional' People Power 1 (Cory's 1986 revolutionary ascent), the 'intra constitutional' but contested People Power 2 (GMA in 2001, per Estrada v. Desierto), and now People Power 3, which 'catapults Noynoy with unquestioned constitutionality' and is fittingly embodied in 'the 1987 Constitution of Cory.' Yet he itemizes avoidable failures: the clustering that, as he had predicted, assigned 'only one... BEI and one PCOS machine to 1,000 voters' (he and his wife waited 45 minutes; Noynoy 'sweated many hours'); wasted votes from 'PCOS machine malfunction, oval misalignment, ballot rejection, and printing errors'; weak training and voter-list exclusions; and 'small covers... half the size of the ballots' that violated secrecy -- captured by the Inquirer photo of Estrada's exposed ballot -- disenfranchisement that, he agrees with Sen. Jamby Madrigal, 'must still be investigated.' He also warns that the celebrated 'instant transmission' and the PPCRV, GMA7 and ABS-CBN parallel counts all drew 'from the same election returns spewed out by the PCOS machines,' so none explained 'how the PCOS machines counted the individual votes,' leaving 'no check on how the machines tallied' after the Comelec 'inexplicably disengaged' a voter-confirmation safeguard. Still, he 'heave[s] a sigh of relief' that nationwide failure, source-code corruption, holdover and military rule 'did not come to pass,' hailing 'the miraculous start of a peaceful transition of power.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 7 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 6), CJP's May 23, 2010 Inquirer column, identifies the 'most vexing problem' awaiting Noynoy Aquino: the prosecution of grafters -- the heart of his 'Kung walang corrupt, walang mahirap' mantra and his pledge to pursue 'the alleged excesses and ill-gotten wealth of the Arroyos' -- which is 'easier said than done.' Cory, he recalls, had 'one year of revolutionary rule -- undeterred by legal niceties' to 'dismantle the Marcos machine,' name a new Court and change the Constitution, plus five more years, 'yet these were not enough,' since 'the chase for the... Marcos wealth has not ended.' Noynoy faces 'more daunting odds': he 'would not enjoy that one year of free rule' and must immediately confront 'the gridlocks of democracy and the many constitutional checks that could be misused... to stymie his reforms,' because GMA 'carefully selected all the members of the Supreme Court and the Office of the Ombudsman' -- so, by public perception, 'she and her cronies would be beyond the reach of our laws.' The early flashpoint was Noynoy's vow to 'refuse to be sworn in' by GMA's new Chief Justice Renato Corona, whose appointment followed the Court's reversal of 'half a century of jurisprudence banning midnight appointments' -- a sign that his crusade 'would surely flounder' without 'a cooperative Ombudsman and an unbiased judiciary,' bodies armed with 'fixed terms' and independence. CJP draws two comparative lessons: Franklin Roosevelt, his New Deal gutted by the US Supreme Court, tried to 'pack' it and lost, yet 'prevailed anyway' when Justice Owen Roberts 'switched positions'; and Brazil's Lula, after 'moderating his ideas,' lifted his country into 'BRIC' and earned Obama's G20 praise as 'the most popular politician on earth.' His counsel: with the media's '100 days of honeymoon,' Noynoy must 'seize the momentum' and use his People Power capital -- not 'frontal criticisms' -- to win over the constitutional structures still 'dominated by appointees of the predecessor.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 8 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 6), CJP's May 30, 2010 Inquirer column, argues that what propelled Noynoy Aquino was 'destiny and legacy, not dynasty' -- Time Magazine's word -- and shows how the 'tsunami of votes' could be turned against corruption and poverty. The landslide 'so impressed the international community' that ambassadors of the US (Harry Thomas Jr.), China (Liu Jianchao), Japan (Makoto Katsura) and the EU (Alistair MacDonald) congratulated Noynoy 'even before... canvassing had begun,' and Time featured him twice in under a month, making the Philippines 'the darling of the world again.' This 'shining moment,' CJP urges, should be leveraged to draw 'new investments, funding grants (like from the US Millennium Challenge Corporation), and favorable trade agreements' -- and, concretely, to negotiate 'sovereign debt waivers' or 'at the very least, a moratorium of say three years' on international-debt amortizations, freeing 'meager funds' for 'pump-priming and job creation.' For the source of Noynoy's 'passion to liberate his people,' CJP turns to Ninoy Aquino's August 25, 1973 prison letter (shared by retired Justice Flerida Ruth Romero), written under martial law to explain -- after consulting Salonga and Tañada -- his refusal to join the 'one-sided' Military Commission, an 'act of conscience' and 'protest against the structures of injustice' by which he 'decided to walk into the very jaws of death.' Unable to leave wealth, Ninoy bequeathed the family name kept 'untarnished,' apologized for the 'great responsibility' on his son's 'young shoulders,' and urged him to stand by his mother and inherit her 'indomitable spirit and... silent courage,' closing: 'live with honor and follow your conscience... the ball is now in your hands.' Like Cory, Noynoy 'had no plans of seeking the presidency' until his mother's August 1, 2009 death 'altered history' -- so, against the 'dynasty' label, CJP credits destiny and legacy.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 10 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 6), CJP's October 24, 2010 Inquirer column, lays out how President Aquino can prevail in the 'crucial cases' before the Supreme Court -- the one body that 'can scuttle' his anti-corruption and anti-poverty programs because it is 'independent and apolitical' and bound to 'the Constitution and the rule of law,' which, per CJ Corona, 'will never bend to the ever-shifting political winds.' In a 'tête-à-tête' with presidential allies (Drilon, Purisima, Abad, Soliman, Bautista, Santos, Cruz), CJP had discussed four cases: 'the impeachment of the Ombudsman, the... Truth Commission, the validity of midnight appointments, and the legality of public-private partnerships (PPP).' The Court had issued two status quo ante (SQA) orders -- barring the House from hearing the Gutierrez impeachment, and stopping the firing of alleged 'midnight appointee' Bai Omera Dianalan Lucman -- plus an earlier SLEX TRO. SQAs, he explains, are 'worded more benignly than TROs' to spare co-equal branches but 'have the same effect,' biting immediately because they need no bonds; and their issuance 'implies that the Court has found the petitions to be prima facie meritorious,' so the respondents (the House and the administration) 'must rebut the prima facie case... to win.' That is what happened in the SLEX matter: persuaded by the respondents, the Court lifted the TRO and, in Francisco v. Toll Regulatory Board (2010), 'unanimously upheld' the SLEX/NLEX/Skyway PPPs -- Justice Velasco balancing 'the paramount common good for infrastructure' with 'a reasonable rate of return' to investors, and answering the ADB's call that 'the judicial system will uphold contractual rights.' Finally, CJP offers two models of how cases are decided -- the 'analytical' (facts × law = decision) and the 'sociological' (personality × stimuli = decision) -- and counsels that P-Noy must 'strategize patiently and properly,' using 'persuasion' rather than 'frontal criticisms,' remembering that 'in the end, the law is what the Supreme Court says it is.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 15 of 'Love God, Serve Man' is CJP's November 3, 1992 speech at the Hotel Inter-Continental before a joint meeting of the Bishops-Businessmen's Conference, FINEX, the Makati Business Club, the Management Association of the Philippines, Philippine Business for Social Progress and the Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry, delivered while he served as the chamber's general counsel. He began from the premise that peace is everyone's concern -- espoused by Christianity, Islam and Buddhism alike, wished daily in every Mass, and sought by every government, family and person -- and greeted his audience with the same wish. The gathering's purpose, he said, was to make the country's leading business and professional groups aware of the Ramos government's Peace Process and to ask what the 'middle forces' could do to hasten it, since the 1986 EDSA revolution had shown that non-violent revolutionary change requires a partnership between street marchers and the middle class. He traced the private sector's peace effort to the first Multi-Sectoral Conference at the Asian Institute of Management in June 1992, where the Workshop on Administration of Justice he chaired recommended the Peace Process as a government priority, and to the second conference at De La Salle University that October, where it was hailed as a leading achievement and endorsed for the next 1,000 days. He then defined true peace negatively and positively: not the absence of violence, the victory of superior arms, or 'the eerie silence imposed by dictators and strong men,' but the resolution of the social, economic and political imbalances behind armed conflict -- Jose P. Laurel's humanization of laws and equalization of social and economic forces, John Paul I's solidarity of those who have more with those who have less, PCP II's harmony of heart and social order. Justice being impersonal, he argued, peace also requires love and sacrifice, and he closed pledging solidarity with the poor and re-dedicating the country to peace, justice and love.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 10 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' collects CJP's address on the 'Globalization of Justice' to the First Global Biotechnology Forum in Concepcion, Chile, organized by UNIDO and the Chilean government. He opened by claiming affinity with his hosts, since the Philippines is often called the only Latin American nation in Asia, the only Christian nation in its part of the globe and the only one colonized by both Spain and the United States, and linked that affinity to the FEALAC or FOCALE ministers' meeting held in Manila that January. He then stated the traditional postulate that laws and judicial decisions are territorial, flowing from the view that sovereignty is absolute only within a state's boundary, and argued that international tribunals, telecommunications, migration, technology and an ever-shrinking world had modified that absoluteness. Globalization, he said, was more than trade: it was an interconnected process of institutional, demographic and cultural connection, and human rights had been propelled by it ahead of trade, citing Hans Köchler for the view that sovereignty must be redefined against human rights as norms of jus cogens, while the wars on terror had transformed the concept of just war. He offered two borderless viruses as proof. SARS respected no boundaries, showed that medical questions were at heart questions of human rights and social policy, exposed both the suppression of reporting in closed systems and the legal barriers to quarantine in open ones, and made the WHO the only credible authority, teaching that the right to health could be secured through local courts. The 'ILoveYou' virus, created by a Philippine student, crippled systems worldwide yet left its author unpunished, since no Philippine law then covered computer crimes and the double criminality clause blocked extradition. He surveyed the coming bio-age docket -- genetic engineering, embryo disposition, cloning, cryogenics, GMO labeling, DNA identification and patents -- urging uniform national decisions to avoid forum shopping, and closed that globalization is not necessarily antagonistic to nationalism.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 11 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' is CJP's lecture on judicial excellence in the bio-age, opening with a family Christmas in Orlando and, more consequentially for him, a tour of the Kennedy Space Center at Cape Canaveral. He retold how the Cold War drove the space race -- Yuri Gagarin orbiting first, Kennedy vowing America would reach the moon, Armstrong and Aldrin fulfilling that vow on July 20, 1969 -- and then observed that the 1990s replaced competition with cooperation, as Russia and the United States jointly built the International Space Station and fourteen other nations joined them. That shift, he argued, typifies globalization in every field: the personal computer, the Internet and the cell phone have made the world one global village in which traditional legal borders no longer deter human progress, and advances in trade, banking, telecommunications, transportation and migration have diluted the territoriality doctrine, so that a new paradigm demands the universalization of laws and of the rulings interpreting them. Quoting columnist Federico Pascual Jr.'s joke defining globalization through Princess Diana's death, he moved to his substance: a survey of bio-litigation organized under the Australian Institute of Health, Law and Ethics theme 'Hatching, Matching, Snatching and Dispatching.' Under hatching he discussed Kass v. Kass and J.B. v. M.B. on the disposition of frozen pre-embryos and Woodward on the inheritance rights of posthumously conceived children; under matching, EU labeling of GMOs, Monsanto v. Tilly, Schiff v. Prados, People v. Privitera and the rise of DNA evidence, including Time's report of nearly eighty DNA exonerations; under snatching, Moore v. Regents of University of California, the Maryland lead-paint study and Pate v. Threlkel on disclosure, consent and fiduciary duty; and under dispatching, Diamond v. Chakrabarty, Monsanto v. Schmeiser and the divided oncomouse rulings on patenting engineered life. Because such disputes will occur worldwide, he urged that national tribunals resolve them similarly, avoiding forum shopping by globalizing justice, and concluded that it is no longer enough for judges to be walking encyclopedias of law -- they must command the humanities, economics, medicine, the digital sciences and now the biosciences as well.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 13 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' is CJP's brief round-table contribution at the UNIDO Global Biotechnology Forum, where discussants were asked to describe their regions' preparedness for the controversies the new biosciences would bring. Allotted ten minutes for the whole of Asia, he said he could only skim the surface as a general introduction to the open forum. He began with scale, adding the populations of China, India, Indonesia, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Japan, the Philippines and Vietnam to reach roughly three billion people, half the world, and dated the region's political, scientific and economic renaissance to the fall of the Soviet Union in 1989 and the spread of the free market. He then sketched the region country by country, pairing scientific or economic advance with judicial condition: China prospering amid the global financial crisis, with the Beijing Genomics Institute under Dr. Huanming Yang and a judiciary being reformed under Supreme Court President Xiao Yang; India a burgeoning center of cyber-technology with an independent but backlogged judiciary; South Korea's startling cloning breakthrough, reported by Time, in which Seoul National University researchers created more than 200 cloned embryos, grew thirty to the blastocyst stage and derived a self-perpetuating stem-cell colony; South Korea and Japan's demanding bar examinations and specialized training; Thailand's recovered currency and its Constitution Court's 8-7 vote upholding Premier Thaksin Shinawatra; Vietnam's market-oriented communism; Malaysia's pegged currency and Petronas Twin Towers; and Singapore's newly reformed judiciary aiming to become the world's first paperless system. Of his own country he said the Philippines prides itself on an independent and competent judiciary ready for the bio-age, constitutionally empowered to review lower courts and to strike down acts of any branch, including the Presidency and Congress, tainted with grave abuse of discretion, with administrative power over the courts and the legal profession, fiscal independence and rule-making authority. He noted a growing regional interest in alternative dispute resolution, which suits the Asian ethic of settling disputes without loss of face, and concluded that Asian judicial systems are adjusting with equal velocity to the information and biotechnological ages before opening the floor to questions.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 14 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' is CJP's forum address on ethics in the biotechnological revolution, built on the premise that the ability to do something does not equate with entitlement to do so -- ability is not equivalent to permissibility, and between 'I can do it' and 'I may do it' lies the divide known as morality or ethics. He applied that divide to a cascade of questions: whether the power to modify organisms entitles us to feed the world that way, whether re-engineering human cells automatically empowers scientists to improve medicine, whether the capacity to manipulate the embryo permits unrestricted use of the new sciences against diabetes, cancer, Alzheimer's and Parkinson's, whether science should be limited at all, and, ultimately, whether it would be ethical to clone humans. Answers, he said, come from three separate sources. Religion has always exerted an enduring influence on human conduct, from ancient voodooism and pluralistic deism to the Ten Commandments shared by the Mosaic faiths and the Christian summary of loving God and one another, out of which grew the Catholic pro-life theology quoted from Pope John Paul II, that the mere probability a human person is involved justifies an absolutely clear prohibition of any intervention aimed at killing an embryo. Philosophy begins with human ends -- James Watson's needs and wants, Bentham's utilitarian pleasure and pain -- but the insistence on rationality leads instead to dignity, which is why, in his hypothetical, the healthy liver of a comatose reckless driver may not be taken for a revered leader, since rights cannot be removed without consent even in the guise of the greater good; this premise, he added, underwrites liberal democracy and constitutional law, though rights proliferate and conflict, as when procreative liberty collides with the scientist's claimed right to re-engineer people. Because of that confusion, a third proposition holds that the truly authoritative source of ethics is human covenant -- the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the covenants on civil, economic and children's rights, professional codes and his country's Ethical Standards Law. He closed on the polarization between the libertarian and restraint camps and on two proposed responses, Fukuyama's call for regulation, particularly international regulation, and EINSHAC's I/STREF, insisting that either way these ethical questions are worth discussing in every forum of the dawning bio-age.
